finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: Treasuries’ Link to AI Shows Sharp Shift as Haven Trade Returns
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Ruth Carson and Masaki Kondo

paragraphs.text: Ruth Carson and Masaki Kondo
Thu, October 22, 2026 at 8:19 PM MST 3 min read
(Bloomberg) -- For much of this year, Treasuries offered investors little of their traditional protection when technology stocks stumbled. This week, that role has bounced back sharply.
Most Read from Bloomberg

A gauge of the inverse relationship between US government bonds and AI-focused stocks has strengthened to levels last seen a year ago. It's a sign the deepening tech selloff is sending investors back into bonds for safety, reviving a haven role that had faded as inflation worries and higher interest rates weighed on Treasuries.

Driving the shift are concerns about the sustainability and eventual payoff of artificial intelligence investment, which have sent tech shares tumbling. Those worries are also spilling into the broader economic outlook, prompting traders to dial back expectations for a rate increase this year.

"Bonds are — gasp — working as your hedge again," Charlie McElligott, a cross-asset strategist at Nomura Holdings Inc., wrote in a note. "The market seems to be real-time repricing the probabilities of a US 'growth scare' off the back of the AI reset."

Treasuries had their best day in more than a year on Thursday, surging across the board as the deepening rout in AI-related shares, market turmoil in France and fresh Middle East tensions all combined to make US government debt the investment of choice for anxious traders.

The rally continued even as Brent crude climbed above $113 a barrel following deadly attacks in Saudi Arabia. Just weeks ago, soaring energy prices were hammering bonds by stoking inflation fears. Now, it's also being seen as a threat to growth, adding to demand for US debt and prompting traders to push back expectations for a quarter-point rate hike to January from December.

Treasury yields tumbled, with those on shorter-dated debt falling as much as 20 basis points on Thursday. The benchmark 10-year yield dropped below the key 5% level and held around 4.97% in Asian trading Friday.

(Bloomberg) -- Copper headed for a third weekly loss in four as a selloff in technology stocks deepened, sapping risk appetite across markets including for the metal that's used in data centers and power infrastructure.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Futures traded above $14,150 a ton in London, down almost 2% this week and extending a retreat from a record set in September. The global slump in tech stocks intensified on Friday, as earnings from major companies failed to reassure investors about the durability of the artificial-intelligence trade.

The stock selloff is "putting great pressure" on metals from copper to gold, said Fan Rui, an analyst at Guoyuan Futures Co. "It is affecting short-term sentiment on metals given demand from other sectors remains bland."

Copper remains about 14% higher this year, with gains aided by a major influx of metal into the US on speculation that the Trump administration with introduce a levy on refined metal. Still, there have been some doubts among traders over whether Washington will actually follow through with the move.

On the supply front, output may tighten as Chile's production is expected to fall 8% to 9% this year, according to Finance Minister Jorge Quiroz. That stands to worsen the outlook for a slump in the top-mining nation, which has seen pits affected by a string of deadly accidents and extreme weather.

In China, a shortage of material is also forcing smelters to deepen production cuts ahead of negotiations on next year's concentrate supply. Refiners in the country plan to process less concentrate, with some starting maintenance and running at minimal rates, according to people familiar with the matter.

Copper was 0.6% higher at $14,160 a ton on the London Metal Exchange at 10:59 a.m. in Singapore, after swinging between gains and losses. Other metals were mixed, with nickel down 1.5% at $15,875 a ton and zinc marginally higher.

(Bloomberg) -- Metrics across global bond markets are signaling their biggest risk-off sentiment in more than a year, as a selloff in AI stocks and growing geopolitical tensions caused investors to seek out safe-haven assets.
Most Read from Bloomberg

On Friday, spreads on dollar bonds of higher-rated Asian companies widened to their highest levels since last July, moving in tandem with credit markets more broadly. The move mirrors a jump in corporate bond yield premiums globally, which surged to their widest since May 2025, reaching up to 129 basis points, a Bloomberg index shows.

President Jon Gray said there's no cause for concern as demand is "almost parabolic."

At the same time, US Treasuries, viewed as a safer investment vehicle, rallied for their best day in more than two years, rising on all levels. There was also a wave of buying in Treasury futures, as traders rushed to unwind bearish bets and cover short positions.

technologyreview.com/2026/10/23/1147610/.headline: In the biotech world, you can’t see everything
technologyreview.com/2026/10/23/1147610/.author: Jessica Hamzelou

paragraphs.text: Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything, the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes.

I went in not really knowing what to expect. I’d avoided spoilers (and won’t be giving anything away here, either!). I was wondering what new information this film could reveal, given how familiar many of us are with the Theranos story thanks to years of media coverage, the best-selling book Bad Blood, and the Hulu series The Dropout, starring Amanda Seyfried.

Like many others who have seen the film, I came away feeling unsettled. But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the somewhat disturbing interactions between the subjects. The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything.

In case you’re rusty on the details, Elizabeth Holmes dropped out of Stanford University in 2003 to run Theranos, a diagnostics company she founded, when she was just 19. She went on to claim that her company had invented a way to run over 100 diagnostic tests on just a few drops of blood.

Holmes raised hundreds of millions of dollars for Theranos, which was valued at $9 billion in 2014. Forbes named her the youngest self-made female billionaire—she was worth $4.5 billion when she was just 30 years old.

Things started to unravel in 2015, when an investigation by the Wall Street Journal raised concerns by former Theranos employees that the tests didn’t work. Some also said that the company’s device had not been tested properly, and that blood samples had been analyzed on machines from other companies instead. MIT Technology Review named it one of the biggest technology failures of 2015.

Forbes had revised Holmes’s worth to $0 by 2016. That year, a damning government report said that the company’s lab was struggling with basic procedures and gave patients results even when they knew they could be wrong.

In 2018, Theranos, Holmes, and former company president Ramesh Balwani were charged with “massive fraud.” In 2022, she was sentenced to a little over 11 years in prison for defrauding investors. She began serving her sentence in May 2023.

It was around a month before this that filmmakers Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, and their colleagues began documenting Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, at home with their two young children. I’m not giving anything away when I say it’s an extremely intimate portrayal—at least of how the two adults interact with Fielder, who is also a central character in the film.

As you might know if you’ve seen the trailer, there are plenty of super close-ups. I felt as if I spent most of the film staring straight into the faces of those people. And almost the whole way through, they all seemed to be trying to figure each other out. Holmes is known for her dishonesty, but she invited cameras into her home in an apparent bid to reframe the narrative and position herself as an honest person with an unusual mind. Will anyone believe her?

I couldn’t help feeling some empathy for Holmes, a mother we see preparing to leave her two kids for a lengthy prison sentence. And even though I have long known the facts, Holmes is clearly an effective manipulator. You can see her plant the seeds of doubt in Fielder’s mind. At times, I felt she was convincing me, sitting in my cinema seat. Maybe she really didn’t mean to lie?

But then I remembered how other journalists felt after being taken in by her claims. “I blew it,” Fortune’s Roger Parloff reflected in 2015, a year after profiling Holmes and her company. “I’m pretty sure she lied to me,” STAT’s Matthew Herper wrote recently, having interviewed Holmes in 2015. Even the former employee turned whistleblower Tyler Shultz, who knew the product didn’t work, said that he could “have a five-minute conversation with her and walk away feeling like my work was changing the world,” he said in 2022.
I didn’t cover Theranos in the 2010s. If I’d interviewed Holmes, would I have fallen for it all?

One of the early red flags in the Theranos case was the lack of published, peer-reviewed data. Much of the company’s work was classified as a “trade secret.” Scientists tend to publish their work in journals—a slow process that involves having the work evaluated by often anonymous experts in the field, who provide feedback, highlight questionable conclusions, and often ask for clarification. Peer review is meant to add rigor to the publication process. You should be able to trust published scientific papers.
Except that sometimes you can’t.

Scientists aren’t perfect. Some will exaggerate their results or inflate their importance. Some manipulate data to serve a hypothesis. Sometimes these infractions are caught during peer review, but not always. There are plenty of examples of scientific findings that could never be replicated by other labs and ended up collapsing under the weight of real evidence. Many papers ultimately end up with corrections. Some are withdrawn—10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023.

At any rate, there’s been a shift to sharing research in other ways. Today, many scientists opt to publish their work at preprint servers like arXiv, medRxiv, and bioRxiv before they submit them to established journals. Those outlets bypass peer review. So do company press releases, social media posts, and many conference presentations. And I get a lot of my stories from conversations and interviews.
I’ll admit I’ve looked at a scientific finding and thought: A scientist has just said they’ve done that. How can I be sure they really have?

I like to think that I hold myself to high journalistic standards here, as does everyone at MIT Technology Review. I would never publish a story about some new scientific development without doing my own form of peer review, and asking scientists—ideally people I know and trust—what they think of a new claim.

But the film is a stark reminder of how easy it can be to fall for an appealing narrative. While most scientists are, I hope, pretty honest, and Holmes is certainly an outlier, we should all continue to interrogate the claims being fed to us. If you’ve seen the film, let me know what you think!
This article first appeared in The Checkup, MIT Technology Review’s weekly biotech newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Thursday, and read articles like this first, sign up here.

cnbc.com/2026/10/23/france-debt-euro-zon.headline: France is flashing euro crisis signals. This time, the fault lines are different
cnbc.com/2026/10/23/france-debt-euro-zon.author: Jenni Reid, Chloe Taylor

paragraphs.text: As France's economic and political woes mount, investors are asking whether the country's debt problems risk contaminating the rest of the euro zone.
Markets are flashing alarm bells over the euro zone's second-biggest economy. The euro has remained under pressure, falling almost 5% against the dollar since the start of the year.
France's benchmark borrowing cost, the yield on its 10-year bond, rose above 5% for the first time since 2002 this week before moving sharply higher.

Meanwhile, the spread between French and German 10-year bond yields — a closely watched metric of distress — reached more than 170 basis points on Thursday for the first time since the euro zone debt crisis of the early 2010s. The cost of insuring the French government against default, as measured by credit default swaps, is also the highest since that period.
Euro zone contagion

The big concern is fragmentation, when countries that share a currency face sharply different borrowing costs, compounding market stress and risking spiraling debt repayments for the worst-impacted countries.

As the euro zone sovereign debt crisis of the early 2010s showed, market stress in one country can spread rapidly through economies that share a currency and a central bank but retain separate fiscal systems. The crisis began in Greece before spreading to countries including Portugal, Ireland, Italy and Spain.
Governments were expected to rescue struggling banks, which held large amounts of sovereign debt, creating a vicious cycle.
The crisis only eased after rescue programs tied to sweeping austerity measures, and ECB President Mario Draghi pledged in 2012 to do "whatever it takes" to preserve the euro.

Economists are warning that a new vicious cycle is being created — not only in France but in big economies from the U.S. to the U.K. — as investor concern over rising government debt pushes up yields and interest costs, which in turn add to the debt burden.

A slowdown in bond purchases raises "the specter that the government will be forced into default because it simply doesn't have the cash to pay interest and principal on its debt," Nobel laureate Paul Krugman wrote in a blog on Oct. 8.
"Fear of default then leads to even more capital flight, which increases fears of default and the interest rate," he said.
France's debt risks

France in particular has one of the highest deficit-to-GDP ratios in the 21-nation euro area and a growing national debt pile. Its economy has slowed to a crawl, with the government cutting its 2026 growth forecast to just 0.5%.
Those fiscal strains come as political volatility and social unrest raise doubts about the government's ability to deliver measures aimed at stabilizing the public finances.
"We are deep into French crisis territory," Carsten Brzeski, ING's global head of macro research and chief euro zone economist, said by email.
"There is no risk of an imminent liquidity issue for the French government but the lack of trust of bond markets and the ongoing crisis should finally bring a high sense of urgency to Paris."

John Stopford, head of multi-asset income at Ninety One, said France has gone from being a core or semi-core European country for fixed income investors to increasingly being considered on the periphery, which he labeled "bizarre" given the history of France in relation to the EU and its economic power in the continent.

"We as investors, have just chosen for the time being to pretty much avoid all of the non-core countries in Europe – it's too fluid a situation with too much uncertainty to really want to get involved," Stopford said on a call.
Why 2026 is different

Nonetheless, analysts CNBC spoke to broadly agreed that reforms meant that even if the market is behaving in similar ways to the post-financial crisis period, the contagion risk remained limited this time around.

Ninety One's Stopford said spreads would likely need to be trading "in the 200s" before the situation is broadly perceived as a genuine crisis — but, he added, that the situation in France "doesn't look great."

"French spreads are now wider than they were at the peak of the peripheral crisis of the early 2010s, but they're still much narrower than the extreme levels that we saw in Spain, Italy, Greece and Ireland back then, so... I think the market's assumption is that things will need to get worse before we get to a point where EU institutions start to look to try and limit further damage," he told CNBC.

BlackRock strategists noted the current environment is "materially different" to the one that preceded the 2011 to 2012 euro zone debt crisis, with the region now better equipped to weather financial stress, but they added that "further volatility and spillovers remain possible."

"The French bond sell-off illustrates how competition for capital is reshaping fixed income markets amid a global rate reset," they wrote. "Rising government borrowing and AI-related investment are pushing up financing costs, exposing borrowers with deteriorating fundamentals to greater scrutiny."

George Lagarias, chief economist at Forvis Mazars, said France was already in a debt crisis, citing its debt-to-GDP ratio of 119% at the end of the second quarter of 2026 — close to Greece's of 128% in late 2009.
A spillover would mean a wider French-German yield spread followed by higher credit default swap prices – the cost of insuring debt, he said.

"Italy, Spain, would see higher borrowing costs, and have to curtail fiscal expenditures, possibly raising political backlash in their own countries," he told CNBC. "The European periphery would come under tremendous pressure, even if their finances are in much better order than a few years ago."
However, Lagarias said crucial structural differences minimize the risk of a wider spillover akin to the early 2010s, which he estimated at 10% to 20%.
"Greece had a very bad trade deficit. France also has a trade deficit, but the numbers are much more benign," he said by email.
He added that the Insee, France's national statistics body, was "not likely to lie about the deficit" and contrasted this with Greece.

In 2009, Greece sharply revised its projected budget deficit from 3.7% of GDP in the spring to 12.5% by October, undermining confidence in the reliability of its public finances and helping accelerate the crisis.

"[French] debt levels are worrying but known. Markets can deal with known risks. They hate surprises," Lagarias added. "What sunk Greece was a deficit that was suddenly revealed to be five-fold versus the official estimate. This catalysed a crisis."
Alex Everett, investment director for rates management at Aberdeen Investments, agreed that the current environment should be treated "primarily as French risk rather than a systemic euro-area risk."

"Compared to the early 2010s, the Eurozone has stronger banks, greater integration and numerous tools designed to limit the risk of sovereign fragmentation," he said. "I anticipate contagion to be short-lived."

npr.org/2026/10/23/nx-s1-5983813/gen-z-c.headline: Gen Z candidates in both parties aim to tackle high housing costs
npr.org/2026/10/23/nx-s1-5983813/gen-z-c.author: Jennifer Ludden

paragraphs.text: WEST HARTFORD, Conn. — "My bus is running slightly behind," Olaleye Onikuyide texted ahead of our meeting at a coffee shop on West Hartford's main street. The 28-year-old Democrat running for Connecticut state representative still made it on time and said he loved riding public transit.
Onikuyide also lives with his parents, though he said that's by choice to save money, unlike the many young adults who can't afford to live on their own.

Still, as part of a generation that faces record-high housing unaffordability, he started obsessing years ago over how to make it cheaper. Now that the cripplingly high cost of both rent and homes has become an urgent national conversation, he likens it to being a fan of a niche music group before everyone else caught on.
"All of a sudden, it's blown up and everybody's at the concerts and you're like, 'OK, this is a bit of a crowd here now,'" he said with a broad smile.
Nationwide, housing costs are a top issue for voters in a midterms season laser focused on affordability. A chronic housing shortage has pushed up prices, and the fallout cuts across generations.

Younger people are renting with roommates into their 30s. They're struggling to save for a down payment and wondering whether it even makes sense to buy, given today's sky-high prices. Empty nesters looking to downsize can't find an affordable place to go, and longtime homeowners are reluctant to move at all, given current high mortgage rates.
Generation Z candidates from both major parties said their age group has a lot at stake and is uniquely positioned to help create solutions for everyone.

"We're in the thick of it," Onikuyide said, citing not only high housing and gas prices but also student loan debt and a tough labor market. "We might be the generation that is more educated and yet worse off than our parents."

His policy goals include creating more mixed-income housing and walkable cities. Adding density to urban areas can be controversial, as longtime residents worry about more traffic or strained infrastructure. But Onikuyide and others also see an opportunity for bipartisanship. And if elected, he would feel well-placed to make life less expensive for his constituents.
"I keep one eye on the national conversation about it," he said, "but the action is happening at the state level."
"The experience of being a renter"

About an hour away in New Haven, Conn., 26-year-old Eli Sabin found a quiet room for talking inside the ornate City Hall. He's also a Democrat running for state representative, and he has worked in this building.

When he was a sophomore in college, he started serving on the Board of Alders. That's "our old-fashioned term for the city council," he explained. "We changed some of the zoning rules to allow for denser development and more affordable units."
Elected officials at all levels in the U.S. are overwhelmingly homeowners. Sabin said it makes a difference that he is a renter, like about 70% of residents in this city.

"I think it's the experience of being a renter and just the insecurity and instability that you feel," he said. His lease is up in May, and he has no idea whether the rent will go up or whether the landlord will even allow him to stay.
He would like more protections against eviction and would also like to make it easier to buy a home.

Older people have told him how they bought 30 years ago on a teacher's salary but could never do that today, while younger people feel "pushed out of the community." Some have moved to states such as Texas, Tennessee or Florida, "not because that's where they have the best job opportunities or where they want to be, but because simply that's the place they can afford," he said.

Sabin won a three-way primary, beating both a democratic socialist and a longtime incumbent first elected more than a decade before he was born. "I think people feel like we need fight right now," he said. "We need energy, we need new ideas and we can't accept that the status quo is all right."

Like Onikuyide, he credited New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani for igniting political energy around tackling the everyday cost of living. But Sabin also pointed to Republican-led states such as Texas and Montana as role models for bipartisan legislation on housing affordability.
A market gap in starter homes

In Kalispell, Mont., Republican Lukas Schubert is only 21 and campaigning for reelection as a state representative. "I'm not even recently the most youngest," he laughed. The state allows people to run for office at age 18.

On Schubert's campaign website, housing is at the top of the issues page, along with Christianity and taxes. "It is a top priority among Republicans as well," he said "It's not just, you know, a Democrat issue."

Home prices in Montana jumped sharply during the COVID-19 pandemic as more people moved there. Gen Z and millennial lawmakers were part of a push to overhaul zoning and red tape. A 2023 package of laws dubbed the "Montana Miracle" aims to make it easier and cheaper to build housing.

Those changes are rolling out, but the housing challenge remains vast. Schubert would like to rein in large foreign corporations that buy up homes and noncitizens who own large parcels of land and property but don't live in the state. He also sees a big gap in the market.

"Seemingly all of the new development is apartment buildings or big, you know, 5, 10 million-dollar mansions," he said. His main focus is on starter homes, either single family or duplexes. "That's what we need to be really getting rid of government barriers to producing."

This past session, Schubert proposed a major tax break for developers that sell a newly built starter home for less than 85% of the local median value. It did not pass, but he plans to try again to boost homeownership.
"That has been one of the biggest factors in wealth retention and development for the middle class in this country," he said.
Like the Democratic candidates in Connecticut, Schubert wants to keep the American dream alive for new generations.

cbsnews.com/live-updates/iran-war-trump-.headline: Iran War Updates: Trump envoy says war could last another year as oil prices continue rising
cbsnews.com/live-updates/iran-war-trump-.author: Frank Andrews

paragraphs.text: October 23, 2026 / 5:38 AM EDT / CBS News
What to know about the Iran war today:

• U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz has told the Financial Times the war with Iran could last another year, but the Trump administration envoy said he hopes the Iranians "come to the table" before that.

• The price of Brent crude oil hit $114 a barrel Friday after Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed to have disabled seven tankers near the Strait of Hormuz. President Trump accused Iran Thursday of lying about attacks on ships to drive up oil prices before the U.S. midterm elections.

• State-owned energy giant Saudi Aramco said Thursday that the amount of oil flowing through its East-West pipeline, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, had more than tripled from 2 million to 7 million barrels per day, as uncertainty hangs over exports across the Middle East.
U.S. ambassador to the U.N. says Iran war could last another year
U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz has said the war with Iran could drag on for another year.
In an interview with the Financial Times published Friday, Waltz said the U.S. could still be fighting the war President Trump initially said would last "four to five weeks" 12 months from now.
Waltz told the FT the U.S. will not have achieved its key goals in Iran until the country disposes of its highly enriched uranium and accepts a "meaningful agreement on their domestic enrichment."
"I'm not going to put out hypotheticals. One would hope that they'll come to the table in a meaningful way before that," Waltz said, referring to the possibility of another year of war.

He added that Mr. Trump "and the U.S. Navy can maintain this blockade [on Iranian ports] for the foreseeable future," and said the administration was still "tightening" its economic pressure campaign against Iran.
Mr. Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have renewed their threats to launch new strikes on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3.
Foreign ministers from Europe and Gulf region to discuss Strait of Hormuz and Iran conflict

Foreign ministers from seven nations in Europe, the Middle East and elsewhere will hold talks in Istanbul Friday focused on the Strait of Hormuz and the interlinked crises in the Middle East, as well as the Ukraine war.

Ministers from the so-called E3 group – Britain, France and Germany – will meet counterparts from the newly created R4 group, composed of Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt, to discuss the Israel-Palestinian crisis, developments in Yemen and the Strait of Hormuz, and ways to end the Russia-Ukraine war, a Turkish foreign ministry source told AFP.

British Foreign Minister Ed Miliband's office said the talks would revolve around "the Strait of Hormuz and the situation in Saudi Arabia," as the Saudis back Yemen's beleaguered government in its decade-long civil war, which has flared up amid the U.S. war on Iran.

"Despite positive progress from the U.S. and regional partners, passage through the Strait remains under threat, with traffic through the waterway sharply down on pre-war levels," a U.K. foreign ministry statement said.

It said Miliband would "advocate for a diplomatic solution to the crisis that restores full navigational rights and freedoms" and stress "how Iranian tactics are being replicated across the region, with attacks on Saudi Arabia further destabilizing the region and increasing pressure on vital waterways and global chokepoints, such as Bab el-Mandeb and the Suez Canal."
"The U.K. is stepping up to help stabilize the region, having this week committed RAF Typhoons to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks in their airspace," it added.
Saudi Aramco says volume bypassing Strait of Hormuz via pipeline has surged

The president of Saudi state-owned oil company Saudi Aramco, whose facilities have been targeted by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants repeatedly for weeks, says the amount of oil moving through a pipeline that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz has more than tripled.
The East-West pipeline's capacity has surged from 2 million to 7 million barrels each day, President and CEO Amin Nasser said in an interview with Saudi-owned television Al Arabiya Business.

Built in the early 1980s, the pipeline has played a crucial role in Saudi Arabia's ability to export oil amid disruption to shipping via the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran war. It carries crude from Saudi oil fields and production facilities in the east, on the Persian Gulf, to the Yanbu oil terminal on the Saudi Red Sea coast on the other side of the vast kingdom, from which it can be shipped to global markets.

That route, which, unlike the Gulf, has two available exits, has also been threatened and attacked by the Houthis, who have vowed to stop Saudi shipments via the Red Sea's southern gateway, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Nasser said Saudi Aramco has used drones to assess damage caused to infrastructure, including sites key to the East-West pipeline, by Houthi attacks, and to help with firefighting.
Trump accuses Iran of lying about strikes on ships to drive up oil prices
As crude oil prices hit their highest levels since May, President Trump accused Iran on Thursday of lying about attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz to drive up global energy prices.

"Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the U.S. Midterm Election," Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social. "They are even making up fake hits, mines, and everything else, because more Oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the Conflict."
Brent crude, the international standard for oil, hit $112 a barrel Thursday morning, its highest price since May 18.

Iran claimed to have struck four vessels in the Persian Gulf Thursday after they transited the Strait of Hormuz using a U.S.-endorsed route that Tehran rejects, and it said three others hit sea mines in the region after using the same shipping lanes. All of the ships were damaged along or after using southern shipping lanes in the strait near the Omani coast, which the Trump administration has insisted for weeks is open to traffic.

The U.S. military has escorted tankers out of the Persian Gulf using that route, boosting the quantity of oil leaving the region, but it is a costly process. Overall instability in the Middle East has kept energy prices high despite the recently increased supplies.
