There’s a lot of Barack Obama talk in this week’s Mailbag, which reminded me of something that I think tends to get forgotten in assessments of Trump-era politics: It was Mitt Romney, not Donald Trump, who made a hard break with the Bush-McCain interest in some form of “comprehensive immigration reform” with a path to citizenship for the majority of long-resident undocumented immigrants. It’s true that Trump in his 2016 campaign amped up the rhetoric somewhat from where Romney was, but the actual policy gap between Trump and Romney on immigration was modest compared with the very large gaps between Romney and McCain on immigration or between Romney and Trump on Social Security or Medicare or marriage equality.

I bring this up because I think in a lot of ways the core difference between the Slow Boring worldview and the conventional wisdom among Democrats is that most Democrats see Trump’s success as a counterexample to the idea that moderation has political benefits while I see Trump as an illustration of the principle. He is dragged down by a lot of personal misconduct but boosted by having moved to the center to neutralize Obama’s best attacks on Romney. His immigration politics is way to the right of where Bush and McCain were but only modestly to the right of where Romney was.

Conversely, a lot of Republicans are convinced that Trump won where Romney lost because Trump is a scumbag and Romney was an honorable and decent man. This serves to rationalize all kinds of scumbag behavior when the simple truth is that Romney — or some other honorable and decent person — could easily have won if he had Trump’s views on Social Security and Medicare.

Greg M: Given that the least hospitable place on earth is 1000x more hospitable, manageable, more easily constructed, resourced, and populated than literally anywhere else NOT on earth, why the obsession with colonizing the moon or another planet?
Who is this question directed toward? I’m not moving to the moon, I’m with you.

I mentioned this in a totally different context in last week’s Mailbag, but I think your question is a great example of a topic where what I really want is a clearer index of what the conventional wisdom is. Are there a lot of people obsessed with colonizing other planets? Obviously Elon Musk specifically is very interested in this, but my sense is that he’s pretty idiosyncratic in this regard, just as you don’t see a lot of people who combine hard-right politics with enthusiasm for solar energy. But I might be wrong and tons of people are obsessed with colonizing Mars when they should really be thinking about why nobody wants to live in northern Canada instead.

Romulus Augustus: Could you suss out a bit on how Obama post 2014 election disappointed you? I feel the same way because I think he veered into a “proto Woke” policies on the sort of Kendist view that any disparity in school discipline was evidence of racism and his unliberal view on due process for young men accused of sexual assault on college campuses. I would also suggest he gave too much credence to the BLM narrative about the police at times during these years.
Are there other issues you had a problem with during those years and how do you rate him overall?

I might quibble on the margin, but I think the way the Obama administration handled B.L.M. was basically fine. Where I criticize late-Obamaism is on three fronts — all of which ended up making it a lot harder for Hillary Clinton to win in 2016.

aeon.co/essays/why-a-world-without-frict.headline: Why a world without friction is a world without progress
aeon.co/essays/why-a-world-without-frict.author: Jennifer R Vail

paragraphs.text: In conversations, few words catch my attention faster than ‘friction’ – and especially talk of making things frictionless. From the workplace to grocery shopping, our societies seem to be striving to remove friction from everything. The motivation appears to be that decreasing resistance makes life easier and smoother.

Having spent a career as a tribologist, studying friction, wear and lubrication scientifically, I have some opinions on this. I’ll confess that, in most of my career, I too have sought to reduce friction, developing new materials, designs or even instrumentation in order to lower friction in a jet engine or reduce emissions from your car. However, I’ve also found myself trying to figure out how to increase friction to remove plaque on teeth.

The reality is that friction, despite seeming so antagonistic, is necessary and even productive. The force that resists motion has, since humans first struck a spark from a stone, been the very thing that propels us forward. And this paradox offers a lens through which to reread humanity’s entire technological history.

In order to appreciate all that an understanding of friction has helped us to accomplish, it’s necessary to start at square one and state what friction actually is. We define friction as the force that resists motion, and that means friction is rather ubiquitous. If things are moving, whether they’re sliding around or rolling, there’s friction. Solids, liquids, gases? Doesn’t matter. If there’s movement, friction is there to resist it. Unfortunately, because friction’s job is to resist, we’ve developed an aversion to it as a nuisance. But it’s a very important force, and we’ve thrived by expanding our understanding of it. By the 1960s, after millennia of evolving with friction, we finally accepted that friction is such a critical part of our world that a scientific field of study needed to be devoted to it: tribology.

Tribologists like me study this force in all its forms. Tribology is the science of interacting surfaces in relative motion, concerned with the wear of materials, friction and lubrication. Basically, tribology is the specialisation of things rubbing against each other. You may raise an eyebrow at a field of science focused on this, but when you pause to consider how much motion is going on inside us, around us and throughout the Universe, you can appreciate that tribology is vast. More than anyone, tribologists know the problems friction can cause. But they also know the achievements that have followed as we’ve come to understand resistance better.

Although tribology as a formalised field is relatively modern, friction has long shaped humanity’s technological innovations. For example, consider its pivotal role in people’s journeys from A to B over the centuries. I’m willing to bet that whenever you need to move unwieldy furniture or carry home that giant bag of cat litter, your instinct is to find a cart to help you. Early humans had a similar thought, turning to log rollers to move heavy objects, and coming up with one of our greatest inventions: the wheel. Rolling makes it easier to move objects because it reduces friction between the object and surface you’re moving it against. There are far fewer surface interactions in the process of rolling versus sliding. Plenty can be said about the wheel, including the fact that even in 2026 we can’t seem to agree on the origin of its discovery, but there is zero doubt that it’s a brilliant innovation for dealing with friction. But wheels also need friction: when we exert a force to move a wheel forward, the force between the ground and the wheel – static friction – keeps it from spinning freely, which would result in us going nowhere. Once forward motion begins, the resistance to motion becomes dynamic friction, which is just as important. If you’ve driven on ice, you know the danger of too little friction.
However, if people hadn’t continued improving on these basic principles, even the wheel would be rather inefficient due to friction.
The Vikings’ longships minimised form drag so they could cut through the water quickly

The ancient Romans discovered this in their amphitheatres. Roman chariot races didn’t come without their headaches. Or rather, foot aches. I’m certain the drivers likely complained about their hot feet, caused by friction between the wheels and axle heating up the surrounding parts. In Odes, a collection of lyric poems, the poet Horace described how chariot wheels would glow during racing. Today, scientists know that this glow is from turning the energy of motion into thermal energy. Roman designers eventually figured out that they could temper the problem by putting axungia (animal fat) grease between the wheel and axle. By doing so, they were applying tribological knowledge already exploited by the Sumerians: that fats and oils work more effectively than water as lubrication between surfaces. However, that created a new conundrum: if the grease got hot enough, it risked catching fire. The solution? A coolant. In this case, they splashed water on the chariots, in the ancient equivalent of a pit stop.

While all roads led to Rome, you could say all seas led to the Vikings. They, too, cleverly adapted to the resistance that met them as they journeyed through the oceans. Moving through fluids produces a type of friction known as drag. Even within drag there are subsets. Skin drag is from the friction between the surface of the ship and the water, whereas form drag stems from the shape of the hull as it moves through the water. When they had to transport cargo safely, the Vikings used sturdy ships with wide hulls. This wider hull increased form drag and slowed them down, but the stability provided was more critical. Their famous longships, however, were long and slim, minimising form drag as much as possible so they could cut through the water quickly.

As with all friction scenarios, however, the Vikings found themselves having to balance some competing demands. Faster longships are better, yes, but it was also imperative that the ships not break apart into pieces from the waves. They needed flexibility and strength, while keeping the ships as light as possible to ride higher in the water to reduce drag. To do this, the Vikings used their ‘clinker’ technique of nailing together long planks of wood. The rivets and overlapping planks would increase drag compared with a more polished, smoother design but these individual planks gave the ships the ability to twist and flex to weather storms. If I was on a boat trip in the middle of the ocean, I too would be happy to sacrifice a little bit of drag reduction to avoid capsizing from a rogue wave.

Looking at boats and ships today, it’s clear that we didn’t just accept these Viking designs as the culmination of nautical perfection. Likewise, we aren’t driving around in Roman chariots today. We have since made incredible leaps forward in understanding how to quantify friction and thus design for it, finally approaching friction scientifically. In the 1920s, Chrysler’s head of engineering Carl Breer had the idea to design cars with aerodynamics in mind. Planes seemed to slice seamlessly through the air. Shouldn’t cars do the same? Breer tasked the engineer William Earnshaw to consult with none other than Orville Wright to learn how to design a car in a wind tunnel. The resulting teardrop-shaped Chrysler Airflow was considered a flop, as many disruptive designs can be when they’re just too jarring for taste, but that flop revolutionised how we design cars. Wind-tunnel testing remains a standard today, and friction’s presence is as expected as the air itself.

Tribology testing is routine for the automotive industry today, and there are tribology labs scattered throughout a variety of industries, from medical to food. In these labs, you’ll find instruments designed to measure friction at macro-scales down to the atomic level. My PhD lab at the University of Florida had tribometers measuring friction in force ranges that covered three orders of magnitude. I’ve even worked in a lab that had a tribometer built to test an actual train wheel against a railway. Tribologists are incredibly clever with innovating ways to measure friction, given how persnickety friction is. Friction is dependent on the conditions of the operation – how fast things are moving, how much force they experience, and what temperature and environment they’re in.

Temperature in particular is a fun variable to contend with, because friction itself leads to temperature changes; indeed, frictional heating can be extreme in some cases. Like with Roman chariots, greases can ignite at certain temperatures making it imperative to control friction heating in order to avoid accidentally reaching that temperature. And for applications like jet engines, which get very hot anyway, we have engineered solid materials with low friction to withstand the heat.
When tribologists run into a wall, we develop a new instrument to understand what friction is trying to tell us

You may think tribology is already a niche field, but we have specialisations within it. Mine was solid lubrication, and I worked on developing and testing materials for jet engines and automobiles. In some cases, the conditions of the end use were so aggressive that the steel I was running my material against would experience enough friction heating to completely change the colour of the steel. That’s how you know you’ve reached the extremes in tribology, but those extremes must be met and they obviously are. After all, we have space stations orbiting Earth and landers on Mars.

Which brings us to another critical point about friction’s role in human progress: resistance is a consequence of progress, and its existence is a sign of progression itself. We wouldn’t have the now-robust business of solid lubricants if we had not advanced technologically to design turbine engines, which themselves were the result of us figuring out powered flight. By achieving that, our progress led us to new resistance. I think this is critical to remember anytime we find ourselves confronting unexpected resistance, and it’s something I remind myself of whenever I get halted in my work. I wouldn’t be stumped by this new resistance if I hadn’t managed to advance myself to this position where the resistance exists.

Often when tribologists run into a wall, we find ourselves developing a new instrument to help us understand what friction is trying to tell us. Tribometers have been designed to mimic all of the variables mentioned above, and that alone is quite a feat of human engineering, but now we also couple them with other techniques that allow us to somehow see what is happening while it’s happening. From maps of frictional heating during operation to how friction is influencing cellular movement, instruments and techniques have enabled us to usher friction into a new era to drive us forward, doing more than just finding clever ways to overcome friction. We can harness it as a tool.

In terms of friction, the 20th century can be thought of as the century in which humans accepted the resistance, and established engineering rigour around friction to propel our technological advances forward. Critically, it’s when we formalised how to overcome friction to be more efficient. As a tribologist, however, I’m far more excited about what the 21st century has brought us. Instead of just overcoming friction, we began fully realising how to harness that resistance to bring in a new era of progress. Exhibit A is once again found in our cars, where friction has been deployed as a tool in sustainability. Braking requires friction, so engineers asked: why don’t we use the consequences of that friction to our advantage? The heat from friction in braking is now used to create electricity in regenerative braking in EVs and hybrids. We must continue to use this creative and fresh perspective when dealing with friction, as opposed to always driving towards frictionlessness. Imagine if those engineers had been so fixated on the negatives of friction that they didn’t harness its power.

Using friction as a tool has come to us only as we’ve evolved to understand the depths of friction, including its behaviours and where it may be lurking. We know it is involved in dynamic processes, so let’s use it to control such processes. Yes, we’ve done so for a while with mechanisms like brakes and dampeners, but expanding this beyond machines has really taken hold in recent decades. Now, we’re looking at how friction may be a tool in perhaps the most impressive machine there is: the human body. It’s possible friction may be a lever to help us better model and understand biological processes and, in turn, help in the development of therapeutics. The rate at which a virus ejects from its protein shell or capsid can dictate whether it results in an active infection or instead remains dormant in the cell. If we want to use viruses to intentionally infect and defeat other viruses or bacteria, then controlling the virus’s ejection rate is crucial. Friction is the key to unlocking this possibility. In 2023, researchers found that, by packing the coils of virus DNA in certain ways, they could increase friction during ejection and slow down its rate of ejection.
Every advance we make generates new friction. We solve one problem, and friction presents another

Recently, our knowledge of friction has taken us to even more surprising places, extending even to helping us understand dark matter. The concept of ‘resistance is your reward for progress’ may be best illustrated by the astrophysicist Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar. Despite the fact that established scientists mocked his theories, Chandrasekhar would go on to become a founder of astrophysics, and is the reason we understand the evolution of stars and interstellar dynamics. In the 1930s, he was interested in how the interactions between stars could lead to their collisions. He calculated the timescales of such collisions and realised, though only after publishing, that things weren’t adding up quite right. This led him back to the drawing board, where he spotted there was a resistance present that no one before had identified: dynamical friction. This friction is a gravitationally induced drag that acts on objects as they interact and move through space.

Fast-forward to the 21st century, and dynamical friction has been used as a tool to infer the presence of dark matter. In 2024, researchers in Hong Kong realised that orbital times weren’t matching up with a couple of stars they were studying that were believed to be circling around black holes. They looked at Chandrasekhar’s concept of dynamical friction and wondered what would happen if they incorporated the contribution of friction from the dark matter surrounding the black hole. Voila! Suddenly, the predicted and calculated orbital times of the stars matched with what they were measuring. Friction was present when humanity first started experimenting with fire and the wheel. Now it’s there as we probe the frontiers of our Universe.

We need friction to move. Without its resistance, Earth’s plates would be in constant motion. We could not walk, or drive, or even hold objects. Understanding how to achieve what we want, in a world requiring this resistance, has been essential in our development.

Yet there is a deeper paradox at work, one that William James captured when he wrote that life is built ‘in the self-governing resistance of the ego to the world’. Every advance we make generates new friction. We solve one problem, and friction presents another. We step forward, and new resistance awaits. This is what progress means: that we have moved into territory that demands new understanding.
Roman engineers learned it when their chariot wheels caught fire. Chandrasekhar discovered this when his calculations didn’t add up. And we will continue to encounter resistance as we push forward.
When people speak of a frictionless world, they imagine ease. But ease without resistance is a wheel spinning in place, motion without progress.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq4g1p974wxko.headline: Five Israelis wounded and two suspected Palestinian attackers killed in West Bank shooting
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq4g1p974wxko.author: Tom Bennett

paragraphs.text: Five Israelis have been wounded and two suspected Palestinian attackers killed by Israeli security forces following a shooting in the occupied West Bank, Israeli officials say.
Unverified footage shared on social media shows an intense gun battle between soldiers and the gunmen, at a military checkpoint at the entrance to the city of Hebron.

The attack comes at a time of high tensions in the West Bank, with extremist Jewish settlers targeting Palestinians during the annual olive harvest, and Israel's general election taking place in four days time.

The Israeli military said it had found a large quantity of ammunition in the attackers' vehicle. The military said they believe the gunmen had intended to carry out a much larger attack on the nearby Route 35, but unexpectedly ran into the checkpoint - so instead decided to open fire there.

Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has built his election campaign on promising security, said he had instructed the military to prepare for a full lockdown of the West Bank, beginning later on Friday. The West Bank was already expected to be placed under lockdown for the election on Monday and Tuesday, according to Israeli media.
Netanyahu added that his Likud party would cancel campaign events for the morning.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmwyqn6ejyd4o.headline: Hispanic voters helped bring Trump to power - in Texas, the tide may be turning
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmwyqn6ejyd4o.author: Gary O’Donoghue

paragraphs.text: It was just before dawn in the Rio Grande Valley in Texas and the congregation were arriving for the Friday service at the tiny La Lomita Catholic Chapel.
The whitewashed building, which has been here since the days of the American Civil War, rises from the surrounding scrub and sits about 200 yards from the Rio Grande river itself.
As cars pulled up to the chapel, the sound of Father Roy Snipes' barking dogs signalled his arrival. He has been the priest here for almost half a century - and is known locally as the Cowboy Priest.
"I'm not sure why I picked that up, but it's nice," he said of the nickname.

In truth, it is pretty obvious why. Snipes wears a Stetson in place of the more traditional priest's hat. And moments later, the chapel was filled by the sound of a Roy Rogers song - the singer and actor known as the King of the Cowboys.

During the first Trump administration, Snipes resisted plans to seize the chapel's land to build the US president's border wall. Eight years on, at the early Friday service, he focused his short sermon on the actions of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
"There's no good excuse to detain, incarcerate and deport poor, good folks who are our neighbours," Snipes told the congregation of about 30, mainly Hispanic worshippers.
Texas accounted for roughly one-third of all ICE arrests nationwide in July 2026 - a larger share than any other state - according to government figures obtained by the Deportation Data Project.

"They said we're gonna seek out, capture, detain and deport the worst of the worst," Snipes said in his sermon. "Well, we're here on the border and the cartel is the worst-of-the-worst. So we thought, well, that's a good thing.
"But it turned out, you can hear almost every day, some poor guy going to work and they stop him and detain him and start a big fight."
After the service, two members of the congregation stopped to chat. "We're educators, and we have a lot of students that are having to go back because their parents are getting deported," one said.
"The cruelty that we're seeing - I think that's turning the tide, at least I hope so," their friend added.
Turning the tide politically is what Democrats are hoping they can do in Texas in the midterm elections on 3 November. But that will not be easy.

This stretch of the Rio Grande was once one of the busiest crossing points on the US-Mexico border. Under former President Joe Biden, hundreds of thousands of migrants came through here, with more than two and a half million apprehensions recorded in a single year.
Trump promised to stop these illegal crossings during his 2024 election campaign, and in large parts he has delivered.

Border crossings are now at their lowest level in decades. And it was that promise which in part drove Trump's astonishingly high level of support in the state, taking around 55% of Hispanic votes in Texas alone - a record for a Republican presidential candidate.

Javier Villalobos is the Republican Mayor of McAllen, one of the biggest cities in the Rio Grande Valley. He expects Republicans will find it tough this time around, but credits the Trump administration with stemming the border problem.

"I remember I put out a video… thanking the administration for immediately securing the border. That was great," he said. "And I think generally most people are okay with the deportation of criminals, violent people, or people that really are not productive at all."
But if you start deporting people that are productive and law-abiding, that is where the problem is, he added.

Recent polls suggest much of Trump's support among Hispanic voters has ebbed away since 2024. Surveys taken since late summer indicate a majority of Texan Hispanic voters disapprove of the president. They also suggest Hispanic voters are favouring Democrats over Republicans by a significant margin.

"When I voted for President Trump, I voted for him because we saw an influx of immigration during the Biden administration," said Mario Guerrero, a young Mexican-American businessman who leads the South Texas Builders Association. It needed to be fixed, he said.
"We thought that we were in the right by voting for Trump, and that he was going to do what was best in order to fix the crisis on the border.
"And I think to myself, we were really not told the extreme that they were willing to go to make a point," he added, before referencing recent shootings involving ICE agents in US cities.
Guerrero is a reminder that, for many who live and work close to the US-Mexico border, security and immigration enforcement are two distinct issues.
A voter here may be supportive of securing the border and stopping illegal crossings, but oppose the actions of ICE and how the administration is enforcing its crackdown on undocumented migration.
Guerrero voted for Trump three times in a row - but is planning to vote Democrat in November, in part due to his unease with that crackdown.

"There's a man that I know that… last year, had 35 workers that were working for him every day," he said. "Right now, he just told me two days ago that he would be lucky if he would get four to six guys to show up to work."

Even though Guerrero plans to vote Democrat, he describes himself as neither Democrat nor Republican. And that, according to Mike Madrid, a leading Republican consultant and expert on Hispanic voters, is key to understanding the largest ethnic demographic voting group in the country.
"Latinos are more likely than any other racial or ethnic group to identify as independents rather than Republicans or Democrats," he said.

It was in part the belief that Hispanic voters were shifting permanently towards the Republican Party that led Trump to press states such as Texas to redraw their congressional maps early, before the once-a-decade census.

The strategy was intended to capitalise on what Republicans saw as a realignment in Hispanic voting behaviour, particularly in border districts that had been Democratic strongholds for more than a century.
Texas's 15th congressional district was among those that were redrawn, and has become one of the clearest tests of whether electoral maps can guarantee political outcomes.

The seat was redrawn after the 2020 census and was won by a Republican in 2022. It was redrawn again in 2025, creating a notional 18-point majority for Republicans in these midterms. Even so, current polling suggests a Democratic lead of five or six points.
Bobby Pulido is the Democratic candidate hoping to win the district. As a popular Tejano singer and winner of two Latin Grammys, he is already a household name in the Rio Grande Valley.

At an event just weeks before the vote, he delivered a stock political speech followed by a musical performance. "A lot of people are disillusioned with both parties," he told the BBC shortly before he took the stage. "And I hear them."
To win in this part of Texas, you need to be a conservative. Pulido has distanced himself from the national Democratic Party brand and focused deliberately and consistently on economic issues.

"This isn't New York, this isn't LA," he said. "When you lead with issues like social justice, climate change and other topics, that's not what people want to hear first. They want to hear about the economy."
That message is consistent with what many current polls are suggesting - the economy, and the cost of living specifically, rank top on the list of most voters' priorities.

At a local avocado festival, a fruit that is a staple among Hispanic communities in the valley, a couple, Dave Baldwin and Veronica Salazar, began discussing rising prices as soon as they were asked about the upcoming elections.
When asked who they blame for spiking costs, the answer was swift. "The president," they said.
"He is in control of our destiny with all that, and right now he's not doing a very good job," added Baldwin.
Among many Republican campaigners here, there is a feeling that they are are on the back foot just weeks before the vote.
Alexis Uscanga, a student volunteer tasked with knocking on doors and checking on likely Republican voters in the district, was realistic about what he is trying to achieve.
"The midterms are just purely a game of turnout," he said. "It's not trying so much to convince individuals to vote one way or the other, it's about trying to get our people mostly to show up."

Tano Tijerina, the Republican candidate in the neighbouring, Democratic-held 28th district, credited Trump with "breaking through barriers" but acknowledged the "national political headwinds are real".

The Hispanic shift towards President Trump in 2024 was one of the most striking political facts of the past decade. While this expanding demographic may not have much love for either party, in a two-party system voters are mostly forced to make a choice.
And if polling is correct - and there is no guarantee of that - even a modest swing back to Democrats in November could reshape races not just across this state but far beyond.
In Texas, it could even be enough to put a US Senate seat in play - and Democrats haven't won one of those in the state in more than 30 years.

Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

theguardian.com/uk-news/2026/oct/23/megh.headline: Duchess of Sussex ‘deeply distressed’ over child sexual abuse image claims against father
theguardian.com/uk-news/2026/oct/23/megh.author: Caroline Davies

paragraphs.text: The Duchess of Sussex has said she is “deeply distressed” over accusations involving child sexual abuse images against her estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr, and revealed she was made aware of “disturbing allegations” against him in 2018 by the Metropolitan police.

Meghan issued a statement after the Sun newspaper published claims that her half-brother Thomas Markle Jr alleged he had found a stash of images belonging to their father at his former home in the Philippines.
In an interview with the Daily Mail, Markle Sr denied possessing child sexual abuse images, calling the accusations “sick lies”.

It is understood that authorities in the UK had previously told Meghan that allegations made about her father in a 2018 letter sent to Scotland Yard, and subsequently shared with her by the police, were being investigated.
In a statement through her spokesperson, Meghan said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.

“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.

“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them.
“I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.

“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”
The 2018 letter was understood to have been shared with Meghan by the royalty and specialist protection unit within the Met police.

Markle Sr has been estranged from the duchess since he failed to attend her wedding to Prince Harry on health grounds, and has never met his grandchildren, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five.

The Sun reported that Markle Jr told detectives in the Philippines he had discovered “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images on computers and mobile phones stored in four large boxes at the home in Cebu where Markle Sr was living until he returned to the US in May after having a stroke.
Markle Jr, 60, said he had also contacted the FBI in the US, the Sun reported.
Meghan’s father has vehemently denied possessing child sexual abuse images, telling the Daily Mail that the accusations were “sick lies”.
He told the newspaper the computers had not been in his possession since he left Rosarito, Mexico, with his son in January 2025 and moved to the Philippines “for a fresh start”.

Speaking from a rehabilitation centre in Florida, where he is learning to walk with a prosthetic limb after his left leg was amputated because of a blood clot, he told the Mail: “I’m shocked, I’m hurt and I’m very upset that my son is making these accusations against me. I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.
“This is bullshit. It’s just a bunch of lies. It’s sick. I have no idea why Tom is trying to destroy me with these lies.”

cnbc.com/2026/10/23/janeese-lewis-george.headline: Democratic socialist set to become D.C. mayor — and face Trump's pushback
cnbc.com/2026/10/23/janeese-lewis-george.author: Irit Skulnik

paragraphs.text: Zohran Mamdani famously brought democratic socialism to the largest U.S. city when he became New York's mayor. Now another member of the Democratic Party's progressive flank is poised to lead Washington, D.C.

Janeese Lewis George, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America and a city council member, is set to become the next mayor of the nation's capital, which has been led for more than a decade by Democratic Mayor Muriel Bowser. Lewis George defeated moderate Democrat Kenyan McDuffie in the June Democratic primary and will face off against independent and Green Party candidates in November in an election that is all but decided in the overwhelmingly Democratic city.

As she prepares to take office, looming questions remain about how much she will be able to accomplish in a city that's home to the federal government, which has significant authority over its governance, and whether her leadership will be primarily symbolic under the larger government's thumb.

Her supporters, however, hope she will stand up to President Donald Trump, as she pledged she would do during her campaign. Trump has previously federalized the city's police department and has deployed thousands of National Guard troops for the past 14 months across Washington, with plans to keep them in place until his term ends in 2029.

"Myself and basically every other D.C. resident I know, we don't take kindly to threats from the federal government on our ability to self-govern," said Kurtis Hagans, chair of the Metro DC Democratic Socialists of America chapter. "I'm going to be happy if she's showing a willingness to fight for us."

Lewis George is part of a larger swell of democratic socialists gaining power on local and federal levels. In Seattle, Katie Wilson became mayor last year in a close win over incumbent Democrat Bruce Harrell. In Los Angeles, Nithya Raman is leading in a tight runoff for mayor against incumbent Democrat Karen Bass.

There are also several democratic socialists running for Congress this election cycle. In Michigan, the far-left Abdul El-Sayed is challenging former Rep. Mike Rogers. El-Sayed has rejected the DSA label, though many of his positions align with the organization's goals.
Lewis George's campaign declined CNBC's requests for an interview.
Lewis George's agenda as Washington mayor
One goal of the DSA is universal childcare, which Lewis George has campaigned on, and Hagans said he hopes to see her deliver.
Lewis George also wants to focus on affordable housing and lowering utility costs, her website says.
Additionally, she supports a new business activity tax, or BAT, though she told The Washington Sun that she doesn't support tax hikes on working- or middle-class families.

Her BAT proposal would target unincorporated partnerships such as law offices, lobbying shops and other firms that are based in Washington but whose owners live outside the city and who, under federal tax law, can avoid paying the district's business franchise tax. It would exempt the first $200,000 of economic activity from taxation.

According to the DC Fiscal Policy Institute, a 2% BAT policy could raise about $500 million in additional revenue for the city annually. Lewis George said during the Democratic mayoral primary debate that revenue from the BAT could help fund her policy goals.

The D.C. City Council in July ordered a feasibility report on implementing a BAT. This month, the council held a nine-hour hearing to debate tax proposals, including the BAT, as the council attempts to mitigate budget shortfalls for fiscal year 2028.
Proponents of the tax said at the hearing it would make taxation fairer across the city's business community, and Lewis George has previously said it closes a tax "loophole."

Malcom Fox, executive director of Opportunity DC, an independent expenditure group that has supported moderate candidates including McDuffie and says it supports reducing the cost of living and doing business in Washington, said the BAT would hurt the city by raising taxes on small businesses.
"It's a self-defeatist approach that is punishing the small businesses we need to bring our economy back," Fox said.
Congress, Trump ready to limit mayor's power
In light of the potential BAT and other tax proposals, Republicans in Congress are preparing to limit the city — and Lewis George's — authority.

This summer, Rep. James Comer, R-Ky., introduced a bill that would effectively allow Congress to block tax increases the city approves. The D.C. Taxing Authority Review Act advanced out of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, which Comer chairs, on July 22.

"Radical DC Democrats want to solve their spending problem by reaching deeper into taxpayers' pockets and driving further on the path to socialism. Let's be clear: higher taxes will not fix the financial mess they created," Comer said in a press release.
Lewis George responded to the legislation on X by encouraging Congress to reject the bill.
"Let the people of D.C. govern D.C.," she said.

The next step would be for the proposal to go to a full House vote, though it is unclear if that will happen. Ankit Jain, a District of Columbia shadow senator, told CNBC he thinks the odds of the bill surviving both chambers of Congress are slim.
Lewis George will also have to fight Trump, who in August 2025 seized control of Washington's police department, a move Bowser's critics said she complied with too easily.

Trump said his federal takeover of city police, as well as the deployment of hundreds of National Guard soldiers, was meant to crack down on crime, despite violent crime having fallen in the city from earlier peaks. Trump used Section 740 of the 1973 Home Rule Act, which allows a president to take control of Washington's police for emergency situations for 30 days, unless Congress grants an extension.
Trump has repeatedly threatened to federalize the city again and called Lewis George a "communist" in June.
On a local level, D.C. Chamber of Commerce President and Chief Executive Chinyere Hubbard said the group looks forward to working with Lewis George.

"Janeese Lewis George has said that as mayor, she really wants to create a thriving economy that works for everyone to ensure good-paying jobs, and we share that goal at the chamber," Hubbard said. "It doesn't matter how someone's labeled or anything, but whether they implement policies."
The bounds of authority as D.C. mayor

David Barker, a political science professor at American University, said he thinks Lewis George's mayorship will be more symbolic than anything else, noting the Washington mayor, like mayors in general, has limited power.

"What is the mayor going to do? They can't actually pass any kind of legislation that's going to massively increase some minimum wage or massively increase tax rates on residents and redistribute it or anything like that," Barker said. "They're gonna, you know, fix some potholes and stuff and put up lights."

However, Lewis George's willingness to say no to Trump, unlike Bowser, will have an impact on Washington residents, said Nick Cosgrove, co-chair of the Young Democratic Socialists for America chapter at the University of Maryland.
Cosgrove also noted that, being in Washington, she will have less executive power than other mayors.

"Even in a best case, I don't think she's going to be the Mamdani in D.C.," he said. Mamdani has become well-known for quickly advancing his policy goals, including rolling out initiatives such as a pied-à-terre tax and free childcare for low-income children.
"But I do think that she's going to be a vast improvement over Mayor Bowser," Cosgrove added, referring to Lewis George's pledge to say no to Trump.
Bowser's office declined to comment.
Nadia Brown, a professor of government at Georgetown University, said Bowser has had to learn when to work with Trump and when to fight him.
"I think Janeese Lewis George is going to have to thread that needle as well," Brown said.

npr.org/sections/planet-money/2026/10/23.headline: Why Meta is charging to post more hyperlinks
npr.org/sections/planet-money/2026/10/23.author: Cooper Katz McKim

paragraphs.text: Outside of Atlanta, two gas stations got into a price war. The Atlanta TV station WSB-TV reported that, over the course of a day, prices dropped from $2.54 down to $1.44, $1.39 and eventually down to just 97 cents. When drivers took notice, the traffic jam began and police intervened. BUT while it was happening, one driver said she only spent $15 to fill up her truck. It usually costs $90. "Look at God, baby! Look at God!" she said.
In our team's Slack, co-host Wailin Wong responded to the low prices, "make it up on volume!?" Jeff Guo wrote, "how is this real." But like, actually. How is this real?
Coming up:
• Why Facebook is charging you to post hyperlinks
• How fake data centers can still drive up electricity costs
• How one man is dealing with a rental car agency
News We're Watching
Why websites make it hard to leave

What To Know: Social media sites don't love it when users leave. If you've ever used Instagram, it's not the easiest place to post links. You need to include them in bios, or through a special button on stories. Well now, if you run a Facebook page, you can only post TWO hyperlinks for free per month. $49.99/month will get you a Meta One Advanced plan, allowing you to include eight hyperlinks in posts or reels. With the $499/month Max plan, you can post an unlimited amount. Ashley Gullen, who runs a game design company, posted on Mastodon, a decentralized social media platform, "Facebook achieving absurd new heights of enshittification" in response to the news. This isn't totally unique. Nieman Lab did a whole study finding that posting links hurts news publishers on X.

Why are companies doing this?: Attention is money for social media sites. They want to keep you inside their walls! David Evans, managing director at BRG, a consulting firm, wrote a simple explanation as to why platforms want you to stay on their site: "Attention platforms use content to get consumers to spend time on their platform and sell marketers the ability to expose these consumers to messages."
Even FAKE data centers could be driving up electricity costs - The Wall Street Journal

What To Know: Developers are desperate to get their data centers up and running. They need it to help power their precious AI and whatever other computing is needed. BUT, developers won't just say, "This is the only location we'll accept for this project." No, they'll put out requests to all sorts of locations for their centers. The problem is, utilities are still considering data centers that likely WON'T GET BUILT in their electricity forecasts. Energy research firm Wood Mackenzie estimates that only a mere 23% of data-center requests are considered "high confidence," according to The Wall Street Journal. The rest are speculative!

How this affects YOU: Electricity costs could rise even if the data centers don't get built. Hoowwwwww does that work now? Because utilities are still planning for expected demand. They can't just suddenly integrate a wildly power-demanding data center without new substations or transmission lines. It's possible for the utility to pass on some of those grid investments onto consumers, even if the data centers never come to pass. Some power markets also set prices based on future demand so… There are lots of ways these projects could mess with your electricity bill.
Another oil reserve gets tapped - U.S. Department of Energy

It's your weekly update on diesel prices! This week, the Trump administration has found a NEW way to try and lower prices, which seems to be a core issue ahead of the midterms. This time, the U.S. Department of Energy has authorized an exchange from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve. It would release roughly a third of the reserves for heating oil. The Chief Energy Advisor for Gulf Oil thinks it won't make a difference on prices.

What's interesting, this reserve has only been tapped ONCE, and that was after Hurricane Sandy. According to the DOE's history, that's the sort of thing it was meant for. "The intent was to create a buffer large enough to allow commercial companies to compensate for interruptions in supply during severe winter weather." Here, the DOE will loan out up to 315,000 barrels of heating oil in hopes of lowering prices. It's called an exchange because borrowing entities, like a regional heating oil retailer, would be required to replace the same volume at a premium ahead of next year.
Today's Indicator
Why Oracle's debt load could be your problem

If you HAVEN'T listened: We keep hearing about the AI boom that's propping up the U.S. economy. Well, Oracle is a part of that story. The enterprise software company has moved into building out data centers to serve the AI industry. Now, they have a huge deal with OpenAI worth $300 billion over five years. Here's the problem. Oracle has been spending freely with the assumption that this OpenAI deal will deliver. But what if it doesn't? Oracle already has $169 billion in total debt and a growing credit risk. They're one link in an interconnected chain of enormous tech companies. If that link breaks, it could spell trouble for the economy.
Listen to the full episode

If you HAVE listened: Lindsay Tyler, credit analyst, explains in the piece that Oracle is making a bet on data centers. "The analogy might be you have 10 apartments, you've pre-signed leases with, for those 10 apartments, and you're thinking, 'Should I build another floor?'"
On the surface, this doesn't seem plausible. Isn't computing demand insatiable right now? Yeah, right now. But…
• AI is getting so much more efficient to run. Research from Epoch AI found "the cost of achieving a given level of AI performance has fallen about 47% per quarter since 2023, or 13× per year."
• The chips powering these AI models "have a useful lifespan of one to three years due to rapid technological obsolescence and physical wear."

Some economic historians like to compare the AI buildout to the railroads, but this one is different. Rails last longer than one to three years. The cost of shipping does not plummet 13x per year. And maybe Oracle is at the center of these economic forces colliding: a railroad-type investment boom building castles made of sand.
Rest of the WeekWe can inflate away the national debt… at a cost
Piercing the American taboo of talking about income and class
Can a "Moneyball" system work for campaign funding?
Listener Mailbag

Context: Last week, we ran an episode full of consumer rage stories. One included a story about someone charged for damage to a rental car that was impossible to disprove. Stay to the end for a surprising twist.
Listener Jim Zerefos sent in a response from Colorado.

I share the frustration of the person who complained about dubious damage claims from a rental car company. I've been fighting Alamo for nearly a year now over a $1,600 damage claim. Alamo sent me photos of very minor damage taken AFTER our rental, but never provided photos from BEFORE our rental. [The car] had some 23k miles so seems possible (likely?) the scratches occurred some time before our rental.

My spidey sense here smells a scam: "rental companies now scan cars for damage and so are trying to find scapegoats for all prior damage"? Alamo's reaction to me (and my insurance company) has been to ignore us - never sending the "before" pics and never acknowledging that's an issue. They just keep sending us invoices. They now are threatening collection action and have banned me from renting from the Alamo rental family (as if I would). So, the story on the broader scam? Or story on which credit cards still offer primary rental damage coverage (which we THOUGHT we had)?

By the way, here at The Indicator, we reached out to the car rental company and they responded in a statement through a spokesperson from Enterprise Mobility: "Customer satisfaction is our top priority, and we are always open to further conversations with customers regarding damage claims. Our team is actively reviewing this matter through our escalation process and will reach out to the customer to share an update today."

And we already have an update: Jim tells us Alamo has since dropped the claim and will make no further collection efforts. Alamo's "risk" department instructed the Cleveland manager to drop the claim, according to Jim.
Jim's response: "Sad to see that you got more action in a day than my insurance company and I got in nearly a year."
In Our Spare Time
Co-host Wailin Wong is reading Under Story

This fall has yielded a bumper crop of big new fiction releases. My favorite from the last couple of weeks of reading is UNDER STORY by Chloe Benjamin. This novel is about a fungi expert who goes to Antarctica after a family tragedy. She's hoping to anonymously wash dishes at a research station. However, a strange light phenomenon and the arrival of her physicist ex-husband pull her back into the scientific world. This was an exciting, imaginative, and beautiful story about grief, family, parallel universes, trees, and mushrooms. (Bonus rec: This book also makes for a good pairing with Emily St. John Mandel's new novel, Exit Party.)

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6ev38dj1g8zo.headline: At least one dead and four injured in Paris suburb shooting
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6ev38dj1g8zo.author: BBC News

paragraphs.text: One person has been killed and four others injured in a Parisian suburb, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has said.
The "very serious events" happened in Trappes, to the west of Paris, Lecornu wrote on social media, adding that the suspected attack had been "apprehended and placed in police custody".
A police source said a man opened fire from a vehicle on Friday, according to news agency AFP, and was later arrested in the nearby town of Coignières at about 10:30 local time (08:30 GMT).
Reports in French media suggest the number of injured may be higher and that a 12-year-old child may be among them.
Lecornu said the National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's Office has announced it is monitoring the situation.

finance.yahoo.com/media-advertising/arti.headline: Rogers Beats on Sports Revenue as Wireless Remains Sluggish
finance.yahoo.com/media-advertising/arti.author: Stephanie Hughes

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Rogers Communications Inc. beat analyst earnings expectations on gains from sports assets, but the company's core wireless business is still struggling to find growth.
Most Read from Bloomberg
Canada's biggest mobile phone provider earned C$1.29 per share on an adjusted basis in the third quarter, more than the C$1.23 average estimate in a Bloomberg survey of analysts.

Rogers' media revenue rose to C$821 million, up 9% from a year ago. The company doubled its stake in Maple Leaf Sports & Entertainment last year, and as of Oct. 1, it owns 100% of the company that runs the Toronto Raptors basketball club and Toronto Maple Leafs hockey team.

Rogers already owned Major League Baseball's Toronto Blue Jays and it plans to sell a minority stake in a consolidated sports, media and entertainment company, targeting a deal in the first half of 2027.

"The close of the MLSE transaction marks a significant milestone in our plan to unlock shareholder value from our sports and media assets, which continue to show global breadth and scale," Chief Executive Officer Tony Staffieri said in a statement.

Revenue in the wireless segment, Rogers' largest business, was C$2.69 billion, up 1% from a year ago. The company added just 6,000 net postpaid mobile subscribers during the quarter, less than the roughly 33,000 expected by analysts. A year ago, it added 62,000.
Adjusted Ebitda was up 1% from last year's third quarter in both the cable and wireless divisions. Ebitda is earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization.

Temporary foreign workers and international student visas have been restricted in Canada under an immigration tightening that began in 2024, limiting the pool of new users. Telecom firms had been using aggressive discounts to encourage customers to switch providers.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: Chipotle’s Softening Sales Force Analyst to Throw in the Towel
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Peyton Forte

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- A long-standing Chipotle Mexican Grill Inc. bull has moved to the sidelines, citing concern that a slow start to the fourth quarter suggests softer sales for the year ahead.
Most Read from Bloomberg

TD Cowen analyst Andrew Charles lowered his recommendation on the shares to hold from buy on Wednesday, just ahead of the burrito maker's earnings report next week. He also cut his 12-month price target to a Street-low $32 from $44, while his bear case assumes the stock could drop to $25 per share.

Charles says that while Chipotle's third-quarter results should be slightly better than consensus, medium-term same-store sales forecasts are too high as the brand relies less on price increases to prioritize growing traffic.

"The start of the quarter is showing underlying softness at a time when the business ought to be clicking," Charles, who'd held a buy-equivalent rating on Chipotle since 2019, said in an interview. "Now that we believe that it's more likely Chipotle is going to miss 2027 estimates more materially, we thought now is a good time to move to the sidelines."

Chipotle shares have shed 24% this year and are trading near a three-year low, making it one of the worst performers in the S&P Composite 1500 Restaurants Index, which is down 6.6% in 2026. Restaurant stocks have broadly struggled amid deteriorating consumer sentiment.

Chipotle has seen some success in assuring customers who've grown weary of high-priced "slop bowls" that its prices are justified, an issue that triggered sales declines in recent quarters. The company's latest earnings release showed sales performed better than expected thanks to buzz around limited-time offers like honey chicken, in addition to promotions via its loyalty app.

Still, Charles fears these initiatives may not be enough to overpower macro headwinds while warning that other sales drivers such as high-efficiency kitchen equipment and catering are "less proven," setting the stage for a challenging 2027.

TD Cowen lowered its fourth-quarter same-store sales growth estimate to 1% from 4%, well below the 2.9% gain analysts polled by Bloomberg are expecting. Charles's 2027 projection was cut to 2.1% from 3.8%, compared with the consensus estimate of a 3.1% increase.

Wells Fargo analyst Zachary Fadem — who cut his price target to $40 from $45 on Wednesday — said Chipotle shares are back to lows as investors lose patience with the company's strategy. Early quarter trends are soft despite easier year-over-year comparisons, he added.
Raymond James last week cut its Chipotle price target to $37, with analyst Brian Vaccaro questioning whether more work could be done to more directly communicate Chipotle's value proposition.

Despite the near-term headwinds, Wall Street is still generally bullish on the stock. Chipotle has 23 buy-equivalent ratings to go along with 12 holds and just one sell, according to Bloomberg data. Charles said he'd like to see Chipotle accelerate traffic without having to lean on promotions.
"This is a premium brand with premium ingredients," he said. "I don't think it should be degraded by doing more value advertising."
Here are other notable analyst calls and commentary this week:

• Goldman Sachs upgraded shares of CoreWeave Inc. to buy from neutral, saying that the neocloud looked attractive following a recent selloff sparked by its debt falling to levels that typically indicate distress.
• Kohl's shares jumped Thursday after Gordon Haskett Research Advisors upgraded their rating on the retailer's stock to buy from hold, becoming the only Wall Street bull.
• Loop Capital Markets downgraded shares of Apple Inc. to hold from buy citing a reduction in iPhone shipments.
• Block Inc. got a new bull when BMO Capital Markets upgraded shares to outperform from market perform, citing "multiple compelling opportunities on the horizon."

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: BofA’s Hartnett Sees Risk-Off Mood Lasting Until Mid-November
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Levin Stamm

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Investors' risk-off mood is likely to continue well into November, according to Bank of America Corp.'s Michael Hartnett, in another sign of how jitters around the artificial intelligence trade and the US midterm elections have held back equity markets.
Most Read from Bloomberg
"We stay tactically risk-off until mid-Nov," the strategist wrote in a note to clients Friday. "Expect down-in-yields, down-in-stocks, down-in US dollar trade."

Hartnett said the market still needs to fully price a Democratic victory in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, which would be negative for earnings growth as it would result in an end to the current low-tax, low-regulation regime.

Another factor that would signal a revival of risk appetites would be the European Central Bank or French government stepping in to reverse the rout in French bond yields, Hartnett said. A peak in AI hyperscaler debt spreads, which have spooked markets recently, could also be brought about by cuts to capital spending or an "extreme equity issuance announcement," he said.

Investors are continuing to pile into the AI-related sectors. EPFR Global data cited by the bank showed the largest weekly inflows into technology stocks since July. A Bank of America survey this month also showed that global investors are the most exposed to tech since August 2020.

In recent days, though, they've also taken a defensive turn, looking for shelter from a series of risks ranging from climbing oil prices and higher borrowing costs as well as worries that the AI trade is starting to exhibit bubble-like conditions.

Billionaire Ken Griffin warned this week that investors are "almost certainly" in the midst of an AI bubble. An equal-weighted version of the S&P 500 Index — a proxy for market breadth — on Thursday had its best day since 2024 relative to the market-cap weighted S&P 500. Defensive consumer staple stocks, meanwhile, are on track for their best month since 1998.

technologyreview.com/2026/10/23/1147628/.headline: The Download: testing six tech promises and biotech’s blind spots
technologyreview.com/2026/10/23/1147628/.author: Thomas Macaulay

paragraphs.text: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
Are we there yet? A reality check on six big tech promises

Some seemingly impossible feats are too good to give up on. Decoding a pet’s yowls and yips? Absolutely. Scrubbing the world of forever chemicals? Yes, please. Rocketing to Mars in a fraction of the time? Sounds great, but how close are we, really?

In the new Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review, we ran progress reports on six potentially transformative technologies and ideas that have been “just around the corner” for years, or even decades. From exercise in a pill to nuclear-powered spaceships, we asked experts what’s holding them back and how far they’ve come.
Check out our stories on how they all stacked up.
Over the coming days, we’ll unpack each of the six technologies in The Download. So stay tuned!
In the biotech world, you can’t see everything
—Jessica Hamzelou
Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything, the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes.

Like many others, I came away feeling unsettled. But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the disturbing interactions between the subjects. The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything.The film is a stark reminder of how easy it can be to fall for an appealing narrative. This is why it left me questioning how we cover science.

cnbc.com/2026/10/23/airfare-airline-capa.headline: Fewer people are flying as airfare soars. Here's why airlines aren't worried
cnbc.com/2026/10/23/airfare-airline-capa.author: Leslie Josephs

paragraphs.text: Fewer people are flying this year, but with airfare this high and climbing, airline executives say that's just fine.

The number of people screened at U.S. checkpoints is on track for its first annual decline since 2020. Major U.S. carriers have said capturing higher fares is more important than fully filling their planes or flying record numbers of travelers.

"We're actively prioritizing yield versus load factor and really happy as we see it. It fits right in with the premium investments that we're making," American Airlines Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper said on the company's earnings call Thursday.
American's load factor, a gauge of how full planes are flying, fell to 83.4% in the third quarter from 86% in the same quarter of 2025.
Fares keep climbing
The price of plane tickets has skyrocketed as airlines grapple with a spike in jet fuel prices, their biggest expense after labor, and pass more of those costs on to customers.

Fares in September were up more than 22% from a year earlier, according to the latest inflation read. Fare tracker Hopper said it expects this holiday season to come with the most expensive ticket prices in years.

The average Southwest Airlines fare in the third quarter, for example, was $231.69, up close to $50 from a year earlier. That doesn't include Southwest's new fees, like its extra charges for checked bags or a seat closer to the front of the plane.
The airline's count of revenue passengers, however, fell 3.2% from a year ago, to about 33.5 million people.
Still, both fares and the passenger counts exceeded Southwest's expectations.

"Passenger fares came in about $3 above what our forecast was and the more important thing is that passenger volumes also exceeded our expectations," Southwest CEO Bob Jordan said on an earnings call Thursday.

Since April — when airlines began warning in earnest about profits taking a hit from the spike in jet fuel — through Thursday, about 9.3 million fewer people were screened at airport checkpoints compared with the same period of 2025, according to the Transportation Security Administration. While that's down less than 2% from last year, it follows years of growth.

With jet fuel prices more than double year-ago levels — as seen in U.S. Gulf Coast spot prices going for $4.63 a gallon, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration — airlines have been focused on recovering as much of the fuel spike as possible.
Even despite some drops, airline executives said during their earnings calls that travel demand overall is robust, especially for profitable premium cabins like business class.

And not every carrier is seeing a decline. United Airlines flew 2.4% more passengers in the third quarter than it did a year ago, and said its unit revenue rose by 16%, the biggest increase since the pandemic.

"I've been pleasantly surprised at the industry's ability this year to raise yields and pass through much of the increase in fuel prices," CEO Scott Kirby said on the company's earnings call Wednesday. "So it's possible that airlines will continue to focus on yields at the expense of load factor and that alone could get us to double-digit margins next year."
Profit hit
Most airlines are anticipating that fuel costs will continue to bite, but executives say they're confident in their pricing power.
United, for example, said it expects to pay an average of $4.80 a gallon for fuel in the fourth quarter, up from an average price of $3.90 a gallon in the third.

American, United, Delta Air Lines and Southwest all cut their profit forecasts for 2026 this month when they reported earnings. American is the only one of the four that expects to post a loss this year.

American and others have also reduced growth plans or warned the industry could dial back on its goals for expanding capacity, which could keep fares elevated. Reduced capacity can make bookable seats scarcer, driving up prices even more if demand holds.
The carriers said demand has been particularly strong for premium seats, which command hundreds, if not thousands of dollars, more than coach tickets.

Smaller airlines set to report results in the coming weeks, including Frontier Airlines and Allegiant Air, have traditionally focused on more price-sensitive customers, which could show if those travelers are pulling back at all.
One factor that could also affect air travel is the demise of Spirit Airlines, which went out of business in early May.
"Some of its customers have likely stopped flying," Bank of America said in a research note Thursday.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: Carney ‘Disappointed’ by US Envoy’s Election Interference Accusation
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Nojoud Al Mallees

paragraphs.text: Fri, October 23, 2026 at 7:33 AM EDT 2 min read

(Bloomberg) -- Prime Minister Mark Carney says he's disappointed to see the US suggesting that Canada has tried to interfere in its elections, and that his government has been very careful to not even be seen as engaging in such activities.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Speaking to reporters Friday in Istanbul, Carney said there is "no merit" to the claims made by the US Embassy in Canada, which recently published a fact sheet with quotes from federal ministers and premiers that the document said "openly describe plans to influence American politics."

"I'm disappointed that their envoy sees that it's his role to make these suggestions," Carney said, adding that Canada has been "very, very careful to not be seen to" interfere in the US's democratic processes.

"Our global affairs group, well in advance of these fact sheets and allegations, has been reminding everybody: be careful who you are even seen with physically in the same place as, so that such unsubstantiated allegations can be made," the premier said.

Bloomberg reported on Thursday that Canadian diplomats working in the US have been directed to stay away from candidates running in the midterm elections, and to keep a low profile to avoid allegations by the Trump administration of political interference.

Carney said while he didn't want to participate in a tit-for-tat response, he suggested the media can judge for itself "the extent to which very, very senior US officials have directly intervened, so to speak, in Canadian sovereignty, Canadian democratic processes, encourage certain outcomes."

The prime minister said his government continues to engage with the Trump administration and remains ready to sit down and negotiate a trade deal that's in both countries' interests. Asked whether a deal could come before the US midterms, Carney said "it's up to the United States."

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: GM Analysts Say Buy the Dip as Stock Eyes Worst Week Since 2025
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Jordan Fitzgerald and Paul Roman

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- General Motors Co. stock is set to record its worst week in more than 20 months, but bullish Wall Street analysts are doubling down.
Most Read from Bloomberg
The carmaker's stock has fallen 8% through Thursday's close, putting it on pace for the largest weekly drop since January 2025, and analysts are saying investors should buy the dip.

On Tuesday, the company narrowed the top- and bottom-ends of this year's profit guidance range, and its Chief Executive Officer Mary Barra warned that GM faces "clear external headwinds," sending the stock down 6.8% in the worst session since July 2025.
"The bar was high," said StoneX analyst Mickey Legg. "It's a buying opportunity. Most of what spooked the market is timing rather than earnings power."

StoneX's Legg, who has a buy rating on GM, is not alone in his call. None of the analysts tracked by Bloomberg recommend selling the stock after Wells Fargo dropped coverage of the company amid an analyst departure last month. Still, GM shares are down year-to-date, declining 5.1% as the S&P 500 climbed 12%.

Analysts at BNP Paribas, Evercore ISI, and RBC Capital Markets echoed the call to buy the dip after Tuesday's earnings. BNP's James Picariello reiterated his buy-equivalent rating, citing GM's "severely discounted valuation" and unparalleled execution.
When GM last reported earnings in July, quarterly profit beat and management hiked its outlook. Shares rallied over the next few days to touch a record high.
But the stock has retreated since amid lofty oil and high costs, elevated interest rates, and weak consumer sentiment.

"The market has focused excessively on these near-term headwinds while overlooking the company's improving operating performance, margins, and cash generation." said Ivan Feinseth, chief investment officer at Tigress Financial Partners.
