theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/23/ebola-.headline: Mystery over source of Ebola infection in Nigeria fuels concern about spread of virus
theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/23/ebola-.author: Carlos Mureithi

paragraphs.text: Health officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient ⁠in more than a decade ⁠became infected, amid fears the outbreak could spread further after reaching a fourth African country.

The Swiss foreign ministry said on Friday the patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of ⁠Congo, where the outbreak was first detected in mid-May before spreading to Uganda, Kenya and now Nigeria. The woman was believed to have contracted Ebola while travelling with her husband in Uganda, the ministry added.

The new information contradicts accounts from Uganda, which previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo, and will raise concerns about the ability of authorities to contain the outbreak, which is already the most geographically widespread in history.

The Ugandan government reported Ebola cases in May and June before WHO declared it Ebola-free in August. A Ugandan government spokesperson told Reuters on Thursday that Uganda had no Ebola cases and that, if it did, it would make that information public.
The World Health Organization said investigations were continuing to establish the likely source of infection for the Ebola patient in Nigeria.

The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention is investigating whether the patient may have come into contact with an Ebola patient in Kenya, as both travelled from Uganda’s Entebbe airport on 3 October, said Dr Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the organisation.

Catherine Smallwood, a WHO Ebola incident manager in DR Congo, told a UN briefing in Geneva via video link on Friday that WHO staff in DR Congo had no information showing the patient in Nigeria had travelled to the country.

Smallwood said a link to the case in Kenya was possible, but added that officials would need to compare the timing with when the Nigeria patient’s symptoms began to tell whether the infection more likely happened at the Ugandan airport or elsewhere.

Marion Koopmans, a Dutch virologist and member of the WHO’s Ebola emergency committee, cast doubt on the theory. “I think that is very speculative unless there is evidence of sharing the same space in a manner that could explain that,” she said. “Random presence at the same location, a large airport, is not a supported epidemiological link by any standard of what we currently know.”

The Nigerian health minister, Muhammad Ali Pate, said Nigeria’s case remains contained and that contact-tracing was continuing. “We are trying to contain it so it doesn’t go out to the communities. Hopefully, it won’t get to that and we are working hard to ensure that,” Pate said.

Melaku Yirga, vice-president for Africa at Prosper Global (formerly Mercy Corps), said the confirmation of Ebola in Kenya and Nigeria reinforces the need for countries to work closely together to prevent further transmission.
“What matters most now is speed, sharing information across borders without delay and ensuring frontline health workers and local organiaations have the resources to respond quickly,” he said.

Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding.

The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected more than 9,500 people and killed nearly half of them.
The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in DR Congo’s history and second only globally to the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, which infected more than 28,600 people and killed more than 11,000.
Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/23/netany.headline: Netanyahu orders ‘very extensive’ operation in West Bank after two Israeli soldiers killed
theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/23/netany.author: Lorenzo Tondo

paragraphs.text: Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered the army to prepare for a “very extensive” operation in the occupied West Bank after two Israeli soldiers and two Palestinians were killed in an exchange of fire near a checkpoint in Hebron.

Netanyahu said the military would go house to house and demolish homes in an operation on a scale unseen in the occupied West Bank for decades, after the Israeli military said it had thwarted a “terror attack” by two armed Palestinians on Friday, amid heightened tensions before next week’s election.

According to the Israel Defense Forces, the two assailants opened fire on soldiers at a temporary checkpoint outside Hebron after failing to reach a nearby highway, where the Israeli military believes they had intended to attack civilians. According to a preliminary military investigation, the ensuing gunfight lasted more than 20 minutes, leaving five Israelis wounded, two of whom later succumbed to their injuries.
An AFP photographer who was en route to another assignment and witnessed the gun battle saw two Palestinian men armed with a handgun and an automatic rifle exchanging fire with Israeli forces.
Netanyahu’s office later said it had instructed security forces to immediately cordon off Hebron and prepare for a full closure of the West Bank starting on Friday.

After the shooting, the Israeli prime minister held an emergency meeting of his security cabinet and officials from top military and security agencies. He said Hamas was “planning a major attack aimed at murdering innocent civilians”.

During a visit to Hebron after the attack, Netanyahu later said Israeli forces would enter the neighbourhood of the attackers and displace its residents. He said the military would apply a model previously used in refugee camps in the northern West Bank.
A large-scale military operation named the “Iron Wall” launched in January 2025, forcibly displaced tens of thousands of people across several refugee camps, according to the UN rights office.

“We will evacuate the residents, we will go from house to house, we will also seize the weapons there, and all the terrorist infrastructure will be dealt with and destroyed,” Netanyahu said, according to his office.

Closures of the West Bank are becoming more common. Friday’s lockdown was the fourth time in the past month that Israel had imposed restrictions across the territory, shutting gates and checkpoints connecting Palestinian villages to major roads, which will remain open to Israeli drivers, including settlers, who can still travel through the area.

Bezalel Smotrich, the far-right Israeli finance minister who also holds a position within the defence ministry, called for a military campaign in the West Bank “exactly like in Gaza”. He said: “There is no other option but a comprehensive military campaign to dismantle the Palestinian Authority, collect weapons and eliminate terrorists. Exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon.”
Smotrich added: “In the next government this will be one of the first measures that we must demand and apply.”

Human rights groups warned that Netanyahu and his government could use the attack on Israeli soldiers to justify tougher measures against Palestinians and bolster their security credentials before the election.

“Every day in the West Bank is a dramatic day for the Palestinians,” Yariv Oppenheimer, the former director of Peace Now told Al Jazeera. “The Israeli army is getting into the Palestinian cities, the settlers are attacking Palestinians, and the situation is impossible.

“There will be house demolitions. We will see [a] curfew. We will see more soldiers … making arrests, and definitely we might see the settlers trying to target Palestinians in revenge for this attack, and trying to take advantage of this situation in order to escalate the situation even more.”

Voters go to the polls on Tuesday in an election that will help to determine whether Netanyahu secures another term as prime minister. The vote comes three years after the Hamas-led attacks on Israel that triggered the war in Gaza.
Israeli settlers are increasingly taking over Palestinian properties, and authorities have stepped up demolitions of homes lacking building permits, displacing families.

The campaign has intensified since the war in Gaza started in October 2023 amid accelerating land seizures and settlement expansion across the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers, whose violence has surged during the annual olive harvest.

On 16 October settlers attacked Palestinian villages, burning cars and trees and injuring a Washington Post photographer. The next day they attacked European diplomats, a French mayor and Palestinian olive pickers, injuring three people and damaging a diplomatic vehicle.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/23/lab-testing-gi.headline: Lab testing giant Quest Diagnostics confirms patients’ personal and health data was compromised during breach
techcrunch.com/2026/10/23/lab-testing-gi.author: Zack Whittaker

paragraphs.text: Medical lab testing giant Quest Diagnostics has confirmed a cyberattack and data breach affecting an as-yet unspecified amount of sensitive patient information stored in its systems, according to a legally required disclosure with U.S. regulators.

Quest said in an 8-K filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission that it learned of a cyberattack on Wednesday targeting one of its lab testing systems, Quanum, which allows doctor’s offices, hospitals, and healthcare practices to request lab tests for patients while also handling billing. The platform stores a large amount of patient health and medical records, as well as associated diagnostic and billing data.
The company said the unauthorized access included the accessing of “certain patient records.” Quest said it notified law enforcement and is investigating.

The cyberattack on Quest is the latest major cyber incident to affect the healthcare industry this year. A series of cyberattacks and data breaches have sparked weeks of disruption and allowed the theft of millions of patient electronic health records and other medical information. Healthtech companies have become a major target for financially motivated cybercriminals, who aim to steal as much sensitive data as possible and threaten to publish it if they aren’t paid a ransom.

In recent months, a cyberattack resulted in the mass-wiping of employee devices at medical tech maker Stryker in March, and a hack on medical implant manufacturer Boston Scientific in August forced the company’s network offline for weeks, sparking “global disruption” to its operations. Meanwhile, separate hacks throughout the year caused massive breaches of patient data at medical recordkeeping company CareCloud, Scotland-based healthtech provider Craneware, and U.S. pharmaceutical distribution giant McKesson.

Quest did not say when the breach began or whether any hacking group has contacted the company with demands, such as payment in exchange to not release the stolen data. A spokesperson for Quest did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment on Friday.
The lab-testing giant has not yet said how many healthcare customers, or patients, had information stolen during the attack on its Quanum systems.

Quest’s website and materials say Quanum is used by about half a million clinicians in thousands of locations across North America. It’s unclear how many health records Quanum holds, but one 2026 case study on Quest’s website shows how a single health system with more than 6 million patients can hold hundreds of millions of related medical documents and charts.

In a note on its website, Quest said that some patients’ protected health information was taken, including “personal information and patient records,” but the company is still investigating what specific kinds of data were taken. (The website post currently contains “noindex” code, which tells search engines not to list the page in search results, making it far more difficult for people to find the page.)
This is Quest’s second known major data breach in a decade, after losing 11.9 million patient records in a cyberattack on a third-party billing company in 2019.

nytimes.com/2026/10/23/technology/person.headline: Review of iPhone Duo: A New Chapter That Redefines a Smartphone’s Purpose

paragraphs.text: Whenever I take a plane to go on vacation, I have a renewed appreciation for my iPad. Its roomy, bright screen makes movies, books and comics look great.
But then I return home, where I rely on a laptop and a phone. The iPad goes in a drawer. Only occasionally, like when I’m taking public transportation, do I wish I had my tablet to read a book.

How often you find yourself in that situation — yearning for a tablet when it is impractical to carry one — should be the central question you ask when considering whether Apple’s $2,000 iPhone Duo, which the company released on Friday as its first two-in-one, foldable tablet phone, is worth your money.

Because that’s the whole point of it. The Duo is a miniature tablet that can be folded up into a phone that fits in your pocket so you can carry it everywhere. To that end, what’s most important to evaluate about the Duo is its usefulness as a tablet. Everything else, including the camera, is secondary.

If having a tablet everywhere is not important for you, stop reading this review and continue enjoying your old-school, rectangular phone. You have plenty of time to think about it anyway. In a sign that this is the iPhone of our K-shaped economy, people eager to have every shiny new Apple thing bought all the iPhone Duos minutes after online orders opened last week. Any orders placed on Friday are estimated to ship in 2027.
I had a day to test an iPhone Duo before its release, so I mostly used it the way I use a tablet — for watching movies, reading books and doing some lightweight work.

My verdict is that commuters and business travelers who spend a lot of time on trains, buses and planes will probably like the Duo, as will avid book readers and people who watch lots of TV. Everyone else may feel frustrated with what is otherwise a funky, so-so smartphone.
Here’s what to know.
The Pros and Cons of the Duo
The Duo’s name refers to two devices. Closed up, it has a 5.4-inch outer screen for people to use as a normal smartphone. It opens up to reveal a 7.6-inch inner screen to become a tablet.

Every foldable phone released in the last eight years has had compromises, and the Duo is no exception. Its 5.4-inch phone screen looks like a cute, dainty device resembling a passport. But when used, it feels thick and stubby, which makes it cumbersome to operate with one hand. While trying to type a text message with one hand, I could not reach some letters with my thumb.

The Duo’s camera also lacks a so-called telephoto lens, which means it cannot zoom in as much as Apple’s other expensive iPhone, the $1,200 iPhone 18 Pro. (This is not a deal breaker because photos taken with the Duo’s camera looked quite good.) More annoyingly, the Duo doesn’t have a face scanner for unlocking the device, relying on a fingerprint sensor embedded in a button on the side of the phone, and it takes longer to unlock.
So the question comes down to how often you would use the Duo as a tablet to forgive the trade-offs, because the device begins to shine when it is opened up to take advantage of its bigger screen.

For watching movies, reviewing photos, reading books and writing emails, the Duo excelled. As an owner of many iPads of different sizes over the years, I found the Duo to be the most versatile and interesting tablet I’ve used.
Watching Videos

As soon as I set up the Duo, I fired up the Amazon Prime Video app to stream some movies and shows. Some videos looked better than others. “The Expanse,” for example, was shot in an aspect ratio that took up most of the Duo’s screen and looked nice. But movies in widescreen, like Christopher Nolan’s “Memento,” showed thick black bars, detracting from the viewing experience.
Still, the screen felt roomy enough to satisfyingly stream videos, which I rarely feel compelled to do on my normal iPhone.
When I got tired of holding the tablet, I simply folded it 90 degrees and set it down as if it were a miniature laptop to continue watching hands-free.
Reviewing Photos

I opened the Photos app on the Duo to scroll through the thousands of photos I had taken of my family, including Homer, a golden retriever, and Max, a corgi. Having grown accustomed to reviewing photos on a phone, I had forgotten how much better they look on a larger screen. I realized I hadn’t noticed details captured in past photos, like a chip on Homer’s tooth.
Reading Books

E-books, which are no fun to read on a tiny phone screen, were a delight to consume on the Duo. Even better were comic books. Graphic novels produced in color looked crisp and vibrant, and the screen’s matted texture reduced glare from ambient light.
While my book reader of choice is still a Kindle, I’d consider a Duo if I wanted to get into the habit of reading more often, because it would become a book reader that I carried with me everywhere.
Getting Work Done

Tablets for years have not been conducive to productivity, but are great for lightweight tasks like email. Apple’s Mail app made good use of the Duo’s software interface. With the Duo folded shut, the small outer screen showed a simple list of emails. With the Duo unfolded into tablet mode, the app adapted to list the emails on the left side and show their contents on the right side.

The biggest plus to productivity is the ease of typing on the larger screen. As a tablet, the Duo is thin and compact enough to easily compose emails and Slack messages with two thumbs, which was very difficult to do with larger iPads.
Bottom Line

Many tech reviewers have dunked on the iPhone Duo’s smaller screen because it diminished the experience of using the device as a normal smartphone. But when the Duo arrives to customers, I expect people will prefer to unfold it for use primarily as a tablet.

This is a new beast and should be treated as such. It may not be as fun to mindlessly scroll through TikTok using one hand with the Duo, but perhaps that means you will end up opening it up to consume deeper content, which would be a win.

While the Duo probably isn’t for me (a person who commutes on a motorcycle and tries to minimize screen time), I’ve been sold on the concept of foldables after testing many in the last few years because they help us get larger screens without adding much bulk.

I’m quite fond of my rectangular iPhone, but wish it were thinner and more compact in my pocket, which would mean it would have to fold up into a tiny square. That feels like the inevitable next step for the quintessential phone.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/articles/us-co.headline: US Consumer Sentiment Slips to Five-Month Low on Inflation Woes
finance.yahoo.com/economy/articles/us-co.author: Maria Paula Mijares Torres and Jeffrey Sparshott

paragraphs.text: Maria Paula Mijares Torres and Jeffrey Sparshott
Fri, October 23, 2026 at 9:00 AM CDT 2 min read
(Bloomberg) -- US consumer sentiment edged down to a five-month low in October as high prices and rising interest rates depressed morale.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The University of Michigan's final sentiment index eased to 48 from 48.1 in September, according to the survey released Friday. Even so, that was an improvement from the preliminary reading and topped all estimates in a Bloomberg survey of economists.

Consumers expect prices to rise 4.7% over the next year, up from 4.6% in the previous month. They also saw costs climbing at an annual rate of 3.5% over the next five to 10 years. Both were the highest since May.

"After five years of above-target inflation, both short- and long-term inflation expectations have ticked up in recent months, exposing risks that elevated inflation expectations could become entrenched," Joanne Hsu, director of the survey, said in a statement.

Consumer sentiment continued to deteriorate in October amid persistent inflation, tepid hiring and elevated mortgage rates. Prices at the pump remain well above $4 a gallon, compounding longstanding frustrations with the cost of living.
In recent months, price increases have outpaced pay gains, further pressuring household budgets. Data out last week showed consumer prices rose in September at the fastest pace in five months.
Economic issues like the cost of living remain front and center for Americans in the final stretch of midterm campaigns.
"Consumers of all political persuasions agree that inflation is overwhelmingly the greater risk to the economy in the year ahead than unemployment," Hsu said.
Sentiment among Democrats and Republicans improved somewhat in October, while sentiment among independents fell for a third straight month.

A gauge of buying conditions for durable goods fell to a record low in October, with the report citing higher interest rates and rising affordability concerns. Nearly 70% of consumers expect interest rates to rise in the year ahead, the highest in more than three years.
The current conditions gauge sank to the second lowest on record, while an index of consumer expectations improved for the first time since July.
The survey period includes responses from Sept. 22 to Oct. 19.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: Amex to Cut 5% of Headcount Globally as Cost Pressures Mount
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Paige Smith and Romaine Bostick

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- American Express Co. is cutting 5% of its headcount globally as Chief Executive Officer Steve Squeri seeks to keep a lid on the company's rising costs.
Most Read from Bloomberg
Squeri told Bloomberg TV that the company has 78,000 employees, meaning the move will affect about 3,500 jobs.

Financial firms have been cutting jobs in recent months, with some companies attributing the changes to the increased use of artificial intelligence. This week, Barclays Plc said it would eliminate 5,000 jobs. HSBC Holdings Plc is planning job reductions across its UK wealth-management business, Bloomberg News reported earlier this month, and Citigroup Inc. has also been lowering its headcount.
Squeri said on a call with analysts Friday that the job cuts reflect the desire to make the company more agile and efficient, and find ways to reduce layers and speed up decision making.

The company has also been facing consistent pressure to keep and retain its premium card members. To do that, Amex has been refreshing certain cards, adding a raft of new perks last year to its Platinum card. Earlier this month, the company said it would work with Airbnb Inc. to allow for certain luxury rentals on its travel site to count for the cardholders' annual lodging credit.
Overall, that's boosted costs. The New York-based firm said expenses climbed about 9% to $14.5 billion in the third quarter, although it was less than the $14.8 billion estimate from analysts.

Costs for member rewards were up 10% in the quarter, while marketing expenses rose 11%. Chief Financial Officer Christophe Le Caillec had previously said to expect marketing expenses to increase by around 10% in the second half of 2026 compared with last year.
"It's been highly competitive," Squeri said about the fight for premium cardholders on the call. "And our assumption is that it will remain highly competitive."
Amex shares were down 1.8% to $319.45 at 9:35 a.m. in New York trading Friday, extending this year's drop to nearly 14%.

The workforce cuts were announced after Amex posted third-quarter earnings that beat estimates, with adjusted earnings per share of $4.68 surpassing the $4.49 average analyst estimate in a Bloomberg survey.

The company also raised its full-year earnings guidance, saying it expects earnings per share of $18.30 to $18.60 in 2026, according to a statement Friday. Previously, the figure was expected to be $17.30 to $17.90.

But billed business — a measure of transactions on credit cards and other products — came in at $454 billion in the third quarter, shy of the $456.9 billion average estimate in a Bloomberg survey. The company said it had exited some small-business co-brand deals, which affected results.
That slower growth in billed business is likely a slight disappointment, according to Truist Securities analysts including Brian Foran.
"The headline is good — Amex beats on earnings and raises full year guidance," the analysts said in a note to clients. "The details are more mixed."

The company's results were also affected by the sale of Amex's equity interest in in Global Business Travel Group Inc., which resulted in a $751 million after-tax gain. Amex used a portion of the gain to fund a $253 million after-tax restructuring charge tied to efficiency initiatives. The gain, net of the restructuring, is excluded from the adjusted results.
"Our business momentum continues, with strength in billings, new acquisitions and card member retention, and excellent credit quality," Squeri said in the statement.

The company is also facing a $350 million fine due to anti-money-laundering violations. The US Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Reserve brought enforcement actions against Amex earlier this month, alleging deficiencies in the firm's anti-money-laundering systems.
Amex said at the time that the penalty won't affect the full-year 2026 guidance it previously issued or any 2027 outlook, and the orders don't impose an asset cap on the firm.
(Updates with cost details starting in fourth paragraph, shares in ninth.)

finance.yahoo.com/economy/articles/us-bu.headline: US Business Activity Expands, Prices Surge by Most Since 2022
finance.yahoo.com/economy/articles/us-bu.author: Jeffrey Sparshott

paragraphs.text: Fri, October 23, 2026 at 8:45 AM CDT 2 min read
(Bloomberg) -- US business activity grew at a slightly slower pace in October but remained close to a multi-year high as robust demand pushed new orders, employment and prices higher.
Most Read from Bloomberg
The S&P Global flash composite index fell 0.8 point to 57.6 in October, data released Friday showed. That was the second-highest reading since 2022. Figures above 50 indicate expansion.
A gauge of selling prices rose at the fastest pace in more than four years, reflecting a sharp rise in the cost of energy, transportation and raw materials.

"Cost pressures remain a key concern, notably as the renewed surge in oil prices reverberates through to impact a wide variety of goods and services," Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said in a statement.
Bottlenecks are also getting worse. Supplier delivery times lengthened the most since 2022, with S&P Global citing material and labor shortages as well as overloaded suppliers and shipping delays.
Even so, Williamson said that, outside the pandemic reopening, US businesses are enjoying their strongest period of growth since 2015.

Strong consumer spending, AI-fueled investment and defense outlays have all bolstered US businesses this year. New orders, a gauge of demand, posted the fastest growth in four-and-a-half years in October.

Firms are responding by adding more workers. The composite index for employment was the second-highest in four years, and the manufacturing index showed factory headcount advancing at the fastest pace since 2012.

Looking ahead, investment in artificial intelligence and related technologies is anticipated to support demand and the broader economy next year, too. Forecasters raised their estimates for private investment growth in the third quarter and across all of 2027 in the latest Bloomberg News survey of economists.
The group's overall manufacturing index inched up to 56, the strongest since May 2022, while a gauge of activity at service providers eased.
--With assistance from Julia Fanzeres, Dana Morgan and Aidan Williams.

cnbc.com/2026/10/23/php-vulnerabilities-.headline: AI's 'Black October': Critical PHP flaws set off global security scramble
cnbc.com/2026/10/23/php-vulnerabilities-.author: Ashley Capoot

paragraphs.text: Cybersecurity teams around the globe are rushing to patch PHP programming language flaws this week, in an artificial intelligence safety moment that's being described as "Black October."
Nearly 70% of all websites use PHP, according to some estimates.

"In the last 2 days there have been several dozen cyber attacks which, in isolation, would each have been the worst to happen in an entire calendar year," John Milinovich, senior director of product management at Figma, wrote in a post on X on Thursday. "Every sector from government to education to big tech and banks is being massively affected, and people are starting to freak out."

Researchers at Google's Wiz and the AI firm Calif discovered major vulnerabilities in PHP in August by using advanced AI models from OpenAI and Google. But by Tuesday, the warnings had spread online, prompting governments and businesses around the globe to scramble to contain the fallout.

Major AI companies have been warning about the technology's advancing cybersecurity capabilities since April, when Anthropic announced a limited rollout of its powerful model called Mythos. Concerns mounted in July, when OpenAI disclosed that two of its models escaped containment, accessed the open internet and breached a company called Hugging Face.
Experts believe the PHP security flaws serve as the latest example of what's to come.
Jason Clinton, deputy chief information security officer at Anthropic, wrote in a post on X on Thursday that the cybersecurity landscape is likely to get "a lot worse" before it gets better.
"Security leaders, never let a crisis go to waste: please go to your boards and ask for help right now," Clinton said. "Not for ai, for the basics. (we need to hold on for ~18 months.)"

While many large companies have access to advanced models that they can use to harden their systems, serious bugs could be more challenging for small- and medium-sized businesses to address, Chris Krebs, former director of the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, told CNBC on Friday. He encouraged smaller companies to "constantly" scan for vulnerabilities, deploy patches as fast as possible or take legacy systems offline.
"This is a significant week or two in cybersecurity," Krebs told CNBC's "Squawk Box." "As I mentioned, 3% of all critical vulnerabilities ever discovered have been found in the last month."

Figma's Milinovich encouraged individuals to set up two-factor authentication for "everything," use a password manager, set up an identity protection app and move smart devices to their own network. He added that people should lean in and experiment with AI to understand how powerful the tools have become.

"While I still firmly believe that AI will be a net positive for humanity, it's more clear to me than ever that the societal and individual risk is very real, and is playing out NOW," Milinovich said.
Krebs added that company leaders and employees should check in on their security teams.
"Make sure they're doing okay," he said. "They've had a heck of a week."
—CNBC's Isabel O’Brien contributed to this report

latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-22/.headline: Man forced way into Arcadia home, killed teenage girl, police say
latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-22/.author: Iris Kwok, Richard Winton

paragraphs.text: Authorities said a teenage girl was killed after a man she was dating forced his way into a residence in Arcadia and shot her. The man then fled and attempted to take his own life in a shooting in Pasadena, officials said.
A witness told The Times there were multiple people who saw the Pasadena shooting, which took place on a sidewalk in broad daylight.
On Thursday around 11 a.m., Arcadia police responded to a call about a possible shooting in the 800 block of West Huntington Drive. The caller said a man was inside the residence and had fired a gun.
Officers arrived to find a girl with a gunshot wound, according to a statement Thursday afternoon from Arcadia police. She was pronounced dead at the scene.
“We heard a woman screaming,” Daisy Valdez told KTLA. “We heard her asking for an ambulance. It sounded like it was a mom for sure.”

By the time officers arrived, the man, identified by the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department as 20-year-old Paul Anthony Cruz Jr., had fled the scene, according to the statement. Arcadia police did not share the victim’s name.
The case remains under investigation and is being handled by the Sheriff’s Department Homicide Division, according to Arcadia police.
Authorities believe the man fled to Pasadena, where he attempted to take his own life about an hour later.
The Sheriff’s Department said Cruz was in a dating relationship with the victim. He had “forced entry” into the Arcadia location, according to the department.
Pasadena city spokesperson Lisa Derderian said the man was found with a self-inflicted gunshot wound in the city on Thursday about 12:30 p.m. and was transported to a hospital in critical condition.
Auto shop workers across the street from the incident told KABC that they heard a gunshot, then saw police handcuffing a man outside.

“We look out the window, there’s this guy, he’s laying face down on the floor. A couple seconds later, police officers show up and they close off the area,” said Michael Amini, manager at Alliance Auto Body Works, told the station.
The Sheriff’s Department said he shot himself as Pasadena Police Department officers were preparing to contact him. He remained in critical condition as of about 7 p.m.
Amini told The Times the neighborhood was “pretty busy” at the time of the shooting, and there were several other witnesses.
The suspect, who was being pursued by police, parked his car in the Petco parking lot, walked over to the sidewalk and pulled out the gun, Amini said.
After the shooting, Amini said, he saw the man lying face down. Police arrived about “five seconds” later, he said.
“It was really fast,” Amini said.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: Private Fund Valuations, AI Risks to Be Focus of SEC Examiners
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Nicola M White

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Securities and Exchange Commission examiners will step up scrutiny of private fund valuations and artificial intelligence, the latest sign of regulatory concerns about emerging market risk.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Investment advisers, brokers, clearing agencies and others can expect staffers at the Wall Street watchdog to focus on fees, expenses and valuations in private funds, according to the agency's Division of Examinations priorities released Friday. The agency also plans to zoom in on how firms prepare for AI-related cyberattacks.

The focus on private fund valuations and credit comes as the SEC considers expanding retail investor access to private markets, including private equity and early-stage startups that have been historically off-limits to the general public.

At the same time, private credit managers have faced a wave of redemption requests as anxious investors try to cash out. Examiners will spend time on what the SEC calls retail investor protection, particularly for complex, higher-risk, and illiquid products, the agency said.

Although artificial intelligence has been listed as a priority for examiners in previous years, the SEC went into further details this year to reflect rapid changes in technology, including cybersecurity.
Examiners will focus on how AI-fueled attacks may affect firms' businesses or customers, such as through phishing messages and deepfake voice and video used for social engineering.

The SEC publishes its examinations priorities every year to signal how it aims to promote compliance, identify fraud, and monitor risks. Exam staffers sometimes escalate findings to the agency's enforcement division for further investigation.
The staff also examines so-called self-regulatory organizations, such as the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, the regulator for broker-dealers.

"Examinations are one of the Commission's most important tools for promoting compliance with the federal securities laws and helping protect investors," SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins said in a statement.

This year, the examinations staff added the US audit regulator, the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board, to its list of examination targets. Queries could include whether the board, which regulates auditors, would include whether the organization is is following its own policies and procedures.
The report also included a new section about how the SEC is coordinating with fellow Wall Street regulator, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which oversees the derivatives market.

Some firms operate in both the commodity futures market and the equity options markets and are subject to exams from the two agencies. Both regulators have said they want to coordinate examination planning to figure out opportunities for joint or aligned reviews.

finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.headline: Blackstone Bet on Chips Drove a Debt Boom That’s Upending Credit
finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Paula Seligson and Dina Bass

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- "What is a GPU?" Blackstone Inc. executives asked CoreWeave Inc.'s leadership. Also: "Is AI real?"
Most Read from Bloomberg

These were entirely logical queries in the early innings of the AI boom, and at a time when CoreWeave was still a little-known AI cloud company on the hunt for funds to buy chips. Blackstone's tactical opportunities group was convinced by the answers it received, and led a $2.3 billion private credit loan in 2023.

This marked the first major deal of its kind and became a blueprint for chip-backed debt that, three years on, is on track to become a trillion-dollar market, eclipsing even the borrowings used to build the data centers housing the chips.

It's a testament to how intertwined the global AI expansion and credit markets have become in such a short time. Just this week, Blackstone President Jon Gray called demand for AI almost "parabolic." But CoreWeave is also emblematic of the anxiety around the money being poured into the space — its stock and corporate bonds have been battered in recent weeks as investors question whether AI revenues can ever justify the breathtaking spend.

The market's projected growth has drawn in virtually every major US bank and alternative-asset manager, along with backstops from AI chipmakers Broadcom Inc. and Nvidia Corp., which have a combined value of roughly $7 trillion.

Broadcom is working with Wall Street firms on a $60 billion debt transaction for a special entity that would buy chips known as tensor processing units and lease them to Anthropic PBC. Meanwhile, SpaceX is in talks to raise $40 billion for Nvidia chips. That follows Nvidia's announcement of a $500 billion partnership with six major lenders to help customers purchase its graphics processing units, or GPUs.

The scale of the spending risks leaving debt markets dependent upon AI's profitability. The deluge also threatens to drive up borrowing costs for AI and other sectors as tech firms compete for finite capital amid rising interest rates. JPMorgan Chase & Co. analysts predict chip spending could exceed $3 trillion through 2030, with the majority likely funded by borrowing.

"You have vendor financing being done at a scale that we've never seen before, and being done in a way that the risk is concentrated," said Jason Pompeii, a senior director at Fitch Ratings. "That just increases the chance that if AI ends up being a disappointing story, there will be ripple effects throughout the supply chain."
The strategy rests on the conviction that demand for computing power will outstrip supply for years to come.

"These financings are attached to the thing of most value in the market, which is the compute capacity produced by the chips," said Rich Myers, global head of structured products and private capital markets at Morgan Stanley. "There's a lot of evidence that demand for compute will continue to go up and is outpacing supply of compute."
Yet there are risks to the build-out's continued momentum.

Local opposition has sparked a data center moratorium on new projects in Texas, while Oracle Corp. has taken steps to put off payments on a New Mexico project mired in regulatory setbacks. Meanwhile, OpenAI and Anthropic are discussing a slower rollout over safety and existential concerns following a spate of incidents.

But much of the spending is already locked into mega data centers under construction, ensuring chip demand as those sites come online. With vendors largely sold out and severe memory shortages driving costs up, companies that make servers containing Nvidia's AI chips informed customers in August that prices will rise by more than 15% in many cases.
"This is a new part of the economy that needs to have an orderly mechanism to finance it," said John Watson, a senior managing director at Blackstone in the firm's tactical opportunities group.
For Watson, there's a parallel to the early, uncertain days of the automotive industry and Ford's mass-market Model T car.

"If you were financing the Ford Model T, you would have asked, 'What am I doing? Are people really going to drive cars?'" he said. "The automotive finance market is robust and well understood and is enormous in scale. It became the most bought machine in America. We have a similar vision for compute."
Fueling these capital needs is the reality that chips cost two to four times more than the data centers housing them, yet depreciate over about five to six years.

At AI cloud provider Nscale's flagship development in West Virginia, for example, the on-site power plant is expected to cost $6.5 billion and the data center and equipment another $18 billion. The GPUs: $47 billion.

Investment-grade cloud giants Alphabet Inc.'s Google, Microsoft Corp., Amazon.com Inc. and Meta Platforms Inc. cover these hardware costs largely through cash or cheap on-balance-sheet bond sales. But OpenAI and Anthropic, burning through billions, lack those reserves and debt market clout. The same is true of neoclouds, companies focused on offering cloud computing for AI.

"The infrastructure build-out is unprecedented," said Mike Liberatore, business finance officer at OpenAI. "There's no playbook that shows you how you go from zero to AGI and raise money through traditional means, given it's a very capital-intensive business," he said, referring to artificial general intelligence.

Consequently, the industry has adapted mechanisms from project and structured finance. By creating special purpose vehicles to ring-fence each deal, issuers raise debt based on a transaction's merits and the quality of the customer, often keeping it off corporate balance sheets.

The SPV is what borrows money to buy and own the chips. The debt is backed by the cash flow from the intended customer, which covers interest payments and fully pays down the debt over time, and the value of the chips themselves.
By aligning the debt's maturity with the chips' expected five-to-six-year depreciation schedule, lenders insulate themselves from risks that the hardware loses value.

Two primary versions have emerged: deals where customers rent chips from an SPV to plug into their own technology stacks, and transactions where neoclouds sell computing capacity to customers and use debt to help pay for buying the chips to build out this service.

Broadcom and Nvidia are taking this a step further by offering to backstop multibillion-dollar deals, promising to support lenders if something goes wrong. This aligns the debt's credit rating with the chipmaker's investment-grade status, reducing the SPV's borrowing costs.

A representative for Broadcom declined to comment and a representative for Nvidia didn't have a comment. Their executives have previously said they consider risks around the funding structure to be limited.
An investment-grade rating is vital to tapping the largest pools of capital — particularly insurance money.

The scale of digital infrastructure financing exceeds what traditional public debt markets can supply, demanding involvement from markets such as project finance, private placements, insurance and commercial real estate, said Apollo Global Management Inc.'s global head of origination Chris Edson.

"We have been focused on high-grade opportunities where risks are mitigated through collateral security, amortization, little to no residual risk or renewal risk, diversification and high-grade off-takers," he said.

Junk-rated CoreWeave, which has made no secret of its desire to become investment grade, was founded in 2017 as a crypto miner before leveraging its GPU experience to quickly pivot to selling AI processing power. Microsoft became CoreWeave's largest customer as the tech giant sought access to additional GPUs to support its partner OpenAI.

To pay for the chips, CoreWeave's founders drew on past experience in commodities. They adapted a model from markets like liquefied natural gas, where customers sign contracts first, then developers use those agreements to secure debt to build facilities.
That first 2023 debt deal was backed by contracts with Microsoft, and CoreWeave had to pay up to borrow at a rate in the mid-teens.
"It was the most challenging diligence I've ever done in my life," recounted CoreWeave co-founder Brannin McBee, who also described the questions Blackstone had asked the company.

As CoreWeave signed subsequent customers, it shifted from private credit deals to cheaper bank facilities. CoreWeave's first taste of investment grade came in March, when it raised an $8.5 billion debt package backed by Meta contracts. Wall Street viewed the risk in line with Meta's high credit rating rather than CoreWeave's junk grade, slicing borrowing costs to roughly 6%.

Others have followed the CoreWeave playbook. Last year, when Elon Musk's xAI needed Nvidia chips to stock its Colossus 2 data center, it raised money through an SPV that included an equity investment led by Valor Equity Partners. Apollo provided nearly $11 billion of debt for the transaction.

Apollo and Blackstone recently did a $35 billion debt deal called Big Sky to support Anthropic. This was the first transaction of a platform between Broadcom, Apollo and Blackstone called AI XPV that could finance 20 gigawatts of capacity — which Bank of America Corp. strategists estimate may require $235 billion of backstopped debt by mid-2029.

A special financing entity was created to raise the debt to buy the chips, which Anthropic would lease. Broadcom provided a backstop, meaning if Anthropic defaults, the chips are re-leased or sold to repay the remaining debt, with the chipmaker covering any shortfall.

This support led to an investment-grade rating for the vehicle's two Broadcom-backed senior tranches. The largest of these pieces pays a 5.75% interest rate — cheaper than Anthropic could get as an unrated, private company — while the riskier $4.5 billion junior tranche priced at 8.5%.
"The sector can have many risks, but some financing structures mitigate those risks more than others," said Ross McAdam, head of alternative debt at L&G — Asset Management, America.

In August, Nvidia assembled a powerhouse coalition of Apollo, Blackstone, BlackRock Inc., Brookfield Asset Management, KKR & Co. and Goldman Sachs Group Inc. to source financing for AI infrastructure, of which it would backstop up to 25% of an opportunity.
Broadcom has held early discussions to arrange financing to help OpenAI purchase custom chips that the pair is developing together, Bloomberg reported this month.

To reach true scale, though, the industry needs to transition from private markets into syndicated debt — where banks arrange bonds and loans to sell and trade among institutional investors. Earlier this year, CoreWeave became the first to enter the syndicated markets with chip deals: two leveraged loans that met solid investor demand.
But the ultimate goal is for these SPV structures to break into the much larger investment-grade bond market — one of the world's deepest, cheapest pools of capital.

CoreWeave's corporate-level junk bonds have taken a hit recently, with some sliding to around 80 cents on the dollar and pushing yields to roughly 15% as investors worry about the company's expanding debt. However, the market views its two chip-backed leveraged loans as separate. Both dipped slightly but still trade near par.

In a statement to Bloomberg following the selloff, CoreWeave Chief Executive Officer Mike Intrator said building a new type of technology company means there are moments where the market has to work through questions about AI adoption.

"That scrutiny is important, but what's also important is to recognize that companies have different technologies, customer commitments, financing structures and records of execution," he said. "We're confident in our business model, our technology, the quality of our execution, and the relentless discipline behind our financial engine."

As capital floods in, lenders are confronting risks. Because most chip deals are private transactions, investors have no easy way to sell their positions in debt deals that have bound a small number of chipmakers, cloud computing giants and neocloud firms together. This creates heavy exposure to a small group of interconnected players.

"The big are going to get bigger," said Dave Snyderman, managing partner and global head of alternative credit and fixed income at Magnetar. "The incumbents are likely going to win because they're the only ones who are going to have access to capital."

Another risk for lenders is how airtight the customer contracts really are. Document protections may prove less ironclad in practice — as they have in riskier credit markets. If AI returns disappoint, tech firms could use their clout to force lenders and neocloud firms into renegotiating deals or leases.

Everyone is assuming these contracts are tight and unbreakable, but "I look at the practical element," said Akhil Bansal, head of asset-backed finance at Carlyle Group Inc. "If you have seven firms that are basically providing all the credit support for the GPUs, who's got the leverage?"

The complexity is keeping some investors on the sidelines. "This is a novel structure," said Laura Parrott, head of private fixed income at Nuveen. "We haven't seen how that plays out if there is some sort of disruption," she said, adding that she's holding off on lending to big investment-grade-rated chip deals until the market develops more.

As the chip market evolves, so too will the mechanisms used to finance the hardware. Early research and real-world usage so far are showing the chips are lasting longer than current accounting treatment suggests, which would make them easier to finance.

The equivalent of the Kelley Blue Book for new and used cars could emerge for semiconductors, enabling chip trading and hedging to develop, said Karen Fang, global head of infrastructure and sustainable finance, and co-head of the global capital solutions teams, at Bank of America.
"When we get to a point where we have enough data history and track record on the chips, then you're going to start seeing a much more robust leasing market," she said.
And raising chip debt could get simpler for OpenAI and Anthropic once they do go public, especially if they can win investment-grade ratings and put together deals on their own.

The ultimate endgame for Nvidia, Blackstone and their Wall Street peers is to turn a unit of computing power into an asset class, where people globally can "finance compute because we understand the economic value of the compute," Blackstone's Watson said.
--With assistance from Carmen Arroyo, Ian King and Sophie Butcher.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/23/what-some-of-a.headline: What some of Anthropic’s backers are reportedly worth before its IPO
techcrunch.com/2026/10/23/what-some-of-a.author: Marina Temkin

paragraphs.text: Anthropic’s public listing, which is expected this year at a valuation of as much as $2 trillion, is bound to be a windfall for both early-stage and later-stage investors. But even at the company’s latest private market valuation of $965 billion, the stakes held by many of those VCs and early backers already total billions. Here is what some backers in the leading AI lab are worth at that last round’s price, according to Bloomberg.

Eric Schmidt: The former Google CEO invested in Anthropic’s Series A in 2021, when the startup was valued at $461 million, according to PitchBook data. Today, Schmidt owns about 1% of the company, and even at its current private valuation, his stake is worth nearly $10 billion.

Iconiq: The investment outfit wrote a $6 billion check to Anthropic last year when the company was already valued at $183 billion. That massive late-stage bet is now worth $17 billion and has the potential to double at the IPO.
Menlo Ventures: The VC firm led Anthropic’s Series D and has invested more than $1 billion in the company over time, a stake now worth $14 billion.

Sequoia: The famed VC firm backed the AI lab for the first time only earlier this year, when the company was already valued at $380 billion. The $3 billion investment gave it about 1% ownership, which means it has already more than doubled its investment.

Sound Ventures: The firm, launched by Guy Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher, invested $35 million in its 2023 Series C round and has since funneled an additional $400 million into Anthropic, resulting in a stake that’s worth billions now. (Kutcher left Sound Ventures this year to launch a new VC firm.)

Spark Capital: The only VC firm known to hold a board seat at Anthropic invested $75 million in that same 2023 Series C round, when it was valued at $5 billion. That position has ballooned more than 90-fold to $7 billion.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6rey3n974g5o.headline: Oil spill washes up on UAE beaches after tanker strike
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6rey3n974g5o.author: Thomas Copeland, Mark Poynting and Tom Spencer

paragraphs.text: An oil spill from a tanker attacked near the Strait of Hormuz is spreading along the United Arab Emirates (UAE) coastline, forcing the closure of some beaches and coastal areas.

Satellite images from Monday show the beginnings of the oil spill from a ship matching the location and dimensions of Gem No.2, which was damaged between 9 and 10 October during a record surge of vessel strikes by Iran.
The slick of oil had spread more than 35km (22 miles) from the tanker by Wednesday, the satellite imagery showed.
UAE authorities said on Thursday that the incident is affecting beaches near the northern city of Umm Al Quwain and verified video from Friday shows the oil washing ashore, colouring the water black.
The UAE's Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Thursday that it "immediately began containment" in order to "limit environmental impacts".

Prof Steve Widdicombe, director of Sharjah Marine Science Research Centre in the UAE, told BBC Verify it was "inevitable that there will be an impact", but researchers caution it is too soon to assess extent of the damage.
Initially a much smaller oil leak could be seen emerging from the ship on 19 October.
But the slick appears to have rapidly spread over two days, according to radar satellite imagery reviewed by BBC Verify and intelligence firm MAIAR.
Oil spills can cause immediate deaths of marine animals and other organisms, for example by physically trapping turtles, smothering the feathers of seabirds or damaging the gills of fish.
They can also cause longer-lasting damage, Prof Widdicombe said, if species remain exposed to toxic compounds from the oil which could impact their ability to reproduce.

Researchers have cautioned the environmental impact at this stage is very uncertain, as it depends on factors including the volume and type of oil spilled, how quickly it evaporates or breaks down and the effectiveness of the clean-up operation.

But the spill does extend towards Siniyah and Khor Al Beidah islands, a globally recognised Key Biodiversity Area containing habitats like corals, seagrasses and saltmarshes, as well as species including green turtles and the critically endangered Halavi guitarfish.
The proximity of the spill to this area is the "most concerning environmental angle", according to Eoghan Darbyshire, a scientist at the Conflict and Environment Observatory.
Tanker hit 14 days ago
BBC Verify analysis of the dimensions and location of the ship indicate they match a crude oil tanker called Gem No.2.

Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard reported the Panama-flagged tanker was "struck by an unknown projectile" on 9 October, just north of the town of Al Jazeera Al Hamra, causing a fire on board that was later extinguished.
Verified footage first posted on social media on 10 October showed the crew running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rose over the ship.
Iranian state media shared footage of a ship matching Gem No.2 which appeared to show the vessel on fire with burning oil spilling into the sea.
The ship had been attempting to exit the Strait of Hormuz via an "unauthorized and dangerous route", according to state media.
All 22 Indian crew members were rescued, the Indian consulate in Dubai said on 11 October.
Gem No.2 is one of a record number of ships that reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz at the start of October.

Security experts told BBC Verify this was part of an Iranian effort to assert greater control over the strait, in response to the US military successfully escorting more vessels through the vital shipping lane.
Tankers and other commercial vessels have come under attack from both Iranian and US forces in and around the Strait of Hormuz amid the conflict between the two countries.
Another major oil slick washed up on the shores of Iran's Qeshm Island in August, which experts said threatened wildlife, protected ecosystems and fishing communities.
Additional reporting by Charlotte Green

cnbc.com/2026/10/23/tiktok-us-compute-ca.headline: TikTok U.S. hunts for multiple gigawatts of computing capacity, sources tell CNBC
cnbc.com/2026/10/23/tiktok-us-compute-ca.author: Kai Nicol-Schwarz

paragraphs.text: TikTok's U.S. entity is looking to secure multiple gigawatts of computing capacity, sources told CNBC, amid a global scramble for digital infrastructure deals.

The company, officially TikTok USDS Joint Venture, operates the social media platform in the U.S. and has sounded out opportunities to obtain capacity over the coming years, two people familiar with the discussions, who asked to remain anonymous as they weren't authorized to share the information, told CNBC.
TikTok U.S. is looking for four gigawatts of compute power by the early 2030s, one source said.
Companies across the world are looking to secure more compute capacity as artificial intelligence workloads become more prominent.
A company spokesperson told CNBC that the company "runs primarily on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure in the U.S. and Oracle will continue to be our primary cloud infrastructure provider."
Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, or OCI, typically runs in facilities that Oracle leases. CNBC has approached Oracle for comment.
There are signs TikTok U.S.' product plans could require extra compute going forward.

The company has numerous machine learning roles live on its website. A job advert posted by TikTok states that the company is "shipping a flagship B2B AI product at the frontier of large-model inference and creative automation."
TikTok U.S. localizes algorithm training

TikTok USDS Joint Venture was established in 2026 in compliance with U.S. President Donald Trump's executive order mandating the divestiture of TikTok in the U.S. from its Chinese parent company, ByteDance.

In January, TikTok U.S. said it would "retrain, test, and update" its prized recommendation algorithm, which is built on machine learning, on U.S. user data. The company's recommendation algorithm will be "secured in Oracle's U.S. cloud environment," it said.

TikTok U.S. has three managing investors, Silver Lake, Oracle and MGX, each holding 15%. The Dell Family Office, the investment firm of Michael Dell, is also an investor. ByteDance retained 19.9% of the new entity.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck87zlpzny15o.headline: Seven shot dead by gunmen at church funeral in Jordan, government says
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck87zlpzny15o.author: Jaroslav Lukiv

paragraphs.text: Six people were killed when gunmen opened fire on a funeral in central Jordan, a government spokesperson has said.
Another 28 people were injured in the church in the village of Hmoud, in the Karak governorate on Friday.

The unidentified gunmen are reported to have arrived in a car, entered the church and opened fire before fleeing, in what government spokesperson Dr al-Momani Mohammad described as a "heinous attack".
Jordan's King Abdullah II said the authorities would "confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties."
Dozens of people had been inside the church for the funeral when the shooting began, Khaled Burqan, one of the mourners, told Jordan's al-Mamlaka state-run TV.
He said two attackers armed with a rifle and a pistol had been firing at the mourners for several minutes.
CCTV footage, verified by the BBC, appears to shows three gunmen making their way from a road toward the church.

Two of the attackers are seen making their way onto what appears to be a vehicle entrance to the church grounds, before retreating briefly and returning with a third man. All three appear to be armed with handguns.
Separate footage believed to be from the aftermath of the attack appears to show several dead and wounded bodies on the ground amid some chaotic scenes.
No-one has so far claimed responsibility for the attack.
A news briefing by interior ministry officials is expected shortly, and al-Momani has said the country's prime minister will chair a meeting of the Security Council to be attended by all ministers.

In his post on X, King Abdullah II offered his condolences to the families of the victims, writing: "Whoever imagines that the bullets of treachery can divide the ranks of Jordanians will fail in his endeavour before our steadfastness and unity."

Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun, a Christian head of state, said the "heinous terrorist attack" on the church "violated the sanctity of death and funeral mourners, contradicts all religious and humanitarian values," according to Lebanese media.
Karak has a sizeable Christian community in the majority-Muslim Jordan.
Such violence is rare in Jordan, but deadly attacks have been carried out in the country in the past.

nytimes.com/2026/10/23/business/energy-e.headline: Why Anger About Data Centers and Energy Prices May Not Swing Votes

paragraphs.text: Electricity costs around 50 percent more in Ohio than it did six years ago. Gas station fill-ups have gone up even more. And where corn and soybeans once grew, banks of computers now sift through data in hulking gray warehouses that glow against the night sky.

The pressures of soaring energy costs and the data center boom have handed Democrats a unique opportunity to make inroads in a state that Republicans have dominated for many years. But persuading voters to connect those issues to races for U.S. Senate and governor has proved difficult.

In more than two dozen interviews with The New York Times, Ohio residents described data centers as threats to their communities and expressed frustration with higher fuel and electricity bills. But few said they had been convinced to cross party lines — or show up to the polls if they usually did not.

Becky Loel, a retired secretary, expects high gasoline and diesel prices to be fleeting. Doyle Bross, a horse trainer with an easy laugh, considers the Republican Party part of his identity. Todd Leonard recently swapped his diesel truck for a gasoline model, and he waited over an hour at a community meeting this month to testify against a data center that had been proposed for a farm near his home.
But Mr. Leonard, a 45-year-old general contractor, has not voted recently and didn’t plan to in November. “It just doesn’t directly impact me,” he said of the midterm elections.

That voting habits are so sticky partly reflects the power of party affiliation and inertia about the act of voting, even at a time of broad discontent with the economy and President Trump’s handling of it.

It also suggests that the data center backlash, which is so fierce that more than a dozen Ohio communities will vote on measures to restrict the facilities locally, is not consistently swaying statewide races, even as Democratic candidates like Sherrod Brown have made it central to their campaigns. Mr. Brown, a former senator, is seeking to beat Senator Jon Husted, a Republican.

Just 3 percent of likely Ohio voters said data centers and artificial intelligence were the most important issue in determining their vote for Congress, according to a recent New York Times/Siena poll. Concerns such as the cost of living and foreign policy were more important.

Ohio also has an open governor’s race, in which Amy Acton is trying to become the first Democrat to win since 2006, running against Vivek Ramaswamy, a Republican. But even though the governor has far more influence than Congress over state policies on energy and data centers, those issues have featured less prominently in that race.

“We have local communities in full-on revolt over data centers,” said David Niven, a political science professor at the University of Cincinnati. “It hasn’t necessarily translated one to one to the rest of state politics, though.”

There are, of course, those who care deeply about stemming the spread of computing facilities, which have grown ninefold in Ohio since 2020 and played a part in rising electricity costs. The Columbus area has turned into the country’s second-fastest-growing data center market, according to Cleanview, a research firm.

Sue Barton, an 87-year-old retired real estate agent, counts herself among them. A Republican who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, Ms. Barton went door to door this summer collecting signatures for a charter amendment that would ban large data centers in her village of Granville, a dozen miles from the state’s biggest cluster of data centers.

But as of late October, other issues were top of mind as Ms. Barton considered statewide races. Mr. Brown had served in the Senate for too long, she thought. She was willing to give Mr. Husted the benefit of the doubt on data centers despite his support for tax breaks for those facilities when he was Ohio’s lieutenant governor, a position he left in 2025.
“When all this started happening, the public did not know and I don’t know that he knew how bad it really was going to be,” Ms. Barton said.

However, she was leaning toward voting for Dr. Acton for governor after Mr. Ramaswamy’s campaign released an attack ad featuring his opponent’s estranged mother. It was, she said, “just beyond what people should do.”

A week earlier, Mike Bellish was driving through his community farther south, where a data center developer had planned to build on a longtime farm. Mr. Bellish, a 63-year-old information technology manager, is a registered Republican who generally voted for Democrats in recent years. But he was unsatisfied by what he had heard from all of the candidates.
“No data centers near neighborhoods,” he said, describing what he wished politicians would commit to. Plus, Mr. Bellish said, tech companies “should be paying for their electrical needs.”

The candidates for Senate and governor have expressed support for those broad principles but refrained from making concrete commitments. They appear to not want to seem too supportive of data centers or oppose them so adamantly as to forgo their potential economic benefits.
Mr. Husted has said that data centers “should only be located where communities want them,” and Mr. Brown said that Ohioans “should get to decide if data centers are built in their community.”
Dr. Acton has backed a conditional moratorium on new data centers, which she said “must” be built on previously developed sites, often called brownfields.
“If data centers can’t follow our strict protocols, they cannot do business in our state,” her campaign said in a statement.
Mr. Ramaswamy said he would “emphasize” brownfields for new data centers and seek to provide free electricity for those living nearby.

“A year from now, if we’re still talking about data centers in Ohio as a problem, then that means I will have failed my job,” said Mr. Ramaswamy, the only one of the four to do an interview with The Times for this article.
Translating broad promises into effective policy will be anything but straightforward.

Electricity prices are lagging, meaning today’s bills reflect regulatory decisions made years ago and recent commodity prices. The same is true of data centers, which typically take several years to permit and build. Even if the next governor and legislature move quickly to change policy, the results may not become evident to voters before the next election. What’s more, Ohio is part of a regional grid and wholesale electricity market known as PJM, which effectively determines a big portion of monthly electric bills.
“You could have data centers in Virginia increasing costs for customers in Ohio,” said Ryan Hledik, a principal at the Brattle Group, a Boston research firm.
Voters are also contending with much more expensive gasoline and diesel.

Ms. Loel, the retired secretary, has been helping some of her grandchildren with gas money, and she left her family’s diesel truck behind on a recent trip to the county fair, taking their gas-powered Honda Pilot instead.

But she said high fuel costs were not a major factor in her voting decisions because she doubted they would last. The 76-year-old registered Republican was leaning toward voting for Mr. Ramaswamy and Mr. Husted.
She did have a request for Mr. Husted, though: “Stop the data centers from coming in.”
Mr. Bross, the horse trainer, planned to vote the same way. “I haven’t voted for a Democrat for a long time,” the 72-year-old said.

A big question for Democrats in the final stretch is whether their efforts to tie Republicans to data centers will sway enough people who are concerned about the issue, said Christopher Nichols, a history professor at Ohio State University. For Republicans, the question is whether they have tacked enough to the center to satisfy voters.
“They aren’t in a position to win on data centers,” Mr. Nichols said of Mr. Husted and Mr. Ramaswamy. “But they are in a position to lose.”
The recent Times/Siena poll found that 48 percent of likely Ohio voters thought Mr. Brown would do a better job on data centers, compared with 38 percent for Mr. Husted.
With less than two weeks until Election Day, Mr. Bellish, the I.T. manager, said he was gravitating toward Mr. Brown and Dr. Acton.
“I feel like Husted has brought in a lot of these data centers. It just seems out of control,” Mr. Bellish said. As for Mr. Ramaswamy, he added, “It doesn’t seem like he would put a throttle on it.”

techcrunch.com/2026/10/23/agent-cloud-st.headline: Agent cloud startup Daytona hits $1B valuation backed by FirstMark and a who’s who of angels
techcrunch.com/2026/10/23/agent-cloud-st.author: Julie Bort

paragraphs.text: Daytona Platforms announced on Friday that it had raised a $60 million Series B round at a $1 billion valuation led by FirstMark Growth. The company says it has now raised a total of $91 million.

The New York-based startup has attracted not just FirstMark (which also led its $24 million Series A in February), but a host of well-known angels in this latest round. Daytona says they include Stripe’s Patrick Collison, Shopify’s Tobi Lütke, Perplexity’s Aravind Srinivas, Zoom’s Eric Yuan, Datadog’s Olivier Pomel, Quora’s Adam D’Angelo (who is also an OpenAI board member), and Mercor’s Brendan Foody. It also names Qualcomm Ventures, Samsung Next, and Okta Ventures as participants.

Three-year-old Daytona is building a cloud specifically for long-running agents, which have different infrastructure needs than yesteryear’s software, the startup contends. “Agents don’t work like the long-lived services today’s cloud was designed for. They spin up thousands of short, stateful jobs nobody planned in advance, and they need a cloud built for that,” founder Ivan Burazin wrote in a blog post announcing the new round. Daytona’s cloud, he said, is like giving every agent its own computer, where agents have access to sandboxed versions of Linux, Windows, macOS, and GPUs, among other services, on the one platform.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/23/commonwealth-f.headline: Commonwealth Fusion Systems gets $85M to build better fusion-ready semiconductors
techcrunch.com/2026/10/23/commonwealth-f.author: Tim De Chant

paragraphs.text: Commonwealth Fusion Systems (CFS) announced on Thursday that it would receive $85 million from the U.S. government to develop advanced chips for the fusion power industry.

Fusion power startups have been racing to complete their first demonstration devices, with CFS aiming to turn on its Sparc reactor sometime next year. But building one reactor is just a proof point. If fusion startups want to build dozens of commercial power plants, they’ll need more durable power electronics and a robust supply chain.

The new CHIPS Act award from the Department of Commerce, which also grants the government a stake in CFS, will help boost R&D and manufacturing capacity for semiconductors in the U.S., the company said.
“Ultimately, that means a more capable, economical power plant and a stronger U.S. supply chain to build it,” Brandon Sorbom, co-founder and chief science officer at CFS, wrote in a blog post.
CFS’s award will go toward supporting five different initiatives.

The first is the advancement of silicon carbide power electronics. The semiconductors are widely used to manage high voltages, and they’re found in everything from LEDs and EVs to cell phone base stations and data centers. It’s also used in fusion machines, where intense bursts of electricity are used to drive the superconducting magnets that confine plasma inside a reactor.

CFS will also use the award to develop next-generation radio-frequency power generators, which the company uses to heat fusion fuel, and advanced electronics that will enable faster control of the reactor and be hardened against radiation. The latter could help extend the lifespan of electronics within a fusion power plant, reducing operating costs.
Lastly, CFS plans to use part of the CHIPS award to adapt AI hardware like GPUs and TPUs for power plants.
“The funding would help improve the U.S. chip and power electronics industries at the same time it accelerates fusion energy’s progress toward the electrical grid,” Sorbom said.

Tim De Chant is a senior climate reporter at TechCrunch. He has written for a wide range of publications, including Wired magazine, the Chicago Tribune, Ars Technica, The Wire China, and NOVA Next, where he was founding editor.

De Chant is also a lecturer in MIT’s Graduate Program in Science Writing, and he was awarded a Knight Science Journalism Fellowship at MIT in 2018, during which time he studied climate technologies and explored new business models for journalism.
