nytimes.com/2026/10/23/us/alaska-senate-.headline: Why Legal Experts See the Justice Dept.’s Alaska Election Challenge as Dubious

paragraphs.text: The Trump administration has filed a lawsuit pre-emptively challenging the certification of Alaska’s Senate election if the Republican candidate narrowly loses. But election law specialists said the litigation lacked any legitimate legal basis.

“It is one of the weakest election lawsuits I’ve ever seen,” said Richard H. Pildes, a New York University law professor who specializes in election issues. “It should have no realistic chance of success in the courts.”

Nevertheless, the lawsuit raised alarms as President Trump has sought to undermine confidence in the election when polls indicate that Republicans are likely to suffer sweeping losses, with control of Congress hanging in the balance. Mr. Trump tried to overturn his loss of the 2020 election, culminating in the Jan. 6, 2021, riot.

Neither the Justice Department nor the associate attorney general, Stanley E. Woodward Jr., who signed the lawsuit with an assistant U.S. attorney based in Anchorage, responded to a request for comment.
Here is a closer look.
What is the lawsuit about?
Voter confusion.

The litigation centers on an oddity in the four-candidate ballot. The incumbent Republican senator, Dan Sullivan, is being challenged not only by the Democrats’ nominee, former Representative Mary Peltola, but also by a novice candidate with almost the same name: Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.

Voters could mistakenly vote for the other Mr. Sullivan instead of the senator. The lawsuit seeks a judicial order blocking the state from certifying the results if Senator Sullivan loses to Ms. Peltola, but would have won had he received votes cast for the other Mr. Sullivan.
Is that outcome likely?
It is possible: Polls suggest that Ms. Peltola is narrowly ahead of Senator Sullivan, with the other Mr. Sullivan pulling single-digit support.
However, Senator Sullivan could still receive votes mistakenly cast for the other Mr. Sullivan because Alaska uses a ranked-choice system.

Under that system, people can rank multiple candidates in order of preference. Votes are tabulated in rounds. Each round, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated and those votes are reassigned to the voters’ next choice until one candidate has a majority. So if a confused voter picks both Sullivans but puts the “wrong” one first, the senator likely still will end up with that vote.
What does the lawsuit say should happen?
The lawsuit calls for an investigation, though it does not explain how one would work.

It asks the court to order “an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan and any further procedures or relief this court deems necessary and appropriate to determine what the result would have been absent Daniel J. Sullivan’s inclusion on the ballot.”
Does the Justice Department have legal standing?
None that is obvious, specialists said.

The Constitution empowers states to administer congressional elections unless Congress enacts a statute to alter such rules. Citing the National Voter Registration Act, the lawsuit claimed the department can sue to force the state to fulfill a duty it claims the act imposes on state officials to “protect the integrity of the electoral process.”

But the lawsuit takes that vague phrase out of context. It is part of the act’s preamble, which explains the law’s purpose but does not itself carry any affirmative legal force. And nothing in the act governs the kind of ballot access and certification issues at play in the dispute over the two Sullivans.

“It’s the worst complaint I’ve ever seen,” said Richard L. Hasen, a law professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, who specializes in election issues. “No federal statute gives D.O.J. the right to sue over these things. The Constitution doesn’t give it standing, either.”
Did Alaska state courts already address the issue?
Yes.

Carol Beecher, the director of the state’s Division of Elections, initially rejected the other Mr. Sullivan’s application to run for the Senate seat, finding that he was not a good-faith candidate and was trying to confuse or mislead voters. But Mr. Sullivan sued, and a trial court held in June that he could be on the ballot. The Alaska Supreme Court affirmed that ruling.
Has Alaska taken steps to reduce confusion?

The Division of Elections has listed Senator Sullivan is on the ballot as Dan S. Sullivan and identified him as the incumbent officeholder and as a “registered Republican.” The ballot identifies the other candidate as “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” and does not list any party registration.

“It’s not a great situation, but the division of elections did an admirable job trying to minimize voter confusion,” Derek T. Muller, a University of Notre Dame law professor who specializes in election issues, said in an interview.
Why is the lawsuit being filed now?

The lawsuit seems too late — the ballot is already finalized. It also seems premature — the election has not happened yet. Either way, election law specialists said, its legal basis is so thin that it appeared to be more about messaging.

“It’s a press-release litigation,” Professor Muller said. “It is litigation that suggests the Department of Justice is fighting for a Republican senator who is facing a confusion campaign, frankly, from another candidate who entered in this race. But it’s left to the political process at this point. There is just not much for the legal process to do at this stage.”

Professor Hasen said one reason for filing before the election could be that courts have rejected legal challenges brought after elections over issues that could have been raised before them. This could therefore be a “place-holder lawsuit or zombie lawsuit” intended to come back to life after the election if Senator Sullivan loses narrowly — except even then, he said, such a challenge would be for the senator to bring in state court, not for the Justice Department to bring in federal court.

latimes.com/sports/story/2026-10-23/brit.headline: Britt McHenry resigns from State Dept. after incident at Wizards game
latimes.com/sports/story/2026-10-23/brit.author: Chuck Schilken

paragraphs.text: Former ESPN reporter and Fox News personality Britt McHenry is no longer a press advisor for the U.S. Department of State, multiple media outlets are reporting. The development comes after viral videos appeared to show her throwing a drink at someone (after one was thrown at her) during an altercation in the stands at an NBA game.

Page Six reported Friday that McHenry was “forced to resign” on Thursday, the day after the alleged incident at the Washington Wizards’ home opener against the Milwaukee Bucks at Capital One Arena. McHenry then told Front Office Sports that she signed a resignation letter.
The State Department told both publications that it does not comment on internal personnel matters.

The incident reportedly started after a group sitting behind McHenry started shouting insults toward Bucks forward Kyle Kuzma about his fiancée, Winnie Harlow. McHenry is said to have spoken up in Harlow’s defense.

Video footage posted by TMZ appears to start a bit later. It shows McHenry talking to a male companion and an usher from her seat while fans seated around her can be heard making negative comments about her, with some chanting, “Kick her out!”

As McHenry and her companion eventually start to leave on their own, a clear liquid can be seen hitting or coming close to hitting her on the back of the head. She responds by throwing a drink in that person’s direction. As she makes her way up the stairs in the aisle, McHenry is seen giving the middle finger and blowing kisses to the crowd as some people heckle and throw towels at her.
Later in one of the videos, McHenry appears to argue with a security worker near at one of the venue’s entrances. As he gestures toward the exit, she appears stunned and asks, “What did I do?”

McHenry worked at ESPN from 2014 to 2017. In 2015, she was suspended for a week after a video surfaced of her yelling at and belittling a towing company employee. McHenry later apologized for the incident.
She announced her State Department job on social media last month.

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/.headline: Thunderstorms, heavy rain and flash flooding predicted for much of Australia
theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/.author: Adeshola Ore

paragraphs.text: Severe thunderstorms and heavy rain will sweep across most Australian states this weekend, adding to the deluge in an already drenched Queensland.

Flash flooding in south-east Queensland this week prompted hundreds of SES callouts and the closure of multiple schools. On Saturday morning, the Bureau of Meteorology had nine flood warnings in place for south Queensland.
The BoM is now warning of severe thunderstorms, heavy rain and flash flooding across South Australia, Victoria, NSW, Tasmania.

Senior meteorologist at the Bureau of Meteorology, David Crock, said severe thunderstorms and heavy rain were forecast across multiple locations in central and eastern Queensland on Saturday, including Rockhampton, Gladstone, Bundaberg, the Sunshine Coast hinterlands and Roma.

Severe storms could also sweep through parts of Victoria, including Melbourne’s eastern suburbs and central and eastern South Australia. Heavy rain is expected to develop in Tasmania overnight into Sunday morning.
“There’s plenty of rain across the south-east, as well as plenty of showers and storms and rain across much of Queensland as well, after what’s already been a really wet week,” Crock said.
The cold front will move across NSW on Sunday, bringing severe thunderstorms to the west of the state as well as north-eastern Victoria, Sydney and Brisbane.
“Tomorrow is a threat for thunderstorms right across eastern Australia, with severe thunderstorms likely through a wide part of inland eastern Australia,” he said.
This week, multiple areas in Queensland were hit by more than twice their average October rainfall across a few days.
“It was an incredibly wet week in Queensland. Much more typical of summer or January or February than this time of year,” Crock said.
The Sunshine Coast hinterlands and Caboolture were hit by flash flooding and recorded a seven-day rainfall total of 300-400mm of rain, with some areas reaching 450mm.

“It’s been notable how persistent this weather pattern has been, how much moisture has pumped in … then how those rainfall totals have accumulated across seven to 10 days through Queensland and northern New South Wales,” Crock said.
On Thursday, torrential rain in south-east Queensland caused flash flooding, water rescues and hundreds of calls for help while several schools were forced to close on Friday.
Thursday’s heavy rain stretched from Caboolture down to the Border Ranges, with some places copping well over 200mm falls.
The Queensland fire department carried out more than 16 swift-water rescues, including using a raft to retrieve an elderly man clinging to the roof of his vehicle at Caboolture.

astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-th.headline: Your Book Review: The Ghost In My Brain
astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-th.author: Scott Alexander

paragraphs.text: [This is one of the finalists in the 2026 book review contest, written by an ACX reader who will remain anonymous until after voting is done. I’ll be posting about one of these a week for several months. When you’ve read them all, I’ll ask you to vote for a favorite, so remember which ones you liked]
In 1999, Professor Clark Elliott is rear-ended by a stranger at a stoplight. He’s shaken but figures he’s fine, and drives to work. Spoiler: Clark Elliott is not fine.

Elliott is severely concussed, and this fact will dictate the next ten years of his life. Elliott’s memoir is based on notes he took while concussed. Reading it is like watching someone try to troubleshoot their broken laptop using the broken laptop.
In the opening chapter, Elliott describes walking from his office to his car after a long winter workday:

“At this point my world had collapsed inward on itself… I looked down at my feet and shouted at myself to walk, but I knew it was hopeless. I had lost the mysterious initiative that impels us all forward when we walk, and I knew that without brain rest I wouldn’t be getting it back. I considered lying down in the snow.”
Over an hour later, Elliott finally manages to cross the parking lot and begins the second phase of his trial: getting into the car.

“I’d lost the concept of center. I had no internal representation, or visual understanding of circle, target, middle, inside. Without these concepts I couldn’t get my hand to move toward the lock, or put the key in the slot.” So he just stands next to the door for another hour and a half.

Around 2 a.m., a suspicious police officer asks why Elliott is loitering in the parking lot, but the officer is too cold to get out of his car and drives away. At 3:30 a.m., four and a half hours after he left his office, Elliott finally arrives home.
Somehow, Elliott lives like this for a decade.

The book’s first mystery is how a person can remain conscious, verbal, employed, and yet so damaged that he can’t get into a car or recognize his own house. The second mystery is: why did he apparently recover through treatments that sound, at first pass, like boutique neuro-quackery?

A disclosure is in order before we continue. I am pretty personally invested in the answers here. About a year and a half ago, I got seriously concussed. Milder than Elliott’s, but bad enough to substantially rearrange my life. On some level, I read this book in hope of a cheap fix, or at least an obvious one. Instead I found myself in the weird borderlands of modern medicine.
A hurricane let loose on 50 million desktop computers
What’s it like to be a human with severe brain damage? Elliott offers a metaphor:

To simulate concussion damage to a human brain then, we’ll need to gather together […] 50 million desktop computers, a 500,000-mile-high stack of paper, and the almost inconceivable amount of information it takes to construct a human mind, then loose a hurricane on the system, ripping out network lines, laying waste to vast sections of memory, and sending landslides to smash hundreds of thousands of computers.

A bit sensational, but you get the picture. One classic model of what’s happening during severe concussions is “diffuse axonal injury”: rapid acceleration and deceleration stretch axons, the neuron projections that send electrical signals, causing micro-tears and disrupting cellular metabolism.

Standard CT and MRI imaging usually fail to detect these microscopic or functional disruptions, and there isn’t really a cure, so patients are told to go home, rest up, and wait to find out whether they’ll be back to work the next day or out of commission for the next decade.

U.S. concussion incidence is commonly cited around 1.6-3.8 million a year, and many go unreported1 . About 15-30% of adults report post-concussion symptoms (PCS) 3-6 months later. Even on conservative estimates, that’s hundreds of thousands of cases a year in the US alone. A much smaller number of those cases will result in something like Elliott’s experience.

After the initial fender-bender, Elliott hands his driver’s license to the other driver. Then, a few minutes later, he hands it over again. He has no memory of having done so the first time, and can’t figure out why people are looking at him funny. This is a recurring theme—Elliott can’t even notice the problem, because the cognition that’s supposed to monitor the behavior has gone offline.

He writes: “when cognitive capabilities go missing they are often so fully gone that the concussive does not miss them in the way a normal person would, or indeed sometimes even realize they’ve gone absent.”

But Clark Elliott is no pushover. He’s a Professor of Artificial Intelligence at DePaul University, a consummate musician, is single-handedly renovating his family home, and runs marathons on the side. The biographical lists serve a purpose: Elliott wants to assure the reader that he hasn’t become less intelligent. His cognitive capacities have just come apart in a way that doesn’t track any nameable cognitive disorder.

He can write, but he cannot read. He can climb stairs but not descend them. He can teach a graduate seminar and then, walking home afterward, fail to recognize his own house. Moving through doorways or down halls poses a significant challenge.

More than once, he describes his state as “alien.” He writes, “we still walk and talk and act as though we are part of the human race, but it doesn’t feel that way inside… Instead, there is a strange feeling of nostalgia, a longing for who we used to be.” He notes that this feeling of disconnection is likely a significant contributor to the rate of suicide among concussives2 : “we have, in many ways, already lost that which makes us human.”

One of the most striking passages in the book is when Elliott, hungry, decides to make himself a snack. He heads to the kitchen to eat a piece of salami and an apple, but finds he can’t. As though trapped in an old Tom and Jerry cartoon, he finds himself literally unable to choose which of the two to eat first. He can’t initiate action selection. He goes to the living room, returns to the kitchen, fails again. He repeats this loop ten times, like “a rat repeatedly traversing a dead-end maze.” Two days pass before he eats.

Elliott calls this “getting stuck.” The bridge between knowing what he wants to do and doing it has broken. In desperation, he finally calls his bemused friend Jake, who tells him: “Okay, go eat the salami first, then eat the apple,” ending the forty-eight hours of struggle.
Somehow, he cobbles together enough coping mechanisms to keep limping along for years. Until he can’t anymore.
Partial death

“This is it,” Elliott reflected. “I am never going to have another normal day, or hour, or ten-minute period again. I am never going to be a real human being again. I won’t be publishing my research, and at some point I am going to lose my job.”

Ten years after the crash, Elliott is approaching a complete breakdown. Or rather, while broken, he adds a small child to the equation. As it turns out, the normal prattle of his two-year-old daughter is concussion kryptonite:

“It was this simple combination—my inability to filter out or process spoken dialogue in real time, and Erin’s continual need to talk—that almost led to a final, catastrophic meltdown.” He calls it “partial death.”
Unfortunately, there are no parenting sabbaticals. In a last-ditch effort, Elliott pulls out his emergency savings and reaches out to a “cognitive restructuring specialist” named Donalee Markus.
Wait a minute, you might be thinking. Elliott hasn’t seen a specialist before??

He has, sort of. It didn’t help. A brief detour through medical history: Elliott hit his head in 1999. The CDC didn’t publish its first major report on mild traumatic brain injury (TBI) until 2003. The NFL concussion crisis broke into public awareness in 2005. Until 2013, the only mention of persistent post-concussive symptoms in the DSM-IV was in the appendix under “proposed criteria set”. After the crash, an ER doctor checks his pupils and sends him home; a neurologist runs a 30-minute test and declares him fine, and shouts at him when he pushes back.

It’s unclear whether Elliott was just unlucky in encountering a cast of extremely unsympathetic medical professionals, or whether this was really the general state of neurology in the 90s. Whatever the case, Elliott quickly writes the whole system off and goes back to calling his friend Jake whenever he gets stuck in doorways.
The Miracle Begins
For ten years, Elliott can’t make himself a sandwich. Then, over the course of a year, he substantially recovers. Enter idiosyncratic concussion specialists Donalee Markus and Deborah Zelinsky.
This is the first time we have a third-person perspective on Elliott. Markus writes:

“Clark Elliott was a mystery to me when we first met. Observing him through my glass front door, I saw that it took him two minutes just to find the doorknob with his hand. When I gave him the simplest of my assessment tests—copying a geometric line drawing—his body went into bizarre contortions as he struggled to complete it.” Markus takes him on as a patient anyway.

Her intervention is simple: she gives him geometric puzzles to solve, specifically trapezoids and three-dimensional dot exercises that escalate in complexity. He has to apply rules to shapes, generate equations from them, and eventually do the whole thing in his head.
(Source): Elliot includes a bunch of these geometric puzzle examples in the book. Sadly, they didn’t alleviate my symptoms.
Markus also refers Elliott to her colleague Deborah Zelinsky, a neuro-optometrist.
Bells and Prisms

Zelinsky’s diagnostic method is a little more involved. The patient closes their eyes, and the examiner rings a small bell at various positions in space. The patient must reach out to touch the bell. The patient will often fail this test, revealing a “visual-auditory mismatch.” Zelinsky will then try different prism lens combinations while the patient’s eyes are closed and ask them to do the bell test again. I repeat, the patient’s eyes remain fully closed. The entire time. She then prescribes the lenses that improve the patient’s performance.

This is called the Z-bell test (presumably after “Zelinsky,” who has a patent on it). While I wasn’t particularly surprised that adjusting someone’s vision when their eyes are open can change how accurately they localize sound when their eyes are closed, I remain deeply confused about how prism lenses could alter accuracy if the patient’s eyes remain closed the entire time.
The claim is that low-level light still passes through the closed eyelids, stimulates retinal activity, and that this stimulation is what’s being modulated by the different lenses.
Zelinsky’s Mind-Eye Institute website:

“By placing various types of lenses across a patient’s closed eyes, we can change the way light spreads over the retina, thus modifying the dynamic relationship between the mind’s visual inputs and the body’s internal responses.”

Depending on wavelength, eyelids transmit somewhere from well under 1% of blue/green light to around 5–6% of red light. But, as anyone with eyelids knows, this is still mostly diffuse reddish illumination—not sufficient to update your visual field, or to localize a bell.

But within a year of meeting Markus and Zelinsky, Elliott has experienced massive improvements and is on the road to recovery. He writes a heartfelt note to Markus thanking her for “giving him his life back.” So I guess the treatments worked?
Into the uncanny valley of concussion science

Let’s take a look at the evidence, starting with Markus. Markus belongs to a fairly large tradition of “cognitive training interventions” for PCS for which there’s some evidence. A 2016 meta-analysis looking at 14 studies on cognitive training in post-acute TBI found a small effect on overall improvement in cognitive function (Hallock et al., 2016).

Unfortunately, “cognitive rehabilitation” is an enormous umbrella and Markus’s specific protocol isn’t in the meta-analysis. Markus published her own protocol in 2007, describing the puzzle-based technique she used on Elliott, but it’s more of a “how I do it” piece, not a controlled trial. The trail of scientific evidence dries up there.
Okay, what about Zelinsky? Do the bells work? There’s a 2019 paper that tried to find out. First author: Clark Elliott.

The paper is a preliminary conference paper on 14 out of the 41 recruited participants. Elliott et al. find that the therapeutic lenses produced a small but statistically significant improvement in bell-touching accuracy compared to the clear-lens baseline. However, the therapeutic lenses didn’t outperform an ‘impaired lens’ condition, which was theorized to push the outcome in the opposite direction, and the full study with all 41 recruited participants has never been published.
This is pretty tepid evidence. With one preliminary, ambiguous analysis its only empirical bulwark against the wave of scientific skepticism, Zelinsky’s method isn’t looking too good.

That said, the testimonial evidence is abundant. “I can move normally again, be active, travel. Mind-Eye has opened up a whole new chapter in my life,” says an avid patient. One testimonial describes the treatment as “like, well, ‘magic,’” while another patient calls it “mathemagical.”

We can add Clark Elliott to the rave reviewers. Within ten days of his first prism glasses, he reports a strange shift. Music sounds different, and he starts re-accessing visual scenes from childhood.

Within a month, Elliott begins to feel like himself again. The “ghost of his true self” had reentered the room. “At last I had enough brain power to support the real me, the complex me. I could see the world through my own eyes again.”

The strongest within-book evidence that the glasses, in particular, are doing causal work comes from what happens when Elliott briefly loses them. Even 33 hours without his prescription produces dramatic regression: exhaustion, handwriting deterioration, visual disturbances, and the return of the “all tasks involve pain in some way” baseline of his pre-recovery life. Once he finds the glasses, he’s back to playing the Beatles from memory and “looking forward to the rest of [his life] again.”

Elliott is writing the book fifteen years after the accident, and the recovery has held. He even claims, with the partial qualification one expects from a man who has nearly lost his mind to a brain injury, that his cognition is in some ways now better than it was before the crash.

A skeptical explanation might be that Elliott was desperate and ripe for placebo effect. Receiving intense attention from clinicians who believed they could help him after years of failed encounters with doctors might have been sufficient to shift his symptoms. Elliott’s recovery was staged over five years with iterative adjustments, which is exactly the protocol that would maintain a placebo effect, and the base rate of spontaneous recovery in chronic PCS is non-zero. So can we be sure that any of these treatments did anything other than give him a pat on the back as the concussion worked itself out?

I think a case can be made for at least some real intervention. While the evidence for Zelinsky’s closed-eye method in particular is thin, the general “prescribe new lenses” approach looks much more promising. There’s even a reasonable causal mechanism on offer.

If you hold up your thumb in front of your face, and then easily switch between looking at something on the wall and your thumb, congrats - your accommodation triad is working. The accommodation triad is the trio of ocular functions that enable close-up vision. In many PCS patients, this system goes awry, resulting in a suite of vision complications. In a study of adolescent patients (n=116), Wiecek et al (2021) found that ~60% of patients had deficits in near point of convergence after concussion. Prism lenses can reduce eye strain by shifting the image on the retina so the eyes don’t have to work as hard to converge, and magnifying lenses reduce accommodation demand.

A year into my concussion, and partially inspired by Elliott, I asked my neuro-opthalmologist for prism lenses. They didn’t help at all. But the magnifying lenses I tried next totally did, almost entirely eliminating my symptoms immediately (unfortunately, they later returned).
It’s possible that Zelinsky’s method actually does work, but not for the reason she thinks. The bell ceremony might just be an unusually elaborate way to arrive at a genuinely useful prescription.

This would explain both her rave reviews and the lack of scientific support. Her Z-bell tinkering isn’t doing much, but the broader lens intervention sometimes works—some percent of the time, prism glasses and magnifying lenses actually do improve people’s concussion symptoms. (Of course, this will result in a hit-or-miss treatment, but you can’t tell because none of the duds post a review).
When averages fail
So what, if anything, can we learn from Elliott’s recovery?

Here’s one obvious point: recovery is possible, but strangely elusive. It took Elliott a decade, several awful medical encounters, and two boutique specialists to find help. While the situation was worse in the 90s, it’s still bad today. In one study, among patients severe enough to reach specialty care, fewer than a third had recovered when surveyed, and the still-symptomatic group had been living with PCS for an average of 4.5 years (Hiploylee et al., 2017).
Perhaps the real mystery is: why is it so hard to treat concussions?

One reason is that concussions resist mainstream medical intervention. Clinical instruments can’t catch the microscopic damage common to PCS, and randomized controlled trials (RCTs) struggle to identify treatments when the population is heterogeneous and the symptoms are varied and subjective. So it takes months to get a PCS diagnosis, and even when you do, many clinicians have no idea what to do with you.

PCS treatment is hard because concussion does not damage an abstract, average brain. It damages your brain, with your particular foibles and weak spots. Specialist concussion medicine has identified roughly six clinical phenotypes, but even when correctly type-cast, each patient responds differently. Clark Elliott and I both had vision issues, but he responded to prisms while magnifying lenses worked for me. PCS may be less like a single disease than a family resemblance category with wildly different failures compressed into one diagnosis.

RCTs are the “medical gold standard.” But perhaps idiosyncratic medical maladies are where the standard hierarchy of evidence breaks down a little. Philosopher of science Nancy Cartwright has argued that RCTs answer a narrower question than clinical practice needs: they tell you that a treatment, on average, produced a particular outcome in a trial population. They don’t tell you whether it will work for you in particular.

So PCS patients navigate the uncanny valley of niche medical science: on the one side, RCTs and rigorous studies that document average effects that might not apply to you, and on the other, N=1 case studies that might solve your exact problem, or be entirely useless. In the middle, there’s a bunch of people trying to sell you metabolism-enhancing lasers for five thousand dollars. Absent clear explanations, patients can find themselves passed between neurologists, optometrists, physical therapists, vision therapists, acupuncturists, psychiatrists, and energy-healers before finding the one thing that happens to work for them.
To get the most juice out of a clinical trial, you need a theory of why the treatment worked, for whom, and whether you’re similar enough to the trial population for the effect to transfer.
But what if you don’t have a mature theory yet?
Z-bell tests and Fijian reef fish

As a species, we’ve been solving problems we don’t understand for a long time. On Fiji’s Yasawa Island, pregnant and breastfeeding women observe taboos against eating certain species of reef fish. When Natalie and Joseph Henrich investigated in 2010, they found that the taboo species mapped onto the fish most likely to carry ciguatera toxin, a naturally occurring marine toxin that’s particularly dangerous to fetuses and nursing infants. Local variation combined with fitness-relevant outcomes and social learning can surface solutions long before the mechanism is understood. (The trade-off is that sometimes they suggest you try bloodletting or child sacrifice).

For poorly understood chronic conditions, treatment often looks less like applying established science and more like janky cultural learning. PCS communities generate variation, share outcomes online, and copy apparently successful interventions.

But what makes the Fijian case work is that there’s a real selector pulling signal out of the noise. Toxic fish made people visibly sick, and useful taboos could be reinforced across generations. The PCS testimonial ecosystem has no comparably reliable selector; variants can propagate just because they’re dramatic or recent or someone’s trying to sell you something. The same dynamics that make it kind of reasonable to try Zelinsky’s Z-bell test might push you toward forty sessions of hyperbaric oxygen at $200 a pop.

Another drawback is that cultural transmission is good at producing outcomes, but overimitates methods. The Z-bell case is actually a nice illustration. Even if Zelinsky’s lenses actually help some patients, the community’s causal story (closed-eye retinal stimulation) might be totally wrong. Cultural transmission will faithfully convey the bells-and-mathemagic ritual along with whatever genuinely works.

Alright, clearly we can’t just trust the forums. In an ideal world, we’d capitalize on the strengths of patient communities (lots of people trying lots of things) and combine it with some kind of rigorous selection mechanism.

Luckily, there’s already a proof of concept for this. In 2020, the Body Politic COVID support group pioneered a novel idea: ask patients stuff. They created the Patient-Generated Hypotheses Journal (PGHJ) and began advising (and funding) major research efforts. Their flagship peer-reviewed paper (Davis et al, 2021), an online survey of 3,762 people drawn from support groups across 56 countries, found that Long COVID affected multiple organ systems, that symptoms persisted well past acute infection, and that recovery often took many months (all borne out by subsequent research).

Some community-amplified hypotheses won’t hold up—great, that’s what science is for! At the least, the PGHJ demonstrates that heterogenous patient communities can do more than swap miracle stories; they can generate structured observations and funnel hypotheses toward controlled studies. For example, do prism glasses actually improve general cognitive functioning in PCS patients with convergence issues? Despite Elliott’s popularization, as far as I can tell there are literally no RCTs testing this.

For medical orphans like PCS, the evidence hierarchy is doing the right things in the wrong order. Population-wide RCTs belong at the top once we know what outcome we care about and what mechanism we’re targeting. Until then, structured patient case registries could help us figure out what actually deserves a trial.
Getting out of the parking lot
Two years ago, if someone asked me how to navigate PCS, I would have said, “Uh, only pursue treatments with clear, scientifically-backed benefits.”

And at first, that’s what I did. My path to recovery started with best-evidenced treatments. But as the months dragged on without improvement, I found myself in testimonial-land—trying things based on Google Maps reviews, and reading this book.

As a concussion roadmap, The Ghost in My Brain is pretty frustrating. Elliott is too ready to accept his clinicians’ explanations and treats his recovery path as way more generalizable than it is. But as phenomenology, it’s excellent. It does a great job of conveying what it feels like when your brain breaks. If you’re intrigued by the extreme edges of human experience, this is for you. If you’re looking for a guidebook, sorry, there isn’t one (yet).

For conditions like severe, persistent PCS, the patients who recover often fall into two groups: the ones who are lucky enough to find clinicians willing to iterate with them, and the ones who have the time and money to experiment on themselves. That’s a small slice of the population.

We can’t just replace RCTs with facebook groups, but maybe we could bridge the weirdness of individual cases and the discipline of controlled science. The rather dark irony here is that the PCS patient community has PCS. Many of us can’t look at screens, nevermind organize case registries. But if even the conservative end of the PCS estimates is right, that’s hundreds of thousands of cases a year. Many of those people are doing exactly what I did—trawling through forums and trying treatments. And whether or not anyone records the results, people will continue to search the solution space. Because when your brain breaks and you’re stuck in apple vs salami hell, you try all the bells and prisms.

Institute of Medicine and National Research Council. Sports-Related Concussions in Youth: Improving the Science, Changing the Culture. National Academies Press, 2014, citing Langlois et al. 2006. This is technically a report on sports and recreation-related TBI and concussion, which are overlapping categories that both often lead to PCS. Given that this is just sports and rec related, the real number must be much higher.

A major JAMA Neurology meta-analysis found a relative risk of suicide of 2.03 after concussion/mild TBI. In two included cohort studies with about 4 years median follow-up, suicide deaths occurred in 0.50% and 0.59% of diagnosed concussion/mTBI patients. That is roughly 1 in 200 over that follow-up period

techcrunch.com/2026/10/23/startups-dont-.headline: Startups don’t need to go viral to win customers
techcrunch.com/2026/10/23/startups-dont-.author: Lucas Ropek

paragraphs.text: Getting initial customers as a startup can be one of the most grueling challenges in business. Even when companies manage to snag some early interest, there’s no guarantee those customers will stick around.

At TechCrunch Disrupt last week, Elia Wallen, founder and CEO of travel startup Engine, Gamma founder and CEO Grant Lee, and Crystal Huang, general partner at Google Ventures, shared tips on how to attract and retain customers.

In the current era — when young AI companies like Cluely and Instinct are building big audiences not just through their products but also through their founders’ colorful online presences — social media can seem like a magic bullet for reaching early customers. But founders who want heighten their business strategy with modern marketing, have to be strategic, according to Lee.

Gamma, which sells AI-powered presentation software, managed to scale its business exponentially with a social media strategy that deployed influencers through its Ambassadors (or “Gambassador”) program. The company adopted the plan before influencer-based marketing was a tried-and-true strategy for smaller companies, eventually reaching a multi-billion dollar valuation.
But simply giving influencers a platform and telling them to promote your brand online doesn’t automatically translate to sales, said Lee. There’s more to it than that.

“If you have a product that can serve many different segments or use cases, then you want to basically have creators that can target each one of those,” Lee said. “If you have folks that are in consulting versus people that do all their marketing and create all the decks for their CMO, there’s all these different segments you might want to go after.”
Lee said sometimes founders seem to treat creator marketing or influencer marketing as a sort of set it and forget it thing.

“I think you’re better served by really spending a lot of time with these creators, because if they’re not able to understand how to articulate the value of your product, it doesn’t matter how much money you spend, it’s just going to fall flat,” Lee added.
The effectiveness of social media depends largely on the type of business. Other ways of reaching customers can be just (if not more) effective.

Wallen would know. His company Engine, which manages lodging and travel bookings for midsize businesses, bootstrapped its way to $150 million in bookings before taking on any outside funding. They also had no visible social media strategy at all. For Wallen, traditional sales tactics can be far more useful than a positive TikTok video.

“We did events and we smiled and dialed,” said Wallen. “We still have a lot of people picking up the phone. A lot of people who didn’t grow up with that or don’t understand it think that it’s outdated or it doesn’t work but it does. It’s a hard thing. There are a lot of companies that just refuse to do it or don’t know how to do it well. But they’re missing out on a very big offline client base.” He added: “The phone still works.”

Wallen also shared an in-person tactic that his company deployed during its scrappy early days: hiring a magician named David to perform tricks for prospective clients at events and encourage them to visit the Engine’s booth. In short, old-fashioned personal engagement can work just as well, if not better, than the latest social media tricks.
Huang, who has managed droves of startups and shepherded them to success, said that once you have a customer, a lot of value can be derived from looking at how they use the product.

“Can you look into usage data and figure out if it’s recurring, if it’s increasing, if they are referring their friends?” Huang said. “It can come across in early usage and retention information as well. And then also, do you see some super fans, right, who even want to work at the company, promote the company, be attached to the brand?” She added: “You need to have ways to create evangelists who are really passionate about the product.”

latimes.com/entertainment-arts/story/202.headline: Stevie Wonder sues to evict reported ex-fiancée from L.A. property
latimes.com/entertainment-arts/story/202.author: Alexandra Del Rosario

paragraphs.text: Stevie Wonder is taking legal action against a reported ex-fiancée, filing a lawsuit this week to evict her after she allegedly lived rent-free at his property in Studio City for nearly four decades.

The prolific musician, whose legal name is Stevland Morris, filed a legal complaint in Los Angeles County Superior Court on Thursday against Carmen Efferson, whom he says has been living for free at a home on Oak Glen Drive since July 1988, according to the complaint obtained by The Times. Wonder seeks to evict Efferson after she allegedly refused to allow inspectors into the property earlier in the summer and failed to vacate the home in August, despite receiving a 30-day notice in late July.

Efferson, whom TMZ reported was once betrothed to the Grammy-winning “Songs in the Key of Life” musician, did not immediately respond to The Times’ multiple requests for response on Friday. A legal representative for Wonder, 76, did not comment and did not clarify the singer’s reported relationship with Efferson. Wonder has been married Tomeeka Bracy since 2017.

According to the musician’s complaint, Wonder and Efferson reached an oral agreement in 1988 that she can occupy the property without paying monthly rent. Tensions began in July this year when representatives for Wonder attempted to access the property multiple times “for purposes of updating and retaining property insurance,” according to an email between Wonder’s legal representatives and Efferson included in the complaint.

One attorney for Wonder notified Efferson on July 23 of a property inspection the following week. Efferson had choice words for the request, emailing another attorney for Wonder on July 25 to “please refrain from your rascist [sic] coldblooded ‘white male privilege’ tone.”
“I’m feeling harassed,” Efferson said, according to screenshots of her email. “Regarding your ORDERS of entering into the place where I am living, I do not consent.”

She ended her email with an explicit statement. An attorney for Wonder responded two days later, informing Efferson that the lawyer who issued the inspection notice “is neither racist, coldblooded, white or male.”

In an email dated July 27, Efferson also threatened to “immediately contact law enforcement” upon further attempts by Wonder’s representatives to enter the property. The next day, attorneys notified Efferson she had 30 days to vacate the home.
“You were given the opportunity to reconsider your decision to deny access and declined,” the notice said, according to the complaint. Efferson was ordered to vacate the property by Aug. 27

On Oct. 6, Wonder’s lawyers issued Efferson a three-day notice to leave the home due to her alleged violation of her oral agreement with the musician. Wonder’s legal representatives also claimed they gave Efferson “three additional opportunities to permit entry” for an inspection, but she failed to respond.

“Owner has been prejudiced by the cancellation of the property insurance policy and is now at substantial risk of economic loss by virtue of your actions to prevent the protection and preservation of the Premises,” attorneys said in the notice, according to exhibits. The attorneys also notified Efferson that Wonder would file a complaint should she refuse access again.

Wonder — celebrating the 50th anniversary of his seminal “Songs in the Key of Life” this year — is seeking forfeiture of the lease agreement with Efferson, legal fees and statutory damages up to $600.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/23/openai-says-it.headline: OpenAI says it will no longer train its AI models on the live internet, citing “significant risks”
techcrunch.com/2026/10/23/openai-says-it.author: Tim Fernholz

paragraphs.text: On Friday, OpenAI said that it will train its models using cached copies and simulated versions of the internet instead of the live web because the models are too unpredictable to be trusted with live internet access.

The frontier lab announced its new policy two weeks after its rival, Anthropic, began limiting its newest and, in theory, most capable models from accessing the live internet. Researchers adopted these policies after months of incidents in which models pursuing training tasks broke into external systems in search of answers, collaborated on obscure message boards, and developed exotic hacking strategies.

“Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access,” the company said in a blog post.

OpenAI said that as recently as September 20, one of its frontier models exploited a misconfiguration to access the internet. That led the company to pause training work for the rest of the month so it could develop and test new approaches to securing its models.
The decision to train these models in sandboxes cut off from the internet is notable because employees at frontier labs have insisted that doing so would be nearly infeasible.

Keeping AI data centers separate from the internet “would need research teams to essentially be embedded inside of data centers in Iowa or wherever else around the world,” former OpenAI researcher Steven Adler told Fortune this month. “It’s a lot of overhead, and it isn’t clear to me that the safety benefits of it are large enough to merit just how large a tax it would be for a company to do it unilaterally.”

“In nearly every post I make on X, without fail, I get between five and ten comments about my inability to secure a sandbox, or asking why the hell we can’t just unplug the model from the internet,” an anonymous security engineer at OpenAI wrote in a September post on X. “These comments reflect a widening gap between where a lot of organizations and people are today and what the frontier labs are dealing with. There is also a general misunderstanding of how model training and evaluation work at these labs.”

The engineer, whose role has been confirmed previously by OpenAI, described how complex the training runs launched by OpenAI engineers are, noting that they require access a variety of resources and tools across many domains, and that thousands of researchers build, modify and test the environments. “So is it as easy as just putting it in a sandbox? No, it’s not,” he concluded.

Now, OpenAI says that “we must always be able to prevent a frontier model from achieving unauthorized, arbitrary access to the live internet.” That comes after the company deployed swarms of agents in red-teaming exercises that attempted to escape from their sandbox. That effort revealed a range of vulnerabilities that convinced the lab to adopt its new approach.

To meet that requirement while still reaching its training goals, the lab said it created a “a vast set of indexed and cached web content with which our models can interact, without risk of affecting external systems.”

Whether that strategy will perform as well as letting models run freely on the open internet remains to be seen, but it is noteworthy that both frontier labs have determined their most powerful technology can’t be left unsupervised on the digital commons.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: Instacart Considers a Potential Sale, Sparking Share Rally
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Dana Wollman and Mark Gurman

paragraphs.text: Dana Wollman and Mark Gurman
Fri, October 23, 2026 at 4:18 PM CDT 2 min read
(Bloomberg) -- Instacart has explored a potential sale of the grocery-delivery company, a process that has included discussions with Uber Technologies Inc., a person familiar with the matter said.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Though Instacart recently shopped itself to Uber, the ride-hailing giant walked away from the discussions, according to the person, who asked not to be identified because the talks were private. The two sides are no longer in discussions, the person said.

The Information previously reported that Instacart also held preliminary talks with DoorDash Inc. as part of a potential sale process. The story sent shares of Instacart up as much as 9.2% to $56.44 on Friday.
Representatives for Instacart, which trades as Maplebear Inc., didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. Uber and DoorDash also didn't immediately comment in response to requests.

Instacart has been working with an investment bank to evaluate its options, the Information said, citing unidentified people familiar with the matter. Discussions with other companies are early and ongoing and may not result in a deal, according to the report.

The grocery company is exploring a sale at a time of intensifying competition, with Uber and DoorDash encroaching further on its grocery business. That could potentially make a sale to a larger rival the company's best path to delivering returns to shareholders and securing its long-term future.
Uber's stock fell 3.4% in New York trading, while DoorDash declined 3.5%.

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/.headline: Embattled Greens senator Jordon Steele-John confirms leave from parliament after allegations against him made public
theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/.author: Sarah Basford Canales

paragraphs.text: Jordon Steele-John has confirmed he will not attend parliament next week as the embattled Greens senator releases a letter detailing the allegations against him.
After days of confusion following historical complaints about alleged misconduct were publicly aired in the media, Steele-John posted a statement to social media late Friday night.

In the statement, the Western Australian senator said he considered attending Senate estimates virtually but was told it would be “unacceptable”. He will instead focus on seeing through an independent investigation to its conclusion, he said.

“Over the past few days there has been a growing chorus calling on me not to attend parliament next week. I have explored attending digitally but have been informed that would also be unacceptable,” Steele-John said.
Steele-John said a precedent of keeping parliamentarians out of parliament after “allegations of allegations” are made had now been set.
“Had an allegation or complaint been made against me, I would have taken these actions immediately,” he said.

The 32-year-old senator’s attendance in parliament for the remainder of the year had been uncertain after a public stoush with the party’s leader, David Shoebridge, over whether he was on leave while an investigation was undertaken into allegations he had acted inappropriately towards women between 2017 and 2025.
The complaints are now subject to an independent investigation commissioned by the WA Greens and have been referred to the Independent Parliamentary Standards Commission.
Shoebridge claimed Steele-John had requested leave and he accepted it last week after seven party members penned a letter to the leader urging an investigation into the claims.

The three-page letter sent on 13 October, and first published by the Nine newspapers, said the authors had been “made aware of multiple allegations of serious misconduct” against Steele-John about his “behaviour in the presence of women”.
The letter referred to an allegation of sexual harassment at a Greens campaign event in 2024 that the alleged victim had not reported out of fear and backlash. The letter provided no further detail.
In another, the authors referred to an allegation of “serious sexual misconduct” in 2025.
Also contained in the letter was a reference to a disparaging nickname for Steele-John – “feels on wheels” – which the authors said implied he had a reputation for acting inappropriately.

“To be clear, all signatories to this letter know that an allegation does not equate to a fact and/or guilt. We simply believe that it is in the party’s best interests to ensure that every allegation is investigated thoroughly, in alignment with community and member expectations,” the letter’s authors wrote.

Steele-John was defiant in a lengthy statement last Sunday, rejecting the allegations against him, denying he agreed to take leave from parliament and accusing an internal faction within the Greens of playing “nasty political games” in their decision to release the letter to the media.

Steele-John said any claims of his alleged behaviour should be investigated “fairly and thoroughly” but accused an “unofficial faction” within the WA branch had released the complaint letter to the media in a bid to oust him from the Senate.
Guardian Australia has confirmed the WA police told Steele-John the investigation was closed in May with no charges.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-23/.headline: Court blocks path for Trump to deploy national guard without state OK
latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-23/.author: Sonja Sharp

paragraphs.text: President Trump illegally usurped Gov. Gavin Newsom’s command of the California National Guard by ordering a surge troops deployed into Los Angeles and across the state amid protests against the White House’s mass deportation program last year, the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled Friday.

The two-one decision split the president’s own appointees to the court, with Judge Eric D. Miller of Seattle siding with Judge Jennifer Sung of Portland, a Biden pick, and Judge Mark J.Bennett of Honolulu dissenting.

“The order exceeded the President’s statutory authority and encroached on Congress’s calling forth power, in violation of the constitutional separation of powers,” Sung wrote for the majority, calling Trump’s order “unconstitutional.”

The decision also appeared to foreclose what California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta called “the Trump Administration’s transparent attempt” to preserve its right to call up California troops again under the same obscure statute — a novel legal maneuver administration lawyers said let the president seize command without invoking the far stronger Insurrection Act.
The 9th Circuit trio was among the first to weigh the law last June, after Trump federalized 4,000 National Guard soldiers in response to unrest over immigration enforcement in Los Angeles.

California sued. US District Judge Charles R. Breyer quickly ruled to block the deployment. But Sung, Bennett and Miller stayed his order, finding that the California deployment could go forward under an obscure and virtually untested subsection of the law.

That decision set a “great level of deference” as the standard of review for deployments, meaning courts had very little power to test the president’s rationale for sending troops into American streets.
At the time, the decision represented one of the president’s most sweeping second-term victories: a plug-and-play legal mechanism to deploy soldiers against civilians in cities across the country.
In Portland that fall, another 9th Circuit panel stayed U.S. District Judge Karin Immergut’s order to stand down troops, using the first trio’s precedent.

The Portland decision — based in part on data the Department of Justice later admitted was false — prompted an extraordinary filing by Judge Jay Bybee, who all but pleaded with the court to rehear the case and interpret the law differently.
“There is no greater threat to the sovereignty of the states than an assertion of federal control over their domestic affairs,” Bybee wrote.

The issue quickly found its way to the Supreme Court, after a 7th Circuit panel found the president had provided “insufficient evidence” for deployment even under the 9th Circuit’s deference standard.

On Dec. 23, the Justices adopted a celebrated Georgetown scholar’s academic reading of the statute, saying it only allowed the president to commandeer national guard troops if the situation had already outmatched the standing army.
Federalized troops were ordered to leave Los Angeles in December.
On Friday, the 9th Circuit held that Trump’s claim that Los Angeles was in the grips of a rebellion last June “did not reflect a colorable assessment within a range of honest judgment.”

Using “the plain text of the statute,” and “dictionary definitions of the disputed term,” the majority found the president had not furnished evidence of a “a violent, armed, organized, open and avowed uprising against the government as a whole” — nor anything close to it.

Instead, Justice Department lawyers had relied on subsidiary definitions of “rebellion” that the 9th Circuit warned would allow the president to call up troops to quell almost any resistance, including peaceful protests.
“Resistance that is not violent, armed, organized, and against the government as a whole generally does not require a military response,” Sung wrote.

“Because Defendants have failed to identify a source of authority that would allow the military to legally execute the laws in California, they have not carried their burden to show that the President had the authority to federalize California’s National Guard,” Sung wrote.

npr.org/2026/10/23/nx-s1-6014742/floodin.headline: Severe flooding hits Four Corners region, more expected through the weekend
npr.org/2026/10/23/nx-s1-6014742/floodin.author: Ava Berger

paragraphs.text: Looking out a window on Friday afternoon, Devin Neeley saw light, puffy clouds and a blue sky in San Juan County, N.M. The county's public information officer for emergency management called it "surreal."
Meanwhile, brown rainwaters were flooding homes in low-lying areas of the county and forcing sewage into the San Juan River.
"[The sky] belies really the danger that is coming down the river in historic levels," Neeley says. "We have not seen flooding like this in generations."

Neeley says, emergency responders rescued people on their roofs after floodwater inundated their homes. The county is under an emergency declaration and residents in susceptible areas were told to evacuate Thursday afternoon.
"These are communities that have beautiful riverfront places to live," Neeley says. "And unfortunately, that's a problem today."
Rare, heavy rainfall started to hit the Four Corners region — which includes New Mexico, Colorado, Utah and Arizona — on Wednesday.
Since then, severe, brown-colored floodwaters have led to road closures, mandatory evacuations and emergency declarations across the four states.
Thick, brown floodwaters
Areas of southern Utah, southwest Colorado, and the northern parts of Arizona and New Mexico were drenched with rain leading to rapidly rising floodwaters, Thursday and Friday.

In response to a post on X that showed brownish-red floodwaters in Hurricane, Utah, Gov. Spencer Cox, wrote on Thursday: "Our hearts are with the families whose homes and livelihoods have been impacted."

The southern Utah city issued an emergency declaration on Thursday after flooding damaged more than 100 homes and Rvs. People were seen leading horses to safety through ankle-deep water, in a video posted by the National Weather Service.
In Farmington, N.M., at the center of the devastation, Police Chief Steve Hebbe said at a press conference on Friday that "this is singular and this is real."
"So far, we have not had any deaths that is very fortunate, but this is not something that should be played with," Hebbe said.
Colorado Gov. Jared Polis declared disaster emergencies for 11 counties. Polis also authorized the use of National Guard members to assist with rescue efforts in southwest Colorado.

The police department for the Navajo Nation, which spans across northeastern Arizona, northwestern New Mexico, and southeastern Utah, said on Thursday that authorities had rescued seven families, 30 people, from their flooded homes. The Hopi Tribe in northeastern Arizona declared a state of emergency on Thursday due to heavy rainfall damaging roads, bridges, homes and other infrastructure.
The Archuleta County Sheriff's office in Colorado warned residents to shelter in place Friday morning, and by the evening had issued an evacuation warning.
The flooding comes after extreme weather hit the Southwest throughout the week. Arizona saw baseball-sized hail and a possible tornado that injured at least one person Wednesday evening.
A record amount of rainfall
The region's mountainous terrain is conducive to flooding. In August, intense flash flooding in the Grand Canyon led to multiple deaths.

Severe thunderstorm warnings started earlier in the week, says Kris Sanders, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service in Grand Junction, Colo. The remnants of Hurricane Trudy, which was active from Oct. 15 to Oct. 18, in the Pacific Ocean formed into a slow-moving low-pressure system that worked its way southwest.

Sanders says a lot of the storms weakened as they came through the region, but the heavy rain did not. Portions of southwest Colorado and southeast Utah saw two to four inches, whereas areas with higher elevations, like the San Juan Mountains, got up to six inches. This caused small creeks and streams and rivers to flood.
"Those rainfall amounts are records in themselves," Sanders says.

While the amount of rainfall is rare, he says, these storms typically happen in the region at this time of year. An event last year caused major flooding in the same spots, "like a carbon copy" of this year, Sanders says.
The threat is not over, he says, and thunderstorm watches are active in many of the same areas through Sunday.

Daniel Swain, a climate scientist with the University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources, says the severe thunderstorms are fueled by the large amount of moisture in the air. He says that moisture comes from the record-warm waters off parts of the West Coast, which are driven by a strong El Niño event and a preexisting marine heat wave (which he attributes largely to human-caused climate change).

The flooding isn't a surprise, he says, pointing to a prediction he and others made in the spring — that if El Niño materialized according to forecasts, southwestern U.S. could see extreme precipitation events through October.
Now, "that is exactly what we've seen," he says, "because this isn't even the first event this fall."
Neeley, the public information officer in San Juan County, N.M., says his community will be on alert for more damage and safety risks throughout the weekend.
"People are concerned about their life and their welfare and their property," Neeley says. "This is going to be a long term impact to this community,"

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/.headline: Helen Haines’s condition improves days after losing both legs from alleged attack
theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/.author: Adeshola Ore

paragraphs.text: Independent MP Helen Haines’s condition has been downgraded to serious but stable after she lost both legs following an alleged attack near her electorate office in north-east Victoria on Monday afternoon.
The Alfred hospital in Melbourne provided an update on Haines’s condition on Saturday morning.
“The patient is in a serious but stable condition at The Alfred on Saturday morning,” a spokesperson for the hospital said.

Haines, the federal MP for the Victorian seat of Indi, had been in a critical but stable condition after she was struck by a car in Wangaratta on Monday afternoon. Surgeons were trying to save her right leg on Tuesday, but both legs had to be amputated due to the seriousness of her injuries.

Police on Tuesday charged Brendan Nugent, 43, from nearby Tarrawingee with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally cause serious injury and the commonwealth offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official. Police have since charged him with two additional offences – cultivating and possessing cannabis – according to court documents.
Nugent appeared in court on Wednesday and did not apply for bail.

On Friday, an update on Haines’s social media accounts said her staff were working to reopen her electorate offices next Thursday. “What happened on Monday has deeply affected Helen’s family and all of her staff. Many of us witnessed the incident and some were among the first to come to her aid,” the post read.

“As Helen takes the time she needs to recover, we will take time to look after ourselves and one another, too. Healing will take time, and we ask for your understanding as we navigate the days and weeks ahead.”
The alleged attack on Haines has reverberated through Australian politics, prompting conversations about the temperature of political debate and mental services in regional Victoria.

theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/23/marc.headline: Rubio tells Cubans ‘now is the time’ to act to see political change
theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/23/marc.author: Guardian staff reporter

paragraphs.text: Marco Rubio urged Cubans seeking political change in their country to act, saying “now is the time” moments after Donald Trump told a Friday rally for candidates in south Florida that US warships could intervene in Cuba on their way back from the Iran war.

The US secretary of state, in his social media post addressed “to those who seek to create positive change”, urged Cubans to capitalize on Trump’s plans. “The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete [sic] partnership with the CIA,” Rubio said.

The top US diplomat, whose parents left Cuba for the United States before the socialist revolution there, seemed to mistakenly use the word “discrete”, meaning separate, rather than “discreet”, meaning private or secret.

Trump first floated this idea earlier this year, but has not mentioned it in recent months. But he revived it in response to a shouted question from the crowd about the island nation. He was campaigning just days before midterm elections in which voters have expressed concern about the impact the US war on Iran has had on prices of goods from gas to groceries.

“We’ll do a little stopover,” Trump said. “Actually, what we’re going to do with Cuba is, we’re going to come back from Iran. Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They’ll raise up their hands. And then we’re going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.”

Rubio and Trump have been bullish on action in Cuba, with Trump previously suggesting the country would “be next” in terms of intervention abroad, following the winding down of the Iran war he has long forecast but which has not yet happened.

In May, he and Rubio raised the specter of US military intervention in Cuba, a renewed threat that took on greater weight after the administration announced criminal charges against the island’s former leader, Raúl Castro. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that previous US presidents had considered intervening in Cuba for decades but that “it looks like I’ll be the one that does it”.

Rubio told reporters separately that Cuba had been a national security threat for years because of its ties to US adversaries and that Trump was intent on addressing it. While saying the Trump administration wanted to resolve differences with Cuba peacefully, Rubio voiced doubts that the US could reach a diplomatic resolution with the island’s current government.
Rubio has not addressed Cuba in depth in public for several weeks, with his last comments coming in a 29 September interview with Fox News host Sean Hannity.

“The truth is Cuba has already fallen. It doesn’t have a functional economy and it’s governed by people who continue to preach about some revolution that has been dead for 20 years that’s never worked,” Rubio said, without alluding to any CIA operation.

“We are hopeful that Cuba will choose a different path. We are hopeful … that there will be some people in there that open their eyes to the reality of what they’re facing. We’re never going to allow Cuba to become a base of operation against American interests or pose a threat to our national security. On that we are abundantly clear.”

Rubio and other top Trump aides have met with Cuban officials in recent months to explore possible improvements in relations. But the US side has come away unimpressed from those talks, leading to even more sanctions imposed on the Cuban government.

During his address to the United Nations general assembly last month, Trump said Rubio – son of Cuban immigrants, who has long taken a hard line against Cuba’s socialist leadership – was “deep into negotiations with Cuba”, saying he would “not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep”.
Days later, Trump told reporters that he anticipated that the two countries “will make a deal”, adding: “I don’t think we’ll need the military. Cuba is failing very badly.”

Earlier this week, the two countries clashed at the United Nations as the Trump administration sought once again to build opposition for an upcoming annual vote condemning Washington’s decades-long economic embargo against Havana.

Cuba has struggled since 2020 with an economic and energy crisis. Its gross domestic product has shrunk , and its 10 million residents have endured blackouts, food shortages and inflation. There have been waves of protests, and hundreds of thousands of Cubans have immigrated, many to the United States.

nytimes.com/2026/10/23/science/space/nas.headline: NASA Is Still Aiming for the Next Moon Landing in 2028

paragraphs.text: Can NASA land astronauts on the moon in 2028?
On Friday, NASA’s administrator, Jared Isaacman, did not promise yes, but he said the space agency was working as hard as possible to meet that target.

“We have the mandate, we have the resources, the support from our stakeholders to be able to execute, and that’s what we intend to do,” Mr. Isaacman said during a news conference that provided updates on NASA’s Artemis program, which aims to put Americans back on the lunar surface for the first time since 1972.

In April, NASA sent four astronauts on a loop around the moon, without landing, during the Artemis II mission. In summer 2027, Artemis III is scheduled to orbit Earth for 14 to 17 days so that astronauts can practice docking procedures with prototypes of lunar landers, which are being developed by two commercial companies: SpaceX, which is owned by Elon Musk, and Blue Origin, Jeff Bezos’ company.

NASA has not yet decided which lander it will use for Artemis IV, the mission scheduled for late 2028 that will put two astronauts on the lunar surface near the moon’s south pole. Both lander designs will have to conduct an uncrewed demonstration flight to the moon before astronauts climb aboard.

Many outside experts doubt that a 2028 moon landing is possible and expect that China will get its astronauts to the surface before Artemis does. At the news conference, Mr. Isaacman and other top NASA officials talked about how they were looking to speed things up without compromising safety.

For example, the agency is exploring the idea of a simpler spacesuit design for the early Artemis moon landings. This suit would not have all of the capabilities that NASA will eventually need when astronauts spend weeks or months on the moon. But it would cut the mass in half, to 250 pounds per suit, saving precious weight that would need to go to the moon and back.
“When you think about what has to be delivered to the lunar surface, that is a really big deal,” said Jeremy Parsons, the Artemis program manager at NASA.

In his introductory remarks, Mr. Isaacman harked back to the space race of the 1960s between the United States and the Soviet Union and the quick progress made during the Apollo program. Only nine months passed between Apollo 7, the first mission with astronauts aboard, and Apollo 11, when Neil Armstrong became the first human to step on the moon.
Today, the superpower competitor is China, which has made strides with its focused and steady space program over the last couple of decades. China aims to send its astronauts to the moon by 2030.

Since becoming NASA administrator last December, Mr. Isaacman has sought to reshape Artemis to take a more step-by-step approach similar to Apollo’s. “It’s a playbook this agency knows really well,” he said.

The first Artemis moon landing was initially set to occur during Artemis III, and would have happened in late 2028 at the earliest. But Mr. Isaacman decided that it made more sense to first test out key docking technologies in Earth orbit before relying on them nearly a quarter-million miles away at the moon. That would also allow NASA to launch sooner and build up its rocket-launching experience.

“The idea of taking longer, costing more, and flying less somehow, leading to better or safer outcomes, I think is a misunderstanding that’s been left uncorrected for far too long,” Mr. Isaacman said.

nytimes.com/2026/10/23/us/politics/justi.headline: Trump Officials Seek Block on Alaska Senate Race Results if the Republican Dan Sullivan Loses

paragraphs.text: The Trump administration has asked a federal court to block certification of the Senate election in Alaska if the Republican incumbent narrowly loses, a highly unusual move that signaled an effort to potentially intervene in the outcome.

President Trump made clear on Friday that he had demanded the lawsuit, acknowledging how directly he has harnessed the Justice Department to carry out his wishes. “I’m the one that said do it,” he told reporters.

The Justice Department, in the lawsuit filed in federal court in Alaska on Thursday, argued that confusion over a candidate on the ballot with a name very similar to that of the incumbent, Senator Dan S. Sullivan, could taint the election result.

Polls show that the senator is in a close race against Mary Peltola, a Democrat. However, the four-person ballot also includes Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., and does not list any party registration. The senator’s line on the state ballot describes him as the incumbent.

The administration’s new legal gambit highlights its intensifying efforts to claim authority over the midterm elections, as control of Congress hangs in the balance. Elections are administered by state and local officials, but in recent weeks, the Trump administration has filed lawsuits seeking to alter how states like Alaska and California do so.

David Becker of the Center for Election Innovation & Research, a nonpartisan group that advises election officials, said he could not recall a similar instance in which the federal government had sought to block certification of an election, “and certainly not 11 days before an election.” State officials have already addressed the issue of the candidate with a similar name, he said.

“D.O.J. making this claim this late smells of political interference and is against D.O.J. policy,” Mr. Becker said. “The feds have absolutely no authority to tell Alaska when and how to certify. The state officials are following Alaska state law, as the Constitution requires.” He said he expected the courts to reject the administration’s lawsuit.

For months, Republicans have tried to get the second Mr. Sullivan off the ballot, arguing he is a Democratic plant meant to siphon away key votes in a thinly populated state where the winner could be decided by a narrow margin. Republicans noted the challenger had only recently registered as a Republican; he acknowledged working with a Democratic strategist to get on the ballot; and he had a history of donating to Democratic candidates, including Ms. Peltola.
Nevertheless, in June, the Alaska Supreme Court ruled that the second Mr. Sullivan could appear on the ballot, ahead of the primary.

Democrats have maintained they have no connection to the second Mr. Sullivan, a retired elementary-school teacher living in the small fishing village of Petersburg, southeast of Juneau. And the candidate himself has said that he is running in good faith, as a moderate Republican unhappy with the incumbent senator’s tenure.

“My intention is not to trick people,” he said in an interview in Petersburg in August. “I would hope people are informed enough to know the difference between an incumbent senator and a teacher.” Still, he acknowledged having voted for Democrats, including Ms. Peltola, in recent elections.

The lawsuit, signed by a senior Justice Department official, Stanley Woodward, argues “there is a realistic chance that, even if a majority of Alaskans wish to vote for Senator Sullivan, Daniel J. Sullivan’s presence on the ballot will result in a victory for Peltola.”

To guard against voter confusion, the suit argues, Alaska should “not certify any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion.” The possibility of such confusion exists, the suit continued, if “(1) Senator Sullivan does not win the election; and (2) had all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan been cast instead for Senator Sullivan and Alaska’s rank-choice process played out accordingly, Senator Sullivan would have won the election.”
Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference, with the tallies used in the event that no candidate secures a majority of the first-choice vote.

Political observers in the state have suggested that system could reduce the impact of a spoiler candidate, because voters who rank both Sullivans would see their votes ultimately go to the incumbent senator, assuming the other Mr. Sullivan is eliminated in an earlier round. But some Republicans have said they fear a scenario where their voters rank only a single Sullivan — and accidentally choose the one from Petersburg — depriving the senator of those votes.

The Trump administration argues that the system could add to confusion in the Senate race, because voters might confuse the Sullivans and rank the candidates in an order different than what they intended.

Mr. Trump has repeatedly attacked ranked-choice voting and criticized the decision to allow the second Mr. Sullivan’s name to remain on the ballot. On Wednesday night, he did so again on social media, writing, “It’s ridiculous that the Court didn’t stop this SCAM.”
