Offerings such as ceramics, crabs, corn and earrings made from Spondylus shells (a genus of bivalves known as thorny oysters) were also placed on low rock platforms near some of the geoglyphs, especially those shaped like trapezoids, Lambers noted in his paper. Spondylus shells are normally found farther north, in Ecuador, but during El Niño events, they can appear farther south, in Peru. These shells, alongside crabs and corn, tend to be associated with water and fertility, Lambers noted.
Related mysteries

Another idea is that the geoglyphs themselves may have been used for ritual processions. Some of the geoglyphs are made with a single, uninterrupted line," Nieves said. "Those are the ones that would lend themselves for processions since people could walk them in a single file."

Some of the activities at the Nazca Lines may have helped foster a sense of community and equality, said Darryl Wilkinson, a professor of religion at Dartmouth University who has written about the geoglyphs. For instance, "walking the lines was a group activity, and participating in such processions would have likely created a feeling of community among those involved," Wilkinson told Live Science in an email. "I interpret the Nasca lines as geared towards the realization of a relatively more equal expression of community."

Whatever the reasons for their construction the Nazca Lines are awe inspiring today. Lambers wrote in his essay that the Nazca people who built them "succeeded in transforming one of the driest deserts in the world, over the course of many centuries, to serve the region’s inhabitants as an expression of their cultural ideas and a setting for their social activities."

theguardian.com/music/2026/oct/24/donal-.headline: Dónal Lunny, ‘colossus of Irish music’, dies aged 79
theguardian.com/music/2026/oct/24/donal-.author: Guardian staff reporter

paragraphs.text: The Irish traditional musician Dónal Lunny has died at the age of 79 from cancer.

Lunny rose to prominence in the band Rakes of Kildare alongside Christy Moore and his brother Frank. He went on to play in bands such as Planxty, Moving Hearts, the Bothy Band and Coolfin among others and toured the world.
A post on his Facebook page confirmed that Lunny died in St James’s hospital in Dublin on Friday morning.

“We are heartbroken to confirm that our beloved Dónal passed away peacefully this morning in Dublin following a short stay in St James’s hospital,” the post said. “Thank you for helping us to remember and celebrate his immense contribution to music, to culture and to so many people’s lives all over the world.”
The Irish president, Catherine Connolly, expressed her “deepest condolences to the family, friends and many musical collaborators of Dónal Lunny”.

In a statement, she said: “Dónal was one of Ireland’s greatest musical figures, a wonderfully talented musician and producer who was central to so many of the most influential moments of the last 60 years of Irish music.

“Dónal will be particularly remembered for his long partnerships with fellow musicians such as Christy Moore and Andy Irvine and for the innovative music he has left behind both as a musician in groups including Planxty, the Bothy Band and Moving Hearts and also as a renowned producer.

“This rich musical legacy, including his central role in the introduction of the bouzouki into Irish music, was appropriately recognised by his fellow artists in Dónal’s membership of Aosdána, as well as the well-deserved recognition which he received in being awarded a lifetime achievement award at the 2025 RTÉ Radio 1 Irish folk awards.
“Beyond his music, Dónal will be remembered for his warmth and the strong connection which he had with audiences all over Ireland and beyond. He will be deeply missed.”
The post ended in Irish, saying his likes will not be seen again: “Ní bheidh a leithéid arís ann.”

Lunny was born in Tullamore, County Offaly, and was a multi-instrumentalist but was best known for his mastery of the bouzouki. He was a talented melody writer and considered central to the revival of traditional music as he produced 17 albums under his record label Mulligan Records.

Paying tribute to the folk musician, the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said he was “deeply saddened” to hear of his passing. “A colossus of Irish music, as a performer, songwriter and producer,” he wrote in a post on social media.
“Uniquely gifted, Dónal carried traditional and folk music to new audiences through Planxty and his many other endeavours.”

Sinn Féin’s president, Mary Lou McDonald, also paid tribute online, saying: “Deeply saddened to hear of the passing of Dónal Lunny. A giant of Irish traditional music, Dónal helped shape the sound of Irish music for generations, bringing our rich musical heritage to audiences at home and around the world. His contribution to Irish music and culture will never be forgotten.
“Ar dheis Dé go raibh a anam [may his soul rest in peace].”

npr.org/2026/10/24/nx-s1-6014811/midterm.headline: This decade has been missing its big-impact midterm
npr.org/2026/10/24/nx-s1-6014811/midterm.author: Ron Elving

paragraphs.text: Given all that's happened in American politics since 2019, it may be hard to believe there's been anything missing.
But the decade of the 2020s has yet to see a midterm that mattered much — or that ranked among the impact midterms of past decades.
That sets the 2020s apart, as every other decade over the past hundred years has produced at least one midterm that made a big difference in Congress and in national politics more broadly.
These big-impact midterms have also shifted power in the statehouses, often signaling changes in state and national political landscapes that have mattered and lasted.

Midterms do not attract the same level of voter participation or voter interest as presidential elections. When the White House is not at stake, "low propensity voters" tend to tune out. Overall vote totals slide by about one-third.

But those voters who show up for midterms elect just as many members of Congress and fill just as many state legislative seats as voters in presidential years. Moreover, midterm voters determine about two-thirds of the nation's governorships.

The big midterms have tended to come in presidents' second terms, when their popularity and political energy may be waning. And just because a president is not on the ballot does not mean he's irrelevant. Historically, each president's detractors have seen midterms as an opportunity, while his supporters have often been complacent — or at least less motivated.
All this contributes to the general expectation that the midterms arriving Nov. 3 will be important, and perhaps momentous.
Flexing midterm muscles

Because this is a decade with three presidential cycles (2020, 2024 and 2028), it is also a decade with just two midterms. One went by in 2022. Some expected at the time that a "big red wave" would sweep then-President Biden's majorities out of Congress.

It did not happen. Democrats held on in the Senate, and the House shifted from barely Democratic to barely Republican. That did bring an end to House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's second (and last) turn with the Big Gavel. But the GOP would spend much of the next two years struggling to unite behind a speaker of their own.
That's a far cry from the big midterms that have at times rivaled presidential elections for responding to the mood of the times and rearranging the landscape.

If we take the last hundred years as our sample, we can start with the midterms that followed the Wall Street "Crash of 1929." That financial panic set off a sequence of events that would be called the Great Depression, and the collateral damage included the closing of an era of Republican dominance in Washington.

That era ended with the midterms of 1930, which cost the GOP eight Senate seats and 52 seats in the House in November 1930. Although the GOP initially retained small majorities in both chambers, they lost it in the House with the results of a few special elections early in 1931.

The Senate remained nominally Republican but featured a working majority of Democrats and progressive Republicans. A page had been turned, and Democrats would take control outright in 1932 and hold that majority through World War II.
After that war had ended, the period of Democratic hegemony under President Franklin Roosevelt also ended, and abruptly, with the results of the midterm of 1946.
Pendulum swings both ways

Republican numbers in Congress had fallen so far in the FDR years (below 100 at one point in the 435-seat House) that it seemed impossible for them to return to power. But in 1946 they stormed back to majority control of both House and Senate in a single midterm cycle.

Midterms have continued to serve as political regulators in the generations since. Dwight Eisenhower won two landslide elections as president in the 1950s, but he lost the House in 1954 and needed the vice president to break ties in the Senate.
In his second term, the re-elected "Ike" did not control Capitol Hill, and in the 1958 midterms saw his party drop to just 35 seats in the Senate.

The Senate Democrats first elected in 1958 established a critical mass that would later drive the bipartisan super-majorities needed to break the filibuster and pass the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

In the same era, Democrats in Congress enacted a raft of social programs that would become part of the language, such as Medicare and Medicaid. It was all part of President Lyndon Johnson's "Great Society" program.
What goes up …
But by the midterm year of 1966, much of the energy from LBJ's landslide election in 1964 had been expended — and much more had been siphoned off by his escalation of the war in Vietnam.

Right on time, the midterm arrived, and while the Democrats only took a haircut in the Senate elections they lost a painful 47 seats to the GOP in the House. It gave the party a new lease on life and encouraged its new emphasis on winning in the South. The redirection would guide the party's 1968 presidential candidate, Richard Nixon, and remain a focus for the onetime "Party of Lincoln" for decades to come.
Also in the midterm of 1966, out on the West Coast, a first-time candidate named Ronald Reagan won the governorship of California. People were starting to use the term "Sunbelt."
Yet another midterm correction

But what the midterms of 1966 gave the GOP, the midterms of 1974 would largely take away. Nixon had been elected president in 1968, pursuing what was called a Southern Strategy, and was reelected in a resounding 49-state landslide in 1972.

But by 1974 it had all gone the other way for Nixon. The "Watergate" scandals emerged from his 1972 campaign's use of burglary and electronic surveillance among other unsavory tactics. An attempt to cover it all up blew back on the White House and forced Nixon to resign on the brink of impeachment in August of 1974 – just three months before the midterm for his second term.
The result was a crushing defeat for the GOP, the loss of 48 seats in the House and several more in the Senate (where the Democrats already had more than 60 votes).

While it is tempting to attribute these losses to Nixon's downfall, the country had — to some extent — rallied behind his vice president and successor, Gerald R. Ford. The underlying vulnerability of the GOP was the state of the economy, which was suffering from inflation and the hangover from the oil embargo of 1973 by Arab members of OPEC, the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries.

That embargo, a side effect of the Arab-Israeli "Yom Kippur War" of 1973, temporarily raised the price of crude oil from $3 to $12 and introduced Americans to the phrases "oil shock" and "energy crisis."
Reagan rises and falls

Reagan became the dominant political personality of the 1980s, defeating incumbent President Jimmy Carter in 1980 and winning a 49-state landslide reelection in 1984. He was able to carry in a majority for Republicans in the Senate and establish a kind of working majority in the House with the aid of conservative Democrats in that chamber.

On the strength of those elections, restrained only marginally by the midterm elections of 1982, Reagan began his second term on top of the world. But he soon learned how hard that height can be to hold. As he neared his second midterm, Democrats were on the march nationally and restoring their strength in the more populous Southern states.

In 1986, Democrats defeated six GOP senators who had been elected with Reagan in 1980. The net gain of eight Senate seats gave them a 55-45 majority. In the session of Congress that followed, the Senate would override Reagan's veto of a highway bill and reject his nomination of Robert Bork to the Supreme Court. Reagan was a spent force.
Yet more dramatic reversals to come

Reagan was able to see his vice president, George H.W. Bush, take the White House in 1988, but the party's hopes for momentum into the 1990 midterms were largely unfulfilled. The presidency was also lost in 1992, when Democrat Bill Clinton won a three-way race with just 43% of the popular vote, defeating Bush and independent candidate H. Ross Perot.

Clinton's lack of a majority and list of frustrations in his first term set the stage for a bruising first midterm election in 1994. But what came was beyond bruising. Republicans stormed to their first majority in the House (54 seats net) in 40 years and recaptured the Senate with eight new seats there as well.
The new GOP speaker, Newt Gingrich of Georgia, was a hard-driving partisan who had portrayed the chamber as a House of Ill Repute, the title of a book he and other House Republicans had published.
The use of a "Contract with America" theme promised lower taxes, less corruption and a healthier economy in a compact agenda that had voter appeal as well.

Gingrich explicitly rejected the go-along-get-along attitude of previous GOP leaders in the House and advocated confrontation. The strategy proved less fruitful once he had the Big Gavel, however, and Gingrich spent much of his time as speaker making deals with Clinton. Internal dissatisfaction with him forced him out late in 1998.
Mood swings in the 2000s

In the new century that followed, parties have continued to prosper when their presidential candidates win and give ground in the midterms. George W. Bush was an exception as the president after the terror attacks of September 2001. In his first midterm the following year, theGOP made gains across the board.

But the larger dynamic caught up to him in 2006, when he and his party took what he called "a thumpin'" in elections at all levels. Bush had initially gained popularity with his "War on Terror" and won a second term. But thereafter, his invasion of Iraq had become an albatross. And in 2006 he paid the historic price, losing both his party majorities in the House and Senate. The new majority in the House made Pelosi the first woman speaker in history.

That created an atmosphere of optimism for Democrats, who elected Barack Obama president in 2008 and gave him majorities in the House and Senate (the latter briefly reaching 60 seats). But Obama felt the sting of the midterms early — much as Clinton had. Republicans in 2010 capitalized on an economy still experiencing the recession that had aided Obama's win in 2008. The GOP also capitalized on fears and confusion surrounding the enactment of the Affordable Care Act, or "Obamacare," in 2010.
Echoing his predecessor, Obama called this setback "a shellacking," and settled in to work with a much diminished Senate majority and a Republican-dominated House under Speaker John Boehner.
Obama managed to thread the needle well enough to win a second term for himself in 2012, but the House remained Republican and the Senate followed suit in Obama's second midterm election in 2014.

That second midterm revealed continuing GOP strength across the South and Midwest and to some degree augured the Electoral College majorities that would make Donald J. Trump president in 2016 and 2024.
If the 2020s are to have a midterm with the kind of impact others have had, roughly once a decade for a century, the last opportunity for that to happen is Nov. 3.

If the once-a-decade rhythm has any rationale, in fact, the pressure for a meaningful midterm ought to be building substantially. And in fact most pollsters, pundits and other prognosticators now predict Democrats could flip control of the House and even the Senate as well.

Just as in the previous 10 cycles, the current cycle combines economic concerns (including energy prices) and negative stories about incumbents in various offices. It is the party perceived as being in power that is exposed in a midterm, and it pays a price when voters perceive that party to have lost its mandate — or at least its momentum.

npr.org/2026/10/23/nx-s1-5995508/russia-.headline: Russia steps up election influence efforts in final stretch of midterms
npr.org/2026/10/23/nx-s1-5995508/russia-.author: Shannon Bond

paragraphs.text: Russian operatives are pumping out fabricated claims about Democratic candidates, AI-manipulated videos of celebrities and fake posts impersonating real news outlets in an effort to influence American voters in the final run-up to Election Day.

Researchers who track online influence operations and lawmakers who've been briefed by the intelligence community say Kremlin-backed groups are renewing familiar tactics they've used to sow distrust and discord in previous elections in the U.S. and around the world.

"It's a carnival out there," Rep. Jim Himes of Connecticut, the ranking member on the House intelligence committee, told reporters this week. "They're throwing everything out there to generate a sense of chaos and anarchy."
The goal is to exacerbate divisions, erode confidence in democracy and, crucially, undermine U.S. support for Ukraine.

"At the end of the day, the main issue for Russia is and has to be Ukraine," said Darren Linvill, co-director of Clemson University's Media Forensics Hub, who has tracked foreign propaganda campaigns for years.

Linvill says the Russian playbook is consistent. A false claim or divisive narrative is seeded on social media or on a fake website posing as a news organization or think tank. It's spread by state media, automated fake accounts or, increasingly, paid influencers, in the hopes that it gets seen and repeated by real people.

"In the same way that marketing companies will pay an influencer to disseminate, you know, 'Nike's a great shoe,' the Russians do it with false information and made-up lies," he said. "They use influencers that know their audience, that are part of that audience, and they know how to give that audience a message that they want to hear," Linvill said.
A Russian operation put that playbook to work this week to spread a baseless accusation against a Democratic U.S. Senate candidate.

Linvill and several other research groups attributed them to Russian operators the research community has dubbed Storm-1516. It's known for staging fake videos with actors and laundering their claims through influencer accounts with large followings.

Two fraudulent videos targeting the Senate candidate were posted on Tuesday on X by an account created last month that had few followers. The account's X profile said it was based in the U.S. but the social media platform publicly flagged it as possibly using a proxy such as a virtual private network, which could disguise its location.

The videos were likely created using artificial intelligence, according to Graphika, a research company that analyzes online communities. Linvill said a hallmark of Storm-1516 videos is the use of real actors whose faces are swapped using AI to look like someone else.

The post was immediately shared by a network of 15 accounts Linvill flagged as bots. About 12 hours later, one of the videos was shared in new posts by three X accounts with large followings, which researchers said have previously amplified other narratives attributed to Storm-1516. One of them has solicited paid partnerships on X. Soon other X accounts began resharing the large accounts' posts in replies to politicians and journalists.

One of the two fake videos racked up roughly 857,000 views within 24 hours, according to an analysis by Alethea, a threat intelligence company. By late on Wednesday, the account that first posted the videos and one of the large accounts that reshared the claim had been suspended by X, and the two other large accounts that amplified it had taken down their posts.

In the run-up to the 2024 presidential election, Storm-1516 posted fraudulent videos making similar unfounded accusations against Democratic vice presidential nominee Tim Walz and purporting to show ballots for President Trump being torn up.

Linvill says the operation tries to glom on to narratives that are already circulating among Americans. "It is hard to persuade anybody of anything, ever," he said. "But what you can do is reinforce beliefs."
This election cycle, Russian operations have also spread messages about Democrats turning away from supporting Israel and fabricated news reports accusing Democratic candidates of corruption.

"I increasingly have come to think of Russia as essentially a dark money PAC," said Lisa Kaplan, who founded Alethea. "You know they're going to be running advertisements. You want to understand what's out there. You want to understand if they're actually effective in moving people in one direction or another."
Intelligence officials have long said Russia has favored Trump and targeted Democrats in its efforts to erode support for Ukraine in the U.S.

On Wednesday, Himes and Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., vice chairman of the Senate intelligence committee, told reporters they'd seen a recent classified intelligence report on foreign election meddling showing Russia opposes candidates of either party who have backed Ukraine.
Himes stressed that while Russia and other foreign countries have sought to influence voters, there has been no indication that they have been able to interfere with the actual mechanics of voting.
"Nothing out there suggests that there is either the capability or the intent to do interference, whereas there is a pretty robust influence environment," Himes said.

The same Russian operations now active in the U.S. midterms have also targeted elections this year in France, Germany and elsewhere. They've used AI-generated audio and impersonated politicians, celebrities and media outlets, Graphika said in a new report on Friday.

"They have run this playbook in half a dozen other countries in the past six months throughout Europe. We're just the next in line," Linvill said. "They attack with these same themes. Anything that's going to make a candidate seem degenerate, seem corrupt, seem incapable."
Kaplan of Alethea says this focus on polarizing issues in the final stretch of the election is less about shaping voter's views and more about inflaming anger or fear to affect turnout.
"In these final posts in the lead up to the election, it's really more about evoking that emotion," she said.

Researchers tracking Storm-1516 and other groups say they expect more false claims and fake videos to come, and for these operations to focus on voting and ballot processing in the period immediately surrounding election day.
NPR's Eric McDaniel contributed to this report.

theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/24/britis.headline: British woman dies trying to save sons on Bahamas snorkelling trip
theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/24/britis.author: Harry Taylor

paragraphs.text: A British woman has died in the Bahamas while trying to rescue her two sons after a current swept them away as they were snorkelling.
The Royal Bahamas police force said it had launched an investigation after the death of a 36-year-old woman on Tuesday.
The force said they believed she was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island of Bimini when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.
The police said that in an attempt to rescue her boys, “the woman was also swept away”. The children were later rescued from the water.
The Foreign Office said it was in contact with the woman’s family and was providing support.
Bimini is a small island between the largest landmass in the Bahamas, Andros, and Miami in the US. It is the closest point in the Bahamas to the US mainland.
The island is best known for once being home to Ernest Hemingway and is also home to a world-leading shark research centre.

In a statementposted on social media, the Royal Bahamas police force said: “According to the preliminary report, shortly after 10am, officers at the Alice Town police station received information that a female was unresponsive at the North Bimini ferry dock.

“Officers responded and, upon arrival, learned that the woman had been transported to the local clinic for medical attention, where she was subsequently pronounced dead by a local doctor despite efforts to save her life.
“Preliminary information indicates that the deceased was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.
“In an attempt to rescue her sons, the woman was also swept away.
“She was later rescued and transported to the ferry dock, where CPR was reportedly administered. Foul play is not suspected at this time.”
An autopsy would be carried out to help determine the exact cause of death, the statement said.
A Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office spokesperson said: “Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas.
“We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family.”

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c317kxyknwp2o.headline: Seven missing after tall building collapses in Kenya's capital
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c317kxyknwp2o.author: Aleks Phillips

paragraphs.text: A search and rescue effort is under way to find seven people feared trapped under rubble after a building collapsed in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi.
Dramatic footage shows the bottom floor of the block, thought to have been 16 or 18 storeys, giving way before the rest of the building crumples, sending a plume of dust into the surrounding streets.

Dozens of builders had been working on the upper floors when it collapsed, but managed to emerge largely unscathed. Those missing were thought to have been in shops that had opened at the base of the building.
The incident has raised fresh concerns about construction standards and regulations in Kenya.

The block was under construction when it collapsed on Friday afternoon, with footage showing scaffolding still wrapped around the outside of the building. Officials said 11 shops had already opened on the bottom floors.

Interior ministry official Kipchumba Murkomen said 66 of the 67 construction workers in the building at the time had been able to get out unharmed, while the other had suffered injuries that were not life-threatening.

Images from the scene, in Nairobi's Eastleigh area, show the concrete floors of the building piled on top of one another, as rescue workers saw through metal to get to those believed to have been stuck underneath.

Rescue efforts have been complicated by concerns that excavation using diggers could limit the supply of air to those trapped, prompting emergency responders to cease using them, according to the Daily Nation newspaper.
Questions have emerged about why the building suddenly collapsed and whether it met planning regulations.

Kenya's National Construction Authority said in a statement that it had identified the company behind the development, as well as the architect and structural engineer, but did not say whether the site had been inspected before Friday.
Nairobi Governor Sakaja Johnson told local media that the owners of the building did not have the required paperwork for the building to be occupied.
He urged the national government to give local authorities greater powers to penalise "developers who disregard approved building plans and safety standards".
Building collapses are not uncommon in Nairobi, with poor construction or improper planning often cited as contributing factors.

persuasion.community/p/malcolm-gaskill.headline: Malcolm Gaskill on Why Our Ancestors Weren't as Superstitious as We Think
persuasion.community/p/malcolm-gaskill.author: Yascha Mounk

paragraphs.text: Malcolm Gaskill, Emeritus Professor of Early Modern History at the University of East Anglia, is the author of seven books, including Witchfinders, Between Two Worlds, and The Ruin of All Witches.

In this week’s conversation, Yascha Mounk and Malcolm Gaskell discuss how premodern people understood the boundary between the natural and supernatural worlds, why historians are right—and wrong—to complicate the Enlightenment’s story of progress, and what the persistence of superstition tells us about human nature.
This transcript has been condensed and lightly edited for clarity.

Yascha Mounk: I’m really looking forward to this conversation, in part because I always look forward to conversations where I feel like I learn new things, and this is a topic I don’t know that much about. Obviously generalizing over different places, different times, different individuals—what is the nature of the supernatural beliefs people had for a lot of history before “the Enlightenment”, the rational age? And what do we tend to get wrong about it?

Malcolm Gaskill: In the modern age, we tend to draw sharp distinctions between what we think is rational and irrational, natural and unnatural. If we went back 500 years, we would find varieties of opinion, skepticism, disagreement, and degrees of credulity—perhaps more than we might expect from our ancestors. But we would essentially find a kind of consensus that seems alien to us today.

The consensus is that their world—their visible, tangible world—was much more porous to the unseen world. People didn’t always understand mysterious forces; in fact, a state of puzzlement or bemusement was probably most common. But there was an assumption that there was an invisible world beyond this one, and that there was a relationship between daily life, existence, and some kind of world that existed beyond. That was a basic assumption people had, and it shaped all sorts of engagement that we would broadly call religious, or even superstitious. Essentially it was a relationship between the seen and the unseen, the tangible and the intangible, and the sublime.

Mounk: Part of what characterizes our beliefs today is that we’re quite tempted to believe in all kinds of supernatural, superstitious things, but we check ourselves. When we see a dark shadow at night, we might think for a moment, “gosh, that feels like a ghost,” and then say, “ha, silly me—that’s obviously not what it is.” If we look into the sky and didn’t realize there was going to be an eclipse, we think, “wow, that’s a pretty spooky natural phenomenon,” and then we think, “let me check whether there’s some kind of explanation for this.”

If you didn’t have that kind of mental filter, presumably every time you see something scary out of the corner of your eye, or something happens in nature you don’t have an explanation for because you can’t Google it, you’d naturally come up with stories about what might have caused it.

Gaskill: It’s an evolutionary advantage, in many ways, to try to make sense of chaos. But that often means getting it wrong—looking for patterns in things that aren’t there. There’s a condition called pareidolia, which is really where you join up the dots to make a picture where no picture exists. The mind always imposes patterns on strange, totally natural phenomena that aren’t necessarily understood, and out of them makes stories that are meaningful.

Going back to our late medieval ancestors, they didn’t make those stories out of everything. There was an acceptance that there were natural phenomena—extensions of God’s creation that weren’t direct providences, just things about nature that weren’t completely understood—and there wasn’t a constant need to impose some weird supernatural interpretation on them. This comes into witchcraft accusations too, where people often assume our ancestors didn’t understand so many things about illness and disaster, so they blamed everything on witches. That turns out not to be the case. There is a more rational sense to our ancestors than we might imagine, given the way our benighted forebears were produced by Enlightenment philosophes and rationalists into the 19th century, who wanted to force this difference between them and us so as to make us feel better.

Mounk: Let me push you a little on that. I think there are different levels, or different kinds of description, of what rationality might entail. I certainly think our ancestors were about as smart as we are—they had very similar mental faculties, just less knowledge. There were many parts of the natural world they didn’t understand, and they were raised in a much more religious world, where, as you said, the boundaries between the visible world and the invisible world were much more porous. So I agree that they had reasoning faculties broadly similar to ours, and exercised them. It’s not clear to me that we can get from that claim to the idea that they were somehow less superstitious, or believed in the supernatural any less.

There’s a story I learned in graduate school—I’ll keep it brief—about an anthropologist doing fieldwork, I think in the mountains of Ghana. He wants to be taken to see the rainmaker, but has to spend many months there before they trust him. Finally they take him—he crosses a desert, climbs a dangerous mountain—and he asks, “how do you make it rain?” The rainmaker says, “I have a secret stone. If I turn it a particular way and say a particular incantation, most of the time the next day it rains.” He asks to see the stone, and the rainmaker shows him a child’s marble, saying there’s only one of these stones in the world, it’s unique, and so on.

We hope you’re enjoying the podcast! If you’re a paying subscriber, you can set up the premium feed on your favorite podcast app at writing.yaschamounk.com/listen. This will give you ad-free access to the full conversation, plus all full episodes and bonus episodes we have in the works! If you aren’t, you can set up the free, limited version of the feed—or, better still, support the podcast by becoming a subscriber today!
If you have any questions or issues setting up the full podcast feed on a third-party app, please email leonora.barclay@persuasion.community

Later, back in the city, the anthropologist acquires another marble, asks to be taken back to the rainmaker, and says, “look what I brought you—here’s another one of these stones.” The rainmaker is astonished—he thought there was only one. The anthropologist asks, “well, do you think it’s going to work?” The rainmaker thinks for a moment and says, “I don’t know—shall we give it a try?”

This was presented to me by Richard Tuck, who was leading the seminar, as a response to a classmate of mine who was arguing that means-ends reasoning is just a Western construct. It isn’t—this rainmaker has means-ends reasoning. He’s not an idiot; he’s capable of intelligent thought, he has a concept of one thing having a causal impact on another, he even has an empirical mindset: let’s see whether, if I do this, it rains tomorrow or not. What he doesn’t have is a scientific method, and a separation of the visible world from a non-visible one.

So what I easily buy is that our ancestors reasoned critically about phenomena in the world, but were still so steeped in a totally different thought-world that there’s a stark distinction between mainstream beliefs today—setting aside the other kinds of superstitious and religious belief that still exist today, which we can talk about—and the mainstream world then.

Gaskill: It is. There are a couple of things in that. One is the critical thinking required to distinguish between the likelihood of something being totally natural versus the imposition of a demon or an angel.

The other is that it’s very situational. This is where, in a lot of the so-called post-secular scholarship about these phenomena, emotions come in. People’s beliefs—a bit like your story, which is embedded in a very specific situation, a dialogue, an encounter between cultures—don’t float in the air. It’s easy to talk about belief systems and sets of ideas, but a lot of the time these are lived practices. One of the things anthropologists would often do—I think they’re perhaps more sensitive now—but think about someone like Evans-Pritchard going out to the Azande in Africa in the 1930s: really, it’s about trying to reduce everything they believed to functions. He was right, up to a point—these beliefs were hard to describe in the abstract, but you could see them in what people did. They weren’t inferior forms of reasoning; they were extremely embedded in culture and practice.

Sometimes what these anthropologists found—going back to your story—is that the peoples they studied were so baffled by the idea that someone was trying to fit these things into some kind of intellectual template that they had a bit of fun with them. One of the things anthropologists were slow to understand is that these people had a sense of humor, and realized they could play along.

So if we think of these only as sets of ideas and beliefs—belief systems—we slightly miss the point. We need to think of them as embedded in real-life situations and in emotions. Some of our own ideas and feelings—I’ll speak for myself, I won’t speak for you—that we’d espouse confidently and publicly might waver a bit under emotional pressure. It goes back to the old “no atheists in a foxhole” idea. We see this throughout the 20th century: men in battle become more superstitious. So people who, in daily life, wouldn’t hold these ideas, had feelings connected to them that were latent but surfaced because of the particular emotional stresses of the situation. I do agree with you—it’s just another way of thinking about these ideas and beliefs, as practices, as feelings and emotions, rather than codifying them the way anthropologists often wanted to.

Mounk: That I buy. Let me say something more general for a moment. I think there’s a broader historiographical tendency to complicate the easy distinctions we draw, and sometimes I worry it’s a bit of a historian’s idée fixe—partly because you want to rebel against the generation before you, and partly because historians love when things are complicated. The Dark Ages, it turns out, weren’t so dark; things were actually quite good. Secularization—well, in fact, today isn’t really secular, the continuity is much bigger than the discontinuity.

I’m always torn about those, because I think there’s a caricatured view of the Dark Ages as a miserable time of benighted people having terrible lives, which misses a lot of what’s interesting, fascinating, and valuable about those centuries. At the same time, if you compare how long people got to live, the condition of servitude a lot of people endured, and the extent to which the knowledge of the ancient world had been lost—with the rediscovery of these forms of reasoning, the Renaissance, and later the Enlightenment, not yet having happened—something about the short formula “Dark Ages” is not entirely wrong.

It seems to me that when it comes to these questions of how similar or how different the world of belief is, in the era before the Enlightenment and perhaps before the Renaissance, there’s a similar dynamic. I agree that “these people were stupid, superstitious morons, and today we have these great enlightened people who would never fall for anything like that” is far too simplistic—first, because those were people with our natures and our intelligence, not stupid morons, human beings trying their best to make sense of their condition the way we do today, and second, because there’s a lot of weird belief and superstition, modern-day witch hunts and so on, around today too.

So I buy all that. And yet something in me rebels against the idea that there are no distinctions at all. The faculties of the human mind have, by and large, not changed—the mixture of incredible intelligence and venality that characterizes human beings today also characterized us as a species 500 or a thousand years ago.

The other thing you’ve alluded to—I may be getting my history of religion wrong, but I think this was originally Feuerbach’s idea—is that we tend to ascribe to God the faculties we wish for ourselves, and perhaps, more broadly, that God fills a psychological need for us. When we’re really scared, we cling to superstitious practices and beliefs to reassure us. That was true 500 years ago, and it’s true if you’re in a foxhole today, and it’s true whenever the world is scary and you don’t quite understand what’s going on in politics or society. That seems true today too.

So I buy the similarities. And yet it does seem to me very different to have a world in which all the authorities, secular and ecclesiastical, interpret everything through religion and belief in the supernatural, where everything is imbued with symbolic importance—versus a world in which, much as our human nature might tempt us toward that, the authorities pride themselves on not doing it, and we have a scientific method.

Gaskill: There’s simplification in both directions. A grand narrative that’s politically inflected, polemical, even propagandist—think of fascist narratives of history in the 20th century, or communist simplifications of history—these are highly tendentious versions, simplifications with a particular end.

We can go in the other direction too—importing backwards the idea that Newton was “a scientist” unlike anybody else, or importing back the idea that most people were kind of benighted peasants who were all stupid. This comes back to context. Historians do like to complicate things, but that’s not a bad thing—good historians, anyway, try to get between those two extremes: that our ancestors are just like us, or that our ancestors are totally different. It’s largely situational.

When one looks at witchcraft trials, and at the behavior of juries, they’re very discerning. There are different layers and degrees of rationality, and a bedrock of belief they don’t really have the intellectual wherewithal to challenge. There used to be a debate—I know it’s still going on—about whether there were actual atheists in the Renaissance, because it was supposedly impossible to hold that thought, to really believe there was nothing beyond. I never bought that. I always thought it was possible.

Mounk: Tell us about some of those witch trials. This is obviously meant to be a caricature, but I tend to think of the Monty Python sketch—“she’s a witch, she’s a witch,” and immediately the crowd rushes to drown the person, and then she drowns, and I guess she wasn’t a witch. There’s this image of an obviously stupid, idiotic process that everybody gets on board with. You describe the reality as much more complicated and subtle than that. So what did a witchcraft trial actually look like?

Gaskill: Most of the time there were no witchcraft trials. There may well have been suspicions within a village, but the assumption in that Monty Python version is that as soon as you couldn’t explain something, or there was someone you didn’t like, you found out the nearest witch, and there was no legal process—you chased them to the nearest tree and they were hanged, and that was it. Everybody felt an emotional release, and then you got back to normal until the next cow or chicken died, and then you found somebody else, or someone else you didn’t like.

It’s so far removed from the truth. I’ve spent the last 30 years telling people their myths about witchcraft are not right—not because I’m a natural killjoy, but because it misses the opportunity to understand other ways our forebears’ mentalities worked. Typically, there is a bedrock of belief in witchcraft, but most people had no direct experience of it whatsoever. There’s a point where this falls off the written record and we can’t be absolutely sure, but the written records we do have—which are actually copious for the 16th and 17th centuries—give us a pretty good view of the number of witch trials: probably about 110,000 across the 16th and 17th centuries. That seems like a lot for a crime we’d think imaginary, but it’s far fewer than you’d often read. From the Enlightenment onward, the figures got bigger and bigger—they went up into the millions.
Mounk: Also, by the way, against a population far, far smaller than today’s.

Gaskill: Infinitely smaller. The number of people who actually lived—not just the population at one time, but across, say, 1400 to 1700—is absolutely enormous. The number of witch trials is really very small, and very variegated over time and place.
Mounk: 110,000 doesn’t strike me as very small. I don’t want to nitpick, but 110,000 is a lot.

Gaskill: It’s a lot for a crime you and I would agree was imaginary, that people couldn’t possibly have committed. But it’s much smaller than people often imagine. There’s a kind of illusion, I think, between the idea of the Holocaust in the 20th century and what was happening before that—the numbers creep up into the millions and it feels like a very organized thing, a kind of technocratic genocide, which the Holocaust, in the 20th century, really was. But the witch trials are much more patchy. There isn’t a big central authority driving it. Within nations, typically, the central authorities are the restraining forces. The really bad witch hunts happen not because of the strength of law, but because of its weakness in that area.

So it does go against the prevailing narrative we’ve inherited about what the witch trials meant. What those stories have typically done is made our ancestors look stupid, venal, and weak. Whereas actually—taking England, which I know best, though not exclusively—you really have maybe a thousand witch trials across two centuries. That’s far fewer than people assume. It always surprises people that a thousand is a lot, but it also surprises them that you’re going to get 500 convictions out of that—500 executions for a crime that didn’t exist seems like a lot. But in half those cases, jurors stood there and said, “we don’t know,” and didn’t want to hang somebody for a crime they weren’t absolutely sure of, because the evidence wasn’t strong enough for the conviction needed to send someone to the gallows.

Mounk: I don’t know how extensive the record is on the trials that led to conviction versus the ones that didn’t. If you were defending, what kind of argument would you make? Is the prosecution’s case something like: she cursed this family, somebody heard her curse this family—here’s the witness who says, “yeah, I heard her curse her family,” and then three days later the youngest child fell ill and died? And the defense would say—what would they say? “If she didn’t curse them, there’s no evidence of that,” or, “she was seen in the woods collecting dark materials,” and the defense says, “she would always go there to get firewood”? Am I imagining something too muddled?

Gaskill: You are. There is no defense—not before the 18th century. In fact, typically the accused didn’t even get to say anything, because they weren’t expected to speak on oath about themselves—they weren’t on oath. Sometimes they were allowed to say something, and they’d just say, “I never did any such thing.” But it’s not the modern adversarial system. Quite apart from anything else, it’s all over incredibly quickly. The speed of it, I think, sometimes works in favor of the accused, and sometimes it doesn’t.

Mounk: I’m trying to move away from my memory of the Monty Python scene—“she’s a witch, let’s burn her”—and you’re telling me, well, actually there’s a trial, and half the time—but the more I learn about it, the more I feel like I’m getting back to the Monty Python scene. Perhaps there’s—I don’t actually know when British judges started wearing wigs, perhaps that’s later too—but there’s a theatrical nature to the court proceedings. It sounds like there’s some random accusation read out, then a very brief process that doesn’t seem to involve presenting evidence in any structured way, and then the jury somehow comes to a decision. It sounds like a coin flip.

Gaskill: No, it’s not a coin flip. The English legal system is built on an amateur principle—it is, really, even into the 19th century. There’s a lot of resistance in English culture to professionalism of any sort. It’s one of the reasons it was hard to introduce the police force in the 19th century—people thought you shouldn’t pay good citizens to enforce the law.
Mounk: I thought you were going to say it’s one of the reasons Boris Johnson became prime minister.

Gaskill: That’s another area we could go into another time. Corruption is inherent, and they sought to limit it by not paying people to do things. The judges are the only professionals in the system—they’re based in London, they ride out regularly on circuits, and “deliver the jail”: all the accused criminals who’ve gathered there over the last six months are delivered from the jail. That’s why they rattle through the cases—not just witch trials, but whatever’s coming their way. A clerk reads what’s called a jail calendar, a list of names, and people are constantly brought through the dock. So there’s a kind of farcical, almost tragicomic amateurism to all this, but within it there’s this strange discernment, this unexpected skepticism and hesitation.

I think what the jurors feel is an abhorrence at the idea that people might engage with the devil to harm their neighbors, and they may well hold that bedrock assumption that it’s possible. But when they see this before their eyes, I think they, and magistrates, often think, God, this is just neighbors at war, and really you should shut up and go home. We don’t know how many cases were brought before a magistrate—just some bloke interrupting his dinner, a bang on the door, two neighbors standing there, “what is it now?” We don’t know how often he said, “you two really do need to live with each other, and she’s not a witch, look at her, she’s just a pathetic old woman.” It’s a shame we don’t have that record, because I firmly believe that kind of critical thinking, in that particular situation, knowing the personalities involved, was prevalent. It may even have been typical.
Mounk: Right—“this person is just a troublemaker, they continually accuse people of all kinds of things, they’re just querulous, shut up and go back home.”
Gaskill: I really think so. It just doesn’t leave any records.

Mounk: They do have very common characteristics. There’s nearly always a huge tension between religious visions of the future. In southern Germany, it’s often conflict within very small city-states for religious and political dominance. It isn’t theological as much as what they would call themselves “confessional states”—who’s going to be in charge, and what is their confession? Are they Lutheran, Catholic, or what? What religious politics are they going to impose on the whole of their territory, and how is that going to define them? Within southern Germany, in the era of the Reformation, there’s this very intense conflict between these states, and within them, and that produces a kind of toxic energy, a toxic set of emotions, which results in an atmosphere of the possibility that these areas are under a kind of demonic attack, and that it’s existential to do something about it. That characterizes Salem, Massachusetts, in the 1690s, as well.

But it also tends to be that these witch hunts burn themselves out quite quickly. Then there’s a moment of reflection, a restoration of order, because witch crazes are seen as emblems of disorder and chaos. In some of those cases in southern Germany, there are so many people being sucked into this vortex of accusation that there’s a moment of clarity afterward—what on earth are we doing? There are even cases in early 17th-century southern Spain where local people think they’re doing the work of the Inquisition, because they feel the devil is abroad, and they start rounding up accused witches, penning them up, waiting to be congratulated by the officials of the Inquisition, who come round and say, “what on earth are you doing? Let them go.” And they’re rather shame-faced, and they do.

So the historians, I think, looking back on the crazes—and they are exceptional, the exceptions that prove the rule, the rule being restraint—look back on them as symbols of weakness, religious disorder, and weaknesses of governance. That’s what happened at Salem, and it happened in England in the 1640s. England only has one really intense witch hunt, and during it the characteristics were civil war, disruption of the normal law courts, a heightened sense of religiosity, the feeling that England had been backsliding in religion and that Puritans needed to come forward. Young men took matters into their own hands. All those things made that witch hunt possible, but it burns itself out very quickly. In the very first witch trial, in the summer of 1645, you already find dissenting voices in the courtroom—not saying witchcraft doesn’t exist, but saying, hang on, does that testimony really stand up? Can we really execute someone on that basis?

Witch finders—professional witch hunters—always aim to be charismatic. They want to go amongst people and say, look, you probably have your doubts, let me galvanize you, let me lead you through this. Witch finders work precisely because people are naturally hesitant—they’re not sure whether this is witchcraft or not, or they don’t have the confidence to go to law because they feel they won’t be believed.

Mounk: Very interesting. We’re going to skip over a couple of centuries very rapidly here—Enlightenment, age of science—finally we’re all good rationalists who would never engage in witch hunts, who have banished superstition to the weird fringes of our society, where people dabble in tarot cards or horoscopes. What’s wrong with that picture?

Gaskill: It’s such an attractive picture, and it’s a kind of fable we tell ourselves, because it makes us feel like we’re the children of the Enlightenment, able to push that stuff into our background. Of course, that arc of progress into the 19th century was hugely broken by the First World War. Symbolically, one of the things it said was that maybe the age of reason and progress, and industrialization, had led to this—and this is often characterized as a moment not just of slaughter, but of a kind of collective madness.

The First World War also created—well, the myth of a lost generation, but also millions of grieving families who couldn’t deal with their grief the way they might have in an age of enlightenment, an age when spirits and things had been laid to rest. This is where you get the huge rise in the popularity of spiritualism, and indeed in all sorts of religions and practices we’d consider New Age—Buddhism, for example, really takes off in the 1920s, because somehow the old patriarchal forms of organized religion and the churches that had so stood behind the armies of the First World War seemed to have gotten it wrong.

So there’s this disruption in the confidence in that arc of progress, and I think we’ve been living with it ever since—and of course it goes into the Second World War. I think we still want to tell ourselves—and, going back to your earlier point, historians aren’t always these loose relativists about everything who say, well, medieval medicine was just different. No, it wasn’t just different—it was worse. You can make those kinds of value judgments. Nobody wants to be operated on by a medieval surgeon consulting the phases of the moon before making an incision on the operating table. That’s not fun.

But at the same time, I think the things we’ve wanted to suppress in ourselves can surface at moments of extraordinary societal and emotional pressure, and the First World War was certainly one of those. There’s also something about class and education in this—not just the forced suppression of these things within ourselves. Large parts of Western Europe remained relatively unchanged in terms of people’s reliance on harvests, the rhythms of life, the reliance on the seasons. I used to live in a village north of Cambridge—I lived there in the 1990s—and in the 1920s, the beliefs in witchcraft and magic in that village, only ten miles north of Cambridge, were almost completely unchanged from the 17th century. Why? Because people were uneducated, and the rhythm of their lives hadn’t really changed at all. They had the belief in maleficent witchcraft, in counter-magic, the idea that livestock were under attack. It’s extraordinary, but there it was.
Mounk: Whereas today one might argue that the villages around Cambridge may well be rational, whereas the fellows and faculty of Cambridge appear to be less and less so—but that’s a different point.

Gaskill: Well, I do have things to say about that too. I’m not part of Cambridge University anymore, so I couldn’t possibly comment. I think the world has changed. But there is the capacity to act in a mad, collective, emotional way. To take an example like Brexit—Brexit wasn’t a rational thing. Going back to Boris Johnson, and David Cameron—there were lies told about what this meant and what was happening, which people believed because they were very emotionally attached to a version of Britain that had existed during and after the Second World War. That weakness was exploited. In a sense, it conformed to many of the characteristics of superstition.

Mounk: That’s where I get off board a little. It’s interesting—perhaps you’re seeing the glass half full and I’m seeing it half empty, or the other way around, I’m not sure which way to put it. I recognize that in our society today we have a real attraction to superstitious beliefs—people talking about horoscopes get enormous audiences on TikTok and Instagram, and there’s a kind of new spirituality among a lot of younger people. But there’s a question about how seriously people really, deep down, take it. Do they engage with horoscopes as a kind of fun indulgence, or do they actually let it guide their lives in the same way?

By and large, when we’re talking about Europe, at least, and probably North America, people don’t let horoscopes choose their partners, and they certainly don’t consult them before a doctor performs an operation. Perhaps if you meet somebody you like, you look at the horoscope and get a little titillation, thinking about whether you’re well aligned or not. Perhaps if you really believe in horoscopes quite a lot, and you’re already in a fight with your boyfriend anyway, and the horoscope says he’s no good for you, you use that as an internal reason to say, you see, I really should break up with him. But I think the number of people who fall deeply in love with somebody they’re excited about, but don’t go for it because the horoscope says they’re the wrong person, is probably quite limited.

I agree there are these various forms of spiritual and superstitious belief people have—perhaps they don’t want to live on the thirteenth floor of an apartment, or sit in the thirteenth row on an airplane, or they wake up on Friday the thirteenth and think, ooh, got to be a little careful today. But even for the people who engage in that, it’s a little at the edges of their lives—which I think is different from, as you were saying, the doctor who consults the phase of the moon before doing an operation.

And then there’s this kind of metaphorical application of all this to our political adversaries or enemies, which I think is quite different. First, I was against Brexit—partly because I think, for all its flaws, the European Union is on the whole something sensible, and because, having grown up on the Continent, being among other things a German citizen, and having gone to university in England, having studied history at Cambridge, the idea that I could no longer move to Britain whenever I wanted, and feel welcome there the same way, was personally upsetting to me. But I just think that saying the people who voted for Brexit were superstitious, in the same way that people who believed in witchcraft are superstitious, that they weren’t being rational, flattens a distinction between people’s political values—the ways they might care about sovereignty, or have genuine concerns about a democratic deficit in the European Union, or the sense that they don’t really have control over migration, and that there’s too much migration too fast, and so on. All of which you can disagree with—you can say a lot of people regret the vote for Brexit given that a lot of what was promised didn’t come true, you can say there were falsehoods cited in the campaign—but to simply dismiss it as “people voted for Brexit because they’re superstitious”?

Gaskill: No, I agree with everything you’ve just said. I don’t think voting for Brexit was irrational. I think some of the evidence put before people was misleading, and they bought into it uncritically because it tended toward the way they already wanted to go. The idea of getting out of Europe is just an old-fashioned, jingoistic, little-Englander, xenophobic attitude that goes back generations, and I think it just touched that nerve. My father voted for Brexit, my father-in-law voted for it—it’s not like it’s divided our families. I don’t think they’re stupid; these are clever people. And I think, with the change of government, we might even be steering back toward the possibility—we’re told a majority of the population now want to rejoin the European Union. That doesn’t make me think, “look, see, you idiots, you got it wrong.” I think it just means the emotional complexion of the Brexit and post-Brexit era has steered back in another direction.

Maybe the thing is we’ve had a lot of evidence in the last ten years about economic growth, or the lack of it, which we can actually make decisions on. I just don’t think there was the evidence base to leave the European Union, but there was a very strong emotional, nationalist feeling, and nationalism doesn’t really care a lot about facts—what it cares about is inflaming, empowering stories. That’s what I think we had. So I wouldn’t characterize it quite that uncharitably. Any Brexiteers listening in the United Kingdom—I hear you, I understand you, I don’t agree with you, and I hope you think that maybe it’s time to try it the way we tried it before, and that really wasn’t quite so bad.

Going back to something you said before we got into Brexit—the difference between the symbolic, the metaphorical, and the literal: going back to anthropologists, I think sometimes they wanted to find myth and metaphor in sub-Saharan Africa, whereas actually these things weren’t as metaphorical, or as literal, as the anthropologists wanted them to be. They could be either. People could perfectly well tell a story, some origin myth, that was just a form of entertainment. There was an expectation that things needed to be literal or metaphorical that got in the way, whereas really it doesn’t necessarily need to be either.

This idea of—call it paradox, or cognitive dissonance, or aporia, whatever you want to call it—is true in 17th-century England, and you could find it true among the Azande of Africa: that you can think two things at once, that they can coexist. There’s another anthropologist, Nils Bubandt, a Danish anthropologist who wrote a book called The Empty Seashell—an absolutely fantastic book, about an island called Buli in the Pacific, where witchcraft is very sinister there precisely because it’s absent. That’s the paradox—it’s not because there are witches everywhere, it’s because people sense them peripherally but don’t actually have any direct experience of them.

So, again, we think about the ancients, we think about the myths, and we think, well, that was their religion. It could be—but actually, the possibility is that these are just symbolic stories that communicate moral truths, not actually about how the gods created the universe, and they could hold those two things together simultaneously, or depending on the context. I think that’s one of the things that’s hard to grasp—that they were working in a different kind of framework. It wasn’t just the ideas themselves that were different or similar.

In the rest of this conversation, Yascha and Malcolm discuss superstition in the present day and the complexity of human behavior in times of collective madness. This part of the conversation is reserved for paying subscribers…

npr.org/2026/10/24/nx-s1-6014612/medicar.headline: Is your Medicare Advantage plan ending next year? Here's what to know
npr.org/2026/10/24/nx-s1-6014612/medicar.author: Emily Pisacreta

paragraphs.text: A slew of Medicare Advantage plans are disappearing for next year, leaving seniors in many areas with fewer options. In 193 counties across the country, no plans are offered at all.

Medicare's annual open enrollment period kicked off October 15 and runs until December 7, and seniors enrolled in those privatized Medicare plans that are closing in certain markets should carefully review their options.

Medicare Advantage means private insurers run Medicare for older Americans who choose it over traditional Medicare, where the federal government itself administers the program. More than half of the 70 million Americans in Medicare choose Medicare Advantage. It's popular because it covers services like vision and dental, often with lower premiums than traditional Medicare. It also often folds in the "Part D" drug benefit, simplifying that decision.

But a downside of Medicare Advantage is that companies can pick and choose where they offer plans. If a certain community is not profitable, a company can leave that market. And that has been happening on an increasingly large scale the last three years, according to research published in JAMA.
Who is affected
Big swaths of rural America are losing Medicare Advantage choices and so are some major metro areas.

Last year, 2.9 million seniors were in Medicare Advantage plans that closed up shop, according to JAMA. This year, an analysis of insurance company announcements by An Arm and A Leg podcast, shows at least 2 million people will be affected. Other preliminary estimates range from 3.2 million to 5 million seniors. About 35 million people are enrolled in Medicare Advantage.

According to an analysis of federal data by the health policy research organization KFF, the 193 counties that will have zero Medicare Advantage plans are mostly rural. Last year that number was about 120 counties without a plan offered.

KFF's numbers also show that there will be far fewer plans offered in some metro areas. Dallas, Minneapolis, Seattle, Houston and Portland all have between a quarter and a third fewer Medicare Advantage plans for seniors.
What happens next

If your plan is ending, and you don't choose another, the insurance company will assign you to another Medicare Advantage plan or the government will enroll you in traditional Medicare — but without a supplemental or drug plan.

If you want to switch from Medicare Advantage to traditional Medicare and your plan is ending, you can enroll in a Medicare supplemental plan — also known as Medigap — without the same restrictions that you would normally have. If you have a pre-existing condition that has prevented you from enrolling in Medigap before, that could be good news.
Another wrinkle this year is that insurance companies can cap enrollments on some of the Medicare Advantage plans that they do offer.
Which means: If you wait to sign up, a plan you want might already be full.
The companies are supposed to enroll people on a first-come, first-serve basis — and not cherry-pick customers based on health conditions, age, or demographics.
Another reason not to delay is that with so many people on the hunt for new plans, it may take longer than usual to get help.
How and where to find help
Here are some tips for navigating Medicare open enrollment this year:

• Find out if your plan is still offered: First, check your mail. Medicare Advantage plans that are closing should have sent letters the first week in October. You can also log in to your account on Medicare.gov to check your plan's status for next year.

• Try calling your SHIP: There's a State Health Insurance Assistance Program — known as a "SHIP" — in every state to help seniors with Medicare. The name's not easy to remember or particularly descriptive, but it's free, mandated by the federal government, and the staff and volunteers are required to give you unbiased information on all available options. Find your state in the directory at shiphelp.org. Your county may have a specific number that you can find on your state's SHIP website.

• Look for local Medicare counseling services: Friends, family, leaders at your place of worship, and the constituent services of your local elected officials may have the scoop on where you can get one-on-one help. The nonprofit Medicare Rights Center also has a national helpline, and a well-organized library of online guides.

• Brokers can be helpful, but be savvy: You want a broker who's going to talk with you about all your options — including switching to traditional Medicare and a supplemental plan. Ask if they sell plans from all available insurance carriers. And ask if they answer questions about your plan year-round, because insurance never stops being confusing.

• Double check what you see on Medicare.gov: Medicare's Plan Finder allows you to search plans online. But lists of doctors and drugs that are covered can sometimes be wrong. To be safe, double check with your doctor's office or a SHIP counselor, broker, or other Medicare assistor.

• Don't share your personal information with services you find online: Be careful where you share your personal information like your phone number. Some online agencies will sell your information, leading to spam calls and potentially even scam artists.

• Be mindful of the deadlines: Open enrollment for Medicare runs October 15, 2026 through December 7, 2026. The coverage starts January 1, 2027. If your plan is ending, you qualify for a "special enrollment period" to give you a little more time — until February 28, 2027. (For coverage that starts January 1, 2027, enroll by December 31.)
Emily Pisacreta is the senior producer for An Arm and a Leg, a podcast about the cost of healthcare produced in partnership with KFF Health News and distributed by KUOW, Seattle's NPR member station.

npr.org/2026/10/24/nx-s1-6012804/birth-r.headline: U.S. birth rate drops to record low, but older women are having more babies
npr.org/2026/10/24/nx-s1-6012804/birth-r.author: Brian Mann

paragraphs.text: Sarah Harris was 37 years old when she gave birth to her daughter Bridget last year. She describes motherhood as equal parts joy and exhaustion. "When you have a baby in your mid-30s, what you gain in wisdom and experience you also lose in terms of energy," Harris says with a laugh.

Harris, who lives in Vermont, was laid off from a job four months after Bridget was born. She says she's still figuring out what her career and her life will look like with a child. Harris thinks a lot of women are like her. They're wrestling with financial uncertainty and waiting much later to choose pregnancy.

There's also the high cost of raising a child, which Harris said convinced her that one is enough. "I think in another era or another life or another scenario, I might have had more children," Harris says. "I think we're in a difficult societal moment and so that's absolutely affecting people's reproductive choices."

Harris is, in fact, part of a slow revolution in what motherhood and parenting look like in the United States The latest report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention found the general fertility rate for women fell by 1% to a new record low in 2025. That continues a two-decade trend toward fewer children.
Steep drops in parenting among U.S. women in their 20s

The one-year drop for 20-somethings was even more eye-catching. "Certainly the 6% decline in the birthrate for women age 20 to 24 is noteworthy," said Brady Hamilton, a demographer at the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics who co-authored the report. He noted that women in their late teens also saw a 7% decline.

A separate study released last month by the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta found Gen Z women, in their late teens and twenties, "are dramatically less likely to want children" compared with U.S. women of previous generations.

"Several factors have been identified as contributing to this lower desire to have children, such as increased labor market opportunities and agency among women, rising financial costs, changing priorities, and [concerns about] maternal mortality," the study found.

Dr. Tanise Branche, medical director of labor and delivery at Temple Health, a health, research and training network in Philadelphia, told NPR more of her younger women patients are following a different life script.
"They're starting to focus not necessarily just on what they can bring to kids, but what's going to be best for them," she says.
Women in their 30s and 40s saw "significant" birthrate increase
Meanwhile, the latest CDC data shows a small but significant increase in older women, ages 30 to 45, who are choosing to become pregnant.
Branche says more women, including herself, are building careers and stable lives before becoming mothers.

Branche is currently pregnant with her fourth child. "I will be 43 with my last delivery and I started this reproductive journey at 37," she said. "I see the net positive being that we have a choice."
Fewer children because of choice — and affordability

As a consequence of this shift, there are fewer children now in the U.S. The population under age 18 is falling steadily, according to the U.S. Census Bureau, dropping by more than 1 million from 2010 to 2020.
Some experts also believe women would choose to have more kids if they could afford them and had proper supports that include affordable housing, daycare and health insurance.

"The fact that there are a lot of people who still say they want families, but don't feel like they're able to have them [is a concern]," says Anna Louie Sussman, author of a new book on parenting choices called Inconceivable. "Young people say, I can barely take care of myself I can't imagine taking care of someone else."

Sussman herself is part of the trend toward delayed motherhood. Because of her own concerns about affordability and her career, she froze her eggs and waited to have her child until she was in her early 40s.
"I do feel lucky that I'm a little further along professionally than I would have been in my 20s or even 30s," she said.

As women build different lives and birthrates keep falling, the U.S. is changing. The median age is rising rapidly, reaching 39.4 years old in 2025. More states, including Vermont where Sarah Harris lives, are seeing actual population decline, according to the Census Bureau.
"I think about it a lot because I live in a very small place where we're hoping to keep the doors of our elementary school open for as long as we can," she says.

theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/24/kim-jo.headline: Kim Jong-un crosses over newly opened bridge into China
theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/24/kim-jo.author: Raphael Rashid

paragraphs.text: Kim Jong-un has travelled to China over a newly opened bridge marking the North Korean leader’s first known trip abroad in more than a year, South Korean officials have said.

A government source told the Yonhap news agency on Saturday that Kim had arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong, in Liaoning province, after taking a train from Pyongyang to Sinuiju and crossing the New Yalu River Bridge.
Yonhap also reported that the Chinese premier, Li Qiang, had travelled to the city. Kim’s trip was not announced in advance and had not been confirmed by Pyongyang or Beijing by Saturday evening.
China will mark the anniversary on Sunday of its entry into the 1950-53 Korean war on the North’s side.

Japan’s Kyodo news agency said on Saturday that traffic controls had been imposed around the bridge and near a museum devoted to China’s role in the war, and that hotel bookings nearby had been restricted.
Diplomatic sources told the agency the measures were linked to a visit by a senior North Korean official.

The 3km bridge opened in mid-October, 12 years after China finished building it, after being held up by delays on the North Korean side. In early September, North Korea and Russia opened the first road bridge across their own short border leaving Pyongyang newly linked by road to its main backers.

The trip is Kim’s sixth visit to China and his first since September 2025, when he attended a military parade in Beijing alongside the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin. Xi visited Pyongyang in June, his first trip there in seven years.

Relations with South Korea, meanwhile, have deteriorated. Kim’s sister, Kim Yo Jong, has issued about 10 statements criticising Seoul since late September, a frequency South Korea’s unification ministry has called unusual, and has also announced plans to resume loudspeaker broadcasts at the border within days.
Xi will host the Apec summit in Shenzhen on 18-19 November, which has fuelled speculation about a meeting between Kim and Donald Trump.
Reuters reported on Friday, however, that US and South Korean officials see little chance of Kim meeting the US president this year.

cnbc.com/2026/10/24/trump-ai-data-center.headline: Trump is pushing a massive AI buildout. His own voters are wary of what comes with it
cnbc.com/2026/10/24/trump-ai-data-center.author: Luke Fountain

paragraphs.text: President Donald Trump has cast America's artificial intelligence race with China as a national-security imperative, pushing faster development of the technology and an immense buildout of the data centers and power infrastructure needed to fuel it.

But the new CNBC All-America Economic Survey reveals a growing political tension beneath that agenda: Republican voters broadly support the push for AI development, but many oppose building the sprawling infrastructure needed to power it in their own backyards.

Nearly 55% of MAGA supporters want companies to keep developing advanced AI while Congress works on regulations, versus 27% who favor a pause. But only 29% would support a data center within 10 miles of their home, while 40% oppose one. Among all Republicans and Republican-leaning voters — not just those who identify themselves with the MAGA movement — those who say they would support a data center near their home falls to 24%.
Across the electorate, 63% don't want a nearby AI data center and just 13% support one. Democrats lead the opposition: 80% oppose nearby facilities while just 4% support them.
That resistance is increasingly forcing Trump and vulnerable Republicans who once championed data centers to recalibrate as they head into a bleak midterm election environment for the party.

"Many people are annoyed by these data centers," said Brad Carson, a former Democratic congressman from Oklahoma and co-founder of Public First Action PAC, an AI-industry-backed political group pushing for stronger regulation and safeguards.
