"People are also strongly insistent upon reasonable guardrails of AI, and that's going to be hard to beat."

The CNBC survey of 1,000 registered voters nationwide was conducted Oct. 14-18 by Hart Research Associates and Public Opinion Strategies and has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 percentage points. The data-center proximity question was asked of a half-sample of roughly 500 voters, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.38 percentage points.
Read the full survey results here.
The politics have shifted from the early AI boom, when Washington and Silicon Valley sold the technology as an avenue for investment, growth and American dominance.

But as the buildout accelerates, its physical costs are becoming harder to ignore. Communities are fighting data centers over spiking electric bills, soaring electricity and water demand, noise, land use and taxpayer subsidies. Coupled with job-displacement fears from AI, opponents now point to the facilities as a physical symbol of who benefits from the boom and who gets stuck with the bill.
The industry rejects that framing.

“The data center industry provides significant, tangible benefits,” said Dan Diorio of the Data Center Coalition, pointing to jobs, investment and tax revenue while adding that operators are committed to “paying for the energy we use."

But when asked their top concerns if Republicans retain Congress, 18% of voters in the survey cited a failure to regulate AI and data centers. That tied continued military efforts in Iran and outranked continued Immigration and Customs Enforcement deportations at 15%, cuts to health insurance subsidies at 10% and an extension of Trump's tariffs at 5%.
Even among voters who want Republicans to retain control, 17% cited weak AI and data center oversight — second only to a failure to bring down prices.
GOP strategists have taken note.

In August, the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned AI companies that data center backlash was threatening Sen. Jon Husted's reelection in Ohio, calling the issue a midterm "sleeper" that could sour politicians nationwide on future projects, Axios reported.

As Ohio lieutenant governor in 2024, Husted helped announce a $10 billion Amazon Web Services expansion, calling AI facilities "crucial to America's economic superiority." Now, in a tight Senate race against Democrat Sherrod Brown, who has made data-center opposition a campaign issue, Husted is promoting stalled legislation to make large facilities cover their own grid and generation costs rather than pass them on to residential ratepayers.

Texas tells a similar story. Less than a year after Gov. Greg Abbott hailed the state as an "epicenter of AI development," he halted data center permits pending grid- and water-impact reviews and called for ending state tax incentives.

Trump himself is showing signs of the political pressure. In a Truth Social post Wednesday, he said data center developers should pay host communities a financial "dividend" and generate their own power, arguing that local payouts can turn unpopular projects into popular ones.

For now, Democrats hold a modest edge on managing the issue: 32% of voters trust them to handle data center expansion, versus 24% for the Republicans. But 27% said neither party would do a better job than the other.

And the CNBC survey indicates this skepticism runs deeper than local zoning. Overall, 52% of registered voters want advanced AI development paused until Congress passes safety regulations, compared to 32% who favor moving ahead to keep pace with China. Democrats remain far more cautious: 70% favor a pause, while just 18% support pushing forward.

"The debate has shifted dramatically," Carson told CNBC. "A year ago, there were many people who said, 'Let it cook, no regulation at all, exempt the companies from normal rules.'" Carson said sentiment toward AI has "deteriorated a lot over the last six months."

latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-24/.headline: Exceptionally high tides will swamp California. Here's when
latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-24/.author: Rong-Gong Lin II

paragraphs.text: Exceptionally high tides are set to hit California as early as this weekend, sending officials scrambling to prepare for another onslaught along the state’s already battered coast.

The National Weather Service issued a coastal flood warning that goes into effect Sunday morning and lasts through Thursday afternoon, saying it expects “significant coastal flooding” in San Diego and Orange counties that will inundate low-lying homes, businesses and critical infrastructure, with some shoreline erosion in the morning throughout the warning period.

Significant-to-moderate beach erosion is likely in Los Angeles, Ventura, Santa Barbara and San Luis Obispo counties, and “isolated damage of structures due to sea water inundation is possible,” forecasters said. A coastal flood advisory has been issued over the same time period in those four counties.
“Take the necessary actions to protect flood-prone property,” the weather service said.

In the San Francisco Bay and Monterey Bay areas, forecasters warned of up to 1.9 feet of inundation above ground level near shorelines and tidal waterways, with rising tides bringing waves farther up the beach than normal, “restricting escape from beaches and coastal areas.” A coastal flood advisory for those areas goes into effect Saturday morning and lasts through Thursday afternoon.

The shoreline has already been hammered by an unprecedented confluence of threats this year: the arrival of El Niño off the coast of Peru, which has fueled an unusually active hurricane season in the eastern Pacific Ocean; a longstanding and unrelated marine heat wave that has broiled the shoreline for months, and a particular alignment of the Earth, sun and moon seen only once every two decades.

And the threats may only intensify. Tides are expected to get even higher around Thanksgiving, Christmas and Martin Luther King Jr. Day. The coast could be particularly hammered if the exceptionally high king tides coincide with strong winter storms.
“It’s likely to get worse before it gets better,” said Daniel Swain, a UC Agriculture and Natural Resources climate scientist.

Tides could break modern-day records in San Diego and Orange counties in the coming days, the National Weather Service said. When adjusting for how record hot the ocean has been off the coast, tides could reach 7.5 to 8 feet, or even higher, above baseline, which is defined as the average low-water level observed between 1983 and 2001. (Hotter water raises the sea level, as water expands as it heats up.)

Water at the surface at Scripps Pier in La Jolla, a neighborhood in San Diego, reached a high point for the year of around 77 degrees, when the average maximum is around 70 degrees. Just on Thursday, the surface temperature there was around 73 degrees, well above the average of 66 for this time of year.

All that is contributing to unheard-of increases in sea levels. The National Weather Service says actual tides in Southern California are running 1.25 to 1.75 feet above what would expected from just the position of the Earth, sun and moon, given the hotter ocean temperatures.

“As far as I know, this is unprecedented, especially for this length of time,” said Reinhard Flick, a researcher at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at UC San Diego. Water levels have been at least “half a foot above the prediction for months.”

Without accounting for the hot ocean temperatures, La Jolla would expect to see a maximum high tide of 6.14 feet on Sunday morning, 6.44 feet on Monday morning, 6.59 feet on Tuesday morning, 6.55 feet on Wednesday morning and 6.3 feet on Thursday morning, according to federal government predictions published years ahead of time. Actual tides, however, could push it beyond 8 feet.

The problem partly stems from a long-predicted surge in peak high tides, caused by a particular alignment of the Earth, moon and sun. We’re near the peaks of what’s known as the 18.6-year lunar node and 4.4-year lunar perigee tidal cycles, which arise from small changes in the orbit of the moon and affect tide-generating forces, according to Flick.

Another problem has been the record-breaking warm waters off the California coast, which are starting to be influenced by an El Niño-fueled dispatch of warmer ocean waters from the Peruvian coastline. Human-caused global warming is also playing a role, with sea levels having risen by about 1 foot over the past 125 years on the California coastline.

The coastal flooding in the next few days is expected to be different than earlier rounds, which were heavily influenced by powerful swells from the remnants of hurricanes Marie and Rachel. Those tropical storm-influenced swells won’t be present, but the tides this time will be higher.

Such conditions will especially put at risk areas that have already been socked by rising seawater — like the Long Beach Peninsula, where the ocean tore up an historic boardwalk and walloped homes; and Newport Beach’s Balboa Peninsula, which saw days of intense flooding.

“I think it will be on a similar scale,” said Philip Gonsalves, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service office in San Diego. “You’re going to have different contributing factors producing a similar outcome.”

Other areas that have been hit hard this year include Dana Point, where waves damaged beachfront homes, destroyed decks and tore through walls; and Malibu, where a sinkhole is threatening actor Nicolas Cage’s home, and where the ocean has threatened to cut off vehicular road access to Point Dume Beach, known by locals as Westward Beach.

In San Diego County, parts of Carlsbad State Beach have washed away, forcing the closure of the Tamarack day-use parking lot to vehicles. So much sand has eroded at the popular Newport Beach surfing spot The Wedge that remnants of decades-old buried infrastructure, like rusted metal rods and chunks of concrete, have been exposed.

Areas that have already suffered beach erosion or infrastructure damage may be especially vulnerable. Any additional flooding “exacerbates the issue because the damage is already there,” said Todd Hall, warning coordination meteorologist for the weather service office in Oxnard.

One area of concern is on Highway 1 in Ventura County near Point Mugu, where water got underneath the roadway and weakened it, which “makes it more susceptible to additional tidal events,” Hall said. Crews are installing boulders to separate the roadway from the waves.
What is clear is that officials and the public shouldn’t be surprised about coastal flooding this week.

“The warning and advisories are real. People should take them seriously because conditions are favorable for flooding,” said Doug George, an oceanographer with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

Newport Beach has declared a local emergency ahead of the tides and activated its emergency operations center, gearing up for flood prevention and response efforts. The city was also “reinforcing protective sand berms, preparing pumps and tide valves and positioning resources in flood-prone areas,” officials said on social media.

The city said the highest tides it expects are 8.3 feet on Monday at 9:15 a.m., 8.5 feet on Tuesday at 9:50 a.m., and 8.4 feet on Wednesday at 10:28 a.m. Those adjusted figures are 1.8 feet higher than the predictions that don’t take into account hotter ocean water.
Both Newport Beach and Long Beach are also rushing to move sand to shore up eroded beaches.

Newport Beach said about 30 to 40 trucks have been moving sand from an area above Prado Dam to The Wedge, with the goal of moving 2,000 cubic yards by Saturday. Crews have also been installing thousands of sandbags in vulnerable parts of Balboa Island, the city said.

In response to a crack developing beneath Coast Highway, or Highway 1, which connects Newport Beach to Laguna Beach, the California Department of Transportation said it is placing 4-foot-tall, sand-filled barriers beneath the roadway near Crystal Cove. The two lanes closest to the cliff remain closed, with traffic routed on the remaining two lanes, with one lane in each direction.

“The barriers will provide interim protection to the slope by helping to absorb wave energy. The next step will involve installing a fill buttress at the base of the slope, reinforced with large rocks to help reduce erosion and limit further slope movement,” Caltrans said on social media.

Long Beach on Tuesday began dredging Alamitos Bay and is moving sand to the beach on the wave-battered Peninsula, using, essentially, a giant hose. The effort has “already added visible beachfront to the area adjacent to the 72nd Place parking lot,” on the eastern edge of the Peninsula, city spokesperson Jen De Prez said. Repairs have also begun on the Peninsula’s damaged boardwalk.
Metrolink has announced it is suspending commuter train service in southern Orange County and San Diego County for the coming workweek, due to the tide forecast.

In the Bay Area, crews this weekend are shutting down a section of an entire state highway for 55 hours for emergency work to prepare for winter. The ultimate goal is to raise, by 3 feet, parts of flood-prone Highway 37, which connects Marin and Sonoma counties to Napa and Solano counties.

El Niño is a climate pattern characterized by warmer waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean that spur changes in the atmosphere that can affect weather around the world. El Niños are typically associated with coastal erosion in California and more stormy weather than usual to southern United States, including Southern California.

politico.com/news/2026/10/24/trump-alask.headline: Trump makes Alaska the latest frontier in his election power grab
politico.com/news/2026/10/24/trump-alask.author: Andrew Howard, Erin Doherty, Alec Hernandez, Samuel Benson and Lauren Fedor

paragraphs.text: President Donald Trump is escalating his crusade to exert control of America’s elections as his party barrels towards a potentially bruising midterm.

The Justice Department has already filed lawsuits in nearly every state to try and gain access to voter files. Trump revisited his longstanding bid to restrict mail voting, sparking a legal battle that reached the Supreme Court. He sought to make anti-terrorism funds for state and local governments contingent on how they administer elections. He has threatened to withhold federal election funding from states that refuse to change voter registration forms and sparred with Republican lawmakers over a bill to overhaul elections.

But with most of those efforts stalling, on Thursday, just 12 days before Election Day, the DOJ took things even further: In an extraordinary move, it asked a court to preemptively block Alaska’s Senate results if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses, stunning current and former election officials in both parties.

“Boy, they are scraping the bottom of the barrel. It feels like a real desperation play to me, because it has got zero basis in the law,” said Ben Ginsberg, a veteran Republican election law expert who was counsel to George W. Bush’s 2000 and 2004 presidential campaigns.

At virtually every corner, courts have rebuffed Trump’s efforts, and legal experts expect the latest DOJ maneuver to have the same outcome. The requests for voter rolls were blocked repeatedly by members of Trump’s own party and struck down in court. The attempt to restrict mail voting was ultimately blocked by the Supreme Court. Federal judges blocked both the anti-terrorism and election funding efforts. The SAVE Act, which would require voters to provide proof of citizenship at the polls, has stalled in the Senate.
But Trump keeps pushing, telling reporters Friday that he had personally green-lit the Alaska lawsuit: “I'm the one that said 'Do it.’”
The gambit is another sign that Trump is once again ramping up his efforts to exert greater control over how elections are administered — with officials bracing for what may come next.

“I think there is an attempt to lay a foundation to say, ‘If we had won these lawsuits, we would have won the election,’” Gabriel Sterling, a Republican and former senior Georgia elections official who sparred with Trump over his false claims of fraud in the state in 2020, said of the Alaska lawsuit. “So, for them, filing and losing for them is the same difference, tactically speaking, potentially.”

Trump has been claiming elections were being stolen from him since the 2016 primaries, and his wide-ranging legal and political attempts to overturn his 2020 election loss sparked a riot at the U.S. Capitol in January 2021, even as some in his party want him to move on.

“The federal government is his company, and he gets to call all the shots of his company, and that's just never how it's been done before,” said Stephen Richer, Maricopa County, Arizona’s former GOP chief election official.

POLITICO reached out to the offices of every Republican statewide election official in America for a response to the DOJ’s action in Alaska. Four declined to comment, and the rest did not respond. Their silence shows just how powerful Trump remains in the party, and how few are willing to cross him just days before November’s midterms.

"The survival rate politically of people who oppose Donald Trump on this issue is not great if you're Republican,” said Richer, who was ousted by a more conservative Republican in a 2024 primary after defending the county’s 2020 election results against a yearslong campaign from Trump and his allies to try to prove they were rigged.
Arizona Democratic Secretary of State Adrian Fontes railed against the DOJ’s lawsuit, accusing the department of “working as the president's lawyers.”

“The Department of Justice is acting in a monstrously political way, and it's purely inappropriate, and they lose a lot of credibility by putting their thumb on the scales,” Fontes said in an interview Friday afternoon. “This attempt in Alaska, if it comes to Arizona, will also fail.”

The Justice Department, in a statement posted on social media, said "claims that DOJ is trying to stop Alaska’s election are FALSE." Instead, the DOJ argued it was "seeking to protect election integrity, consistent with the National Voter Registration Act (enacted by Congress) and ensure the will of Alaska voters is respected."

Washington state Attorney General Nick Brown, a Democrat, described the legal filing in Alaska as “part of a concerted effort to control the election and to try to dictate the outcome in Donald Trump and the Republican Party’s favor.”
Brown said he worried the administration would contest the results of the midterms.

“That is not hypothetical,” Brown said. “This is what the president has done for years now, and he has the entire power of government, and most importantly, the Department of Justice around elections, acting at his request.”
Sterling predicted the effort would backfire on the GOP.

“By talking about stolen elections, by talking about cheating, they're suppressing their own vote and they're encouraging the votes of their opponents,” he said. “So tactically, I think it's politically moronic.”

The DOJ lawsuit in Alaska comes less than two weeks before a midterm election cycle in which Republicans are bracing for losses across the map. And the Trump administration’s increasing interventions are raising questions about how far his administration intends to go in trying to assert federal authority over elections that by law are run by state and local officials.

A current Georgia Republican election official, granted anonymity to discuss internal deliberations around the Alaska lawsuit, said they are prepared to forcefully push back on any action from the federal government.
“Bring it on,” the official said. “I think there's zero credible way for any entity, much less the DOJ, to say that the election results in Georgia are suspect.”
The lawsuit is the culmination of years of escalating tensions between the federal government and state election officials over election proceedings.

In February, a typically staid gathering of the nation’s top election officials turned fiery when Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson, a Republican and her state’s chief election official, confronted a senior White House aide over the DOJ’s voter roll push.

The DOJ “pretty much slandered all of us to publicly claim that secretaries of state are not doing our jobs and that the federal government has to do it for us. Not OK,” Henderson said to White House Deputy Director of Intergovernmental Affairs Jared Borg, as her colleagues and reporters looked on.

On Wednesday, Henderson’s office received a letter from the Justice Department informing her that election monitors will be sent to her state. Her office responded the next day by distributing instructions to poll workers noting that the DOJ observers “must not interfere with voting” and giving guidance in case “a situation arises involving law enforcement or legal demands.”
Henderson was unsparing in a recent interview with CBS News.
"In the past two elections that I oversaw as lieutenant governor the threats were all external," she said. "But now we also have threats coming from within our own government."
Lisa Kashinsky contributed to this report.

cnbc.com/2026/10/23/alaska-senate-electi.headline: Trump says he ordered DOJ suit to block Alaska Senate race certification if Republican loses
cnbc.com/2026/10/23/alaska-senate-electi.author: Dan Mangan

paragraphs.text: The Department of Justice filed an extraordinary lawsuit seeking to block Alaska from certifying the winner of its upcoming U.S. Senate election if incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses the contest.

The lawsuit, filed less than two weeks before the Nov. 3 election, cites what it argues is likely voter confusion from the name of another candidate appearing on the ballot, retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan.
The DOJ says that could help Democratic nominee Mary Peltola defeat the incumbent, Dan S. Sullivan, in what is expected to be a close contest.
The Alaska race is among several closely watched Senate races that could determine control of the chamber. Republicans currently hold a narrow majority.

The suit asks a federal judge in Alaska to bar the state from certifying "any result that may be impacted by voter confusion ... pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan."
The DOJ did not say how anyone could determine a voter's intent. Doing so might be impossible, given the anonymity of ballots.

"The United States accordingly brings this lawsuit to protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska," says the suit filed Thursday in U.S. District Court in Alaska. In addition to the state, the complaint names Alaska Elections Division Director Carol Beecher, the state's election boards and the state Ballot Counting Review Board as defendants.
President Donald Trump on Friday told reporters that he had set the lawsuit in motion.
"I'm the one that said 'do it,'" Trump said in Fort Myers, Florida while traveling for a political rally. "They have two guys ... named Dan Sullivan, so the Democrats put up a guy."

Before the suit was filed Thursday, Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters that the DOJ had no plans to "improperly interfere with elections or the state confirmation process or certification process."

"There's no circumstances that we would ever do that," he said at a press conference. "Of course I'm not going to say that. But am I planning my days around the election to be somewhere to not certify? Of course not, no, not at all."

The DOJ's suit alleges that Daniel J. Sullivan's "sole purpose" of running for the Senate "is to benefit the Peltola campaign by reducing the number of votes for Senator Sullivan." Sullivan first registered as a Republican earlier this year. He previously was a member of the Alaska Independence Party.

The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates the Alaska Senate race as one of seven "toss-up" contests for that chamber. The election tracking site FiftyPlusOne's average of polling shows Peltola, a former U.S. House member from Alaska, with just a 2-percentage-point lead over Sullivan.

The suit came hours after Trump, in a Truth Social post, wrote, "I am very concerned about the Dan S. Sullivan Race for the U.S. Senate in Alaska in that it is totally confusing, with the Dumocrats putting up another man, totally unrelated to Politics, named Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr."
"It's ridiculous that the Court didn't stop this SCAM. Even 1, 2, or 3% could make the difference," Trump said.

"We are looking at powerful legal options to remove the fraudulent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. from the Ballot, and holding the Democrats accountable for their Election Interference, in the pursuit of Justice and Fairness."

Alaska's general election for the Senate uses ranked-choice voting. Voters rank their candidates in order of preference. If no candidate gets more than 50% in round one, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated in the second round, and that process continues until there are just two candidates and the winner is the one with the most votes.

"Daniel J. Sullivan's presence on the ballot threatens to mislead Alaskan citizens who want to vote for Senator Sullivan," the suit says. "For example, some supporters of Senator Sullivan likely will inadvertently vote for Daniel J. Sullivan."

"Other supporters of Senator Sullivan likely will be confused as to how to rank the three Republican candidates as to defeat Peltola," the suit says. "They might not rank Senator Sullivan at all, resulting in votes for Daniel J. Sullivan to be transferred to Peltola after Daniel J. Sullivan's all-but-guaranteed elimination in the first or second round of tabulations."

In a statement to CNBC, a DOJ spokesperson said, "Alaska's Division of Elections determined that Mr. Daniel J. Sullivan's candidacy was intended to mislead voters and compromise the fairness of the ballot."

"Therefore, the Justice Department, consistent with the National Voter Registration Act enacted by Congress, is taking the necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska's election or the will of its voters," the spokesperson said.
Nate Adams, the campaign spokesman for Sen. Sullivan, said, "We'll let the DOJ complaint run its course."
"Alaskans can tell the difference between a Democrat sideshow and Senator Sullivan's strong record of delivering for Alaska, a record he'll keep building on for the next six years," Adams said.

Harry Child, a spokesman for Peltola's campaign, said, "This is a despicable political threat to overturn an election, designed by Senator Dan Sullivan's allies to suppress the voices of Alaskans because Sullivan is terrified he'll lose the seat that has allowed him to enrich himself at Alaskans' expense for over a decade."

"We will fight to ensure every single eligible voter in Alaska can make their voice heard and that no bureaucrat or politician from the Lower 48 can interfere with our lawful, secure elections," Child said.
CNBC has requested comment from Daniel J. Sullivan, Alaska's attorney general, and state election officials.
Daniel J. Sullivan, in a social media post in June, said, "I entered this race because I am unhappy with the 12 year record of the current Senator and I feel we need a change. It's that simple."

Devan Barber, executive director of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, in a statement to CNBC said, "Donald Trump knows that Dan Sullivan is going to lose the election, so now his Department of Justice is filing a sham lawsuit to overturn the will of Alaska voters and steal an election when he loses."

Daniel J. Sullivan originally was blocked from the state's primary ballot in June, after the Alaska Division of Elections said his declaration of candidacy was not properly filed, and because of a finding that the candidacy was aimed at duping voters who planned to vote for Sen. Sullivan.

The division cited his request to appear on the ballot as 'Dan Sullivan,' his recent switch to the Republican Party and his work with a political consultant described as a longtime supporter of Democratic candidates, including Peltola, according to the DOJ complaint.
Daniel J. Sullivan was added to the ballot after challenging the division's decision in state court. The Alaska Supreme Court later upheld that decision.
Daniel J. Sullivan received just 2.5% of the vote in Alaska's open primary on Aug. 28, but that was enough to win him one of four spots on the Senate general election ballot.
Peltola got 49.5% in the primary, and Sen. Sullivan received 41.4%. Another Republican, Gerald Heikes, received just 1.1% of the primary vote, earning him the fourth spot on the ballot.

Although Daniel J. Sullivan sought to run as a Republican, the Division of Elections decided not to list that party next to his name on the general election ballot. His name is spelled out, "Daniel J. Sullivan," and there are no other words on that line.
Both Sen. Sullivan, who has been in the Senate since 2015, and Heikes have the words "registered Republican" in parentheses next to their names.
And Sen. Sullivan, listed on the ballot as Dan S. Sullivan, also has the word "incumbent" next to his name.
— CNBC's Justin Papp contributed to this article.

nytimes.com/2026/10/24/world/europe/ukra.headline: Speed of Starshield Satellite Network Is Improving, Ukraine Says

paragraphs.text: Ukrainian drones connected to the Pentagon-funded Starshield satellite network have flown at speeds near 250 miles an hour for the first time since the system was throttled last week, Ukraine’s defense minister announced on Saturday. It was the first sign that the speed restrictions, which have hampered crucial drone operations, might be easing.

“This is another example when direct dialogue and the persistent position of the president of Ukraine at the highest level produce results,” Yevhen Khmara, the defense minister, said in a statement. “And this result is primarily important for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics and communications.”

Ukraine uses Starshield for air defense and to guide drones toward targets in Russian-occupied territory. The unexplained throttling of the system deepened a growing rift that has been playing out publicly between Ukraine and the United States. President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Ukrainian civilians had been left more vulnerable to Russian attack, and Ukrainian officials raised fears that the Starshield program had been slowed to force Ukraine into capitulation.

Ukrainian drone operators first saw their drones slowed to speeds lower than 40 miles an hour about 10 days ago. Many drones slowed so abruptly that they lost connection to their pilots on the ground and then fell from the sky, wasting expensive equipment.

It remains unclear who, if anyone, ordered the system to be slowed. No one in Washington has taken responsibility, a fact that only caused further confusion in Kyiv.It has also deepened divides between Congress and the White House over the U.S. approach to Russia. A group of Republicans and Democrats in the Senate warned the White House this week that they would block President Trump’s nominations if Ukraine’s full Starshield capabilities were not restored.

Walking home late one night this week, I paused to register the perfect quiet, the air sweet with the scent of decaying leaves: the city in October, when the cold is still just flirting. The simple delight that Emily Brontë observed — “Every leaf speaks bliss to me / Fluttering from the autumn tree” — seemed attainable. What a waste to go inside and go to sleep when being out in the fresh night feels this good.

Fall is a season that rewards outdoorsy people, those who have been waiting patiently for the heat to break and the mosquitoes to retreat so they can layer on their wicking fabrics and take to the trails. The word “outdoorsy” is one that bedevils me: It’s one of those noun-turned-adjectives that purports to simply describe a person who likes to be in nature, but implies virtue. An outdoorsy person is healthy, active, connected to the earth. An indoorsy person, by contrast, is sedentary, vitamin D-deficient, screen-addicted. I aspire to all the moral characteristics of the outdoorsy set, and so have spent my adult life trying to become a person who can follow color-coded trail markers through the spruces.

Outdoor Boys, a YouTube channel with over 20 million subscribers, features people going to the furthest extremes of outdoorsiness: camping on frozen oceans, building survival shelters in blizzards, catching and cooking snakes. Natalie Berry, a freelancer, wrote about the phenomenon in The Times this week. The videos are “usually enjoyed indoors, by a predominantly male audience, who find comfort in watching others overcome discomfort,” she noted. They’re like housecats watching pumas and jaguars stalk jungle prey from the comfort of their living-room sun puddles.

Getting comfortable with discomfort seems to me to be the key to living a bigger, more fulfilling life. A few years ago, I had the rather rudimentary realization that my aversion to being cold was causing me to shrink my life to fit within the walls of my apartment during winter. I’d decline invitations, measuring the worthiness of an activity by its proximity to a thermostat. When I realized being cold is not an emergency — it’s just discomfort, and discomfort can be tolerated — I got a better winter coat and stopped dreading February so much.

Outdoorsiness as an identity, however, has continued to elude me. There’s a certain amount of skill that goes into erecting a tent, rappelling down a rock face. On message boards where people ask how they can become more outdoorsy, the advice is to start slow: Go to a park and build an evening campfire before planning a weeklong camping trip. Those of us who aspire to outdoorsy might embrace the alternate descriptor outsidey in the meantime. “Outdoorsy is nature for adventure. Outsidey is nature for leisure,” goes a TikTok on the distinction. Mountaineering is for the outdoorsy, it explains, whereas an outsidey person will “frolic upon the meadow.” It’s a lighthearted differentiation, but the ultimate effect is one of inclusiveness. You don’t have to summit a mountain in order to appreciate the foliage. You don’t have to be athletic or intrepid in order to be connected to the natural world.

nytimes.com/2026/10/24/magazine/gina-hin.headline: Gina Hinojosa Believes She’s the One Who Can Finally Flip Texas

paragraphs.text: Democrats have Texas-size dreams this election of flipping a state that has eluded them since the 1990s. While the Democratic candidate for Senate, James Talarico, has gotten most of the attention and money in that fight, another Democrat, Gina Hinojosa, has looked surprisingly competitive against the most powerful politician in the state: Gov. Greg Abbott, the Republican running for an unprecedented fourth term.

Hinojosa is a Texas state legislator who represents parts of liberal Austin. Her political rise began on her local school board, where she was inspired to run for the State Legislature because of cuts to public school funding under Abbott. That became one of her signature issues, which she has carried over into her run for governor.

When she began her campaign, she was seen as the longest of long shots: a Latina with little statewide name recognition and not a lot of financial support. Today, the most recent New York Times/Siena University poll shows her narrowly ahead of Abbott, and national Democrats are finally taking notice, directing money toward the race in these last few crucial weeks. I asked Hinojosa whether that will be enough to overcome an extremely well-funded Abbott, who declined our interview request. We also talked about why she is focusing on affordability, education and data centers rather than what she calls “culture-war issues” and how she is trying to pull in disaffected rural MAGA voters. Can she win? And what will it say about Texas if she does?

I was told by a Texas reporter that in some ways you ran for governor — a position last held by your party in 1995 by another woman, Ann Richards — as a sacrificial lamb. It was the longest of long shots, you had no real chance, but basically some Democrat had to do it and so it might as well be you. Did you see it that way too? No. I wouldn’t have given up a year of my life away from my family to be on the road all across the state to be a sacrificial lamb. I am running to win. It is not an easy endeavor to do this, and it took everything out of me from this last year.

Texas keeps breaking Democratic hearts. What are you doing differently than, say, Beto O’Rourke, who was the last Democrat to run against Abbott? He had a lot of name recognition, a lot of momentum behind him nationally, and yet he still lost by 11 points. I don’t know that I can compare my candidacy to Beto’s. It’s a different time. In 2026, the data centers have been a physical manifestation of a governor doing the bidding of the moneyed interests and leaving the people of Texas to fend for themselves. And so in that way, rural Texas has felt betrayed by Greg Abbott because many of these data centers have descended upon rural Texas where there are no rules really.

I was in the Panhandle, Amarillo, talking to residents where they are fighting the world’s largest data center. It is called Project Matador. Its investors are Rick Perry, our former governor, and his son. They negotiated a deal to get all of their water in this drought-prone area for the data center from the city water supply. When residents asked what happens if we run out of water, the response they told me they got from municipal water was, Well, we will have to turn off the residents’ first. That’s the environment we’re living in in Texas. And so people understand that we are fighting a fight where it’s all of us in the same boat versus like 15 billionaire tech dudes.

When you go to these rural areas, are you trying to get disaffected MAGA voters to turn your way? What is the overall plan on who to persuade, because obviously your time and your resources are finite, so you have to pick and choose who you’re trying to get to listen to your message. It’s everybody. I have not picked and chosen. I have been all over the state with all communities. To be clear, it is not a moderating message. It is reaching out to Democrats, Republicans, independents, with a populist message. And yes, I need Trump supporters to support this race. Trump won Texas, Trump won the Latino vote in Texas. Absolutely, they are invited to be part of this coalition.

What’s been the thing that’s most surprised you when you’re out among communities that you wouldn’t naturally see as supporting you? I mean, you represented Austin, which is one of the most liberal places in the state. I was in Red Oak, Texas, where they have big-acreage lots and a school down the street. They invited me in because they have seven data centers moving into their community, including one that’s 900 acres large right next door to the home that I was invited into. And I was sitting in a living room with MAGA. They knew Greg Abbott had sold them out, but they weren’t sure about me. They had questions. So I sat down and I said: OK, let’s go. Ask me. And they wanted to ask me culture-war questions, right? They wanted to ask me about constitutional carry. I said, “What you call constitutional carry, I call permitless carry, and I voted against it because I believe we should have background checks to have a gun.” They asked me about Shariah law. And I said, “I don’t really know what Shariah law is, but what I worry about is that regular Muslim Texans are going to be discriminated against because people think they are practicing this thing that probably most of them don’t even know what it is.”

And so we engaged, which I think is a rare thing for people of different political parties. It’s rare for elected Democratic leaders to sit down with MAGA and say, “Let’s talk,” and to agree to disagree where we disagree, to find common ground where we do, but then ultimately to recognize, while we have been fighting these culture wars for 10 years in this country — culture wars that are not winnable because they depend on your personal experiences, your lived experience — the only winners have been the tech giants that are amassing our money and our power and all of our data and, if you believe recent reports, are about to blow up the world if we don’t come together fast to save ourselves.

How persuasive do you think you’ve been? I think people are tired of fighting culture-war fights. I think there is an opportunity, if we choose to take it, to forge a new way forward that is almost post-partisan in recognition of disappointment, again, in both parties. Because both parties, frankly, are corrupted by corporate influence. I mean, I see it in the Democratic Party, too. I have seen so many Democrats grandstand on culture-war issues, only to vote with corporate interests, and none of us are better for it.

I want to learn a little bit more about you and your background. Your father was a Democratic Party chair in the state for 13 years and was a judge. Your mom was born in Mexico. What was your family like growing up? My parents started off as legal aid lawyers. They represented farmworkers, and I was born to high school sweethearts. They were very young when they had me, so in some ways I grew up with them. I grew up in Brownsville, on the border with Matamoros, Mexico, and back then we used to cross back and forth all the time. We’d go for breakfast on the weekends to Mexico. We would go shopping for things in Mexico. We were a binational community.

Because you know the area really well, I am curious what you think has been happening down in the Rio Grande Valley. In 2016, it was a 60-point-plus Democratic area, and then, in 2024, Trump won it. What do you think Republicans figured out to catch fire there? There were a couple of things happening. One, Latinos along the border were angry about border security. Remember, this was at a time when we had the caravans crossing. We had people sleeping under bridges. It felt chaotic. It did not inspire confidence. Border communities were angry about that, and those are mostly Latino communities. I also think that Latinos vote their pocketbooks, and Trump was promising to deliver a kind of economic prosperity that was appealing.

But fast forward to today, and yes, we all want border security, but these ICE raids are making us less secure, not more secure. People are really angry about the racial profiling that’s happened. We’ve even had American boys, on their way to enlist in the Marines, pulled from their car by ICE and beaten. We had a man who was killed in Houston a few months ago on his way to work, a case of mistaken identity where they shot first, asked questions later. I could go on. That is the reality we are dealing with in Texas, and Latinos are angry and scared.

As you know, many people see Democrats as weak on the border. Abbott has used his authority to send the National Guard down to the border, among other things. What approaches of Trump or Abbott do you agree with? Because we have seen the border become a much more secure place. Illegal crossings have plummeted under the Trump administration. I think we cannot treat people who have been in our communities for 20 years, hard-working, law-abiding members of our community, like we are treating somebody who needs to be vetted coming across the border. Those are two different kinds of people who need to be treated differently. We should have a path to legalization for people who are here. We should also have order at the border and security at the border.

But what specifically would you do differently than Governor Abbott? Would you repeal S.B. 4, which is the Abbott law that makes unauthorized entry into Texas a [state] criminal offense? Well, I wouldn’t have the power to repeal that as governor.

But would you propose it? Do you think it should be repealed? I don’t support it, and I voted against it, and I stand by my record. But I’m not going to pretend like I’ll have the power to convince the Legislature to do that. Even if I win, we still have Republican control of everything in this state. My agenda will be one that 99 percent of us agree on, which is to secure the American dream, to save Texas public schools, put money in your pocket — a populist agenda, rather than fight fights that I know I can’t win.

That’s interesting. So what you’re telling me is that you might not agree with S.B. 4, which also authorizes the state to remove those here illegally — typically a federal function — but you’re not going to try to change it because you feel like you can’t do it. So then what’s in it for Democrats who want to see substantial changes to the law in Texas, if you won’t be able to deliver on key issues for them? This is not a blue state. This is Texas, where we have Greg Abbott putting the Texas National Guard in detention centers so that these private prison companies can maximize their profits. We have kids being locked up with their parents because Greg Abbott allows for the licensing of these detention centers for little kids to be locked up. We have a governor who turns the other way when Texans are being mowed down on our streets. There is a lot besides the repeal of S.B. 4, and having a governor who has the courage to stand up for Texans will be night and day in this state.

I’m just trying to understand, if you become governor, how you would address some of the things that you see are wrong. What would you do in terms of ICE? I will use everything from the bully pulpit to the courts to defend the rights of Texans.

Do you think ICE needs to be reformed? Reimagined? Disbanded? I think what is happening needs to stop. ICE should not be doing this. They should not be here. What they are doing is causing more danger to the people of Texas than it is protection. People fear them. People are angry at them. It is chaotic. These guys are not trained. They should not be here.

Staying with the border, one of the people you’ve spoken out about is Elon Musk. SpaceX is based in the valley. It even has a town called Starbase there. It employs thousands of people. Musk has pledged $20 million to a local school district down there. You’ve been very critical of him and the way he has operated his businesses in Texas. Tell me why. I’m actually more critical of the way Abbott lets him abuse our resources. I blame him less than I blame our weak leader, who doesn’t defend Texans. The record is that Elon Musk has given Greg Abbott half a million dollars to his campaign, and he has received $1.6 billion in property-tax breaks for his company, Terafab. He’s received tens of millions of dollars in cash from the state of Texas for Starbase. He has received the governor’s intervention in contracting for broadband so that he could receive a $100 million broadband contract. This is the reality we are living in.

Elon Musk has also been an enormous contributor to the Republican Party — tens of millions of dollars being poured into the race in Texas in particular, but all over the country. How do you see his role in the politics of your state? He has an outsize influence, to say the least. You should not be able to spend that much money. It’s gross that he has that kind of influence over our political system.

There must be some tension there because he is a big employer in the state. He moved a lot of his businesses to Texas. You want people to have good-paying jobs. So how do you imagine that you would manage that relationship with someone who clearly supports a different agenda? I launched this campaign with this saying my grandmother used to tell me growing up: No te dejes. There’s not a direct translation for this saying, but it basically means: Know your worth, and fight to defend it. Elon Musk is lucky he is here. Yes, there are good jobs that he is providing, but also he’s getting tremendous taxpayer dollars that is not justified.

Do you think he should get out of the state? He doesn’t need to get out of the state. He just needs to abide by the rules like everybody else does. We all pay our taxes. Why shouldn’t Elon Musk pay his taxes in Texas, too?

You’ve described the way that many Texans feel disempowered and the way that the economy has functioned, in your view, against ordinary Texans. But I do think Republicans would argue that their policies have made Texas one of the most business-friendly states in the entire country. It has the second-largest economy after California. Isn’t that good stewardship of the state? There’s no question that corporations love Greg Abbott and Texas, but the reality is we have the most people without health insurance of any state, despite the fact that Texans worked more hours than the national average. We have the most children without health insurance of any state. We have the most people disconnected from their electricity because they cannot afford to pay their bills. We have the most bankruptcies of any state in America, and it is small businesses that are struggling to keep their doors open. We have over 150 school districts operating at four days a week because they can’t afford to operate at five days a week. Despite the fact that we pay 85 percent more in property taxes under Greg Abbott. That is his record. We have nothing to show for it. So yes, there’s a lot of money that flows through Texas. There is a lot of money that is made in Texas by the people of Texas, but the people are not sharing in that economic wealth.

OK, we’re going to pivot a little bit to something that you’ve talked about, which is seeing yourself as a populist and not a liberal or a progressive. Your voting record in the State House is, by all accounts, pretty liberal. You were, in 2019, ranked the most liberal member of the Texas House, and it was a title that you openly embraced. So I’m curious how you define “populist” and “progressive,” and tell me why you’ve landed on “populist” as a label for yourself. I think “populist” meets the moment of our time. The one fight in this country is about economic power, and populism is about economic power. We see that things are so stacked against working people in this country. Listen, it’s just a label, but if I were to pick a label to describe my politics, it is economic populism. It happens to be a type of politics that is rooted in our Texas history. It was L.B.J.’s grandfather, who was part of the Farmers’ Alliance, that organized farmers against big railroads that were taking advantage of them. Now we have working Texans who are up against big tech. And so I chose this title to define my politics because I think this has to be the politics of the moment to meet the challenges of the moment.

Is part of it also that the progressive or liberal label could be perceived as pretty toxic by certain members of the state that you’re trying to get to vote for you? No, it is not that. But I think those labels have been associated with culture wars, and I just don’t think that the culture wars are the fight of 2026.

Being a progressive could also be about the way you use taxation to redistribute wealth. It could mean the way you want the health care system to work in terms of supporting Obamacare or Medicare for all. It’s not just a label that has to do with culture wars. I think it means more than that. It may mean more than that to you, but to a lot of people, it means the culture-war fights, because those are the fights we’ve been fighting for the last 10 years.

So that comes back to my thing that it’s toxic. No, it’s not that. It comes back to that it doesn’t meet the political moment. It is not what 2026 is about. Look, we are facing an almost existential crisis in this country because tech giants are having their way with us. There is one fight, and we are so caught up in fighting each other in a divided nation, fighting each other over the ways we disagree about social issues and culture wars that we’re all about to lose. And so I’m not going to perpetuate that anymore.

You clearly understand that some of these issues motivate people. You released a very personal ad early in your campaign talking about the issue of abortion. In Texas, abortion is almost completely banned from conception with no exception for rape or incest. In your ad, you discuss something very personal. Can you tell me the story and why you wanted to talk about it? So in my first pregnancy, shortly after I was married, I was diagnosed with a fetus that had trisomy 18, which was described to me by doctors as not compatible with life. I had to make a decision about whether or not to terminate that pregnancy. I had a week’s time to decide that. I consulted with my priest and the nun at my church. I prayed with my husband. We both took that time to figure out what to do. My family was so supportive. I had a small Christian community that held my hand along the way, and I ultimately decided not to terminate that pregnancy and carry it forward to term. She didn’t make it. She died at nine months of pregnancy at birth. And it made me who I am. I probably would not be here had it not been for that experience. It showed me my strength and really put things in perspective for me.

That’s such a very personal and painful story. What were you hoping people would understand about you from that? I think Texans want to know who are you, why are you doing this, what motivates you. It was a formative experience in my life. And I think the thing that I wanted to communicate is that this is first and foremost a human experience. We have politicized pregnancy in this country, but there are so many women, so many families, who have had their hearts broken by pregnancies gone bad. I wanted to try to connect with people on a human level with what my human hardship was and how it made me stronger.

Do you see abortion as a culture-war issue, or do you see it as something that transcends that — as an issue of health care or an issue of human rights? I think it is an issue of human rights. I think it’s a health care issue. There are women who are dying in Texas because they can’t terminate a pregnancy when they are in crisis because doctors are facing 99 years in prison. We just had our governor delay the release of the maternal mortality report in this state until after the election, but we’ve heard so many stories of women dying, and we know it’s going to be bad. So absolutely, it is all of those things.

What would you like to do if you’re governor on that issue, understanding that the Legislature is what it is? I do think that we can come together in a bipartisan way to save women’s lives. That is the commitment I’ve made on the campaign trail.

Obviously, as a woman, you are hoping to appeal to women, including, as you’ve mentioned, MAGA women. I just looked at the latest Marist poll, and you are ahead with women, but not by much. Are you doing well enough with women? Are you worried about that? Well, the only reason we’re winning six major polls out of the last five weeks is because of our strong support from women. So I feel good about our support from women. But look, we take no demographic for granted.

A different demographic: Prominent Latinos wrote a letter to Democratic leadership imploring them to give you financial support. They wrote, “We are asking you to invest in a competitive race with the largest Latino electorate in the country following an election cycle where Republicans made alarming inroads with Latinos.” Do you think the national Democrats ignore Latino candidates like you? I don’t really follow other races, but I would like them to invest in this race. We have an opportunity of a generation to win here. We’ve been dealt a phenomenal hand in Texas, and it would be very helpful to have more national support. There’s no doubt there are big national stakes in this race. We know that Republicans in Austin want to redistrict again in Texas, redraw maps, and they have decided to do so next year if they win. We know there’s no Democratic control of Congress when that happens.

We need a governor in Texas who will veto rigged maps, and I will be that governor. So those are the stakes. And again, this is an opportunity of a generation to win. In 2026, yes, Latinos are key to that winning number. Beto got 64 percent of the Latino vote in 2018. When I get that, I win because there are more of us in the voting population in Texas in 2026. This is not the time to be playing small ball.

Do you think the head of the Democratic Governors Association, Gov. Andy Beshear, was disrespecting your candidacy? Because he was reluctant to invest. I have a good relationship with him. They did send $1 million. I’m grateful for that.
One million dollars is not a lot in Texas. It’s such a big state. It’s helpful. Ninety-five percent of our contributions come from small-dollar donations. I’m proud of what we’ve been able to raise.

You just mentioned that Texas Republicans are planning to redraw the maps, which could be very, very problematic for Democrats in Congress. Did you make the case to the national party about that? Yes, I did make that case, and I have made that case from the very beginning. Absolutely, those are the stakes, and we’ve been talking to anybody who will listen. That’s why I think you’re hearing Democrats across the country really want to make sure we have the investment we need to win, because the stakes are so high and because the opportunity to win is even higher. For the first time, we have a ticket running in Texas. We’ve had Beto in the past, we’ve had Colin Allred in the past, but it was just them. Now we have me, we have James [Talarico], we have Democrats running up and down the ballot. For the first time, we have Democrats running in every Texas House seat, Texas Senate seat, congressional seat. We have an opportunity of a generation to win in Texas.

Well, let’s say you do win. It will be a political earthquake. What do you think it will signify? The thing that I am most excited about when I win is the feeling Texans will feel to know their power again. To know that we can go up against big money, probably the biggest in the country, and entrenched politics — Greg Abbott is probably the most entrenched incumbent there is in America — and that we could win. And I just know there’s going to be this feeling of almost liberation when we feel our power again. That’s the thing I’m most looking forward to.
This interview has been edited and condensed. Listen to and follow “The Interview” on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, iHeartRadio or Amazon Music. Follow us on Instagram and TikTok.

nytimes.com/2026/10/24/world/europe/fran.headline: Looting Left Damage and Fear on Paradise Street in Marseille

paragraphs.text: For more than a century, Rue Paradis through downtown Marseille has catered to affluent shoppers, from the Mediterranean merchants of yore to those seeking designer fashions today.
Now, the avenue, whose name means Paradise Street, lies battered and in crisis.
Cracks snake across many shop windows, and others are boarded up. Some stores have been cleaned out by looters.
“Store is empty,” read a handwritten sign taped to the door of a perfumery. “Closed.”

A week ago, mostly peaceful demonstrations in cities across France devolved into clashes between protesters and the police. Then looters entered the fray, breaking into stores, supermarkets and shopping malls, and hauling off whatever they could.

In Marseille, France’s second-largest city, the pillaging hit the historic downtown hard, with about 500 businesses affected, according to the regional Chamber of Commerce. In one mall, Centre Bourse, looters sacked 32 out of 34 stores. Others set their sights on Paradise Street.

After days of government-imposed protest bans and curfews, a demonstration was expected to go ahead in Marseille on Saturday. As the day approached, merchants were still recovering from the looting while wondering why the police had been so unprepared to stop it.

“We never expected that we would live that,” said Nicole Richard-Verspieren, who heads a local business association. “There was fear. After that there was anger. Now people want to protect themselves.”
She spoke while packing much of the inventory of her wine shop into boxes to be moved elsewhere, just in case.

Other nearby businesspeople were installing security systems or nailing boards over shattered vitrines. Some were considering arming themselves, Ms. Richard-Verspieren said, adding that her association discouraged it.

Social conditions in Marseille, a city of 895,000 people on the Mediterranean, exacerbated the unrest, experts said. While it has an active cargo port, dynamic cultural life and significant tourism, it remains France’s most economically unequal metropolis.

“Marseille is a city that contains real poverty,” said Michel Peraldi, an anthropologist who has long studied the city. Many of its poor live in neighborhoods north of downtown that have benefited little from the city’s development. And a large share are young.
“That explains part of what happened, at least some of the frustrations that were expressed,” Mr. Peraldi said.
Paradise Street begins a few blocks from the city’s Old Port and heads south. Lining its downtown portion are quaint apartment buildings with wooden shutters, small balconies and ground-floor shops.

On the sidewalk, William Naim watched workers affixing boards over the front of his custom-jewelry store. He is a fifth-generation jeweler, he said, whose father left Tunisia for Marseille decades ago.

On the afternoon of the riot, Mr. Naim said, he received a notification that the alarm at his store had gone off, and rushed to the scene. Looters had torn open the metal grate over the entrance and broken in.
“They took all they could take,” he said. He, his father and brothers stood outside the shop until late that night to deter looters. One of them yanked off and stole his necklace, he said.
Like many merchants, Mr. Naim distinguished looters from protesters, whom he supported.
“The protests are important because we are in a country where we can express ourselves and where we can listen to others, whether we agree with them or not,” he said.
Down the street, a woman working for a gold dealer that had been ransacked said she had been shocked by her own children’s responses to the burglary.
Her son, 14, got excited when he saw looters breaking into stores, she said. Her daughter, 15, told her, “We’ll never have a chance to have clothes from Hermès.”

The woman, who spoke on condition that only her first name, Maha, be published, shared feelings common among protesters that the French state was failing its citizens. Her daughter is a good student, but worries that she will not enter a good university. When her son got injured recently, the family waited six hours for care at a state hospital.
“In France?” she said in disbelief.
Nearby blocks were a patchwork of shops that had been damaged and others that had been spared.
Stores housing well-known brands like Nespresso, Swatch and Longchamp were boarded over and closed. Dr. Martens and Intimissimi were also boarded up but remained open.
Outside a store whose sign read, “Hunting Weapons and Ammunition,” a man smoked furiously and declined to speak with journalists.
A nearby hairdresser, Kevin Varnier, 25, said he expected the security forces to act forcefully to prevent further unrest.
“The state can’t leave Marseille at the bottom,” he said. “The violence that was done needs to be paid back.”
To help local merchants, the Chamber of Commerce opened a drop-in center where businesspeople could report problems and seek aid.
Karine Guillem, an official overseeing the effort, said common concerns included how to protect their shops, make insurance claims, cover their rent and replenish their looted inventories.
Many merchants worried that the crisis was not over.
“The question that keeps coming back is, What next?” she said. “What will happen now?”
Sophie Boutière-Damahi contributed reporting.

nytimes.com/2026/10/24/us/politics/vivek.headline: How Vivek Ramaswamy’s Ruthless Ad in Ohio Divided Republicans

paragraphs.text: The most explosive advertisement of the midterm elections has split Republicans and again posed the question of what is fair game for campaign attacks in American politics.

In the days since the leak of the ad from Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for governor of Ohio, many fellow G.O.P. politicians have denounced, disavowed or distanced themselves from the spot. Yet President Trump and Vice President JD Vance have defended the ad, a remarkably ruthless one even by the standards of modern political campaigns.

The ad features the estranged mother of Mr. Ramaswamy’s Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, calling her daughter a liar and urging Ohioans not to vote for her. Ms. Acton has said that she has not spoken to her mother since she was 12 years old, when she was removed from her mother’s custody after her stepfather was arrested and charged with raping her.

The outrage over the ad’s dark backstory has left Mr. Ramaswamy, a billionaire entrepreneur who exemplifies the anything-goes, attack-at-all-costs ethos of Trump-era politics, at the center of a self-created political firestorm.

The Republican disagreements over the ad show that major figures in the party can still become divided over the rules and red lines of political warfare in the Trump era. And they set the stage for high drama on Election Day in Ohio, a state that has trended solidly Republican in recent years but now has outsize importance in the midterms. The overarching political question is: Will a potential backlash to Mr. Ramaswamy hurt other Ohio Republicans in competitive races, especially Senator Jon Husted, who is trying to fend off a well-known Democratic rival in a vital race for Senate control?
There is now a degree of unpredictability in the state. Campaigns in both parties do not know how voters will react.

Mr. Ramaswamy, who along with his aides declined to be interviewed for this article, said at a campaign stop on Friday that he had no regrets. The ad, he suggested, was his attempt to change the rules of engagement for Republicans in Ohio — just as Mr. Trump has done in Washington.

“What we need is a governor at the top just like President Trump is for our country — a governor for this state who stands strong, who says we will not play on your terms,” he told a crowd in Strongsville, a Cleveland suburb. “We will stand for what we know is right and true, and we will not apologize for it.”
A Shocking Ad Emerges Online
There had been rumblings for weeks in Ohio political circles that Mr. Ramaswamy’s top aides were in touch with Dr. Acton’s estranged mother.
Dr. Acton’s troubled childhood was no secret, and had been the subject of reporting during her high-profile stretch as the pandemic-era health director for Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican.
Mr. Ramaswamy had been trailing Dr. Acton in many public and private polls. Like other Republicans, he was confronting voter frustration with high gas prices, tariffs and Mr. Trump’s leadership.

Producing the ad was a politically hazardous move for Mr. Ramaswamy, a 41-year-old start-up founder who has shown a high tolerance for risk since he emerged on the scene during his 2024 campaign for president. During that race, he presented himself as a full Trump acolyte and made plenty of enemies with his brash style before placing fourth in the Iowa caucuses, dropping out and endorsing Mr. Trump.
The Ramaswamy campaign was still testing the ad to gauge its effectiveness when the spot burst into public view late Monday.
D.J. Byrnes, a left-leaning local journalist known as the Rooster, published the ad online, calling it “loathsome.”
The spot, which took little time to spread widely online, showed Dr. Acton’s 82-year-old mother, Donna Arthur, using harsh language to denounce her estranged daughter.
“Don’t let her become your governor,” Ms. Arthur said.
‘Just Plain Wrong’
The backlash was immediate and intense.

As the controversy swirled, Mr. Ramaswamy reached out privately to other Ohio Republicans to gauge their reaction, according to three people briefed on the exchanges. He felt the coverage by the news media was unfair and wanted a chance to explain his thinking, even if it did not lead to public support for running the ad.

Governor DeWine called the ad “deeply, deeply troubling” and “just plain wrong,” and he urged Mr. Ramaswamy — whom he has endorsed — to take it down. Mr. Husted, who faces his own tight election against former Senator Sherrod Brown on Nov. 3, said he would not have run the ad. Republicans in close races in other states, like Representative Ashley Hinson of Iowa, who is running for Senate, said it should come off the air.
Not only has Mr. Ramaswamy so far declined to back away from the ad, but his campaign also bought more than $4 million in Ohio airtime to show it to viewers.
Supporters of Mr. Ramaswamy echoed his contention that he has been treated unfairly by the news media and argued that there had been no public anger when Dr. Acton’s campaign had attacked him.

“Democrats and the media are trying to change the subject from ‘she’s a liar’ to ‘she was abused as a child,’” Beth Lear, an Ohio state representative from just north of Columbus, wrote in an opinion essay published Friday in The Columbus Dispatch. “It’s a masterful attempt to manipulate voters’ emotions by making Amy a victim.”

The ad served as an attempt to shift the focus of the campaign in its final days from frustrations about Mr. Trump’s economy to a referendum on Dr. Acton’s honesty. But in so doing, it placed Mr. Ramaswamy’s own morals and ethics in the spotlight, and reminded voters that Dr. Acton survived a seriously troubled childhood.

Mr. Ramaswamy has, in a sense, run a political psychology experiment on his home state. Will voters in Ohio be outraged that he has tried to secure a political advantage through a woman estranged from her daughter over allegations of rape, or will they better recall the accusation that Dr. Acton is lying?
“We ran an ad about lying,” Mr. Ramaswamy told the crowd in Strongsville. “Amy Acton is lying. She has been lying this entire campaign about me.”

But at a pumpkin festival on Friday night in Circleville, Ohio, Mr. Ramaswamy’s running mate, State Senator Rob McColley, said the campaign did not believe Dr. Acton was lying about her childhood abuse.
“Oh no, that is horrible,” Mr. McColley said. “We are accusing her of lying in her adult career.”
Anger From the Acton Campaign
Dr. Acton’s campaign has almost run out of words to express its disgust over the ad. A spokeswoman, Addie Bullock, has called it “despicable,” “disturbing” and “disqualifying.”
“Ramaswamy will do anything, including embrace child sex predators, to get what he wants,” Ms. Bullock said.

Court documents from Mahoning County, Ohio, back up the descriptions by Dr. Acton and her brother of the events of her childhood. In 1978, when Dr. Acton was 12, her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was arrested and charged with raping her.

He pleaded not guilty and was indicted by a grand jury, after which Ms. Arthur lost custody of Dr. Acton and her brother. A month later, court records show, Mr. Arthur fled the area, and a warrant was issued for his arrest. The Arthurs appear to have lived the ensuing decades in Pennsylvania, and according to Dr. Acton’s brother, they stayed together until Mr. Arthur died in 2004.
In the campaign ad, Ms. Arthur accuses her daughter of lying about her past but does not address the rape allegations.
It is not clear where Ms. Arthur lives now, and she did not respond to messages this week.

She had been living in her car with some cats in the Calvary Church parking lot, just outside Boalsburg, Pa., according to the Rev. Stacy Sublett, the church’s pastor. Mr. Sublett said that he had tried to find Ms. Arthur permanent housing in the area but that she declined the assistance.
He said he was not aware of friends or family who came to see her.

nytimes.com/2026/10/24/business/airlines.headline: Attention, Passengers: High Airfares May Be Here to Stay

paragraphs.text: Airfares soared because of the war with Iran. It’s looking increasingly likely that prices won’t come down anytime soon.
Tensions in the Middle East have risen in recent days, pushing up oil prices. But even if the war ended and fuel costs fell, ticket prices could remain stubbornly high.

Travelers, particularly affluent ones who buy high-end seats, have been undeterred so far by the higher prices. Other costs for the airlines are up. And they are facing less competition. Spirit Airlines, which once offered tickets for less than $100, shut down this spring, and other low-cost carriers are struggling.

“It’s expensive to fly airplanes,” Scott Kirby, the chief executive of United Airlines, told Wall Street analysts in a conference call on Wednesday. Most companies in his industry will lose money this year, so fares will have to remain high, he said. “I think the tide has to rise for everyone or those airlines simply won’t exist.”

In September, airfares were 22 percent more expensive than a year earlier, according to federal data. The average cost of a round-trip Thanksgiving flight within the United States is currently about $389, about 39 percent more than it was at this time last year, according to Hopper, a booking app known for its price-tracking features. Similar flights for Christmas are averaging $452, up 22 percent from a year ago.

Fuel typically accounts for about 25 to 30 percent of an airline’s operating costs, behind only wages and employee benefits. So when jet fuel prices nearly doubled in March, airlines raised fares. Jet fuel prices fell in the spring, but have steadily climbed since July. Today, they are about as high as they have been since the United States and Israel began attacking Iran on Feb. 28.

American Airlines and United each said this past week that their fuel costs in the quarter that ended in September were nearly $1.9 billion higher than the same period last year. United said it had recaptured 72 percent of that cost, though it expected to recover the rest eventually.
Other expenses have increased, too. Landing fees and airport rents were up 9 to 14 percent in the third quarter from a year earlier for several airlines.

Airlines are also paying employees more after negotiating new labor contracts with pilots, flight attendants and other workers in recent years. American, Delta Air Lines and United each spent 7 to 10 percent more on salaries, wages and benefits during the first nine months of this year than they did in the same period in 2025.

Airline executives say ticket price increases are long overdue to cover such costs. Adjusted for inflation, the average fare for a flight within the United States last year was 25 percent cheaper than a decade ago, according to federal data, which does not include fees.
In the past, travelers could expect fares to come down once fuel prices fell. As costs dipped, airlines would have cut prices to win over as many customers as possible.
But the industry is changing. Carriers are less concerned with filling planes and more so with attracting customers who will pay for more comfortable seats and better service.

That is, in part, because budget carriers are no longer the powerhouses they once were. A little over a decade ago, Spirit had some of the industry’s highest profit margins. But Spirit shut down in May, after struggling with high costs and competition, notably from larger airlines that offered no-frills “basic economy” tickets to lure customers from Spirit and other low-cost carriers. The airline’s demise already appears to have contributed to higher fares in some places.

Southwest Airlines, which also had a reputation for bringing down prices, is remaking itself in the mold of American, Delta and United by charging bag fees and removing seats from its Boeing 737 planes to make space for more expensive ones with extra legroom.

Delta and United are by far the most profitable airlines today because they have focused on selling premium seats and keeping customers loyal by offering big spenders generous perks. The sale of economy cabin seats — once the bread-and-butter of airlines — now accounts for less than half of Delta’s revenue. American has said leisure travelers are buying nearly two-thirds of the airline’s premium and business-class seats.

John Dalton is one of the customers airlines covet. Mr. Dalton, an actor who teaches theater appreciation to older people in Miami, has always loved to travel. He first bought a business-class ticket a decade ago for a trip to Europe to celebrate overcoming cancer. Today, he tries to fly business on most long trips, even if it means reducing other spending.

“I was like, ‘OK, I’ll splurge on getting a business class seat,’ and then I liked it, which was the curse,” he said. “All of a sudden, you’re like, ‘Oh, this is the way it could be,’ to the point that I dread having to fly coach.”
Generally, customers have accepted double-digit fare increases with a “limited amount of resistance,” Delta’s chief executive, Ed Bastian, said on an earnings call this month.

And while budget travelers have pulled back a bit, some airline executives said they were not too anxious about losing a few customers. American, Alaska Airlines and United recently said they were flying slightly emptier planes while collecting much more revenue. That is “a trade we would make every day,” United’s chief commercial officer, Andrew Nocella, said on the earnings call.
The question now is whether airlines will be able to resist the urge to lower prices to fill those seats.

Some industry experts said airline executives were using their public statements, especially their conference calls with analysts, to signal to investors and one another that they did not plan to lower fares.
“They will willingly discount-shame anybody who has the temerity to try to break price,” said Robert Mann, an industry consultant and former airline executive.
Mr. Mann said there are fewer airlines in the United States than in the past, which means the remaining companies may feel less pressure to lower fares.

Airlines cycle between flooding the market with seats and retrenching. In 2024, carriers were optimistic about demand and significantly increased the number of flights they offered during the summer. The resulting glut of seats forced companies like Spirit to cut prices. That contributed to Spirit’s downfall, which has reduced the number of seats for sale, thus easing the pressure on airlines to lower fares.
Over a longer stretch of time, the balance could again swing back in the favor of travelers.

This month, Boeing received long-delayed federal approval to start delivering the largest version of its 737 Max plane. United and Alaska are expected to receive 19 and 22 of those planes next year. Southwest also expects to start receiving the smallest Max variant, which was certified in August.

And if the economy weakens and stocks fall sharply, many affluent travelers may rethink their spending on travel, opting for fewer trips, downgrading to economy seats or shopping around for lower fares.
