Even travelers like Mr. Dalton have their limits. As major airlines start offering “basic business” fares that strip away perks like lounge access or extra checked bags, he is becoming more willing to shop around.
“It makes me feel less loyal to an airline,” he said, “if they’re nickel-and-diming everything.”

nytimes.com/2026/10/24/climate/takeaways.headline: 5 Takeaways From Our Investigation of Trump’s Waivers for Polluters

paragraphs.text: They are among the biggest sources of cancer-causing pollution in the United States: chemical manufacturers, steel-making plants, facilities that sterilize medical devices.
In 2024, they were required to take steps to reduce their toxic emissions. That all changed when President Trump returned to office and gave them a pass.
It was the biggest presidential intervention in the Clean Air Act since the bedrock environmental law was enacted more than 50 years ago.

Mr. Trump has gone further than any president in dismantling regulations designed to protect the environment, resulting in dirtier air and water. Even so, his aid to specific polluters stands out. To understand these efforts, The New York Times reviewed more than 10,000 pages of government documents and conducted more than 70 interviews.
Here are five takeaways from our investigation.
Mr. Trump issued more than 200 waivers to some of the worst polluters.
Mr. Trump exempted 202 facilities in 39 states and Puerto Rico from new regulations that the Environmental Protection Agency had adopted during the Biden administration.
The new rules came about because the Clean Air Act requires the E.P.A. to periodically study the latest pollution controls and impose them if they are affordable and effective.

The rules required medical sterilizers, chemical plants and steel facilities to monitor for emissions of cancer-causing gases along their property lines by 2027. If they detected certain levels of the gases escaping into communities, they had to fix the leaks. And they had to post the findings publicly, so that neighbors could see what was in the air.

When it comes to chemical manufacturers, the government estimated companies would have to spend about $440 million to install equipment to comply with the new rules and about $163 million each year after that.
That would amount to less than 1 percent of the chemical industry’s annual sales.
The manufacturers fought the new rules and looked to the president for help.

The chemical industry criticized the rules as expensive, unnecessary and unworkable. Its lawyers filed petitions with Congress, the E.P.A. and federal courts to overturn or at least delay the regulations. It also challenged the scientific findings underpinning the policies.
Yet the industry lost again and again as agency officials and the courts concluded its claims lacked merit.

As soon as Mr. Trump returned to office, though, the industry players saw an opportunity to change their fortunes. Less than two weeks after the inauguration, trade groups asked the E.P.A. administrator, Lee Zeldin, to push Mr. Trump to exempt them from the rules. A trade association for the medical device industry, which uses ethylene oxide, donated to Mr. Trump’s inauguration fund and to his campaign affiliate, MAGA Inc.
They kept their pressure up until they got what they wanted.
On July 14, 2025, the chief executives of Dow, BASF, Eastman Chemical and Huntsman Corporation sent a letter directly to Mr. Trump, and shared it with the E.P.A.

“We write to bring to your attention the urgent need for action on requests submitted earlier this year for presidential exemptions under the Clean Air Act to provide relief from unnecessary and ineffective obligations imposed by E.P.A.,” they wrote.
Three days later, on July 17, Mr. Trump began answering their pleas.
The exemptions handed out by the president were unprecedented.
Never before had a president let specific polluters off the hook with the stroke of his pen.

An obscure provision of the Clean Air Act allows the president to issue exemptions from rules if a manufacturing disruption would undermine national security and the technology needed to comply is not widely available. President Richard M. Nixon signed the law in 1970, but the provision had never been invoked.

Yet Mr. Trump approved the requests for waivers even though the technology was readily accessible and the industry’s national security arguments had little detail to substantiate them, according to documents reviewed by The Times.
The E.P.A. set up a special email inbox for requests for exemptions. Companies flooded the agency with submissions.
The president put former chemical industry lobbyists inside the E.P.A.

The waivers were good for two years, with the possibility of an extension. The reprieve for the companies gave Mr. Trump time to stock the E.P.A. with former industry insiders who worked from within to gut the rules altogether.

For example, Mr. Trump nominated a former top lobbyist for the Advanced Medical Technology Association, or AdvaMed, a powerful trade association, to lead the agency’s air regulation office. The former lobbyist, Aaron Szabo, had been helping the industry fight the regulations under the Biden administration. Now he oversaw the effort to rewrite them. Documents reviewed by The Times indicate that Mr. Szabo helped handle the waiver requests and then pushed employees to pull back on enforcement.
The president’s decisions were a huge victory for an industry that backed his re-election campaign and continued to donate to his pet causes once he took office again.

AdvaMed boasted earlier this year in a letter to members that its lobbying efforts, which included political contributions to Mr. Trump’s causes, had paid off in the form of curbs on air toxics rules that saved companies millions of dollars in upgrades per plant.
“Membership has its privileges,” the group wrote.
The waivers potentially affect the health of around 3.3 million people.
That is how many Americans live within three miles of at least one facility that received a permission slip to pollute from Mr. Trump.
Before the E.P.A. finalized the new rules in 2024, it held meetings to warn people who lived near facilities that sterilize medical devices about the elevated cancer risks.

These facilities use ethylene oxide, a colorless, sweet-smelling, toxic gas. The agency’s research had found that long-term exposure to ethylene oxide increased the risk of leukemia, multiple myeloma and other types of cancer, particularly for people living close to where the gas is produced or used.

“You see these pretty buildings and you think they’re OK,” said Wayne Powell, who lives a five-minute drive from a sterilizer outside of Richmond, Va., that resembles an ordinary warehouse. “But you don’t know that they’re harboring things that are hazardous to our health.”

nytimes.com/2026/10/24/climate/trump-epa.headline: How Trump Gave the Worst Polluters a Free Pass

paragraphs.text: Within sight of a southeast Texas middle school stands a chemical plant that President Trump excused from new federal rules intended to curb its cancer-causing pollution.
About a 30-minute drive from Pittsburgh, a steel-making facility has spewed carcinogenic chemicals near homes for years. Mr. Trump gave it a similar waiver from recent clean-air rules.

And on the outskirts of Richmond, Va., the owners of an industrial warehouse emailed the Trump administration asking for their own waiver. Their wish was granted. Nine months later, the facility accidentally released a large plume of carcinogenic gas into the community.

In total, since taking office again, Mr. Trump exempted 202 facilities in 39 states and Puerto Rico from clean-air regulations that were going into effect. Some were among the country’s worst industrial polluters, including chemical manufacturers, copper smelters and coal-burning power plants. About 3.3 million people live within three miles of at least one affected facility.

The exemptions represent the biggest presidential intervention in enforcement of the Clean Air Act in the half-century since President Richard M. Nixon signed the bedrock environmental law. And that is only one of the ways the Trump administration is dismantling a variety of federal environmental protections.

Before Mr. Trump’s return, the chemical industry was losing its fight to block or at least delay tougher E.P.A. requirements to reduce toxic emissions. It had pleaded with agency officials, filed lawsuits and appealed to Congress. But officials and the courts had largely rejected the industry’s claims of undue expense and regulatory overreach.
Now, Mr. Trump is prioritizing the economic interests of corporations and easing costs for polluting industries, and their immense clout is striking.

The president’s exemptions were good for two years, with the possibility of an extension. The reprieve for the companies gave Mr. Trump time to stock the Environmental Protection Agency with appointees who had lobbied for the industries they now regulate. Those officials then quickly went to work from the inside to gut the rules altogether.

Mr. Trump has taken an expansive view of executive power in his second term. On the environmental front, he has unilaterally shredded regulations, withheld science funding appropriated by Congress and ordered coal plants that planned to shutter to continue running.
Even so, his evisceration of the new Clean Air Act rules stands out.

Many of the details of how the Trump administration aided the chemical industry are being reported here for the first time. In one upside-down moment, industry executives provided the agenda for a meeting with E.P.A. staff and then effectively presided over it.

Mr. Trump also nominated Aaron Szabo, a former lobbyist for the Advanced Medical Technology Association, or AdvaMed, a powerful trade group, to lead the E.P.A.’s air regulation office. Once there, Mr. Szabo helped handle the waiver requests and then pushed employees to pull back on enforcement, documents show.

To understand how Mr. Trump gave a free pass to some of the worst polluters, The New York Times reviewed more than 10,000 pages of government documents and spoke to more than 70 people familiar with the efforts, including former E.P.A. officials and industry executives.

“These companies, with their campaign contributions and the revolving door of former lobbyists and executives that now work in the regulatory agencies — that is where the petrochemical industry gets its power,” said Brent Coon, a Beaumont, Texas, lawyer who has spent decades squaring off in court against petrochemical firms over environmental and health risks.

The Clean Air Act requires the E.P.A. — created in 1970 to protect public health and the environment — to periodically review the latest pollution controls and impose them broadly if they are affordable and effective. The most recent review began under the Biden administration, which in 2024 finalized new, tougher requirements.

In granting the waivers to those rules, Mr. Trump cited an obscure clause in the act that allows exemptions if complying with new rules would threaten national security and if the necessary technology is not widely available.
Yet the president approved the waivers even though the equipment was readily accessible and the industry’s national security claims had little detail to substantiate them, documents show.

The Biden administration pushed through the new pollution requirements after evidence emerged about the health threats posed by ethylene oxide, a colorless gas used to make products like plastic soda bottles and to sterilize medical devices like pacemakers.

E.P.A. researchers had concluded that ethylene oxide was 30 to 60 times as carcinogenic as previously thought, particularly for people who live near plants where the gas is made or used. The agency held meetings to warn community members about the elevated risks.

Outside Richmond, home to one of the country’s largest commercial sterilizers of medical devices, some residents left one of these briefings wondering whether recent cancer diagnoses among neighbors were tied to the plant, though it is virtually impossible to prove pollution caused a specific cancer case.

“You see these pretty buildings, and you think they’re OK,” said Wayne Powell, who lives a five-minute drive from the plant, which resembles an ordinary warehouse. “But you don’t know that they’re harboring things that are hazardous to our health.”

As recently as April, the plant, owned by Sterilization Services of Virginia, had a mishap. A faulty valve caused 580 pounds of ethylene oxide to leak from large drums and waft in a toxic plume over nearby homes, state records show. The plant’s state permit allows it to discharge no more than 400 pounds of ethylene oxide in an entire year.
Representatives for Sterilization Services of Virginia did not respond to calls seeking comment.

The new rules required not only sterilizers but also chemical plants and steel facilities to monitor for emissions of cancer-causing gases along their property lines by 2027. If certain amounts of the gases got out, the operators had to fix the leaks. Some facilities also had to build special containment systems — akin to giant breadboxes — to reduce gas releases.

Though the facilities would still have to follow pollution limits already in place, the industries fought the E.P.A.’s new mandates, calling them expensive, unnecessary and unworkable. They also challenged the Biden administration’s scientific findings.

“It is critical that regulation of our industry is based on sound science and that those regulations reflect a reasonable assessment of the risks and benefits involved,” Brendan Bradley, a spokesman for the American Chemistry Council, an industry trade group, said in a statement.

The Trump administration did not ask companies to present an exhaustive case for why they deserved a waiver from these new requirements. It was as easy as sending an email to the E.P.A. and invoking the obscure exemption language in the act, a provision that no president had ever used.
Taylor Rogers, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement the waivers were necessary to protect American manufacturing.

“Exemptions were issued due to crushing Biden-era regulations that required large swaths of our industrial base to adopt technologies that don’t exist outside the imagination of Biden’s E.P.A. bureaucrats,” she said.
Mr. Trump’s decisions rewarded industries that backed his re-election campaign and continued to donate to his pet causes once he won.

AdvaMed boasted earlier this year in a letter to members that its lobbying efforts, which included political contributions to Mr. Trump’s causes, had paid off, saving the industry millions of dollars in upgrades.
“Membership has its privileges,” the group wrote.
‘A Sense of Urgency’
The chemical plant in Port Neches, Texas, just south of the meandering Neches River, is a vital cog in American manufacturing. It is among the country’s biggest producers of ethylene oxide.

The plant’s owner, Indorama Ventures, is a major employer in the region and supports local schools, including Groves Middle School. It provides a football training complex through which its chemical pipelines run. It also sponsors the annual Fish-O-Rama Fishing Tournament to raise money for local science and math programs.
The plant also has a long history of releasing toxic pollutants into the community, state records show.

On more than 500 occasions since 2003, it has experienced malfunctions or other failures that resulted in releases of air pollution or toxic chemicals, frequently in violation of its permit, Texas records show.

From his front yard, dotted with baseballs and children's bikes, Cody Coburn can see the flares that burn off excess toxic gases from the plant across the street. Some nights they rattle his windows, suggesting a possible malfunction at the plant.
The incidents leave Mr. Coburn and his wife wondering if they are taking a risk living there with their young sons. “We’ve talked about moving away,” he said.
The violations continued after Indorama, based in Bangkok, purchased the facility from the Texas-based Huntsman Corporation in 2020.

A particularly alarming incident occurred in early 2022. A control valve failed, sending 57,000 pounds of pollutants into the air, including ethylene oxide, records show. The discharges continued for nearly a week.
That 2022 incident, and others like it, put Indorama on the radar of E.P.A. officials who were rewriting the rules for chemical plants.
These kinds of facilities had long used models to estimate their emissions. The problem was, no one could say if the estimates were accurate.

The E.P.A. decided to find out. The agency emailed the managers of the Indorama plant and 10 other facilities, ordering them to install temporary devices at the edges of their properties to measure toxins in the air.
Career E.P.A. employees were stunned by the results, said Brenda Shine, then the agency engineer who supervised the data collection.

Based on data provided by the plant, agency staff had estimated the tests for benzene, a gas linked to cancer, would find about 0.02 micrograms per cubic meter of air — a relatively small amount. But the actual air sampling revealed benzene levels nearly 50 times as high. It also found three times as much ethylene oxide in the air as estimated.
Similar conditions were found at other plants, but Indorama’s tests showed the worst results.
The public health implications were enormous.

An additional one in every 500 people who lived near the plant for most of their lives was likely to develop cancer from exposure to ethylene oxide, a March 2024 EPA report concluded. That risk is 20 times the 1-in-10,000 level that the E.P.A. typically considers to be the highest acceptable cancer risk when it evaluates carcinogens.
That cancer threat from the Indorama plant could be cut by 95 percent, the E.P.A. found, if better pollution controls were installed.
“There was a sense of urgency,” said Joseph Goffman, who supervised Ms. Shine’s work as the head of the agency’s air office during the Biden administration. “It really alarmed local communities.”

Indorama executives argued that the E.P.A. had gathered samples while the plant was undergoing maintenance, so the results did not reflect normal operations, records show. But when agency inspectors returned in 2024, they still found ethylene oxide leaking in multiple locations and drifting across the facility’s fence line.
A spokeswoman for Indorama declined to address detailed questions from The Times about the plant and cancer risks because they involve continuing regulatory discussions.

“Indorama Ventures recognizes the importance of protecting the health and well-being of our employees, neighbors and surrounding communities,” Patricia Sakamiti, a company spokeswoman, said in a statement.
The test results were a critical factor in the E.P.A.’s approving the new air toxics rules.

Those rules required Indorama and other facilities to limit leaks from valves and upgrade flares so that they could burn off more toxic gases before they were released. The companies also had to install monitors around a plant’s fence line. The results would be publicly posted, letting neighbors see what they were breathing.

The E.P.A. estimated that similar improvements would cost about $440 million to install and $163 million a year to maintain for all affected facilities. That would constitute less than 1 percent of the industry’s national sales.
For that price, millions of people who live near these plants would be at a lower cancer risk, the agency concluded.

Indorama said the E.P.A. had acted “beyond its statutory authority” when it required the fence line tests and that the demands were based on a “flawed risk assessment.” Executives from plants that use ethylene oxide to sterilize medical devices, including the one outside Richmond, joined the protests.

So did companies like U.S. Steel, which operates a facility in Clairton, Pa., near Pittsburgh. The plant bakes coal at up to 2,000 degrees Fahrenheit, turning it into coke, an ingredient in steel making.

U.S. Steel, in a statement at the time, said it was committed to working with the E.P.A. in supporting regulations that were “well grounded in law” and science. “Unfortunately, the 2024 coke rules do not meet these criteria,” it said.
Lobbyists Turned Regulators

Eleven days into the second Trump administration, Lee Zeldin, the newly sworn-in E.P.A. administrator, received a request from the American Chemistry Council and American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers, the two biggest trade groups for the chemical industry.
They wanted Mr. Zeldin, a former Republican lawmaker, to push the president to give them relief from the Biden-era rules.

The trade associations, in their petition, laid the groundwork for the Trump administration to intervene for national security reasons, arguing that the new requirements could cause them to curb or cease production. “National security includes economic security and protection of domestic production of chemicals vital to public health,” the petition said.
The chemical and medical device industries were also busy writing a flurry of checks to Mr. Trump’s causes.

AdvaMed sent $125,000 to his inauguration fund and $1 million to MAGA Inc., one of Mr. Trump’s campaign affiliates. The latter donation was made on the same day in April 2025 that AdvaMed’s chief executive, Scott Whitaker, attended a candlelight dinner with Mr. Trump at his Mar-a-Lago resort.
“Yes, I met with President Trump and was grateful for the opportunity to introduce our lifesaving industry to him,” Mr. Whitaker said in a statement, adding that ethylene oxide did not come up.

One of the E.P.A. officials who was copied on the request for regulatory relief was Mr. Szabo, a senior adviser who was awaiting confirmation to lead the agency’s powerful Office of Air and Radiation, which oversees regulations intended to curb toxic pollution.

In Mr. Trump’s first administration, Mr. Szabo had served as a White House lawyer, helping review new regulations. But before that term ended, he moved to the lobbying world, representing oil and gas companies, chemical manufacturers and coal-burning electric utilities.

His clients included AdvaMed, and Mr. Szabo secured private meetings with the E.P.A. and the White House through 2024 to help the medical device industry fight the Biden-era changes, records show. Before Mr. Trump’s re-election, Mr. Szabo also helped draft the E.P.A. chapter in Project 2025, the conservative blueprint for a second Trump term.

From his new perch within the E.P.A., Mr. Szabo began participating in gatherings at the agency’s headquarters with former clients and working on the industry’s wish list, according to emails reviewed by The Times.

Brigit Hirsch, an E.P.A. spokeswoman, said in a statement that an ethics agreement Mr. Szabo signed last year permitted him to work on “general” matters that affected various industry players but not “particular” matters that narrowly affected his former clients until one year passed.
E.P.A. officials held at least 40 meetings with chemical industry executives in 2025, agency entrance logs show.

Mr. Szabo coordinated these efforts with two deputies who had joined the E.P.A. after stints in industry: Abigale Tardif, a former lobbyist for the oil refiner Marathon Petroleum and American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers, and Alexander Dominguez, a former American Petroleum Institute lobbyist.
Mr. Szabo also reached out to Emily Underwood, a senior White House lawyer, suggesting that the president could invoke the Clean Air Act exemptions, documents show.
“Thanks Aaron! Can we just see the copy for POTUS’ proposed mention of/remarks on this?” Ms. Underwood responded.
Ms. Underwood, when reached by phone, told The Times that the agency took the lead on these efforts: “The best person to talk to on that would be Aaron Szabo at the E.P.A.”
Mr. Szabo declined to comment. Ms. Tardif did not respond to requests for comment.

The same day that he corresponded with Ms. Underwood, Mr. Szabo appeared before the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee for his confirmation hearing. It was Ash Wednesday, and Mr. Szabo, a Catholic, bore a cross of ashes on his forehead.
Mr. Szabo told senators that he had a personal stake in clean-air rules because he had cystic fibrosis, a lung disease exacerbated by air pollution.
“Growing up, I could feel the impact of poor air quality in my lungs,” he said.
A week later, the E.P.A. created a special inbox to receive requests for waivers from the rules. Companies soon flooded the agency with submissions.
Presidential Exemptions
To understand the newfound power of the chemical industry inside the E.P.A., consider a meeting in May 2025 at the agency’s satellite offices in North Carolina.

Nearly a dozen senior chemical industry executives flew in and gathered in a large conference room. Another 30 industry members joined on a video call. The participants represented some of the industry’s biggest players, including Dow, BASF and Huntsman.
The agenda was set by the chemical industry rather than its regulators.

“To provide some structure to our discussions, we prepared the attached agenda,” Leslie Bellas, a vice president for regulatory affairs at American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers, wrote to the E.P.A. team.
The de facto moderator was Brendan Mascarenhas, a lobbyist for the American Chemistry Council, according to meeting minutes and participants.
Industry officials were not shy about their demands then and at follow-up gatherings with E.P.A. officials, the minutes show.

First, they wanted the E.P.A. to rescind its scientific finding that ethylene oxide was much more likely to cause cancer than previously thought. The determination had formed a legal basis for many regulations, and with it gone, the rules would fall like dominoes.
Companies also wanted to roll back requirements for fence line monitors. And in the event of a leak, they wanted to keep plants running longer before shutting down for repairs.
That same month, the chief executives of Dow, Chemours, OxyChem and the American Chemistry Council gathered with Mr. Zeldin at his office in Washington.

Chris Jahn, the head of the chemistry council, wrote on social media afterward that they discussed transforming the E.P.A. so that it focused on “pro-growth policies,” while also “protecting human health and the environment.”
By July 2025, when Mr. Trump had still not granted the waivers, executives grew anxious.

The deadline for the first of the new pollution controls was only a year away, and it would take nearly that long to install the necessary equipment. So the chief executives of Dow, BASF, Eastman Chemical and Huntsman wrote a letter directly to Mr. Trump and shared it with the E.P.A.

“We write to bring to your attention the urgent need for action on requests submitted earlier this year for Presidential Exemptions under the Clean Air Act to provide relief from unnecessary and ineffective obligations imposed by E.P.A.,” they wrote.
Three days later, on July 17, Mr. Trump began answering their pleas.

He issued his first exemptions for 50 chemical plants and 40 sterilizers. His order said that “the current compliance timeline would undermine our national security,” and that the sterilizer rule relied on “technologies that do not exist in a commercially viable form,” even though the breadbox-like enclosures were already in use in some states.
The E.P.A. pointed to Mr. Trump when asked about the exemptions. “This decision was made by the White House, as it is a presidential authority,” Mr. Szabo wrote to one Texas Republican lawmaker.
Then, two of the former lobbyists within the E.P.A. turned to weakening the underlying rules.

One was Ms. Tardif, who had represented the oil refiner Marathon Petroleum in meetings at the E.P.A. as recently as December 2024. In a June 2025 email, an official at American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers thanked her for “productive discussions” about “reconsideration” of the chemical plant rules and copied an official at Marathon.

The other was Mr. Szabo, who asked his staff this spring to strike the same provisions from the sterilizer rule that he had once represented AdvaMed in opposing, including the requirement to install the enclosures.
He delivered an even bigger victory to his former clients by summer.

In a memo dated Aug. 13, E.P.A. staff members warned Mr. Szabo that removing the fence line monitoring requirement for all affected chemical plants would be “difficult to justify” in court. They also noted that the Clean Air Act required the E.P.A. to address “air toxics that pose the greatest potential health threat,” including those tied to cancer.
Despite those warnings, Mr. Szabo issued the order to kill the mandate that same day.

It would be one of Mr. Szabo’s final acts at the agency. This month he resigned and took another job at a law firm that has represented industry groups in their challenges to some of the same Clean Air Act rules.
Weighing Risks

In Clairton, smokestacks at U.S. Steel’s facility release clouds of steam and chemicals. Thanks to the Trump administration, the plant no longer has to curb some of its toxic emissions, at least for now.

Melanie Meade’s house, in her family for generations, sits on a ridge overlooking the plant. In her backyard, it often smells like rotten eggs or burning rubber, and time outdoors makes her feel lightheaded.
Ms. Meade said she knew she faced an elevated risk of cancer, which killed her older sister and several of her neighbors. But she cannot afford to buy a comparable house elsewhere. So she stays.

A spokesman for U.S. Steel, Andrew Fulton, said in an email that Clairton Coke Works had never been fined for exceeding benzene emissions standards. The company plans to invest up to $2.5 billion in its plants in southwestern Pennsylvania, but none of it will be spent on new pollution controls in Clairton, Mr. Fulton said.
“It would be premature for U.S. Steel or any other regulated company to invest in controls while the rule is under reconsideration,” he said.

In Groves, Texas, which sits adjacent to the Indorama plant, some residents were surprised to learn that Mr. Trump had waived requirements designed to protect their health. Their reactions were mixed.
Chris Borne, the mayor of Groves, appreciates Indorama.
“I have full faith in our facilities where I live,” said Mr. Borne, an electrician who has handled jobs in many of the area’s chemical plants. “Sometimes the rule makers, they go too far.”
Others were angry about the administration’s moves.
“Making things great again — I thought that meant making all things great, including our health,” said Lance Bridges, who voted for Mr. Trump in 2016.
As Mr. Bridges spoke, his 22-year-old daughter pushed a toy scooter carrying his granddaughter in front of their house.
A few weeks later, the Indorama plant had another accidental discharge. Gases started seeping into the community at 6 a.m. on Sept. 11, shortly before students began streaming into school.
State records show that the leak continued for eight hours.
Andrew Chavez and Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

nytimes.com/2026/10/24/us/politics/fishi.headline: They Were Accused of Illegal Fishing. They Ended Up in ICE Detention.

paragraphs.text: Standing along the edge of a canal near Fort Lauderdale, Fla., Edguin Morales Aguirre had just cast a line when officers with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission approached him and two of his friends. They spotted a bucket holding egg-bearing blue crabs, which are illegal to have in the state.

After running checks on their IDs, the officers summoned immigration agents to detain Mr. Morales and one of his friends, who were surprised to learn that the officers were working with federal immigration authorities.
“This never used to happen,” Mr. Morales said. “Before, if they caught you fishing in a place you weren’t supposed to, they would just issue you a citation.”

In Republican-led states, officers who hand out fishing licenses, inspect produce and investigate financial crimes have been deputized by Immigration and Customs Enforcement, using their contact with local residents on a day-to-day basis to broaden the reach of President Trump’s mass deportation campaign.

The increased cooperation among states that have embraced Mr. Trump’s immigration agenda is part of a federal program known as 287(g), which pays state and local agencies to assist with immigration enforcement. Once largely reserved for local police and sheriffs’ offices to increase ICE’s access to local jails, it has expanded under Mr. Trump to include unusual agencies like state agriculture departments, gaming commissions, fish and wildlife agencies, and alcohol control offices.

But these agencies have little experience carrying out immigration arrests, which can get contentious and even violent. Some incidents involving ICE officers have led to fatal shootings. Advocates have criticized the enlistment of the agencies, saying it increases the risk of officer misconduct and deepens fears in immigrant communities that people could be detained by seemingly innocuous authorities.

“We have really serious concerns that these state agencies that have traditionally not been accountable to local communities would see themselves as accountable only to ICE’s agenda,” said Naureen Shah, who leads the American Civil Liberties Union’s immigration policy and advocacy work. “What is it about their training that they receive as fish and wildlife regulation experts or agricultural experts that leads ICE to believe it should entrust them with really fraught situations?”

Civil rights advocates have long denounced the 287(g) program, questioning the qualifications of state and local officers for conducting immigration enforcement. Although the federal government previously required several weeks of in-person training, the Trump administration scaled back to 40 hours of virtual training for deputized officers making immigration arrests in their communities.

The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that those officers “undergo ICE background investigations and clearances.” The department added that it had been having “tremendous success” in making arrests with the help of local law enforcement.

Trump administration officials have urged agencies to sign up, and have called the 287(g) program a “force multiplier.” More than 2,600 agreements have been signed across the country as of late October, up from about 130 at the start of Mr. Trump’s second term.

More than 29,300 state and local officers have been granted the authority to question people about their immigration status and make arrests, according to the Department of Homeland Security. That is nearly five times the number of deportation officers that ICE had before Mr. Trump’s return to office.

The program has become another point of partisan division. Many Democratic-led states, including New York and California, have restricted local law enforcement from cooperating with ICE, drawing the ire of Trump administration officials who say the limits make it harder to arrest people.

Still, the state and local partnerships have become a potent tool for the administration, making up a growing share of ICE arrests, which have hit record highs in recent months. The 287(g) program has also helped Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, achieve his goal of carrying out immigration enforcement in a quieter way.
“We’re still on track pushing as hard as we can,” Mr. Mullin said in a Newsmax interview in May. “We just are doing it in a different way by using local law enforcement to work with us.”

In Louisiana and Mississippi, fish and wildlife departments have similarly partnered with ICE. Even agencies that regulate alcohol and tobacco have signed up in Louisiana and Florida. Nationally, the bulk of immigration arrests are still carried out by ICE, in part because many officers have been deputized in Republican states with fewer immigrants, including West Virginia.

But the partnerships have been especially effective in Florida, which has tallied more than 16,000 arrests through the 287(g) program since August 2025, according to state data. ICE’s most prolific partner in Florida has been the state’s highway safety department, whose troopers have rooted out unauthorized immigrants during traffic stops. The agency has assisted with more than 8,300 immigration arrests.

The state’s fish and wildlife commission has also been one of ICE’s top partners. About 500 federal immigration arrests were made after its officers encountered immigrants, according to state data. The commission referred requests for comment to ICE.

Mr. Morales, a 51-year-old native of Guatemala, said his brush with fish and wildlife officers led to weeks in immigration detention before he was released on bond. He added that he had a pending asylum application at the time of his arrest last year.

Marlene Velazquez Moreno, who was with Mr. Morales when he was arrested, said that she was not detained, because she had a green card. Although she was charged with a misdemeanor, Ms. Velazquez said that someone else unknown to her had left the crabs behind, and that a Broward County judge ultimately dismissed the charge. But she said their friend spent months in immigration detention before he was deported to his native Nicaragua.

In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security said Mr. Morales illegally entered the country and had a prior conviction for driving under the influence. Mr. Morales said the arrest happened more than 15 years ago, and he went to traffic school and paid fines.

Fairuze Sofia, a Fort Lauderdale-based lawyer who represents Ms. Velazquez, said she now regularly hears about immigrants in Florida being arrested by fish and wildlife officers. Another one of her clients, Alfonso Mendoza Perez, is still in immigration detention after he was questioned by them at Lake Okeechobee nearly a year ago. Mr. Mendoza said that he and his brother-in-law frequently caught catfish and tilapia at the popular fishing spot in Central Florida.
“You relax and you catch food for your family,” Mr. Mendoza said in a phone interview from a Mississippi detention facility.

After he was approached by the officers, Mr. Mendoza said he handed over his fishing license, which was valid. But after they checked his driver’s license, he said he was detained on the suspicion that he was in the country illegally. ICE agents later picked him up from the local county jail.

Mr. Mendoza, a native of Mexico, said he lived in Florida for about 17 years and worked as a roofer. Dulce Cruz, his wife, said she and her five children had lost their source of income and now lived in a mobile home with her mother and brothers in South Carolina.

In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security said Mr. Mendoza had been previously arrested for the felony sale of opium drugs. Ms. Cruz denied that her husband had a felony record, and a New York Times search of public records only found traffic-related charges for Mr. Mendoza.
Florida’s agriculture department has also assisted with more than 480 federal immigration arrests, according to state data.

Joshua Chavez, 21, said that he and his father, Mario Chavez Walle, drove to Florida from their hometown in Georgia to sell watermelons at the Jacksonville farmer’s market in late July. They pulled over at one of the state’s agricultural stations to let officers inspect their produce.

According to an incident report from the state’s agriculture department, Mr. Chavez’s father presented his expired Mexican ID to an officer, who then contacted ICE. After ICE confirmed that he had entered the United States illegally, the agriculture officer arrested him and took him to the local jail.
“Undocumented — turned over,” the report says under “offense description.”
Mr. Chavez said the officer questioned them about their immigration statuses, even though he is a U.S. citizen and has a valid driver’s license.

In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security said that Mr. Chavez Walle had been convicted of three D.U.I.s, and had “accepted incentivized departure.” Mr. Chavez disputed that his father agreed to voluntarily depart the country.

The partnerships with ICE have faced intense pushback in local communities across the nation. But some sheriffs said there were clear benefits to signing up. Michael J. Chitwood, the sheriff in Volusia County, Fla., said his office had been awarded $2.7 million in federal funding for making immigration arrests, which it had used to buy new equipment.

He added that officers were not rounding up immigrants, but rather encountering them during their routine work. His officers were scrutinized last year after they arrested a woman who was walking her pug in an area of the beach where dogs were prohibited. After contacting ICE to check her immigration status, the officers detained her, according to an incident report.

Mr. Chitwood noted that sheriffs’ offices in Florida were required to cooperate with ICE under state law, and that the partnership was helping remove some criminals from his community. Although he questioned the need to deport unauthorized immigrants who were not causing trouble, he said his officers were upholding the law.
“If the law says that you should be detained and deported, then we should follow the law,” Mr. Chitwood said.
Sheelagh McNeill and Seamus Hughes contributed research.

theguardian.com/food/2026/oct/24/uk-tsun.headline: No unions, low taxes: why some of Britain’s top chefs are opening outposts in Gulf states
theguardian.com/food/2026/oct/24/uk-tsun.author: Helena Horton

paragraphs.text: Some of London’s top restaurants are opening branches in Dubai because of a “tax tsunami” in the UK and better work ethic abroad, according to a leading restaurateur.
James Robson, a co-owner of Fallow in St James’s Market, regarded as the capital’s hottest restaurant, serving 1,000 people a day, has just signed a deal to open an outpost in the Gulf.

Other restaurants have opened in Dubai, including the celebrity hotspot Scott’s in Mayfair, the two Michelin-starred Indian venue Gymkhana, and the upmarket Chinese restaurant Park Chinois. Isabel’s, a Mayfair institution enjoyed by politicians, has opened in Abu Dhabi. And the trendy Borough Market bakery Bread Ahead has branched out in Dubai.

Despite conflicts in the Middle East, including the US-Israeli war in Iran which caused Dubai to face bombardment and an exodus of expats earlier this year, restaurants continue to open in the emirate.

Speaking from Hong Kong, where he is looking at opportunities in Asia, Robson said: “East Asia, the States and the Gulf are key growth targets for us. America champions business, the Gulf actively encourages and assists, whilst east Asia has a work ethic and taxation system that puts the UK to shame. I’m incredibly keen to start working in these regions over the next few years.”
Fallow has risen to fame partially through Instagram, where it has 650,000 followers, and its striking dishes including a whole cod’s head drenched in a spicy butter sauce.

Restaurateurs have complained of the VAT rate for hospitality in the UK, which at 20% is one of the highest rates in Europe. The European average for restaurants is about 12%. In Italy, it is set at 10% for food sold in restaurants. Chefs are calling for Andy Burnham to use next week’s budget to cut the VAT rate.

“We have had a tsunami of taxes that have got to the point where taking business risk simply does not make sense in the UK,” Robson said, “Sadly the country has sleepwalked into multiple anti-growth taxations the last two budgets and likely more will be forthcoming next week.”
The entrepreneur has asked for VAT to be put more in line with Europe. “Add 25% corporation tax and 40%-plus dividend tax, then you start to question why do businesses any more.”
Jason Atherton, a Michelin-starred chef, spends a third of his time at his Dubai restaurant now and says it is easier to make a profit abroad than in London.

But human rights experts have warned of exploitation and poor worker protections in the Gulf. Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK’s director of campaigns, said: “Dubai might look like an attractive place to do business, but the UAE has a very poor record on workers’ rights and protection from labour exploitation. The UAE has spent heavily on polishing its image in the UK, not least through Manchester City, but that glamour shouldn’t distract from how the people who keep its economy running are treated.

“Migrant workers, who make up the majority of the UAE’s population, remain bound by a sponsorship system that ties them to their employers and exposes them to labour abuse. They are denied the right to form trade unions, leaving them few ways to challenge unfair treatment.

“Any UK business expanding into the Gulf has a responsibility to carry out proper human rights due diligence, to make sure the people working in its kitchens are treated fairly, paid properly and able to raise concerns without fear of losing their job or visa.”

Some restaurants in Dubai are struggling: Dinner by Heston is temporarily closed and has been since the fallout from the war in the Middle East. The Michelin guide came under fire earlier this month because it included 16 restaurants that were either permanently or temporarily closed. It appears that some visits were undertaken by inspectors at the beginning of the year, before the war started.

Robson said he had no resentment paying UK tax. “I am incredibly proud of the taxes I pay and feel privileged that I can contribute to our country’s deficit and will continue to do so,” he said. “My point is UK growth simply does not have any risk-reward balance any more, therefore it’s play incredibly safe here and focus overseas.”

livescience.com/space/the-moon/you-have-.headline: Watch the full 'Hunter's Moon' rise next to Saturn this weekend
livescience.com/space/the-moon/you-have-.author: Jamie Carter

paragraphs.text: October's full "Hunter's Moon" is about to rise, and skywatchers will get two great chances to see it appear on the eastern horizon around sunset.

Although it officially turns full at 12:11 a.m. EDT on Monday (Oct. 26), the Hunter's Moon will appear almost perfectly full as it rises on both Sunday (Oct. 25) and Monday evenings, giving skywatchers two opportunities to observe it.

October's full moon is nicknamed the Hunter's Moon because it was traditionally a signal for hunters to prepare for the coming cold winter by hunting, slaughtering and preserving meat, according to Time and Date. That's an Anglo-Saxon name; Native American names for October's full moon include the Drying Rice Moon, the Falling Leaves Moon and the Freezing Moon.

The first chance to see the Hunter's Moon comes just before sunset on Sunday, when the almost-full moon will rise in the east. The second opportunity comes on Monday, when the moon — still essentially 100% illuminated — will again rise just after sunset. Because it will be in a slightly darker sky, Monday's moonrise will likely be more dramatic.
As it rises Sunday, the moon will appear in the constellation Aries, and Saturn will be to its upper right. On Monday, it will rise above the Pleiades open cluster (M45).

For the best view on either evening, find somewhere with a clear view low to the eastern horizon and be in position shortly before moonrise where you are. An elevated viewpoint, open field or coastline is ideal because buildings, trees and hills can delay the moment the moon becomes visible.
Related stories
Although the full moon will look magnificent with the naked eye, a backyard telescope or good stargazing binoculars can help you zoom in on various lunar features.

The Hunter's Moon may appear unusually large thanks to the "moon illusion," which makes the moon seem bigger when it's seen beside familiar objects, such as trees and buildings, near the horizon. The illusion stems from the fallacies of how our brains use distance to perceive size.

October's Hunter's Moon isn't a supermoon, but it comes immediately before a notable sequence of four consecutive supermoons. The first will be the next full moon, the Beaver Moon, on Nov. 24, followed by full moons in December, January and February. A supermoon occurs when a full moon happens while the moon is relatively close to Earth in its slightly elliptical orbit, making it appear somewhat larger and brighter than average.
How much do you know about the moon? Test your lunar smarts with our moon quiz!

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwkg5md14j8go.headline: Ukraine says Starlink connection 'now stable' after network limits
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwkg5md14j8go.author: Vicky Wong

paragraphs.text: Ukraine now has a "stable connection" to Starlink, its defence minister has said, after its military suffered days of restricted connectivity on the satellite network.

Kyiv relies on the Starlink and its military-grade counterpart Starshield for piloting drones and operations within Ukraine, but last week accused US President Donald Trump of telling owner Elon Musk to place limits on it.
This meant drones would lose connection when travelling at 161km/h (100mph) or more, it said. Trump denied doing so before saying Musk had "put it back".
Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said that speeds of more than 400km/h were now possible on the network, indicating that full capability had been restored.
"This result is above all important for our front, for our soldiers, for the operation of drones, for logistics and for communications," he said in a statement on Saturday.
Ukraine's military uses the network of 10,000 low Earth orbit satellites extensively for military operations, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield.
Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, which Musk said was controlled by the US military when he suggested the Pentagon could be behind the recent issues.
Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.

The debacle over Starlink began last week, and emerged during a broader diplomatic row between Trump and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.
Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move criticised by Ukraine and its European allies.
Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher.
While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war.
Zelensky said that, as well as seemingly limiting Starlink capability in Ukraine, the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump also denied.
Meanwhile, fighting on the ground continues.
Russian authorities said on Saturday there were power cuts in Russian-annexed Crimea following a Ukrainian drone attack.
Sergey Aksyonov, the Moscow-backed governor of the region, said restrictions on electricity and water had been put in place.
Separately, Russian-backed authorities said at least three people had been killed and another wounded in a separate Ukrainian strike in Kharkiv.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-24/.headline: Chad Bianco asks Riverside County to foot legal bills over seized ballots
latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-24/.author: Iris Kwok

paragraphs.text: Bianco’s representative last week filed a claim for damages exceeding $10,000 — arguing that Riverside County should cover his legal costs in four civil proceedings that “arose out of his official actions as Sheriff and caused him to incur reasonable attorneys’ fees, costs, and expenses,” the claim reads.

“If the County rejects the claim, Sheriff Bianco will have the right to sue the County for damages, which he intends to do,” Bradley Hertz, Bianco’s attorney, wrote in an email to The Times Friday evening. He declined a phone interview.
Brooke Federico, a spokesperson for Riverside County, said the county received the claim on Oct. 16 and is determining next steps.

The roots of the issue date back to February when Bianco — then running for governor as a Republican — pursued warrants to seize about 650,000 ballots cast in last November’s Proposition 50 special election from the Riverside County registrar. Bianco said the move was so deputies could review ballots to search for alleged election fraud.

The unprecedented action — for which Bianco obtained warrants from a local GOP-endorsed judge that he’d campaigned for — was quickly rebuked by state Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta. Last month, the seizure was ruled unlawful by the California Supreme Court.
Should the matter proceed to litigation, a central question will be whether Bianco was acting within the scope of his duties as sheriff when he seized the ballots.
Because Bianco “meets the statutory criteria,” he should be able to recover fees and costs for retaining private counsel because Riverside County refused to provide a defense, according to Hertz.

“California law requires public entities to provide for the defense of civil actions brought against employees acting in their official capacity and arising from acts within the scope of their employment,” Hertz wrote in the email.
County elected officials have disagreed.

In April, the Riverside County Board of Supervisors voted 4-1 against funding Bianco’s legal defense. At the time, Supervisor Jose Medina told The Riverside Record: “The criteria that all government agencies use is pretty clear about whether someone should or should not be paid for their legal defense, and that criteria is whether they are acting within or outside of the scope of their position.
“It can be inferred that most of the board didn’t feel like he was acting within the scope of his job,” Medina told the local outlet.
The exact dollar amount Bianco is seeking from the county is still being determined, according to Hertz. Riverside County has until Dec. 2 to respond to the claim, he said.

cnbc.com/2026/10/24/nvidias-role-as-ai-f.headline: Nvidia's role as AI financier faces first big test as neoclouds take market hit
cnbc.com/2026/10/24/nvidias-role-as-ai-f.author: Kif Leswing, Isabel O'Brien

paragraphs.text: Nvidia's emergence as financier for the global AI buildout is facing its first major stress test as credit markets tighten for key partners.

After creating the chips that powered the early stages of the generative artificial intelligence era, Nvidia turned to using its financial prowess to fund AI model developers, data center companies and a host of so-called neoclouds. CEO Jensen Huang's strategy has been to not only build the most advanced technology but to provide customers with investment as well as help them take out loans so his systems can reach many more hands.
That's meant taking full advantage of Nvidia's investment grade credit rating and providing backstop guarantees on mega-projects for OpenAI so that buildouts can get funded at lower interest rates.

As of its last quarterly financial filing in July, Nvidia had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, in addition to its guarantee on up to $105 billion for chips, land and power at a proposed 10 gigawatt OpenAI data center in Ohio. The company signed as a tenant for $20 billion in future data center leases, which will later be assigned to third parties.
For the vast majority of these deals, Nvidia won't have to pay up unless participants in the project default.

"If the demand for compute doesn't meet these really super lofty expectations, we're going to have a problem," said David Trainer, founder and CEO of financial research firm New Constructs, in an interview.
Nvidia declined to comment for this story.

Market conditions may soon test Nvidia's mettle. Shares of neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN, all cash-burning companies in Nvidia's portfolio, are down at least 30% this month. CoreWeave, the biggest of the group, has seen the spread on its credit default swaps soar past 11%, as investors are forced to pay up for insurance against default.
Nvidia has backed other neoclouds that have run into challenges.

The company is an investor in Australian AI cloud provider Firmus, which abruptly withdrew its IPO plans this month, as well as Nscale out of the U.K. and SoftBank-backed SB Energy. Both of those companies filed to go public in the U.S. in September but haven't provided updates on their plans in weeks.
Nvidia wrapped up a third straight down week on Wall Street on Friday, with its stock now off 7.6% in October, on pace for its worst month since November of last year.
Huang reiterated his confidence in the market this week, telling CNBC on Thursday that demand for neoclouds is "off the charts."

"What is missing in the middle is the working capital to fuel that growth," Huang told CNBC's Arjun Kharpal on the sidelines of the company's GTC conference in Berlin. "Because there's just so much demand across so many sectors of AI, there's a scarcity of capital."
Nvidia has taken equity stakes in dozens of companies, including big investments in OpenAI and Anthropic. Its portfolio is worth $99 billion as of the second quarter.
Building the ecosystem

Investors told CNBC that a big question surrounding Nvidia is how the company can use its cash and $5 trillion market cap to get more chips into customers' hands, and how much risk it will assume in the process.

Nvidia graphics processing units are critical for training and deploying AI models. Revenue in the latest fiscal year hit $216 billion, up roughly eightfold since OpenAI launched ChatGPT in late 2022.

Before the AI boom, Nvidia sold graphics cards that could fit into a standard server rack or PC. Its newest systems are much larger and more expensive. Nvidia's flagship Vera Rubin product is a seven-foot rack containing 72 GPUs and weighing as much as a pickup truck. It costs more than $7 million, according to a Morgan Stanley estimate.

While Nvidia still dominates the AI chip market, competition is emerging from the likes of Google, which rents out tensor processing units (TPUs) inside its massive cloud offering, and Advanced Micro Devices, which launched its first AI rack called Helios in July.

Cash is Nvidia's other great advantage. The company generated $70 billion in free cash flow in the first half of this year, while AMD totaled just over $4 billion and Google parent Alphabet went cash flow negative in the second quarter to fund its buildout.

That's a big edge for Nvidia in building out its ecosystem. The company is now offering a full-service platform complete with software, services, integrated hardware and, for many customers, financing assistance.

Nvidia's most recent quarterly financial filing in August outlined over $500 billion in off-balance-sheet commitments over the coming years, with a majority maturing through fiscal 2029. That same month, Huang announced a partnership with six large asset managers on a $500 billion financing push designed to treat compute infrastructure as an asset class. That agreement, which promised financial firms up to $125 billion in residual value guarantees on GPU financings, was in addition to the stakes Nvidia has taken as a limited partner in private equity funds. The company seeded $2 billion in Brookfield's inaugural AI Infrastructure Partners Fund, which aims to raise $10 billion in total capital, as well as other unconfirmed sums in KKR's Helix Digital Infrastructure (an $11 billion vehicle) and Valor Equity Partners' $5.4 billion dedicated compute fund.

"We used to build chips that we sell, and these are technology components that people buy and use," Huang told CNBC, in announcing the agreement in August. "But now, Nvidia's AI factory platform is really an investable asset."
Huang has adopted a marketing mantra to reinforce the unique value of its equipment.
"We're the most rentable. We're fungible, and we're durable," he said on a podcast with investor Brad Gerstner published last week.
20 years of hardware in Ohio
While Nvidia waits for Wall Street firms to pull in investors to expand the GPU loan pool, the chipmaker is already actively fostering record-sized deals in the AI infrastructure space.

Nvidia's biggest single guarantee is for OpenAI's forthcoming facility in Pike County, Ohio, which could be the largest data center in the world. That deal requires use of Nvidia hardware for at least 20 years.
The shift from chips to capital carries significant risks should OpenAI run into trouble.

If OpenAI misses payments or faces insolvency, Nvidia can take over the lease, find a new tenant, or ask the landlord, SB Energy, to sell the facility, guaranteeing to pay the difference for the latter two arrangements up to $105 billion if the release or sale falls below a minimum price. Nvidia could also pay SB Energy a lump sum. On the other side, if OpenAI posts its own collateral, or achieves a high enough credit rating, Nvidia's guarantee ends.
At CoreWeave, Nvidia's investment includes equity and a commitment to buy up to $6.3 billion of its compute if it can't find another taker.

Nvidia's backstops can take many forms, such as guaranteeing a minimum resale price or a minimum hourly offtake price for the chips in the event the lender has to recoup the assets. With Sharon AI and other neoclouds, Nvidia's deals have come with revenue-sharing agreements.

"We believe these AI cloud partners have strong customer demand and robust sales pipelines but are constrained by the large-scale infrastructure that is required to meet that demand," Nvidia said in its quarterly filing.

Huang said this week that CoreWeave doesn't need Nvidia's backstop and that the neocloud's cost of capital is decreasing. CoreWeave has roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, including about $35 billion in notes, bonds and loans. Yields on its bonds maturing in 2031 and 2032 topped 15%.
Brian Stutland, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, said the market jitters reflect concerns about the stability of the business.

CoreWeave and other neoclouds "will sign contracts into the future, and that all looks fine and dandy in their earnings reports, but is that contract going to be stable?" Stutland said. "Is it going to break at some point?"

Nvidia says its financial support can help customers build the infrastructure needed to meet strong demand for its chips. More computing capacity could also help AI labs develop new models and services, creating further demand for Nvidia products.
"They'll do $700 billion in revenue next year," Deepwater Asset Management founder Gene Munster told CNBC last month. "That affords them the ability to finance some of their customers."
Nvidia's credit backstops have mostly kicked in over the past six to 12 months. Its last annual filing, published in February, makes no mention of AI cloud agreements.

Warren Hosseinion, co-founder of AI infrastructure startup Compute Labs, said Nvidia doesn't want to be in the position of insurer, "but they're willing to play that role while the market and the industry catches up."

"They kind of control how things move," said Hosseinion, whose company tokenizes GPUs in order to open up pools of capital for neocloud operators. "They have to be very careful about how they release their technology at what pace, because a lot of that will dictate how the market moves around it."
Not a 'complete panacea'
Nvidia is actively looking for insurers to bear some of the risk associated with the potential loss in value of GPUs.

"Insurers are not yet a complete panacea to this problem," said Tom Hoad, executive director of product innovation at global insurance group Howden. "But they are probably going to turn up and be helpful in the right situations, and therefore open up some commercial transactions."
According to research from New Constructs, Nvidia's net present value of off-balance-sheet liabilities in fiscal 2026 totals over $153 billion, an increase of over $100 billion from last year.

Such liabilities have been growing across the entire AI trade, mainly in the form of lease obligations. Ratings agencies like Moody's have been sounding the alarm. In 2026, guarantees are the fastest-growing type of off-balance-sheet financing arrangements, the agency said.
Moody's doesn't count guarantees as debt when rating corporate buyers, but it's "something we're constantly monitoring," said David Gonzales, a vice president at the agency.

"These things are advanced structures that are unique, and so there is no blanket real approach you can take," he said. Gonzales said it's likely that chips will retain "values in excess of contractual residual value amounts" in the near future, which would mitigate risk in many of Nvidia's financing structures.
Still, how much exposure investment grade AI players can handle is "the question we're evaluating at all times every day," Gonzales said.
"It's the center of all of our discussions right now," he said.
— CNBC's Seema Mody contributed to this report.

torrentfreak.com/ai-assisted-paper-on-z-.headline: AI-Assisted Paper on Z-Library Cites a TorrentFreak Article That Doesn’t Exist
torrentfreak.com/ai-assisted-paper-on-z-.author: Ernesto Van der Sar

paragraphs.text: Home > Opinion Articles >

A fresh academic paper on Z-Library cites a TorrentFreak article that doesn’t exist, and several other sources in the paper are also unfindable. The authors disclose that they used AI tools, which may explain what is going on. The use of AI in an academic paper on shadow libraries is also somewhat ironic, as rightsholders are suing AI companies for using these sites to train AI models.
Z-Library is one of the largest pirate ebook libraries on the Internet, offering millions of books and papers for free.

For students and researchers who can’t afford expensive textbooks and journal subscriptions, it can be a useful resource. At the same time, publishers have spent years trying to take it down, with takedown notices and blocking orders, while U.S. authorities indicted its alleged operators.
This tension is the subject of a paper published earlier this month in the journal New Review of Academic Librarianship, written by two librarians at Nigerian universities.
The paper

The peer-reviewed academic paper doesn’t pick a side and the lead author kindly shared a copy of their work with TorrentFreak. While the conclusions are not immediately newsworthy, there was one reference that stood out right away.
A TorrentFreak Article That Doesn’t Exist

In a section on enforcement against Z-Library, the authors write that major academic publishers, including Elsevier and Springer Nature, have taken similar legal action. The reference is a 2021 TorrentFreak article, as shown below.
The claim

The problem is that this particular legal action is new to us. The reference section lists the article as “Publishers continue crackdown on shadow libraries” and links to the TorrentFreak homepage. However, we have never published an article with that title.

We did report that Elsevier and Springer Nature obtained a UK blocking order against Sci-Hub, and that several Z-Library domains were temporarily suspended over copyright infringement claims. However, we’re not aware of this particular legal action against Z-Library.

Looking more closely, we see more claims that don’t seem to fit. The paper’s account of the Z-Library criminal case, for example, states that the U.S. Department of Justice “arrested individuals” in 2022.
Some references

The DOJ’s own press release says that the two alleged operators, whose indictment we covered at the time, were arrested in Argentina “at the request of the United States.” The title the paper gives for that press release doesn’t exist either.
Plausible but Inaccurate

These non-existent citations appear plausible, as they cite real publications and organizations in a fitting context. However, that doesn’t mean they are accurate. When we went over the full reference list, we noticed that this applies to more sources.

The paper cites a 2019 Harvard Journal of Law & Technology article by IP law professor Daniel Gervais, titled “The future of intellectual property in the shadow of shadow libraries.” The table of contents of the cited issue doesn’t include it, and the cited pages are taken up by two articles on other topics.

The same applies to a 2019 College & Research Libraries article attributed to Carol Tenopir and colleagues. The cited issue has no article by Tenopir. She did co-author a 2019 article on a similar topic, but it appeared in a different journal, under a different title.

Other references that couldn’t be located include a 2019 article credited to Björn Brembs and articles credited to authors named Smith, Piper, Okike and Aronson, as well as a Kaspersky report on “the hidden dangers of shadow libraries.”
In total, we had trouble finding at least ten of the 44 references in the paper, as well as others that didn’t necessarily back the stated claims.

The obvious question is where these mystery references came from. The paper’s acknowledgements may offer a hint in the right direction, as they mention that AI was used in the research and writing process.

“We confirm that Consensus AI was used in sifting through large volume of literature and extract relevant information,” the authors write. They add that ChatGPT was used to improve the language of parts of the paper.

AI chatbots are known to invent references, often with plausible titles credited to real experts in the field. This could explain the findings, although it doesn’t prove that AI wrote these references.

We also ran the paper’s abstract and conclusion through the AI detection tool Pangram. For both sections, the tool reported that “100% of the text is likely AI-generated.” These types of tools are not perfect and can produce false positives, but it would fit the picture.
Pangram’s conclusion

It would be rather ironic if AI caused these errors. It would mean that a paper in a commercial, peer-reviewed journal, published by Taylor & Francis, relied on AI to write about Z-Library. Meanwhile, many rightsholders are suing AI companies for using shadow libraries to train AI models.
Interestingly, the paper explicitly warns that sites such as Z-Library hurt publishers’ revenue, which funds peer review and editing.

“The widespread use of Z-Library poses significant challenges to the sustainability of academic publishing. Publishers rely on subscription fees and paywalls to fund the peer review, editing, and distribution of scholarly works,” it reads, presumably generated by AI as well.
The paper doesn’t mention that peer reviewers generally aren’t paid for their work, an issue that was central to a recent lawsuit against major academic publishers, including Taylor & Francis.
Publisher Investigates

The lead author initially shared a copy of the paper with us, but didn’t answer our follow-up questions about the mysterious references. We also asked Gervais, Brembs and Tenopir whether they wrote the papers that are credited to them, but they didn’t respond either.
Publisher Taylor & Francis did reply and says that it’s looking into the matter.

“I can confirm that this has been referred to our Editorial and Publishing Ethics & Integrity teams, who will investigate the concerns you have raised,” a Taylor & Francis spokesperson informed TorrentFreak.
The publisher will not comment further while the investigation is ongoing. Whether the paper will be corrected or retracted has yet to be seen. —
The paper “Z-Library and Full-Text Access: Democratizing Knowledge or Undermining Copyright Ethics?” is available here.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm86z5n0yvy6o.headline: British woman dies after trying to rescue sons swept away at sea in the Bahamas
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm86z5n0yvy6o.author: BBC News

paragraphs.text: A woman has died after attempting to rescue her two sons when they were swept away while snorkelling in the Bahamas.
The Royal Bahamas Police Force said officers on the island of Bimini launched an investigation into the sudden death of a 36-year-old British woman on Tuesday.

The force said it believed the woman - believed to be from Stapleford in Nottinghamshire - was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.
In an attempt to rescue her sons, "the woman was also swept away", police said. The children were subsequently rescued from the water.
Foul play 'not suspected'

In a statement, posted on social media, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said: "According to the preliminary report, shortly after 10am, officers at the Alice Town police station received information that a female was unresponsive at the North Bimini Ferry Dock.

"Officers responded and, upon arrival, learned that the woman had been transported to the local clinic for medical attention, where she was subsequently pronounced dead by a local doctor despite efforts to save her life.
"Preliminary information indicates that the deceased was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.
"In an attempt to rescue her sons, the woman was also swept away.
"She was later rescued and transported to the ferry dock, where CPR was reportedly administered.
"Foul play is not suspected at this time.
"An autopsy will be conducted to assist in determining the exact cause of death."
A spokesperson for the Foreign Office added: "Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas.
"We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family."
