nytimes.com/2026/10/24/opinion/trump-mid.headline: Dare We Dream of a Blue Wave?

paragraphs.text: We’re less than two weeks out from Election Day. In their last conversation before Americans head to the midterm polls, the national politics writer Michelle Cottle joins the columnists Jamelle Bouie and David French to take stock. While Jamelle makes the case for cautious optimism about a possible blue wave, David worries about what could happen if Trump doesn’t like the results.

Below is a transcript of an episode of “The Opinions.” We recommend listening to it in its original form for the full effect. You can do so using the player above or on the NYTimes app, Apple, Spotify, Amazon Music, YouTube, iHeartRadio or wherever you get your podcasts.
The transcript has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Michelle Cottle: I’m Michelle Cottle. I cover national politics for New York Times Opinion, and I am here this week with my brilliant colleagues, columnists Jamelle Bouie and David French. Gentlemen, how goes it?
Jamelle Bouie: It goes well.
David French: Doing well, Michelle.

Cottle: All right. We are less than two weeks out from Election Day. This is our last episode before the will of the voters becomes clear, and I have so many pressing questions for you, most of which fall into the category of: What in God’s green earth is going to happen?

So I know, I know, we can’t really know, but from everything we’re seeing and hearing, how do we think this is going to play out? And maybe this is just my PTSD from 2020 talking, but how might a certain president try to undermine the results if things don’t go his way? So let’s dive in.

There has been a lot of optimism in the air for the Democrats in recent weeks. Our latest newsroom poll has Democrats leading nationally by 11 percentage points. Are we expecting a blue puddle, a blue wave or, maybe more accurately, what has been termed a “red undertow”? David, you go first.

French: You know, it’s really interesting, Michelle. Everything empirical is saying that this could be a blue wave, this could be a blue tsunami. You’re starting to see things, like polling in South Carolina, in Mississippi, within the margin of error, and it’s becoming so blue-ish in all of the data ——
Cottle: Blue-ish.

French: That a lot of smart people I know are like: Wait a minute, can we trust this data? Because it feels like people have been through this before. They have been through optimistic polling waves. We’ve also been through years and years and years of very closely divided politics, where it doesn’t feel like something like Democrats +11 in a popular vote, if you’re going to like ——
Cottle: That’s not a real thing.

French: Take the whole House and put it at, would it actually end up Democrats +11? Highly doubt that. Highly doubt it. But at the same time, there’s nothing really empirical to point at to diminish the optimism.

I keep going back, though, to the sense I felt when I was in Texas recently. When I was talking to Democrats, I would call it “cautious, guarded, daring to dream, but not really dreaming,” if that makes sense. Which I think is actually a pretty healthy attitude to take.
Cottle: Jamelle?

Bouie: Yeah, I would advise people, if they’re thinking about this, to just stress-test it against previous elections, when you’re thinking about, OK, how, how might this be off? And I think that’s useful, because it forces you not just to look at the polls, but at the larger national conditions. And that’s where I think it’s worth just taking seriously what the polls are saying.

So if you look back at 2018, Donald Trump was not this unpopular. He just wasn’t. He was in, I believe, the low 40s, right? So at the moment, he is about 10 points on average less popular than he was in 2018. And I really think it’s important to stress that he’s never been this unpopular before. Economic conditions under Trump have actually never been this bad before, other than, again, the early days of the pandemic.

And so in a lot of ways, we’re in a situation that is actually quite distinct from previous situations when Trump has been on the ballot — and the results we’re getting in terms of polling are consistent with that. It doesn’t mean that things might be better for Republicans than the polling suggests, but I do think that it’s a good reason to think this is capturing something. The exact contours of what that something is, we won’t know until all the ballots are counted. But as far as where the national mood is and what appears to be competitive, that all seems quite right to me.

Cottle: OK. Well, this makes me feel a little better, because I tend to be a pessimist with a lot of these things, and I tend to look at, say, Maine, where I’m not so sure Susan Collins isn’t on track to pull this out. So if I look at Texas, where, yep, the polling looks good for James Talarico, and I don’t think Beto was ever ahead in the polls.
French: No.
Bouie: No.
French: Never like that.

Cottle: People always compare it to that. At the same time, I’ve been reporting and waiting for Texas to turn blue. I remember doing a story about how the Black and brown coalition was going to turn it blue, I think, like a quarter century ago.

I tend to pick the states and areas that make me the most nervous and obsess a lot about those. In part because one of the just broader things that I’m worried about is that Democrats — not even the electeds, but like a lot of the voters or the activists or the kind of watchers — I worry are playing the expectations game badly, that they’re so excited, that they want to win in Texas.

They want to win in some of these red states — in Alaska, that sort of thing; Iowa — that they’ve got expectations so high that, unless they just completely wipe out the Republicans in the House and claim the Senate, I still worry that they’re going to just be declared underperformers, which is going to give Trump an opportunity to stand up and say, “See? We’re fine, and I can just continue running amok,” and all of that. So aside from the people that you talked to in Texas, David — just like broadly — is anybody else worried about the expectation game being played wrong?

French: Absolutely, Michelle. Let’s put this in perspective for a second. We’ve long been thinking that the Democrats could hold in Georgia. We’ve thought that Ohio could possibly be in play. Ohio is a swing-ish state. Even Iowa, swing-ish somewhat recently. Maine, a relatively blue state. So these are states that nobody would just fall out of their chair in shock about. But now we’re talking about Kansas. We’re talking about Nebraska. We’re talking about South Carolina, Mississippi, Texas. And so I do think, if the Republicans hold those states — sort of ending up by going, “Ha, ha, we narrowly held Kansas” — it’s not the flex that you think that it is. But I do think that expectations are building to such a point that there would be at least some degree of disappointment and upset if Democrats don’t win Kansas. I think there might be some real disappointment, again, if Democrats don’t win in Texas.

To Jamelle’s point — I think Jamelle makes a ton of valid points — about the fundamentals of this race, they are enough to make anyone who’s wanting to see the MAGA era end feel more optimistic. I think those fundamentals are there. It’s just, for me, it’s becoming sort of so overwhelming as state after state and race after race goes from likely R to lean R to tossup, that you start to wonder, could this be something realigning? Could this be something truly resounding that we haven’t seen for some time in American politics? And that’s when all of the skepticism lights start to come on. And we’re just going to have to wait and see.

Bouie: I will be surprised if Adam Hamilton wins in Kansas. That’s kind of a crazy outcome. If Darline Graham only wins by one point, that’s a crazy outcome. But having said that, I guess I’m not as shocked by this development as David might be, in part because of the point I made earlier: The actual fundamentals, the national conditions right now, are different. The closely divided elections of the past since 2016 have all operated under a kind of similar set of circumstances: a relatively strong economy; relatively evenly matched, in terms of popular sentiment, political parties; coalitions that aren’t that fluid because there aren’t any new issues changing the nature of the political debates. And all that stuff has changed, right?

Again, the president’s very unpopular, the economy is sluggish, inflation is still relatively high, still with us. Fuel prices are high. There are these new issues on the table — A.I., data centers — that are scrambling partisan coalitions somewhat. There is the fact that Trump simply isn’t on the ballot. And if you think of Trump as an issue and not just a person — the dividing issue of the past 10 years or so of American politics — him not being on the ballot, and thus voters aren’t being forced to choose about their view of Trump’s role in American politics, that itself maybe opens things up a bit. “Oh, now I’m not voting about Trump; I’m voting about diesel prices. Now I’m voting about the fact that I don’t like data centers.”

So there are all these things happening below the surface of American politics that the divided nature of American politics over the last 10 years may have somewhat obscured, and now, as Trump is leaving the scene, they’re kind of bubbling up again. Again, that’s not to say that I think it’s going to be a big Democratic sweep, but that when you look at a place like Mississippi, which apparently is competitive, the high levels of racial polarization in that state actually mean that Democrats have a pretty high floor, right?
Cottle: Sure.

Bouie: They’re usually winning 45, 46 percent. Is it really that crazy to think that, in an unusually bad time for the incumbent party, some percentage of white Mississippians may decide either to sit it out or switch votes? And in that environment, is it really that crazy that the state becomes competitive? I don’t think so. For so much stuff, it’s like tiny changes on the margins can produce these big effects, and I kind of think that’s what we’re seeing.

Cottle: Well, I do think you touched on something interesting there, which is that it’s not that Republicans need to vote for Democrats; they just need to stay home. You hear these discussions about, “Oh, well, there’s no way with the Democratic brand that somebody who’s been voting Republican forever is going to come out and pull that lever.” But this is a midterm election. Midterm elections are always about who you can get to show up at the polls. I do think that from what we saw, certainly, during the primaries, the enthusiasm gap in Democrats’ favor is enormous, which could always make the difference in these sorts of places.

French: And this is a point in Jamelle’s favor on why you should be looking at some of these polls and saying, “OK, they’re measuring something real.” I can’t remember the last time in an election where you could trace voter anger at specific issues to very specific actions by the administration. Normally, when you’re talking about things like inflation rates or job creation, it’s kind of debatable what’s causing all of the inflation or how are these jobs being created, how much is the government versus the private sector, etc. But here you’ve got: Why are gas prices high? The Iran war. Why is background inflation creeping up again? Why are wages falling behind? Tariffs.

You can look at very specific things that this administration has done, which is one of the reasons I think that that term you used — the red undertow — is very appropriate. You can go issue by issue by issue and say, “On what planet does a smart political party do this? On what planet do you do this if you’re actually trying to win elections?” And rarely have I seen a party squander a victory more thoroughly and more efficiently — and more comprehensively — than what the Republican Party has done to the 2024 victory. It is astounding what the Republican Party and what Trump has done after this vibe shift in 2024. And so that’s to Jamelle’s point: Voters can look at very specific things that Trump and the Trump administration have done that have made their lives worse, and I think it makes it easier to vote against them.

Cottle: Yeah, I think you make an important point there, when you’re like, what party would do this if they want to be successful? It’s not a party. It is one man who has never cared about his political party. Donald Trump has no interest in the success of the broader Republican Party. He is only interested in how people talk about him or what he wants to do. And so there has been, obviously, plenty of frustration among Republican lawmakers about some of these issues. Now, if they were really frustrated about it, they should have stood up and done something before now. But, here we are.

So we’ve laid out basic expectations. Let’s turn now to the kind of dark, weird possibility of what happens if all of this comes to pass — blue tsunami, blue wave, blue whatever — and a certain president doesn’t like the outcome. Does he try to meddle with it, to overturn it? I mean, it wouldn’t be the first time. Earlier this week, the Department of Justice charged 28 people with violating federal voting laws. And after claiming that there are likely 20,000 noncitizens registered to vote in California, I mean, are you guys worried about any of this, and the efforts that seem to be kind of percolating along?

Bouie: So I’m of two minds: The first is that all of this is obviously very bad, right? It seems to be the administration doing what it typically does: abusing its power, harassing innocent people, that sort of thing. The claim that there have been 20,000 noncitizens registered — you know, California disputes that, and every time D.H.S. or the administration has made this kind of assertion, it’s promptly fallen apart, so there’s no reason to believe that it’s true. So all of that is very worrisome, right? I think one should have every expectation that the administration is going to say that the elections were tainted by fraud, etc., etc., etc.

My question always is: OK, so what, practically speaking, does that matter? Because practically speaking, it’s not like the White House can’t overturn the election. When I say that, people are going to hear something like, “Well, that’s illegal. He can’t do it.” No, I mean that in the very literal sense. What specific person talks to what specific person to invalidate 435 congressional elections, to invalidate 30 Senate elections, right? That’s not a thing.
Cottle: It’s just not a thing.

Bouie: It’s just not a thing! And in the event that there is a big Democratic win, that disincentivizes regular Republicans from going along with this stuff, because at a certain point, it’s like, well, what’s the point? What’s the point in causing all this grief if we know we’ve just got our butts handed to us? So I see this stuff very much as a desperate administration lashing out in whatever way it can to try to intimidate people, right? To try to convince people not to turn up, not to vote, to create enough fear and uncertainty to make people think that something truly catastrophic might happen.

But when you think about it rationally, they don’t have much they can do in terms of subverting the outcome. And what they can do is not something they can do without opposition, right? Localities will, states will, the Democratic Party will, in terms of being able to file litigation. There’s all this room for pushback and relatively little room for action from the administration. So for me, it’s these two things at once. It’s a problem and it’s bad, but it’s also not, like, apocalyptic.
Cottle: David?

French: I’m a little darker than Jamelle, not on the front end. I draw a distinction between the voting and counting and certifying. I think it’s just so hard. It is really, truly so hard to mess with the actual voting.

Now, where I’m more concerned is that some of these states, if you win — if the Democrats win Ohio by seven or eight, or Jon Ossoff wins Georgia by eight or nine — I’m not worried about that. But what about Talarico up 0.6 percent on Ken Paxton in Texas? That’s when I’m saying all bets are off at that point. Or you have Hamilton 1 percent or less up in Kansas. And in those circumstances, you’ve got the very red-state election officials. And if there is a contest — the contest in the House, for example — as to who sits in the House is settled by the House. And this is something under procedures that are really pretty cursory and not really fully defined very well.

And then at that point, yeah, Jamelle’s right: There’s lots of opportunities to contest this and to fight this. But as we learned with Jan. 6, and Trump in 2020 and 2021, they don’t even need a credible legal argument. They can get people storming the Capitol over stupidity, like, just lunacy. That’s the thing: The 2020 election conspiracy theories weren’t just wrong; they were stupid and wrong. They were incandescently stupid and wrong, and he got people storming the Capitol in that circumstance. And so that’s where I’m a little bit more worried — the back-end certification challenge in maybe some of these very red states that are suddenly competitive.

Cottle: Yeah, I tend to be more nervous about the structure, and I tend to be specifically nervous about the very low-down officials, like precinct-level type stuff. I just remember, after the Jan. 6 hoo-ha, there was this shift in the Trump world where they were basically readying the playing field to take over. Steve Bannon did this call-out, the precinct strategy, where he called for MAGA people to go in and get elected, or get appointed or volunteer, to take over all these low-level offices, so if there was a question next time, it would be Trump loyalists who would be making the calls about: Did this look like fraud? Should we have this recount? Should we do this, that, or the other?

And then on top of that, of course, you have Trump doing what he always does, which is just to sow distrust and undermine the public’s confidence that any of this works. So that if something gets thrown to this board or that recount, people are kind of primed to think, “Oh, well, there must be something wrong.”

So I have to say, that does make me nervous. On the other hand, I do think that the difference is Trump’s not on the ballot. And on some level, if things don’t go his way, maybe he just wants to throw up his hands and say, “See, you guys are total losers when I’m not there. This just proves that I am the only thing that matters, and I’m just going to go forward for the next two years and fight it out with Democrats, and enjoy my status as the undisputed only Republican that matters.” So his lack of give-a-crap-ness, on some level, makes me feel a little better, I guess.

Bouie: I would say as well that I think it’s just important to think of all this stuff as part of a larger dynamic system, right? So Trump claiming fraud is significant, certainly, but it also has to be weighed against the fact that Trump is very unpopular. So he’ll claim fraud, and what percentage of people will hear that and be like, “Yeah, well, of course he’s going to say that,” and they just move on, right?

The extent to which public sentiment is just not on his side — the extent to which, if it’s a big election victory for Democrats, there’ll be tangible evidence of that — really does, I think, diminish the actual capacity of Trump and his allies to do shenanigans. They may still have the mechanical ability to do it, but you also need some sense that this sentiment is going to be on your side. And an election where, let’s say, Republican turnout collapses — which is very possible — would suggest that it isn’t. So they can do stuff, but I think the response is going to be “OK, whatever,” and you move on.

French: Fox has about 787 million reasons to not go along with stolen election theories this time around. And we’ve actually seen this since 2020. You’ve actually seen, in certain circumstances, when someone goes on Fox and spouts some crazy election conspiracy now, you will have a host come on and say, “There was no evidence. All courts ruled —” etc., etc. And so you are seeing some, for lack of a better term, quality control, editorial standards locking in here a bit. So I do think that’s an absolutely better environment than in 2020 and 2021, and that does give me some optimism. But mark my words ——
Cottle: Mark your words.
French: If it’s Talarico by 0.5 percent, watch what’ll happen in Texas, in conspiracy land.
Cottle: Are you worried about the certification process, Jamelle? I mean, not the voting, but the after — the process.

Bouie: Not particularly. In part because Republicans will be on these ballots, too, right? They’re going to want their offices, too, and the secretary of state, state boards of election, which are responsible for certification, are going to want to certify those people as well. If it were the case that these were the only elections where the competitive Democratic Senate wins, then maybe. But the fact that — in terms of do you get your office, do you get your staff, do you get your salary — everyone’s kind of bound up together. I think that leads me not to worry, not to worry as much.
Cottle: What you’re telling me is that you’re feeling good.

Bouie: What I’m saying is that I think that there is a tendency to treat the desire and will of the president as equivalent to ability and capacity. And so they say, “We want to do these things,” and they make these threats, and I think that there’s a tendency — because of all the crazy stuff we’ve experienced over the last 10 years — to say, “Well, if they say they really want to do it, then it must be a thing that they can do.” And my view has always been: Is it, though? They can both practically — and thinking politically — thinking about the interplay of forces and institutions and people — they may try, but that doesn’t mean they’re going to succeed.

It doesn’t mean people should be complacent, but I do think it means that one should try to, um … I’m going to, I’m going to do a me thing. So in his memoirs, Ulysses S. Grant tells this really interesting story that during the Mexican War, he is out with a writing partner and they hear wolves. And Grant’s like: We’re surrounded by wolves, what are we going to do about this? And his writing partner’s like: Let’s just go check out and see what this is. And they go find the wolves, and there’s only two wolves. And Grant says: There’s always more of them before you count them.
That’s where we are.
Cottle: Nice. OK.

Bouie: There’s always more of them before you count them. Being able to have a clear view of what the landscape looks like I don’t think should, again, make you complacent, but should give you a better sense of what the actual possibilities are here, and how we can deal with those.

French: I hate to contradict one of my childhood heroes, Yoda, who famously said, “Do or do not. There is no try.” There is a try, and the try can be really dangerous and destructive, even when the try fails. Like Jan. 6, for example. That was a very damaging thing to Americans, the American body politic, even though it failed. And I’m with Jamelle. Can they do it? I’m skeptical. Will they try it? If the conditions are at all where there’s any shouting distance, any kind of possibility at all, I think they would try it. And then you’re in the realm of how destructive does the effort get? And that’s what I get worried about.

Cottle: We have been talking about polls and the radioactivity of Trump rubbing off on the Republican Party. It’s not like Americans are really happy with either party. There’s a lot of just general disgust and frustration. That said, as we wrap up this very weird midterm conversation, I want to go positive. Tell me something that you think each team has done well. I mean, obviously, operating within the circumstances that they’ve been given. So give me some high points for each team.

Bouie: I mean, I think Democrats have done an actually exceptional job at candidate recruitment this cycle. Talarico; Hamilton in Kansas; getting Sherrod Brown to jump back into it in Ohio. I mean, when you start looking at the people who are running in these races, Roy Cooper in North Carolina, you’re looking at a set of just strong candidates that match the states, match the circumstances and aren’t really making major mistakes, right? There aren’t a ton of missteps. And it’s a real contrast with, I think, how Republican candidate recruitment has gone, especially in the Senate races.

In fairness to Republicans, when the cycle began, there was no expectation that these races would be all that competitive. So sure, you can let a below-replacement-value person get the nomination because you’re like, “Yeah, well, we’re going to win anyway.” So there’s a certain sense of Republicans not quite understandably realizing where the puck was going. But I think Democrats basically recruited the strongest possible candidates they could, and that, as much as anything, is contributing to their good fortune here.
Cottle: And do you have anything from the red team that you want to say something positively?
Bouie: I mean, no. I can’t ——
Cottle: Fair. Fair.

Bouie: But seriously, seriously, seriously — just in terms of how the Republicans have been trying to, or have been approaching this election cycle, it is genuinely difficult for me to think about or think of a good choice. I mean, they have one very strong candidate on the table: That’s Ashley Hinson in Iowa. Great recruit. But beyond that, the big, strategic mistake Republicans made was to just completely defer to Trump for 18 months, and now they can’t separate themselves from him.
Cottle: They’ve made their bed.
Bouie: Yeah, they’ve made their bed, so.

French: So I would say, if you’re going to look at a red bright spot, it would be Michele Tafoya in Minnesota. That is much more competitive. That race is a lot more competitive than Democrats expected it would be. I think that the Democrats will still pull it out, but if you’re going to look across the country and see where a Republican did overperform expectations, I’m betting Minnesota is going to be at the top of that list. Again, I think the odds are against her. Minnesota’s a blue state. It’s been closer and closer blue, but it’s still a blue state. All the fundamentals are with the Democrats, but I think that this is one race to keep an eye on from the Republican perspective.

On the Democratic side, I think watching the Democrats more intentionally compete for the faith-based vote is one of their better decisions, quite frankly. And this is something I wrote about at some length, about the “God gap,” where in 2024 it wasn’t just white evangelicals who came out in large numbers for Trump; 18 of 22 Protestant denominations moved more red, including some of the more liberal and most liberal denominations in America.

So you had a faith-based problem. The Democratic Party had a real problem with faith-based voters. Now, Black Protestants still went overwhelmingly, obviously, for Kamala Harris, but you saw even movement in those numbers in a more red direction.

And so I think by getting candidates out there like Hamilton, like Talarico and others — and Raphael Warnock, in many ways, showed that way and blazed that trail in Georgia — to have very faith-forward candidates, no, you’re not going to peel off too many of the conservative white evangelicals. They’re too closely wedded to the Republican Party, but those are not all the people of faith in this country. And so diving in and fighting over that turf and over that ground, I think, has been very, very smart by Democrats. Necessary.

Cottle: Yeah, and I think, beyond the specifics of the individual candidates, what the Democrats are trying to do is shuck some of their aura of being extremist and anti-traditional and anti-everything along those lines. So I think that this helps. I do think that this helps with that on a bigger picture.

I take the point that Republicans have done some truly wretched things in the recruiting department, most of which can be tied to the MAGA brands like Paxton or the situation in Georgia, where Ossoff is up against a very weak Mike Collins. But I also think that where they’ve got their swing state moderates like Susan Collins in Maine, the party — and by that you have to say Trump in particular, has let them separate themselves. I mean, I guess that’s damning with faint praise, but, you know, it is what it is.

And as far as the Democrats, this time they seemed to have gotten serious about trying all kinds of different things to appeal to the particular electorates. So in addition to the great candidates within the party that they have put forward, they’ve also — say, in Nebraska, you guys know I went out there to talk to Dan Osborn, who’s an independent running against Pete Ricketts — the Democrats have fully thrown in behind him because the Democratic brand in Nebraska is a disaster, and they are looking at this as: It’s better to have a like-minded independent in the race than to just throw in behind somebody with a D just for the sake of it.

So that’s it. But before we go to recommendations, I’ve got to take a minute, and I want to let folks in the New York City area know that on Nov. 5, just two days after the midterms, the three of us will be together live and in person, taping “The Opinions” at the Central branch of the Brooklyn Public Library. We really would love to see our fellow political sickos come out while we chat with one another altogether for the rare, rare face-to-face confab. So see our show notes or check out the Brooklyn Library’s events pages for more info. You know you want to come out and see these guys in their hats live and in person. So I look forward to seeing everybody there.
And with that, it’s everybody’s favorite moment. It’s time for recommendations. David?

French: So I’m going with a little bit of lighter fare this time, Michelle. And this is not a new show. It’s been around for a few years, but my wife and I just discovered “The Gilded Age” on HBO, and it’s a historical period drama. And I say lighter because the stakes in any given episode are not necessarily huge, because it’s a story about social life in Gilded Age-era Manhattan. And so sometimes the stakes are things like, is one of the main characters going to get invited to a box at the opera house, signifying ——
Cottle: Very important.

French: Like, increasing social status. And you’re thinking: Why would anybody watch that? Well, it’s incredibly well acted. I’m a sucker for history, for anything that is set in real-world history and modeled, at least to some degree, on real-world history. And it’s just really well done. It’s not as dark and murdery as my typical fare that I’m watching. So every now and then you need a break from it, Michelle. Just every now and then.
Cottle: Are the costumes pretty? Because this is important to me.
French: Oh, everybody is dressed, like, this is the kind of thing ——
Cottle: That’s what I need to know. That’s what I’m here for.
French: Where people are going to dinner with their family in tuxedos. That’s the kind of thing.
Cottle: There you go. I’m sold. Jamelle?

Bouie: I have a recommendation that involves the same time period. I recently watched the 1975 Peter Weir film “Picnic at Hanging Rock,” which is this very important film in Australian cinema. It’s the film that made Peter Weir a big-name director, and it is about the mysterious disappearance of a group of girls at a picnic in 1900, at a place called Hanging Rock. The best way I can describe this movie is that it feels like you’re watching someone’s memory of a dream. It’s a very enigmatic film. With the mystery that doesn’t really resolve itself, but you’re there as much for the vibe as you are anything else. And I was really taken with it.
Cottle: Where can I watch this?

Bouie: I believe it’s on the Criterion Channel. Or you can just rent it from Apple TV or whatnot. It’s like an hour and 40 minutes. It’s not particularly long. But I found it kind of enchanting, and very strange, but enchanting.
French: Jamelle, one day you will recommend a movie that I have seen. And it is not this day.

Cottle: Hope springs eternal. All right, well, it’s October. We’re coming up close on Halloween, and as pod fans may know, I’m a fool for Halloween. My house turns into — it’s like Spirit Halloween threw up in my front yard. The neighbors wait on it. We have a party. That sort of thing. So I watch horror movies or horror series during the month, because that’s just how I roll, and I want to recommend something that I thought was going to be absolutely horrible but turned out to be wildly entertaining, and that is the Mike Flanagan mini-series just remaking “Carrie,” the original Stephen — I think that was Stephen King’s first novel.
Bouie: Stephen King, yeah.

Cottle: But it’s actually kind of fantastic. They play around a little bit with the supernatural element of it. I won’t get into details; I don’t want to spoil anything. It’s not a big commitment. It’s streaming. Mike Flanagan, for those who follow this sort of thing, he’s the guy who did “The Haunting of Hill House,” “The Fall of the House of Usher.” He does horror movies as well, but they tend to be smart, and they’re not slasher movies. So anyway, that’s my recommendation for the Halloween spooky season people out there. Check it out. And with that, we’re going to land this plane. Guys, it has been delightful, as always. I will see you on the other side of Election Day.
Bouie: Yeah. See you, and we’ll find out what happened to our country.
Cottle: Speaking of spooky. So spooky.
French: Looking forward to it.

You’d think we’d be weary of flimflam artists, tech vampires and alternative realities by now. But no.
It’s like Gertrude’s lust for Claudius in “Hamlet”: “As if increase of appetite had grown / By what it fed on.”
In a time of deceit — political, algorithmic and every other way — a meditation on deceit has taken the culture by storm.

Meditation is not the right word, actually. It’s more like a film noir thriller, with a manipulative femme fatale, a destructive romance, a man who’s meant to play the fall guy, and an atmospheric cottage by the sea.

The three-hour documentary about Theranos fraudster Elizabeth Holmes, “You Can See Everything,” is paradoxically titled, because you can’t see much of anything. (Except her naked narcissistic fiancé preening in the shower.) Holmes is busy obscuring the truth and building an illusory world where her dangerous fraud about comprehensive medical testing with a pinprick of blood was just an innocent hiccup.

“I know I didn’t commit any crime,” she assures the filmmaker Nathan Fielder, training her big, blue Furby eyes on him. She doesn’t think she has ever lied in her life, she says. It was all just a misunderstanding. Never mind the threatening lawyers like David Boies she sicced on anyone who questioned her phantom technology.

Holmes abandoned her Steve Jobs black turtleneck in favor of J. Crew-looking soccer mom sweaters. But she remains the perfect avatar for our age: She promised tech that would help humanity and then unleashed a deception that could have hurt humanity.

Holmes and her partner, who had two children before her 11-year sentence for fraud began in Texas in 2023, wanted a sympathetic documentary charting her last weeks with her family before she got locked up. They stumbled upon Fielder, who directed the movie along with Lance Oppenheim, and ended up starring in it.
Fielder originally did not intend to appear onscreen, but Holmes irresistibly drew him into her web, and the resulting game of cat-and-mouse between the two magicians is astonishing.

The deadpan Fielder is a Canadian-born satirist who worked with Sacha Baron Cohen on the 2018 mockumentary “Who Is America?” and on his own shows, “Nathan for You” on Comedy Central and “The Rehearsal” on HBO, where he has built elaborate ruses. He is a master at spinning his own absurd reality, and so is Holmes.
The sparring of these two raises the question: ls there any point searching for the truth or is it better to settle into our own fractured, subjective realities?

At 30, Holmes became the first self-made female billionaire, after she dropped out of Stanford at 20 and started Theranos. But she’s no role model for women. When she got in trouble she embraced victimhood, turning from a confident Silicon Valley founder who dominated every room into a damsel in distress. In court, she blamed her lover/partner, Sunny Balwani, who got an almost 13-year sentence for helping Holmes defraud investors of more than $700 million. She said he abused her psychologically and sexually and controlled everything, from her clothes to her diet. The jury was unconvinced.

Holmes tries to turn Fielder into a film noir sap, someone who will believe her lies about her lies, be drawn to her emotionally and come to her rescue. And the documentary projects, then calls into question, a scenario where her current lover/partner, Billy Evans, is manipulating her, asking for a cut of the documentary’s profits supposedly behind her back, taking over her X account and putting up foul-mouthed posts pretending to be her, releasing a hologram of Holmes that he nonchalantly acknowledges might be used by some men online for porn.

The woman famous for her guile — suckering George Shultz, Jim Mattis, Henry Kissinger, Sam Nunn, Larry Ellison, Rupert Murdoch and other brainy older men — plays guileless, acting as if she can’t even scramble eggs without her controlling fiancé’s help, or understand the simplistic joke in the classic Abbott and Costello “Who’s on first?” comedy routine. Fielder jokes that if Holmes had “just said that Theranos was a comedy bit, maybe you could get off scot-free.” The couple talk about building “monuments of love” to each other, but it’s more like monuments of manipulation.

Tyler Shultz, George Shultz’s grandson, who was an intern and researcher at Theranos and then left and blew the whistle on Holmes, said on “CBS Mornings” that Holmes took in Fielder enough to allow doubt to creep in about Holmes’s guilt.
“She knows that she was lying,” Shultz said, “because she created this whole web of lies that you would not have needed to create if you actually believed the lies.”
Shultz said the harm to real patients was horrible and Fielder never laid out the dimensions of her crimes.

“We told people that they had H.I.V. when they did not,” he said. “We told people that they had cancer when they did not. We told expecting mothers that they had lost their unborn child when they had not.”

Amanda Seyfried, who won an Emmy for playing Holmes in Hulu’s “The Dropout,” also wonders if Fielder is too “protective of her.” The actress reprises her role in some scenes in the documentary and visits Holmes’s family after she goes to prison, getting chided by Evans for her Hulu portrayal.

Evans is a handsome, buff man, the scion of a wealthy hotel family who is now determined to work with Liz, as she is known now, to straighten out the problems with her blood-testing method. But as the film goes on, there’s a Dorian Gray effect, where his face grows scarier, twisted into a mask of rage and subterfuge. Is Evans, not Fielder, the sap? As in film noir, the boyfriend carries a rod and is vowing vengeance.

Whether or not you think Fielder isn’t tough enough on Holmes, it is impossible to look away from her. Her unblinking gaze is like the disembodied blue eyes in the haunting billboard in “The Great Gatsby,” and both represent the same thing: moral decay.

cnbc.com/2026/10/24/spirit-airlines-plan.headline: Why popular airplanes are getting scrapped years early
cnbc.com/2026/10/24/spirit-airlines-plan.author: Leslie Josephs

paragraphs.text: GOODYEAR, Ariz. — An Airbus A320neo, one of the world's most popular planes, rolled off the Mobile, Alabama, factory line in July 2022, painted bright yellow for its next destination: Spirit Airlines.

It was built to fly for decades. But this May, less than four years later, it was stripped for parts worth millions and crushed, the steel teeth of an excavator tearing through its fuselage at a facility on the outskirts of Phoenix.

More aircraft are getting dismantled years, if not decades, earlier than expected, industry executives told CNBC. It is the result of a shortage of parts, none more precious and expensive than aircraft engines, that has exasperated airlines and driven up costs for years.
Even after the engines are removed, firms are looking for parts as varied as landing gear and antennae to sell.

"It's the first time in my career that involved purchasing an aircraft that's less than five years since date of manufacture," said Bill Thompson, vice president who leads aircraft and engine acquisition for the Americas at aviation asset management and trading firm EirTrade Aviation, which bought the less than 4-year-old Airbus A320neo earlier this year.

He said the company paid "single-digit" millions each for that airplane and a similarly aged one, and it expects to make a profit from selling the more than 1,000 parts it took off them before they were crushed.
"I don't know if you're going to sell the coffee makers but you never know. Sometimes you do," he said.
'Don't fall in love with the metal'

Twenty-one newest-generation aircraft were torn down from June 2025 through this past August, according to aviation data and advisory firm IBA Group. The scrapped planes were 6.4 years old on average, and included mostly Airbus but also some Boeing planes. That compares with an average retirement age for narrow-body airplanes of 21.7 years, IBA said.

"Anytime that you end up with any period of market softness in aircraft availability, engine availability, it's going to cause investors to look at other options," said Simon Goodson, CEO of AerFin, a company that buys, sells, repairs and leases aircraft and parts. "We always say to our aircraft and engine traders, 'Please don't fall in love with the metal.'"
Hundreds of aircraft are retired each year as manufacturers ramp up production for airlines, so older planes are swapped out for newer, more fuel-efficient models.
But aside from retiring aging planes, some owners don't want to wait around for replacement parts or repairs on younger jets.

"A year might not sound that long, but does three or four years?" said Dave Querio, CEO of Ascent Aviation Services, a company that repairs, modifies, stores and disassembles aircraft, based in Marana, Arizona, outside of Tucson. "That's the issue for the aircraft that came in in '23, '24 and '25."
In some cases, owners can reap more for the parts than they can selling the plane or paying storage costs and waiting for it to get back in the air again.
Querio said he hasn't seen "the volume of younger aircraft being torn down as I'm seeing today."
Hot engine market
A major reason for the young retirements is the long wait and rising prices for jet engines.
One problem is that cutting-edge engines that burn hotter and use less fuel are coming up for maintenance far earlier than airlines expected.

The maintenance requests have kept engine repair and overhaul facilities backed up, from those owned by manufacturing giants GE Aerospace and RTX unit Pratt & Whitney to smaller, independent ones. Airlines and leasing firms have been hunting for spare parts and engines anywhere they can find them, like here in Goodyear, Arizona.

The trend has added more fuel to the already hot secondhand parts market. An engine fan blade could cost $50,000 or even more than $100,000 for bigger jets, Goodson said. Engines that power some Airbus A320neo aircraft have 20 of those blades. A disc for the engine, meanwhile, could cost between $1 million and $2 million.

An engine recall because of a manufacturing defect has backed up repair shops and grounded hundreds of Airbus planes around the world. Spirit Airlines bore the brunt of that problem in the United States, years before the airline collapsed.

The engine is made by Pratt & Whitney, which issued the recall in 2023 after discovering contaminated powdered metal used in making some parts. Those engines are worth close to $17 million this year at the high end, up 60% from the upper end of the range in 2019, according to IBA.
Airlines are removing some engines off retired planes to keep current aircraft flying while they wait for engines to come back from the shop.
"So you're just playing Legos and moving engines on and off aircraft," said Mike Stengel, a partner at AeroDynamic Advisory, an aerospace consulting firm.
The problems are driving up the cost to buy or rent one of the popular engines to record levels.

Renting one is ranging from about $160,000 to $180,000 a month, according to IBA data. A competing engine for the A320neo family made by CFM International, a joint venture of GE Aerospace and France's Safran, is far from a bargain, renting in a similar range of $130,000 to $180,000 a month.
Spirit Airlines' ghost planes
The problems with young retirements predate Spirit's collapse.
The 4-year-old Airbus plane that was torn down outside Phoenix in May is a key example. The aircraft was put in storage because of the engine recall, and it stayed until it was torn apart.
But the company's demise has brought more of its Airbus fleet to the market, forcing owners to figure out if it's worth the wait for engines or other parts.

CNBC visited AerSale's facility in Goodyear on a scorching day in late June, less than two months after Spirit collapsed, where dozens of the idle yellow planes were stored. It was so soon after the airline's demise that a former Detroit-based Spirit captain, Glenn Zecchin, popped in and asked about opportunities to ferry Spirit's aircraft to the desert, and to peek in on his former airline's planes.
"I knew the airplanes were there, and I wanted to see what happened," said Zecchin, who is now flying corporate jets.
A jet parked at the storage facility and maintenance hangar still had Spirit in-flight menus and safety cards in the bungee cord seatbacks. Pilot manuals were still in the cockpit.

Not all of these aircraft will be destroyed. Some companies that owned Spirit's planes before bankruptcy will just sell their parts, but some may keep the planes in storage. Other aircraft may go on to fly for other airlines, with potential carriers ripping out Spirit's tight 28-inch seat pitch for something roomier.

But as long as they're not flying, it means paying storage fees, which vary by aircraft type. Some planes in desert facilities — selected because the arid climate can preserve the aircraft better and avoid corrosion — can sit for decades.
Others won't make it back into the air if there's enough demand for the parts and too long of a wait to get the plane flying again.

"After you get rid of all the valuable equipment and sell it back into the aftermarket, what's really left is just a metal carcass that you will literally take a crane and crush," said AeroDynamic's Stengel. Then the owner can "sell it to recyclers that will make of it what they will, maybe into beer cans or something outside of aerospace."
Ascent's Querio said some owners opt to take that route.
"It's a little melancholy to watch it at times," he said. "But sometimes, it's kind of a thrill to ... see how fast an aircraft can be crunched up and sent off to the smelter."
— CNBC's Erin Black contributed to this report.
This weekend, perhaps even as we speak, auditions are being held in London to cast the next Bond.
James Bond. Double-oh—well, you know.
Deadline reports that at least three actors will be screen tested: Jack Lowden, Josh O' Connor, and Callum Turner, who are all fine, experienced British actors and...how do I say this? Hunks.

The Bond selected by Amazon MGM Studios will succeed Daniel Craig, who has owned the role since Casino Royale in 2006, following a parade of other fine, hunky British actors stretching way back to Sean Connery, who starred in Dr. No in 1962.

The literary Bond — a name poached from Dr. James Bond, an American ornithologist who wrote the field guide, Birds of the West Indies, when author Ian Fleming was living in Jamaica — was a Cold War creation. Fleming wrote Casino Royale in 1953, when Great Britain was feeling diminished. Brits had won World War II, with pluck and skill, but were losing their empire. British agents (Guy Burgess, Kim Philby) kept slipping out to Moscow with official secrets before British intelligence could discover they were spies.

It was all damaging to Britain, and embarrassing. But then James Bond strode into the pages of popular culture, dapper and deft. The Soviets and their allies might have sophisticated weaponry and boundless barbarity. But did they drink their martinis shaken, or stirred?

The great espionage novels of Graham Greene and John LeCarre depicted spycraft as a grimy, compromising business. But Fleming's 007, and the onscreen Bonds who played out those stories, dispatched danger in exotic locales, and without rumpling the pleats on their dinner jackets.

Of course ogres and adversaries can shift shapes over decades. I find myself more curious about what forces will next threaten the world when James Bond, whoever plays him, returns to film. So many devices can now listen to, watch, and track our lives second by second, and feed us information they hope will steer our opinions. It may make you think of a line in Dr. No, where Bond tells the scientist who believes he can control the world with his inventions, "Our asylums are full of people who think they're Napoleon. Or God."

npr.org/2026/10/24/nx-s1-6015414/shootin.headline: Gunmen open fire at a church during a funeral in Jordan, killing 7 and wounding 40
npr.org/2026/10/24/nx-s1-6015414/shootin.author: The Associated Press

paragraphs.text: JERUSALEM — Gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan on Friday, killing seven people and wounding 40 others, authorities said.
The shooting took place at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, about 90 kilometers (55 miles) south of the capital, Amman.

Footage broadcast on Jordanian state television showed two gunmen who appear to be holding pistols approaching the church and firing shots. A third man who appears to be holding a semiautomatic rifle then approaches and opens fire, and all three then run toward the church.
Video footage taken by witnesses shows broken glass and pools of blood on the floor of the church.

Dorgham Halasa, who was among the mourners inside the church, said intense gunfire erupted 15 minutes after the funeral had started, and then people started running. "It was a weird situation, and heavy gunfire," Halasa said.

He did not see the gunmen, but said other people reported seeing four of them. The Associated Press could not independently verify the number of assailants, and Jordan's security services did not immediately release details.

A government statement said that the attack was "carried out by unknown assailants," but didn't say whether any gunmen were captured or killed. It said that "investigations are underway at full speed."
Jordan declared three days of national mourning, according to the kingdom's Petra News Agency.
Karak is home to a minority Christian population.

In 2016, gunmen ambushed police in a series of attacks in Karak, including at a Crusader castle popular with tourists, killing 10 people, including seven officers, and wounding dozens. Jordanian security forces killed those gunmen after a long standoff.
Jordan's Health Minister Ibrahim al-Budour said two of those wounded are in critical condition.

King Abdullah II said on X that Jordan "will confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties" and offered his "deepest condolences to the families of the martyrs, and our wishes for recovery to the wounded."

Jordan's Prime Minister Jafar Hassan said during a security meeting in Karak on Friday evening that the attack was a result of terrorist ideology and blind extremism. He said the assailants will be punished and legal measures taken against those who seek to introduce extremism.
Condemnation of the slayings came from around the region, including from Lebanon, Syria, Egypt and Oman.

Ahmed al-Tayeb in Cairo, the grand imam of Al-Azhar, the Sunni Muslim world's foremost religious institution, offered his condolences to the families of victims in Friday's shooting, calling it a "heinous terrorist attack."
Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein called his Jordanian counterpart and "affirmed Iraq's solidarity with Jordan in the face of terrorism," Hussein's office said in a statement.

U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the attack during a funeral as "especially heinous," spokesman Stephane Dujarric said. "The secretary-general also calls for all those responsible to be found and to be held to account."

nytimes.com/2026/10/23/us/politics/in-us.headline: In U.S. Gas Talks With Kremlin, Hidden Financing for Alaska Project Emerges

paragraphs.text: At first blush, the proposed venture looks like it would further the Trump administration’s goal of global “energy dominance.”
An American energy company intends to buy Russian technology and use it to access a massive supply of natural gas in Alaska, liquefy it and export it to allies abroad.

The Kremlin and the White House were interested in the idea. President Vladimir V. Putin discussed the plan last month with President Trump’s peace envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, people familiar with the negotiations said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomacy. It is one of a series of energy deals White House officials believe could help smooth relations with Moscow and eventually pave the way to end the war in Ukraine.

But it turns out that the company was not an all-American affair. The multibillion-dollar project has received secret funding from the same powerful Russian company that was to provide the technology, according to the energy executive who until last month led the U.S. firm and two others involved in company negotiations.

Joel Riddle, who was chief executive of the company, Polar LNG, until he resigned in September, said he had been misled about the sources of the start-up funding, which ostensibly came from a company in the United Arab Emirates.
Instead, Mr. Riddle said he learned, the true source of at least some of Polar LNG’s money was Novatek, a Russian energy giant under partial U.S. sanctions.
“It’s not only unlawful, but it’s not in the U.S. interest to have Russian technology controlling the commercialization of Arctic gas in the North Slope,” Mr. Riddle said in a brief interview.

These previously unreported tensions were also detailed in legal memos that Mr. Riddle attached to his resignation letter, which was reviewed by The New York Times. The memos, prepared by Baker Botts, an international law firm, said the Treasury Department’s sanctions enforcement unit had raised concerns that Polar LNG had ties to Novatek that might present “potential Russia-related sanctions concerns.”
Polar LNG on Friday issued a statement announcing a new acting chief executive, Tim Talkington, and described Mr. Riddle as a “disgruntled former employee.”

But in a statement to The Times, Novatek said on Friday that in fact, it was moving to acquire “minority shareholder” status in the Polar LNG project — a striking effort by the Russian energy giant to seek ownership of American gas production.

The project, if it happens, is a long way off. In addition to the sanctions issues that would have to be negotiated, the technology envisioned is highly complex and must overcome some of the most brutal weather conditions in the United States. It also is competing with another Alaska gas plan that already has the support of the Trump administration. But that the Polar LNG deal is being discussed at all shows how business deals of almost any stripe are on the table during the talks with the Kremlin.
The sequence of events illustrates the unorthodox, opaque mixture of deal-making and high-stakes diplomacy that has defined Mr. Trump’s attempts to end Europe’s bloodiest conflict since World War II.

There is no indication that Mr. Witkoff or Mr. Kushner were aware of Polar LNG or its ties to Novatek, even as the broad outlines of the deal came up in their talks with Mr. Putin beginning last year. A U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss the closed-door talks, said that the deal had only been broadly mentioned and that no granular discussions had occurred.

The project, should it ever come to fruition, would doubly help Novatek, one of Russia’s biggest energy companies, first by using Novatek’s technology and second because the company would own an equity stake.

The Alaska gas discussions have taken place alongside talks to sell off part of another Russian energy giant, Lukoil, to the U.S. government and other investors, including some with business ties to Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner, causing consternation among some Washington lawmakers and outraging some of Ukraine’s supporters. The pair have also discussed the possibility of U.S. involvement in future Russian gas exports to Europe. (The administration has said that Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff were guided only by U.S. interests.)

Geoffrey R. Pyatt, who served as an assistant secretary of state for energy resources during the Biden administration, said the idea of bringing Novatek into the high north of Alaska is a terrible one. “It is terrible on environmental grounds, it is a terrible idea on economic and geopolitical grounds, and most importantly this feeds the belief that Putin can get an out-of-jail-free card.”

The efforts to bring Novatek equipment to Alaska have also included a businessman, Gentry Beach, with ties to the Trump family. A college friend of Donald Trump Jr., the president’s eldest son, Mr. Beach served as a finance vice chairman for Mr. Trump’s 2017 inauguration. Mr. Beach said in February that he had held negotiations with Novatek about bringing its natural gas technology to Alaska.
Mr. Beach could not be reached for comment. It was not clear if he remained involved in the project, or whether he was aware of Novatek’s potential ownership stake in Polar LNG.

A spokesman for Donald Trump Jr. said the two men were no longer close, adding that Mr. Trump was not involved in the Polar LNG project. Novatek’s statement said that Mr. Beach had no role in its discussions to take a stake in Polar LNG. The U.S. official said Mr. Beach was not involved in the administration’s discussions related to Novatek.

Mr. Riddle is one of at least three Polar LNG executives who recently resigned. As they departed, Trump officials were notified about their concerns related to the secret Russian financing. Mr. Riddle said the executives had urged administration officials to investigate the matter. The Energy Department, where the warning was sent, did not respond when asked about the matter.
“I felt like I did the right thing to notify authorities at the appropriate time,” Mr. Riddle said.
Buried Riches
The Polar LNG plan called for the company to tap into the giant load of natural gas available in the northern reaches of Alaska, a byproduct of extensive oil extraction underway in the region.
Currently, there is no way to move most of the gas that is produced along with the oil, so energy companies inject it back into the earth.

Polar LNG’s proposal calls for it to buy a giant, 640,000-ton concrete-and-steel device from Novatek called a gravity-based structure that would be placed on the seabed just above the northern coast of Alaska, in an area known as Milne Point.

On top of that platform, equipment will be installed that would refrigerate gas supplied by an area oil producer, transforming it into a liquid that can then be loaded onto ships that travel through icy waters and deliver it to customers in Asia.

Novatek uses a similar approach to export natural gas from the Russian Arctic in a project called Arctic LNG 2. Mr. Putin said publicly last year that “we are discussing with our American partners” the possibility of using Novatek technology to produce liquefied natural gas in Alaska.

Korean-made ships with a special ice-breaking design that Polar LNG plans to use were initially built for Novatek, but delivery was stopped by the manufacturer after the United States imposed sanctions on the Arctic LNG 2 project.
From the start, Novatek was slated to supply the gas liquefaction station. But financing for the project was not supposed to come from Russia, according to executives involved in the effort.

Emphasizing the point, Polar LNG features images of the American flag and a bald eagle on its website, boasting that “Polar LNG helps ensure the United States leads,” adding that the project is “America’s Arctic Advantage.”

The company hired lobbyists in Washington and in Alaska to help push the project, according to federal and state records. In Washington alone, the company is spending $380,000 a quarter on lobbying, hiring a former Trump-era Interior Department acting assistant secretary, Adam Suess.

Novatek is already under U.S. sanctions that would require the Treasury Department to issue a license for its equipment to be used in Alaska. Recently passed sanctions legislation named after deceased Senator Lindsey Graham, Republican of South Carolina, makes things even harder: The bill specifically targets Novatek, as well as its Arctic LNG 2 project, because of the company’s ties to Mr. Putin.
However, Mr. Trump temporarily waived the law’s Russia sanctions last week, presenting the move as necessary to keep peace talks going.

During a meeting held at the Four Seasons Hotel in late August in Abu Dhabi between executives of Polar LNG and its parent company, Tech Wave Industrial Projects Management, top executives from Novatek were present. That was when Mr. Riddle began to appreciate that Novatek was directly involved in approving funding to keep the effort going, text messages reviewed by The Times indicate.

Tech Wave is an Abu Dhabi-based company that specializes in managing oil, gas and construction projects. Its chief operating officer is Bjorn Gundersen, who a decade ago was listed in oil industry trade publications as a senior executive at Novatek supervising LNG projects.

A second Tech Wave executive, Ahmed Farghaly, also worked for Novatek until recently. According to his LinkedIn profile, he left around the time the United States first imposed sanctions on one of Novatek’s LNG projects. Mr. Gundersen, Mr. Farghaly and Tech Wave did not respond to requests for comment.

Denis Solovyov, Novatek’s deputy chairman, as well as Leonid Mikhelson, the company’s chief executive, discussed their company providing as much as $15 million to Tech Wave to bankroll Polar LNG, the messages say. Asked about the messages and the Abu Dhabi meeting, Novatek said it could not comment on private correspondence, but that the company and Polar LNG had agreed to “provide each other with open communication.”
“All the necessary decisions were made at the meeting in Abu Dhabi,” Mr. Solovyov wrote in one message to Mr. Riddle sent in early September. “The first 5 million were supposed to arrive by today.”

It was several weeks after this exchange that Mr. Riddle resigned. Two other top Polar LNG executives, Dan Chandra, the company’s chief financial officer, and Jim Smith, a former Exxon Mobil executive who served as Polar LNG’s executive vice president, also have left in recent weeks.
Polar LNG, in a statement Friday, said that “Riddle was recently terminated from the company for cause,” adding: “The company is investigating claims concerning Riddle that may result in litigation.”

But Mr. Riddle resigned six days before the company issued him a letter saying it would terminate his employment immediately, in part because he had raised concerns that some of the company’s actions could be “subject to sanctions,” documents obtained by The Times show.
Questions about the potential ties to Novatek had by late this summer already reached Trump administration officials, according to a memo prepared by an outside law firm for Polar LNG, Baker Botts.
“Concerns regarding a perceived connection to Novatek will likely affect licensing or other regulatory approvals,” Baker Botts wrote in a memo to company executives that was shared with The Times.

In addition, the letter said that federal officials had already made clear in communications with the company that they were concerned that an investor in Polar LNG “has ties to Novatek and may be acting on Novatek’s behalf with respect to the project.”
Paul Luther, a Baker Botts lawyer who worked on the matter, declined on Friday to discuss it further.

Polar LNG would need a series of approvals from the federal government before the deal could move ahead, including a sign-off from the Treasury Department authorizing it to acquire the Novatek seabed platform, given that parts of the company are under sanctions. It would also require a permit from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to build a gas export facility.

Questions have already emerged about whether the Novatek device will function at the planned Milne Point location because of shallow waters there and the “potential disruption to traditional whaling and local opposition, particularly from the local native Alaskan population,” a lawyer for Polar LNG wrote in an internal company memo.

Certain Trump administration officials had already expressed skepticism about the Polar LNG plan, according to internal company documents seen by The Times and interviews with some of the people involved.

Part of the concern is that the Polar LNG project would be pitted against an even more ambitious plan to build a $50 billion, 800-mile natural gas pipeline to move natural gas from the northern slope to the southern coast of Alaska, where it could be more easily shipped out from existing ports there. That plan would also potentially supply Asian markets.
Both the Biden and Trump administrations enthusiastically embraced the gas pipeline project, which Japan and Korea may help finance to increase their reliable supply of natural gas.

“The pipeline makes far more sense,” said Matthew McManus, who until April 2025 served as a deputy director at the State Department’s Bureau of Energy Resources and is now at the National Center for Energy Analytics. “The Polar LNG project would face years of permitting and concerns about ties to Russia.”

Mr. Talkington, Polar LNG’s acting chief executive, said his company sought to seize “a generational opportunity to advance U.S. energy dominance, unlock profound benefits for the state of Alaska, and strengthen American Arctic navigation.”

The fact that discussions are even going on about using Russian equipment — and potentially a Russian-financed company — to move American natural gas to international markets is a further insult to Ukraine, and should not be a part of talks over a possible end to the war, said Ilya Zaslavskiy, a gas industry consultant who previously worked in Moscow and New York who now does research on Russian sanctions and energy issues out of Washington.

“Any approach by Novatek to transfer technology should be seen as a Kremlin attempt to co-opt U.S. policymakers in order to undermine U.S. foreign policy toward Ukraine and our allies,” Mr. Zaslavskiy said.

livescience.com/artificial-intelligence/.headline: AI giants are one big mistake away from catastrophe. They could learn a lot from the nuclear industry.
livescience.com/artificial-intelligence/.author: Akhil Bhardwaj

paragraphs.text: The largest artificial intelligence (AI) firms increasingly understand that they are hostages of one another. If one firm pushes ahead recklessly, others may feel compelled to follow. If one deploys a dangerous model without adequate safeguards, others may see it as a green light to do the same.

The debate over AI has centered on what governments should do to regulate this frontier technology. That remains essential. But a more immediate question is emerging: Can the companies building these powerful systems take action independently before they lose credibility and suffer legal consequences?

That question no longer looks theoretical and is being recognized as an urgent challenge. We've already seen AI firms lose control of their models — for example, in Australia, a rogue AI hacked a government healthcare website. If we are not careful, it's only a matter of time before one of these incidents causes large-scale, real-world harm, like shutting down an electricity grid or municipal water system, or a mass misdiagnosis in a health system. If this trend continues, the entire industry could become tarnished.
But there is a blueprint for self-regulation in a risky business: the nuclear industry, which has built up layers of oversight, controls and self-scrutiny over decades.

Frontier AI may require something similar: private regulation among competitors that do not trust one another but have a mutual interest in preventing outcomes that could damage them all. This does not appeal to the better angels of human nature — it's self-preservation for the industry itself.

There is a historical precedent for this kind of arrangement. The nuclear sector did not become safe because every actor suddenly became benevolent. It became safer through a layered system of peer scrutiny, technical standards, information-sharing and external oversight. International organizations such as the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), which was established in 1957, emerged to coordinate monitoring and verification, while national regulators and industry bodies gradually built professional norms around catastrophic risk.

The result was not perfect safety, as the Chernobyl disaster in 1986 clearly attests. But nuclear governance architecture is designed around the recognition that in high-risk technological systems, one actor's failure can become everyone's problem. This was seen following Chernobyl: global nuclear safety increased significantly after the disaster, with upgrades to reactor designs, improved training and international monitoring networks.

And this movement to self-regulation also occurred in the U.S. nuclear sector, following the Three-Mile Island nuclear accident near Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, in 1979. The reactor suffered a partial meltdown after a relatively minor cooling malfunction. Investigations later revealed design flaws in instruments and alarms, along with inadequate emergency response training, were the root cause of the incident.

The event nearly killed the nuclear energy industry in the U.S., causing public support to fall from a record high of 69% in 1977 to 46%t in 1979. The entire industry suffered because of failures at one facility. In response, the U.S. nuclear industry established the Institute of Nuclear Power Operations (INPO) in December 1979 to improve operational safety.

The analogy to AI should not be overstated. Nuclear materials are easier to count than algorithms, and nuclear facilities are harder to hide than model weights. The outcomes of a catastrophic AI blunder are also less existential, although its use in weapon systems is not without risk. In September, an AI hallucination almost led to the U.S. intercepting a Chinese ship suspected of carrying nuclear material to Iran.

Yet the comparison remains useful because the core governance problem is similar. In both cases, competitors operate in an environment where the downside risk of unchecked rivalry is borne by society while the upside is private gain for these firms. The challenge is to create institutions that make restraint the rational default — even when no actor fully trusts the others, and the inner workings of the industry are not readily visible to outsiders.

For AI, that could mean reciprocal evaluation of frontier models before deployment, secure mechanisms for sharing safety information, agreed red lines around certain capabilities, and independent third parties empowered to audit compliance. Such mechanisms would not replace government regulation. They would instead serve as an intermediate layer: stronger than voluntary ethics statements but more adaptive and technically informed than legislation alone can often be in fast-moving domains. The state would act as a background enforcer.
AI governance is often discussed as if the only choices were laissez-faire innovation or heavy-handed state control. History suggests a third path.

AI executives appear willing to look for solutions too, with Elon Musk recently suggesting a peer-review system before advanced model release, and Demis Hassabis, co-founder and chair of Google DeepMind, putting forward a framework for an AI Standards Body, similar to the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority.

Skeptics will object, with reason, that industry-led governance can become cartel behavior or public-relations theater. Companies may use "safety" language to entrench incumbency, slow rivals or deflect binding regulation. Those are real dangers. The lesson from nuclear history is not that private coordination works automatically. It is that private coordination works only when nested inside a broader system of transparency, verification and public authority. Without those elements, private regulation becomes little more than trust-me rhetoric.

Still, dismissing private regulation altogether would be a mistake. Governments do not yet possess the technical capacity, speed or international alignment needed to oversee frontier AI on their own. And if the leading labs already see themselves as bound together by shared exposure to catastrophic risk, that recognition can become the basis for institutional design. The question is how to turn mutual fear into durable rules.
Exclusive to Live Science Pro

That is where the nuclear analogy is most powerful. It reminds us that industries facing existential hazards do not need perfect trust in order to cooperate. They need mechanisms that make cooperation preferable to defection. In practice, that means inspections, peer review, incident reporting, professional norms and a state-backed enforcement perimeter. AI governance is often discussed as if the only choices were laissez-faire innovation or heavy-handed state control. History suggests a third path: structured private coordination under public shadow.

The real opportunity, then, is not to celebrate the newfound (apparent) prudence of technology executives, it is to recognize what their comments reveal. When even fierce rivals begin to argue for mutual scrutiny, they are admitting that competition alone cannot govern the frontier. That admission should be treated not as reassurance but as evidence that the risk has become collective.

The policy task now is to build institutions that fit that reality. Governments should push for mandatory reporting, independent evaluation and legal backstops. But they should also encourage enforceable forms of peer oversight among the handful of firms whose systems may shape the trajectory of the technology. Frontier AI is becoming an industry in which the leading actors are hostages of one another. The nuclear age showed that such conditions can produce serious governance. The hope is that AI firms learn that lesson before they learn the cost of ignoring it at the peril of the public at large.
