The War on Terror coincided with the rise of the internet, when freshly concerning digital attacks became known as cyberterrorism. Now a new threat has appeared: AI terrorism.

Over the past few years, reports from governments, intergovernmental organizations, and think tanks have warned that AI is likely to fuel terrorist activity, demanding preparation and response. In 2021, the United Nations Office of Counter-Terrorism co-published a report on the “malicious use of artificial intelligence for terrorist purposes.” Cyberattacks such as malware and intrusion featured heavily, as did physical attacks via autonomous vehicles, facial-recognition spoofing, deepfakes, and—the coronavirus pandemic was still raging—engineered biological weapons. Earlier, in 2019 and 2020, the Middlebury Institute of International Studies published two reports on the risks that language models, still mostly unheard-of at the time, would pose to propaganda and radicalization. And just this week, a group of Harvard Kennedy School researchers published a working paper that assumes that the “first major AI-enabled terrorism event” is a credible threat and speculates how it might come about.

Cyberterrorism was already a confusing term, partly because hacking or disabling computer infrastructure might be carried out by state actors and without violence—properties that aren’t normally associated with terrorism. Among the reasons terrorism is bad, a very minor one is that the term has no fixed definition. In revolutionary France, it referred to violence exercised by the Jacobin state, in many cases by guillotine. By the late 19th century, it had shifted to the nonstate violence of anarchist would-be revolutionaries. Terrorism began to overlap with independence movements in the 20th century, drawing it closer to separatist conflict or guerrilla warfare. By the late 20th century, this ideological motivation for terrorism became mandatory. Terrorism amounted to violence designed to produce a psychological effect.

The hijackings and hostage crises of the 1970s exemplify this revised purpose. So do domestic attacks, such as that of Timothy McVeigh, who bombed an Oklahoma City federal building in 1995. Today, a quarter century after the September 11 attacks, terrorism often carries a political judgment instead of describing an act or a type of actor: Nearly any adversary whatsoever might be called a “terrorist” now.

Given the slippage of the term, AI is, in a way, terroristic by nature: It threatens to take your job, steal your money, ruin your children’s education, eradicate art and culture, take away your health care, colonize your town, destroy the climate, make electronics forever unaffordable. You have also been told that AI is inevitable—and that only immensely wealthy Silicon Valley companies, possibly run by sociopathic leaders, have the resources and talent to advance it (which they must do, even if it means the destruction of humankind).

But the older sense of terrorism still persists. The technology could also facilitate, in addition to the familiar chaos that AI threatens to unleash, terrorism in the sense of state- or nonstate-enacted violence or disruption, such as disabling your electric grid and unleashing a bioweapon at your workplace.
[Ian Bogost: The thrill of wanting AI to destroy the world]

The people who study AI terrorism raise different concerns than those raised by whistleblowers inside the AI industry—or AI leaders themselves. Superintelligent-AI-driven extinction events do not top the list of risks, nor do the rogue AI agents that might, in theory, become autonomous. Instead, researchers, intelligence officials, and scenario planners seem principally interested in the ways that AI might allow bad actors to carry out more sophisticated activities with reduced effort. The Las Vegas Cybertruck bomber, for example, asked ChatGPT for advice about how to detonate an explosion, a use that suggests terrorists might be stupid in addition to being enterprising.

Today’s frontier AI models are powerful, cheap, and widely available. They can accomplish (or help accomplish, or appear to accomplish) many types of tasks without having been explicitly designed to do so. Criminals, terrorists, and even governments have tended to use existing communication, transportation, and industrial infrastructure to do bad things. AI offers another such tool. This conclusion is both reasonable and a bit humdrum.

Consequently, most of the reports on AI terrorism that I have read are conservative in their concerns. They stress that carrying out acts of violence or other physical attacks is difficult and that AI can’t magically solve those problems. They are, perhaps, responding to years of cyberterrorism-threat overstatement, the most famous example of which is the idea of an “electronic Pearl Harbor”—a devastating attack on digital infrastructure that incapacitates the nation. That metaphor, which has been in circulation since at least 1999, was made more concrete in 2012, when then–Defense Secretary Leon Panetta warned Congress about a “cyber Pearl Harbor” that “could be as destructive as the terrorist attack on 9/11.”

Many international-policy experts have argued that cyber Pearl Harbor amounts to a mixed metaphor. The attack on Pearl Harbor was an intricately planned act of state warfare, not a rogue operation. More likely, smaller cybersecurity incidents could cascade into bigger ones, or cause unpredictable secondary effects. Real, damaging cyberattacks on physical infrastructure have been possible for many years. AI’s role in cyberterrorism is likely to be the same as the internet’s: an amplified capacity to produce and disseminate propaganda, confusion, and political manipulation.

Panetta justified the warning about a cyber Pearl Harbor on the grounds that the risk was possible even if it wasn’t plausible. A similar justification appears to motivate the Harvard Kennedy School researchers in their paper. The co-authors describe their methodology as a “pre-mortem,” which involves assuming that such an event has taken place and working backwards to understand how it came about.

I asked Stephen Casper, one of the paper’s co-authors, whether artificial intelligence creates new catastrophic capabilities or simply makes existing malice easier, faster, or cheaper. “It’s more the latter,” he told me. Specifically, AI models that possess information about dangerous capabilities, such as how to disrupt infrastructure and construct a chemical weapon, could allow malicious actors to use them to nefarious ends. Max Kamachee, another co-author, told me that new models “can meaningfully assist a novice in creating a known severe biological threat absent safeguards.” Put more simply, bad people with ill intent could use AI to carry out bad acts. The paper goes into much greater detail, including making reasonable suggestions about how different types of models might be controlled or regulated to prevent harm.

The Harvard paper presents two candidates for the first major AI-terrorism event: One is a cyberattack that would cause several billion dollars’ worth of economic damage; the other, a biological-weapon attack that would kill more than 100 people. I asked Casper and Kamachee whether terrorism was the right name for the two scenarios. The paper derives these litmus tests from definitions in recent U.S. laws governing the development and management of models in the AI industry. But Casper acknowledged that those bad outcomes might not be ideologically motivated. “We call it terrorism,” he told me, but he also said that an equivalent name would be “the human-led misuse of AI for malicious ends.” Kamachee called the risk “catastrophic malicious use.”
[Adam Becker: The useful idiots of AI doomsaying]

Predicting the future is foolish, and guessing about whether truly terrible events might or might not come to pass is even worse. On the one hand, Casper and his co-authors seem justified in warning about the worst scenarios that AI could facilitate, even indirectly. On the other hand, AI terrorism risks devolving into the fearmongering rhetoric that cyber Pearl Harbor did.

I pressed Casper to connect the dots between what AI makes possible and which outcomes are likely. He cited the shockingly rapid evolution of capability in the models, along with the fact that some AI companies are directly building AI-driven-biological-research facilities. Anthropic, for example, has built wet labs for Claude-enabled DNA and protein research. Those labs could be breached, or the model weights discovered inside them could make their way out and into the wrong hands. “It’s a big world—lots of people, lots of groups, lots of states, lots of motivations,” Casper said. “The precedented misuse of current AI systems for terrorist-type activities is, you know, a pretty decent sign.” A sign of what? That the AI industry is going to experience what Caspar called “a Challenger or Chernobyl or 9/11 or Enron moment.”

And yet, those historical catastrophes are all quite different. Challenger was doomed by a structural failure that had been overlooked because of organizational mismanagement; the Chernobyl disaster was caused by a design flaw magnified by operator error and stifling bureaucracy; September 11 was an ideologically motivated nonstate attack facilitated by ease of access to expertise and realized thanks to national-intelligence blunders; the Enron scandal was accounting fraud allowed by regulatory failure and auditor complicity. Two of the examples were industrial accidents, one was an unintentional outcome of deliberate misconduct, and only one counts as a terrorist attack.

The actual risks created by AI don’t require terrorism to inspire worry, and thinking about terrorism may confuse or distance us from taking the right preventive actions. Because they act at the fringes of society, terrorists have a tendency to adopt whatever technology and infrastructure that contemporary life makes available. They choose their tools, their weapons, and their targets based on not merely what will cause harm or attract attention but also what they can get hold of. This was true of explosives such as dynamite at the turn of the 20th century and car bombs by mid-century; the newspapers, radio, and television media that would produce notoriety for attackers; commercial aviation once it became mature but not sufficiently secure; and banking exploits and off-books financial networks, among them cryptocurrency. Nobody called McVeigh a rental-truck terrorist or an agricultural-fertilizer terrorist, but those two resources proved convenient and effective for his desired purpose—which was indeed terrorism.

Throughout its history, terrorism has repeatedly appropriated civilian technologies, especially unproven or insufficiently managed ones. Conveniently, such infrastructure also tends to make the public feel danger, which accelerates our fear of vulnerability. Like terrorism that uses railways, cars, airplanes, dense urbanism, and the internet, terrorism that makes use of artificial intelligence is possible and even likely. Preparing for its contingencies is wise, if speculative. In that sense, AI terrorism is not new, even if it is still frightening.

theatlantic.com/ideas/2026/10/fbi-prosec.headline: A Very Suspicious Prosecution of Two Former FBI Officials

paragraphs.text: Not too long ago, the Department of Justice could generally be trusted to prosecute cases in which lawyers believed that real wrongdoing had occurred. Now DOJ frequently unveils lawsuits that seem designed mostly for securing likes and reposts on right-wing social media—the actual facts be damned. Any high-profile criminal case brought by the Trump administration arrives with an air of suspicion.

Today, Jeanine Pirro, the top federal prosecutor for Washington, D.C., announced an odd set of charges against two former FBI officials for allegedly lying to Congress during testimony in 2023. “When senior FBI agents lie to Congress believing they are above the law, it’s time to bring the hammer of justice down on them,” Pirro posted on X. For all of the fanfare, DOJ provided little evidence to back up its claims. But the timing of the charges—they’ve arrived just more than a week before the midterm elections—and with the puzzling substance of the allegations and the administration’s crowing online, does not inspire confidence in the integrity of the prosecutorial work.

The charges concern several statements made by the defendants, Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, in the course of a congressional investigation into supposed “weaponization” of the government against President Trump. In brief, the Justice Department is alleging that Floris and Benavides lied to the House Judiciary Committee regarding their level of knowledge about the FBI’s handling of Hunter Biden’s laptop. Lawyers for Floris issued a statement saying that DOJ “has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts.” Benavides’s lawyer likewise described the charges as “baseless.”

The saga of the Hunter Biden laptop has now spanned four federal elections, and the specifics of the story may, reasonably, no longer be top of mind. Understanding its relevance here requires a deep plunge into far-right mythology. But the quick version is that MAGA became obsessed with the possibly stolen laptop, and the material it contained documenting Biden’s drug addiction, after the New York Post published an article about the laptop in the lead-up to the 2020 election. Social-media companies, burned by their experience of Russian election interference in 2016, worried that the underlying documents might be Russian misinformation. (This suspicion was never confirmed.) They responded aggressively by suppressing links to the Post’s story—which outraged the right. The laptop would go on to play a starring role in the coming years as the GOP used congressional investigations to tell a story about the victimization of the right, supposedly having been a target of a sprawling network of government-backed online censorship and unfair treatment by the FBI.

This was the context in which Floris and Benavides were testifying in 2023. The two had held leadership positions in the FBI’s Foreign Influence Task Force (FITF) during 2020, a section created to respond to foreign interference after Russia’s 2016 election meddling. There they had crossed paths with the laptop. In recent years, congressional Republicans have pointed to various decontextualized snippets of that testimony and internal FBI documents as part of their efforts to suggest that the FBI was working against Trump in the 2020 election.

By then, for a certain kind of very online Trump supporter, Floris and Benavides had already become familiar if relatively minor villains in the anticanon of deep-state enemies. The criminal charges today make sense in this larger narrative. In his X post announcing the charges, FBI Director Kash Patel referred to the agency’s past “political weaponization targeting their opponents.”

Just because MAGA hates someone does not mean that they are innocent. But Floris and Benavides’s work as described in the affidavit seems unremarkable. And the document is opaque when describing what the two defendants are actually alleged to have lied about. To be prosecutable under the relevant statute, a lie to government authorities must be told “knowingly and willfully,” and it must be “material” in a way that substantively affects the investigation in question. Some of Floris’s and Benavides’s alleged misstatements, as described in the affidavit, don’t initially appear to be misstatements at all. For example, Floris said she was not involved in the criminal investigation into Hunter Biden during which the FBI seized the laptop; in fact, her work at the FITF really was separate from the criminal probe, which was carried out by a different team.

Other supposed lies might well be better understood as forgetfulness. The two defendants were high up in the bureau and wouldn’t necessarily recall the minutiae of an incident that took place three years before they testified. In one instance, the affidavit alleges that Floris lied about her involvement in “an assessment to discredit the Hunter Biden investigations,” but contains no further mention of this supposed assessment nor any quotes from the relevant testimony. Perhaps DOJ will be able to provide more evidence for its allegations as the case goes on, but as things now stand, the charges appear less than airtight.

How the Justice Department chose to bring this case also invites suspicion. The charges were filed via a criminal complaint, a method the government uses in many investigations that must move quickly, because a complaint does not require the immediate involvement of a grand jury. The need to rush here is hard to see, given that the relevant testimony was three years ago. Conversely, it’s easy to imagine why DOJ would want to push out incendiary allegations without having to convince a potentially skeptical grand jury—an all-but-certainty in D.C., where jurors have delivered a number of high-profile rebuttals to federal prosecutors. In the next 30 days, if the department wishes to move forward with the case, it will have to seek a grand jury’s indictment. By then, though, the Trump administration may have already gotten the propaganda boost it was looking for.

At a hearing today, Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui appeared skeptical of the case, noting the government’s decision to delay seeking an indictment and describing the defendants’ “sparkling backgrounds.” As many judges have commented over the past year, the traditional “presumption of regularity” awarded to the Justice Department’s work has been eroded by the Trump administration’s habitual use of criminal prosecutions as a tool to harass the president’s enemies. With this case, DOJ has provided little material to reassure its critics.

theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/24/israel.headline: Israeli soldiers raze neighbourhood in Hebron, driving families from homes
theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/24/israel.author: Julian Borger

paragraphs.text: Israeli troops have levelled a neighbourhood in Hebron, driving out hundreds of families, in collective punishment for a militant attack on an army checkpoint outside the West Bank city, local Palestinian authorities said.

The Hebron municipality estimated that 35 hectares (86 acres) had been destroyed or marked for destruction and about 1,500 people had been evicted from their homes by Saturday afternoon in the district of Ein Deir Baha. The whole city of 250,000 people was sealed off by checkpoints on every point of entry.

Videos sent by a Hebron resident showed a substantial area of devastation with every house over several blocks flattened in an urban area. One video showed soldiers marking Palestinian houses with a sprayed black cross, another showed a bulldozer tearing down a stone wall on a hillside and another showed a large residential building festooned with Israeli flags.
People said the building was the home of a prominent Hebron family that had been commandeered as a temporary military headquarters.

The large-scale demolitions follow an attack on Friday on an Israeli military checkpoint outside Hebron by two gunmen. After a 20 minute gunfight, two Israeli soldiers were killed, three injured and the two gunmen were also killed.

The attack came four days before Israeli elections, and the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and the extreme-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, travelled to the site of the attack to promise an immediate and ferocious response.

Netanyahu said Israel would “act to destroy this place”. Smotrich who is standing for election in a smaller coalition party, had himself filmed wearing body armour in front of a Palestinian building being demolished. He said he had ordered “the immediate demolition of a wide row of illegal Arab structures adjacent to the attack site”.
Smotrich also called for “a comprehensive military campaign … exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon”. Ein Deir Baha, the focus of the demolitions, was alleged to be the home district of the two gunmen.

A spokesperson for the Hebron municipality said that about 300 families had been evicted. Some had taken refuge in the homes of friends and relatives, while the municipality said it had opened community halls and children’s play areas to shelter others.

A Palestinian news agency, Wafa, reported Israeli plans to displace a further 2,500 people. “We are being collectively punished for something we neither did nor supported,” a Hebron civil rights activist, Issa Amro, said. “Our suffering is being turned into political material for Israel’s elections, while innocent families pay the price.”
Amro said his sister’s family was one of the hundreds driven out of their homes.

“We are talking about hundreds of families who left their homes because of this, and they are not at all connected to what happened yesterday [Friday],” Amro said in a telephone interview. “It’s a very big area and we don’t know what’s going on, whether it is only election propaganda or if it’s a serious plan from decisions on what to do after the election.”
The Israeli army was approached for comment on the operations and on videos showing extensive devastation.

bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/c6q8nd.headline: Gianni Infantino: Fifa president says he is backed by 'vast majority' in world football
bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/c6q8nd.author: Laura Scott

paragraphs.text: Fifa president Gianni Infantino insists he has the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football, as he laughed off questions about whether he had considered resigning over the World Cup sell-off debacle.

In a rare interview, he struck a defiant tone to BBC Sport about his own position in the wake of the controversial Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, and said it was not always easy to bring different points of view "under one roof".

"There is nothing bad in disagreeing," he said. "We see it every day in so many countries in the world. It's OK to disagree. It's OK to have different points of view, but then we need to be able to move on."
Two months ago, Infantino was facing mounting calls to stand down as president of the organisation he has led since 2016.

The heads of European football's governing body Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf, which runs the game in North and Central America, signed a letter accusing the Fifa president of breaking trust "through deception".

Last week Uefa demanded that Fifa release all key documents relating to FFE by 2 November, with Uefa general secretary Theodore Theodoridis saying that the organisation had failed to address "a number of fundamental questions".
Under FFE, which Infantino scrapped within days, a portion of the commercial rights of competitions run by football's world governing body would have been sold to a private investment firm.

Since the delivery of the letter, Infantino has been travelling the world, appearing in Morocco, the Dominican Republic, Cape Verde, and Japan, managing to shore up support to the point where his re-election as president for a fourth term next year now looks inevitable.
He has also proposed to increase the amount of money handed out for football development across the world by $3.4bn (£2.6bn).
Fifa has done some things 'maybe less good'

During the interview he reflected on having been "fully endorsed" by the Asian Football Confederation - following a U-turn by its president Sheikh Salman - and having the backing of "all African countries".
But only last week, he apologised to the Fifa Council over the "communication and consultation" regarding FFE.
He was told by Council members in that meeting that he was not "fit to be Fifa president" if he did not give them the documents they have asked for, including the rationale for FFE.
Yet, when pressed on when he would be providing the requested papers, he did not give a clear answer, saying they had to follow a "legal process" and that they were "working on it".
"We'll answer of course all the questions that are asked as far as the process allows, as far as we can," he said.
Speaking from the first Under-15 World Cup in Azerbaijan, he said he and the Fifa administration were doing "as best we can" but admitted they have done "some things which are maybe less good".
He also said that they need to have dialogue "more often" with Uefa, in an effort to repair their strained relationship.

Asked by the BBC if he was fit to be Fifa president, and whether he had considered standing down, he laughed, before saying: "Well you know I was elected by 211 member associations from all over the world.
"I think what is important is that in an organisation like Fifa, there can be different views, different points of view.

"But if we are serious about democracy, about the democratic process, about believing that everyone has the same vote and the same voice all over the world, that football belongs to everyone, if we are serious about that, then we need, to respect as well the views of the vast, vast majority.

"I'm just coming back off Tokyo where the Asian Football Confederation has fully endorsed me. I was in Cape Verde where all [Confederation of] African [Football] countries have endorsed me. I'm speaking to all associations everywhere in the world."

He continued: "There are different points of view it's not always easy to bring them all under one roof but we need to respect and I do respect all opinions all views and then it will be up to the Fifa member associations to decide who they want as a president and how they want Fifa to be run."
The deadline for candidates to confirm they are standing against Infantino for the election in March is 18 November - although none have yet filed and he could stand unopposed.
England among teams at U15 World Cup
Infantino arrived in Baku on Friday for the Fifa Under-15 World Cup and Festival, which is being held in Azerbaijan and features teams from 189 member associations.

England, Spain, France, Argentina and Brazil are all taking part. Russia have also sent a team, marking the country's first appearance in a Fifa-sanctioned tournament since the world governing body, and Uefa, suspended Russian teams from international competitions in February 2022 following the invasion of Ukraine.
This tournament is only for boys, with next year's tournament being girls only, and then from 2028 Fifa's plan is to have boys and girls competing in the tournament annually.
Matches are played in an 8v8 format, on smaller pitches and with 20-minute halves.
"It's just beautiful to bring the world together at such a young age to create something like this," Infantino said.
"When some of these boys participate in a World Cup 10 years, 20 years from now, they will all remember that their first World Cup was here."

phys.org/news/2026-10-ancient-stalagmite.headline: Ancient stalagmites reveal exceptions to Asia–South America monsoon seesaw over the past 450,000 years
phys.org/news/2026-10-ancient-stalagmite.author: Krystal Kasal

paragraphs.text: October 24, 2026 report
by Krystal Kasal, Phys.org
edited by Lisa Lock, reviewed by Robert Egan

In places like South Asia, Africa and parts of the Americas, monsoon rains supply water for drinking, crops and hydropower for billions of people. Understanding the patterns that monsoons tend to follow can help people plan for drought risks affecting agriculture, reservoirs and hydropower across distant regions.

While past research has established patterns between Asian and South American monsoons, in particular, a better record of past monsoons can help researchers understand when these patterns have broken down in the past and which climate changes might explain those exceptions. A new study, published in Nature, lends insight into these dynamics with the help of stalagmites from a cave in Peru.
A monsoon seesaw

Researchers know that Asian and South American monsoons generally behave like a seesaw: one region experiences strong monsoons while monsoons in the other weaken, bringing drier conditions. This occurs seasonally, over the course of a year, but also over much longer timescales of thousands of years. Scientists have linked this to changes in Earth's orbit and axial tilt over time, which affect how much sunlight reaches the surface in different areas.

The authors of the new study write, "The global monsoon is controlled by the location of the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) and the strength of incoming solar radiation (insolation) in each hemisphere. For this reason, variations in monsoon precipitation are typically antiphased between the two hemispheres and reflect the mean position of the ITCZ as a direct result of orbital (Milankovitch) forcing."

Past research utilized cave records inferred from stalagmite analysis to trace Asian monsoon changes over roughly 690,000 years and show strong links to orbital cycles. Earlier Southern Hemisphere cave records have been more sparse, generally covering only the last two ice-age cycles. While these records pointed to the seesaw effect, a longer record of rainfall activity in South America would help to support the idea and provide further insight.
Insights from Peruvian caves

In an effort to map out monsoon activity over a longer timescale in South America, the team combined oxygen-isotope measurements from 30 stalagmites in three Peruvian caves near the Andes Mountains, using radioactive dating to establish their ages. The resulting data spanned roughly 450,000 years of summer monsoon variability with a few gaps. The researchers checked the rainfall interpretation against modern cave monitoring, nearby lake sediments and other South American cave records. They then compared the reconstruction with Asian monsoon records, other ancient climate evidence and existing ocean-circulation simulations.

Comparison with Asian records confirmed that the two monsoons usually changed in opposite directions, broadly following Earth's roughly 23,000-year orbital wobble. However, the team identified 10 episodes when the records showed simultaneous weakening or strengthening instead. The shared weakening occurred during several transitions out of ice ages and during some warmer intervals, challenging the simple north–south rainfall seesaw.

The two episodes of shared strengthening occurred during the penultimate ice age, which lasted from roughly 194,000 to 135,000 years ago. The researchers say that the synchronous events lasted for several thousand years before the two records reverted to their previous behavior.
Causes of shared highs and lows

The researchers think that these anomalous synchronized periods might indicate that ocean temperatures, greenhouse gases and temperature contrasts between hemispheres can modify the usual orbital influence. It seems that the global monsoon reorganizes itself in response to these changes, especially during intervals of rapid warming.

The study authors write, "Among the 10 synchronous monsoon events of the past 450 ka, interhemispheric weak monsoon intervals (WMIs) during terminations occur regularly, with a periodicity of about 100 kyr. These interhemispheric WMIs occur within intervals of major increases in atmospheric CO₂ and global temperature, which were intervals of reduced meridional temperature gradient.

"As monsoons are driven by temperature gradients (that is, the temperature-driven pressure differences between land and sea), the global reduction in meridional temperature gradients during terminations may be partly responsible for interhemispheric WMIs."

Additional long cave records may reveal whether other monsoon systems shared these unusual episodes. While the proposed drivers are not conclusively established and the study does not predict when similar changes might happen under modern warming, the results offer a long-term benchmark for testing how well models reproduce major rainfall reorganizations. And while the evidence does not provide a ready-to-use forecasting tool, it does offer potential for improving risk assessments.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/crypto/article.headline: Netanyahu Says Israel Mulls Crypto Ahead of Possible Sanctions
finance.yahoo.com/markets/crypto/article.author: Galit Altstein

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Benjamin Netanyahu said he is exploring the use of cryptocurrency to circumvent potential financial sanctions on Israel, drawing criticism from opposition figures who said it would turn the Jewish state into an economic pariah like Iran.
Most Read from Bloomberg

"We need to prepare ways to evade banking sanctions through an alternative economic system," the prime minister said in an interview with Israel's Channel 10. "You know what that means — the currencies that can bypass them. I'm working on that too." Asked whether he meant crypto, the prime minister said: "Very correct."
Netanyahu was speaking ahead of the Oct. 27 election, where he faces a strong challenge from former general Gadi Eisenkot.

Opposition leader Yair Lapid said the prime minister's proposal for evading potential sanctions "belongs to countries like Iran, Russia, and Venezuela — nations whose banks are cut off from the world, whose companies cannot accept payments, and whose young people are fleeing."
"That's his vision," Lapid added in a post on X.

Last month, 12 major countries led by the UK pledged coordinated measures against Israeli settlements in the West Bank. UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the moves would also cover individuals and companies providing financing, construction and other services to the settlements.
That raised fears of sanctions on Israeli banks that could rattle the tech-export-driven economy.

"The concern is that foreign banks will cease providing correspondent services to their Israeli counterparts, effectively severing Israel's ability to conduct international economic activity," said Yair Avidan, a former banking supervisor at the Bank of Israel.

Netanyahu "is finally admitting that Israel faces a real danger of diplomatic isolation and economic sanctions, yet instead of explaining how he intends to prevent them, he is already talking about preparing a 'sanctions-bypassing economy,'" said former Finance Minister Avigdor Liberman, leader of Israel Beytenu, an opposition party. He vowed to "break Israel out of diplomatic isolation and eliminate the threat of sanctions" if the opposition takes power.
In the interview, Netanyahu also warned that decades of US military aid would end, forcing Israel to finance its defense on its own.

"If you think we will continue receiving what I secured twice — tens of billions of dollars in American aid for the defense budget — you'd better prepare yourselves and get used to the idea that this will not continue," he said. "That is because America has changed, not because Israel has changed. It will end. It is only a matter of time."
Netanyahu said Israel has two more years with US President Donald Trump, but must prepare for a less favorable Washington after he leaves power.

The US and Israel have agreed a memorandum of understanding which runs through 2028 and provides $3.8 billion annually, largely for military procurement from the US. Washington extended a supplement of at least $15 billion during three years of war triggered by Hamas' October 2023 attack on Israel, which claimed the lives of 1,200 Israelis.

Netanyahu said Israel could afford higher defense spending after robust growth, despite three years of war. "For years, we kept defense spending under control to encourage economic growth," he said. "Now the economy must support defense, because without security, there will be no economy."

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: JetBlue Lenders Organize After Stock, Debt Fall to Record Lows
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Reshmi Basu and Dorothy Ma

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- JetBlue Airways Corp.'s creditors are organizing with advisers as the airline comes under intensified pressure ahead of its third-quarter earnings report, according to people familiar with the matter.
Most Read from Bloomberg

A group of creditors, including holders of $2 billion in bonds due 2031 and a $742 million first-lien loan, are working with PJT Partners and Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing private information. The debt and JetBlue shares reached record lows this week.
Representatives for JetBlue, PJT and Akin Gump did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The Wall Street Journal earlier reported the adviser appointments.

Creditors of the junk-rated carrier were spooked this week as other airlines slashed their guidance and warned of a prolonged impact from soaring fuel costs. JetBlue's bonds, which are backed by collateral tied to the company's loyalty program, lost 10 cents this week to about 45 cents on the dollar. The loan has fallen 13 cents to 45 cents, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

JetBlue has been closely watched by distressed-debt investors after budget carrier Spirit Aviation Holdings Inc.'s bankruptcy. On Wednesday, United Airlines Holdings Inc.'s Chief Executive Officer Scott Kirby warned some industry peers face deeper stress after Spirit's collapse, though he didn't name specific operators, as his company cut its full-year outlook.

JetBlue is projected to face a free cash flow deficit of about $1 billion in 2026, as higher jet fuel prices delay its turnaround, S&P Global Ratings analysts said in a June 8 note as they lowered its credit rating one notch to CCC+.

The company reported $6 billion of unencumbered assets and about $2 billion in cash on its balance sheet in the second quarter. The rating agency noted that while JetBlue has sufficient liquidity and ample borrowing capacity, it warned "an increasing debt service burden exacerbates an already pressured cost structure." It had about $8.5 billion in total debt as of the end of June.

finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.headline: UK Vows £100 Million for Biosecurity Lab With OpenAI, Anthropic
finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Jacob Reid

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- The UK announced £100 million ($134 million) for a AI Biosecurity Lab which will be supported by OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind, part of a raft of measures designed to improve the government's ability to understand and tackle the risks posed by the technology.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The lab will use AI to detect and monitor biological threats, with the funding coming alongside up to £200 million in AI model credits from OpenAI and Anthropic, according to a government statement. The lab will also work in partnership with Google DeepMind and life sciences company Basecamp Research, while the government announced a separate £65 million for developing countermeasures for pathogens.

"As AI becomes more powerful, Britain must have the capabilities to protect its people and shape its own future," said Kanishka Narayan, Britain's AI minister. "That means staying ahead of emerging threats, from cyber attacks to biological risks, while building more of the critical technology our security depends on."

The lab "will be a major new global institution, bringing together world-leading scientific expertise to protect people from emerging biological threats and ensure Britain leads the world in AI safety and security," Narayan added.

Its creation makes the government's AI strategy increasingly clear: forming institutions outside of existing government departments to research, monitor and harness different aspects of the technology.

The announcement also included £120 million in extra funding for the AI Security Institute, which is the best-funded government agency focused on regularly evaluating cutting-edge AI models, and £23 million more for the AI Economics Institute, which is being set up to analyze the economic impacts of the technology.
'Honest Broker'

The strategy is a key part of the country's attempt to remain relevant in the AI space despite lagging behind the US and China on cutting edge AI models. It's trying to act as an "honest broker" for monitoring and regulating, and taking a distinct role from the European Union, which has strongly regulated the tech.

"AI is changing both the biological risks we face and the nature of biological discovery, and we applaud the UK government's foresight in opening the AI Biosecurity Lab," said Matt Clifford, who leads International Affairs at Anthropic, and was the Prime Minister's AI advisor until last June.

"Bringing together frontier AI, the UK's scientific strength, and government expertise to detect threats earlier and speed up the development of medical treatments will contribute to the safe deployment of AI across industry and society," he added.

The government also announced £130 million to use AI to identify cyber vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure and the economy and improve the country's cyber defenses. That comes after governments and companies around the world rushed to patch two critical flaws in widely used technology on Thursday, which AI helped to find.

There will also be a £120 million boost to the Sovereign AI Fund to broaden its remit to include physical and industrial AI such as robotics, autonomous systems and advanced manufacturing, and expand its procurement program for British start-ups.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261023.headline: Could lowering high blood pressure be as simple as stimulating your ear?

paragraphs.text: A small device that delivers gentle electrical pulses through the ear could offer a new approach to treating stubborn high blood pressure. In a clinical trial led by researchers at Queen Mary University of London, the technology proved safe, well tolerated, and practical for patients to use at home.

Although the treatment did not significantly lower blood pressure compared with a placebo device across all participants, researchers observed encouraging results in patients with more severe hypertension. The findings suggest that stimulating nerves in the ear could eventually help certain people whose blood pressure remains elevated despite taking medication.

The results come from the SCRATCH-HTN trial, published in Hypertension, a journal of the American Heart Association. Researchers emphasize that larger studies are needed to determine whether the approach can provide meaningful benefits and which patients might respond best.
How Ear Nerve Stimulation Could Lower Blood Pressure

The experimental treatment uses a technique called transcutaneous autonomic neuromodulation (tAN), which aims to influence the autonomic nervous system. This network of nerves automatically controls essential bodily functions, including heart rate, digestion, and blood pressure.
By delivering mild electrical signals to nerves in the ear, researchers hope to influence the body's natural mechanisms for regulating blood pressure without requiring an invasive procedure.

The handheld device, developed by Afferent Medical Solutions, uses two small clips positioned on the tragus, the small flap of cartilage located just in front of the ear canal. These clips deliver gentle electrical stimulation, allowing patients to administer the treatment themselves without visiting a clinic.
Clinical Trial Tests the Device in 63 Patients

The clinical trial, funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), enrolled 63 people with uncontrolled hypertension. All participants were already taking at least one medication to lower their blood pressure, but their readings remained above recommended levels.

Researchers randomly divided the participants into two groups. One received active nerve stimulation, while the other used a sham device designed to serve as a comparison. This approach helped investigators assess whether the electrical stimulation produced benefits beyond those associated with using the device itself.
Participants used their assigned devices for 30 minutes daily during the first two weeks. For the following 10 weeks, they reduced their sessions to once per week.

The results showed that the treatment was safe and generally comfortable for participants. Most also followed the prescribed schedule, suggesting that the technology could be practical for regular use at home.

However, when researchers compared blood pressure changes across the entire study population, they found no statistically significant difference between patients receiving active stimulation and those using the sham device.
Promising Results in Patients With Severe Hypertension
Despite the lack of a significant overall benefit, the researchers identified a potentially important finding among participants who entered the trial with more severe hypertension.

A prespecified subgroup analysis, meaning the researchers had planned this comparison before examining the results, revealed a greater reduction in blood pressure among these patients when they received active nerve stimulation rather than the sham treatment.

This finding raises the possibility that the technique may work better for people with particularly difficult-to-control blood pressure. However, the trial was relatively small, and the subgroup results require confirmation in larger studies before any conclusions can be drawn about its effectiveness.
Dr. Ajay Gupta, Chief Investigator, Clinical Reader at Queen Mary University of London and Consultant Physician at Barts Health NHS Trust, said:

"This is an exciting, highly patient-acceptable technology that could ultimately provide a cheap, scalable solution for millions. Although the trial did not achieve significance across the broad unselected group, those with more severe hypertension exhibited a clear blood pressure reduction in the active group compared to sham.

"As the first and most thorough study of its kind, this points towards important new research directions that could help us understand whether non-invasive neuromodulation can benefit particular groups of patients with uncontrolled hypertension."
A Potential New Option for Hard-to-Control Blood Pressure

High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, is a major contributor to cardiovascular disease and increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes. It places additional strain on blood vessels and the heart, potentially causing serious damage over time.
Although medications help many patients manage their condition, a substantial number continue to have blood pressure readings above recommended targets even while receiving treatment.
This ongoing challenge has encouraged scientists to explore additional approaches that could complement existing therapies.

Ear nerve stimulation is one such possibility. Because the device is small, does not require surgery, and can be used at home, it could offer a convenient option if future research establishes that it reliably lowers blood pressure in certain patients.

For now, the findings represent an early step rather than proof of an effective new treatment. The researchers say larger clinical trials will be essential to confirm the encouraging results in patients with severe hypertension and identify which groups, if any, could benefit most from this approach.

cnbc.com/make-it/2026/10/24/peptides-saf.headline: Fact vs. fiction: Doctors share whether peptides are safe and effective
cnbc.com/make-it/2026/10/24/peptides-saf.author: Renée Onque

paragraphs.text: From YouTube influencers to Reddit threads, the health and wellness side of the internet is full of talk about peptides.

The term refers to a class of chemical compounds made up of short chains of amino acids. In the wellness market, synthetic peptides are often sold to consumers as injectables, which some health influencers say can bring a wide range of health benefits from muscle recovery and longevity to improved sexual function. Some peptides, including GLP-1 drugs commonly used for weight loss or diabetes, are heavily researched and federally approved for medical use. Many other forms of peptides are not.

Yet even some lightly researched peptides may be on their way to pharmacy shelves. The Department of Health and Human Services is reportedly planning to allow specialty pharmacies to compound certain synthetic peptides that have the support of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who told podcaster Joe Rogan that he is a "big fan" of the injectables in a February 2026 interview. As reported, the move would be an interim access policy covering some specific peptides not currently approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

Such a move would be controversial from a regulatory point of view: Multiple peptides, including one of the compounds reportedly included in the health department's proposal, appear on an FDA list of injectables that "may present significant safety risks." That compound, known as BPC-157, has shown potential anti-inflammatory effects in some animal and lab studies but has not yet been subject to large-scale human testing for safety or effectiveness.

"There are a few reasons why, but one of the main ones is the absence of evidence," including robust human studies on safety and effectiveness, says Dr. Caleb Alexander, a professor of epidemiology and medicine at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.

Yet consumer interest and regulatory momentum for peptides are growing. So here's what you need to know about peptides, from why they're the subject of such conversation to whether or not they're safe or effective to use.
What are peptides?
Peptides are "kind of like the building blocks of proteins," says Dr. Alison Dempsey, a dermatologist at the Weill Cornell Medicine and NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital.

Several different types of peptides are naturally found in the body, like insulin and endorphins. Peptides can also be synthesized in labs, according to Harvard Health Publishing. GLP-1s, like Ozempic, are FDA-approved synthetic peptides, Dempsey says.

Injectable variations of synthetic peptides that haven't been approved by the FDA — such as BPC-157 and GHK-Cu, the latter of which has been marketed as a potential anti-aging drug — are the peptides that are making headlines at the moment, says Dr. Pieter Cohen, an associate professor at Harvard Medical School and internist at Cambridge Health Alliance.
Why are peptides gaining popularity among wellness influencers and some other consumers?

One likely factor behind synthetic peptides gaining more attention has been the success of drugs like Ozempic at addressing health concerns such as obesity and diabetes, according to Cohen. "That probably opened up [the idea that] there must be this magical world of these other peptides that we can have access to, that will do these sort of similar magical things in other areas," he says.

However, Cohen and other health experts have their concerns. After all, a compound's status as a peptide "doesn't mean it's close to Ozempic in any way, shape or form ... in terms of both its chemical structure or its effects on the human body," says Cohen.

Synthetic peptides advertised on social media and sold on the so-called gray market — often produced by overseas sellers and sold to U.S. consumers outside the normal American drug regulatory system — come with marketing claims such as boosting longevity, improving sleep quality, strengthening the immune system and even enhancing skin health and sexual function, according to Alexander.

Particularly among the people who consider GLP-1s a form of miracle drug, consumers may simply want to believe that the weight loss medicine's chemical cousins could have similar effects on other elements of human health. "Unfortunately, when it comes to peptides marketing, word of mouth has strongly surpassed where we are with any type of research," Dempsey says.
What do health experts recommend for consumers?

The health experts who spoke with CNBC Make It recommend against using any injectable peptides that aren't approved by the FDA, especially if you're unsure where or how they were produced. Always consult with a medical professional before making any major changes that can affect your health.

"My recommendation is not to use any of the novel, unstudied injectable peptides because we simply do not know if they work. And if they do work, if they're safe," Cohen says. When buying peptides on the gray market, you can receive entirely different compounds or doses, and some may be contaminated with bacteria or other concerning materials, he says.
"There's concerns both about the potential risks, but also about the unclear level of benefit from these products," Alexander says.

"We have a great regulatory system governing prescription drugs in the United States," Alexander adds. "For advocates of these products that really believe in them, I hope that they'll put their money where their mouth is, and do the studies that are necessary so that we can understand the true safety and effectiveness of the products."

bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/ck4g14.author: Shamoon Hafez

paragraphs.text: Nicolas Jackson scored twice as Aston Villa ended Manchester City's 100% winning start to the Premier League season.
Here's how I rated the players and how you rated the players.
Aston Villa
Zion Suzuki: Good in the air, decent distribution and made three important stops to deny Iliman Ndiaye, Rayan Cherki and Josko Gvardiol with a brilliant, fingertip save. 7
Matty Cash: Battled all game with Jeremy Doku and though he was booked for a push on the Belgian, he managed more tackles than any other player. 7
Victor Lindelof: Threw his body at everything that came his way but outmuscled for Haaland's goal. 6
Pau Torres: Calming presence at the back without being too ruffled. 6
Ian Maatsen: Could have scored early on but blazed a volley over. Vital header away to deny Erling Haaland's goalbound header late on. 6
John McGinn: Picked off Marc Guehi to lay on the opening goal and created more chances than anyone else on the pitch. 7
Boubacar Kamara: At the heart of everything good from the home side, sniffing out the danger. 7
Joao Gomes: Mucked in alongside Kamara by keeping the ball ticking and contributing three interceptions. 6
Alysson: The 20-year-old Brazilian impressed against Viking in the Champions League and showed why he was given a start again with another eye-catching performance. 7
Johan Manzambi: Switzerland international displayed sparks of his undoubted talent and could have had a penalty in the first half. 6
Nicolas Jackson: Brimming with confidence. Took the opening goal brilliantly, firing high into the roof of the net, before stroking in a second. 9
