bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-league/articles/c6.headline: 2026 Rugby League World Cup: What England need to avoid group stage exit
bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-league/articles/c6.author: Emma Smith

paragraphs.text: Sixty-eight. That is the magic number for England.
For Brian McDermott's side to reach the semi-finals of the Rugby League World Cup, a specific series of events needs to happen next weekend.
On the backfoot since being humbled 32-10 by Tonga in their opening game, England responded with a crushing 82-0 victory over France to keep their dreams alive.
It means England need to beat co-hosts Papua New Guinea in their final group match in Wollongong next Friday – then hope Tonga beat Samoa, two days later in Sydney.
If Samoa win, England will be eliminated because of their inferior head-to-head record against Tonga. They will also be knocked out if Tonga and Samoa draw.
But if Tonga win, it comes down to points difference between England and Samoa.
England's difference, after the Tonga loss and France win, is +64. Samoa, following hefty victories over the French and PNG, is +132 – which is 68 better than England.

So, 68 is the number to remember. If England beat PNG by 68 points or more, then any Tongan win is good enough for McDermott's men. Less than 68, and they must hope Tonga are really inspired by Pacific rivalry to put one over their island neighbours.

England hope the numbers go in their favour to avoid an unwanted first. In 16 previous Rugby League World Cups, staged in varying formats, neither England nor Great Britain have ever finished outside the top four. And every time the format has included semi-finals, they have got there.
Group B-C: The remaining games
• Fri, 30 Oct: England v Papua New Guinea: Wollongong, 09:05 GMT
• Sun, 1 Nov: Lebanon v France: Parramatta, Sydney: 06:40 GMT
• Sun, 1 Nov: Tonga v Samoa: Parramatta, Sydney: 09:05 GMT
'I'm not sure what else we could have done'
"What we have done today is enormous, given the context," McDermott told his post-match media conference in Perth.
"Knowing we had to win big - and we have had candid conversations about that this week - we have done that without getting hot. Everything was measured and planned.
"Whatever the results next week, we have to finish strong - if we go home next week, we will be disappointed, but I'm not sure what else we could have done."
McDermott's final comments may allude to the controversial format of this men's World Cup, which features an unbalanced group stage that has not helped England's prospects.
Pool A has four teams - Australia, New Zealand, Fiji and the Cook Islands - fighting for two semi-final places in a round-robin format. Simple enough.

But Pools B and C are combined into one six-team league, from which only the top two will make the semi-finals. England, drawn in Pool B, play the three Pool C teams - Tonga, France and Papua New Guinea.
It means while England are competing with Samoa for a semi-final place, they will not actually play each other.
It also means that while New Zealand lost their opening fixture against Australia, their path to the semis remains simple – win their final two group games.
England too had to win their last two pool matches but also needed snookers.
There is some reason behind the maddening format, introduced after France – who were supposed to host a 16-team men's World Cup last summer – pulled out because of money troubles.
Australia stepped in with New Zealand and Papua New Guinea, with the number of teams involved shrunk from 16 to 10 to cut costs.
This format also means every team plays three group games, there are no fallow weekends and the whole tournament can be done in a relatively tight five weeks.
'We have given ourselves half a chance'

But it is unquestionably harder on sides in Groups B and C. The fact Australia and New Zealand are in Group A won't help the perception of the tournament being skewed towards the southern hemisphere giants.
"We were the best we could be," England captain George Williams said of the France win. "The situation has been difficult, but we have given ourselves half a chance."
It also leaves England fans with a nagging feeling their side are only producing their best when they are already halfway home.
After a sluggish, disconnected showing against Tonga, England were slow starting against France before finding their mojo - no tries until the 23rd minute; by the final whistle they had run in 14.
England's UK based players took nearly 48 hours to travel out to Perth. BBC Sport understands that the tournament organiser planned England's travel itinerary for the World Cup.
The convoluted route featured a bus journey to London, then flights via Singapore and Sydney rather than straight to Perth, where they played their first two games.
McDermott's side did not play a warm-up fixture and completed just two full training sessions before taking on Tonga.
"We have been together for only five field sessions; we are building something here," said McDermott. "The tries we scored before half time were what we are chasing.
"With a long build up, we could have achieved some special things."
Ifs, buts and maybes. All England can do now is aim for 68 points, and hope.

cbsnews.com/news/ukraine-starlink-drone-.headline: Ukraine says it regained full use of Starlink, after more than a week of disruption

paragraphs.text: Ukraine's military has regained full use of Starlink satellite links for its drones and other fast-moving equipment, the defense minister said Saturday, ending speed restrictions that Ukrainian officials said had disrupted front-line operations for more than a week.
The Defense Ministry's monitoring systems in Ukraine reported stable connections on objects traveling faster than 250 mph, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara told reporters.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday that checks were conducted and it was determined Starlink and Starshield were running at the correct speed.
"Now the speed is what we need," Zelenskyy said. "The restoration began last night, and in the morning there were already speeds sufficient to use this connection. This is very important."
"This is significant for our front-line logistics, for protecting Ukraine from reactive 'Shaheds,'" he continued, referring to the Iranian-made drones regularly launched by Russia.

The limitations placed on Starshield — SpaceX's military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service and the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communication — last week alarmed the country's military and government officials, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions.

The restoration comes as U.S. envoys launched a new push to end the war. Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month. On Friday, Kyiv and Moscow also agreed to a localized ceasefire brokered by first lady Melania Trump around Oleshky, a war-ravaged, Russian-occupied town in Ukraine's southern Kherson region.

The episode added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington, a relationship already strained by President Donald Trump's reported deal with Moscow on Russian diesel imports, which Ukraine viewed as a betrayal.

Khmara credited "direct dialogue" and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's diplomacy with Washington, adding that the outcome mattered most "for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics and communications."
Zelenskyy on Saturday thanked Americans and "all our partners, who took all this seriously and are really helping us."
Questions have persisted since last week about who ordered the interruptions to the Elon Musk-made satellite internet system that Ukraine has relied on for years to counter Moscow's attacks.
Trump has maintained that he didn't make the call, while also saying Musk should not be blamed. On Tuesday, CBS News reported that Musk was behind the disruption.

cbsnews.com/news/hitler-eagles-nest-moun.headline: Suspect arrested after fire "completely engulfed" Hitler's Eagle's Nest mountain retreat in Germany
cbsnews.com/news/hitler-eagles-nest-moun.author: Duarte Dias

paragraphs.text: A suspect has been detained in Germany following a fire at Adolf Hitler's mountain retreat, known as Eagle's Nest, German police said.
Authorities were alerted to a fire at the Nazi leader's mountain residence on the peak of Obersalzberg at approximately 9:15 p.m. local time on Friday, Upper Bavaria South police said in a statement.
The building, also known as Kehlsteinhaus, was "completely engulfed in flames" when firefighters arrived, police said, but no one was found inside and no injuries were reported.
Fire trucks had some difficulty accessing the site "due to the local conditions," authorities added.

"Shortly after the fire broke out, a suspect came into the focus of investigators," the statement said, adding that the cause of the fire is now under criminal investigation and one person was taken into custody.

At an elevation of 6,017 feet, Hitler's Eagle's Nest was completed in 1938 and occasionally used by the Nazi leader as a temporary seat of government. The site was spared from Allied bombing during World War II, largely preserving its original state.

Since then, it has become a popular tourist attraction, which also operates as a restaurant and beer garden. According to its website, the Eagle's Nest is "one of the few undamaged monuments of the Hitler era" and it "stands for the insanity of the regime."

fortune.com/article/jamie-dimon-poached-.headline: Jamie Dimon poached Warren Buffett’s protégé to run a $10 billion fund—he says Buffett’s response was ‘at least he’s going to you’
fortune.com/article/jamie-dimon-poached-.author: Marco Quiroz-Gutierrez

paragraphs.text: Jamie Dimon poached a senior figure from Warren Buffett’s inner circle, and the legendary investor was surprisingly OK with it.

The longtime JPMorgan Chase CEO hired former Geico CEO Todd Combs away from Berkshire Hathaway in December 2025, hand-picking him to lead a $10 billion investment group as part of JPMorgan’s Security and Resiliency Initiative aimed at helping companies accelerate manufacturing.

During a U.S. Chamber of Commerce event this January, Dimon said he had called Buffett personally to tell him the unwelcome news. He claimed Buffett accepted the outcome, preferring his former executive land at JPMorgan than elsewhere.
“It’s a free country, and people make their own decisions,” Dimon said. “I did call Warren. He probably wouldn’t have preferred it, but he said, ‘if he’s going anywhere, at least he’s going to you.'”
Buffett’s assistant confirmed the accuracy of the account.

In a market saturated with executive moves, Dimon’s Combs hire matters because Berkshire Hathaway is a decentralized empire that draws its strength from the long tenures of its leaders with minimal churn at the top. Its executives are often seen as stewards of a culture, built over Buffett’s own six-decade tenure, that prizes patience and discipline.

Combs, a former hedge fund manager, had been at Berkshire since 2010 and was brought on by Buffett to serve as one of two investment managers tasked with picking stocks for Berkshire. During the succession race to replace Buffett, Combs was positioned as a key leader to assist Greg Abel, who took over as CEO from Buffett in January. Yet, he also served nine years on JPMorgan’s board, according to his hiring announcement.

Since joining JPMorgan in January, Combs quickly put his investment experience to work. His investment group has already committed $5 billion of the $10 billion initially allocated to it, according to a recent announcement.
Meanwhile, Berkshire has also entered a new era with new leadership after Buffett was replaced as CEO by Abel in January after 55 years with the legendary investor at the helm.
The 96-year-old also officially stepped down as chairman last month, handing the role to his son Howard. Buffett remains on Berkshire’s board.
In announcing the hiring, Dimon specifically called out Combs’s investment prowess and his work with Buffett.

“Todd Combs is one of the greatest investors and leaders I’ve known, having successfully managed investments alongside the most respected and successful long-term investor of our time, Warren Buffett,” Dimon said in a statement.

Combs’ hiring may have been directly influenced by his respect for Buffett, said University of Maryland finance professor David Kass, who runs a Warren Buffett blog, in an interview earlier this year with Business Insider.
“Dimon may very well have viewed Combs as a close proxy for Buffett himself,” Kass told the outlet. “Although Dimon could not hire Buffett, he could hire one of his protégés.”
Dimon has long admired Buffett. In May 2025, as Buffett announced he was stepping down from the CEO role, Dimon praised him as a friend and said he had learned from him.

“Warren Buffett represents everything that is good about American capitalism and America itself — investing in the growth of our nation and its businesses with integrity, optimism, and common sense,” Dimon said at the time, according to Reuters.
Though a couple decades younger than Buffett, Dimon, 70, has also faced questions about when he will step aside.

Dimon, who has served as CEO of JPMorgan since 2006, has been reluctant to put a clean end date on his tenure. He spent years responding to retirement questions with a rolling horizon, and only changed his tone in 2024 saying the timeframe had shortened and succession plans were “well on the way.”
This year, Dimon again suggested he was in no hurry to retire, telling an audience in January he wanted to remain CEO for “at least” five more years.

In June, JPMorgan elevated two executives, Doug Petno and Troy Rohrbaugh, to co-presidents, and in July Dimon said the timetable for his retirement was essentially unchanged and ultimately up to the bank’s board.
A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on Jan. 16, 2026.

cnbc.com/2026/10/23/corruption-midterm-e.headline: Corruption is voters' top issue ahead of midterm election, CNBC survey shows
cnbc.com/2026/10/23/corruption-midterm-e.author: Kevin Breuninger

paragraphs.text: Voters are now more concerned about government corruption than any other issue, including high grocery and gas prices, according to the final CNBC All-America Economic Survey before the Nov. 3 midterm election.

The finding follows a monthslong messaging effort by Democrats to link widespread economic dissatisfaction with what they allege is rampant corruption by President Donald Trump and his Republican allies.

CNBC's survey of 1,000 registered U.S. voters found 36% of respondents pointing to government corruption as one of the most important issues facing the country right now. The cost of food and groceries came second with 34%, followed by protecting democracy and the price of gas, which garnered 23% each.

The nationwide poll, which gauged attitudes about the economy, Trump, Congress, artificial intelligence, the Iran war and more, was conducted Oct. 14-18. It was co-led by Democratic pollster Hart Research Associates and Republican pollster Public Opinion Strategies, and carries a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 percentage points.
Read the full survey results here.

To be sure, the question asking voters to name their top concerns lists several economy- and cost-related topics separately, subdividing an issue that might otherwise rank higher if lumped into a single category.
But the results nevertheless align with other recent polls showing corruption has shot to the top of voters' list of pressing worries.

A Fox News poll published last week found 60% of registered voters are extremely concerned about government corruption, surpassing concerns about inflation and high prices. A Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll released Sunday found some two-thirds of respondents think Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself, up 10 percentage points since September 2025. Gallup recently found perceptions of government corruption in the U.S. have hit multi-decade highs. And an August poll from Reuters/Ipsos found nearly 7 in 10 Americans believe Trump's businesses influence his presidential decisions.

Republicans have also tried to seize on growing anti-corruption sentiment. The Trump administration has launched a task force led by Vice President JD Vance aimed at cracking down on fraud, while the president frequently accuses his Democratic enemies of crookery.

"I just want to say that from day one of my administration, we've waged an unprecedented war on corruption and fraud, and will not let our country be looted and plundered by thieves and pirates and foreign fraudsters and basically scum," Trump said Tuesday while unveiling a new reward program for whistleblowers.

But with Republicans in charge of the federal government — and as high costs linked to Trump's tariffs and the Iran war have put the GOP on defense — Democrats have been able to cast blame more directly.
"Americans have spent well over $100 BILLION extra on gas because Trump chose to go to war with Iran," Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., said Wednesday on X. "His ego-fueled decisions cost you thousands."

Their arguments often spotlight Trump, attempting to draw a contrast between Americans' widely felt financial struggles with the president's surging net worth, his family's lucrative business dealings and his focus on pricey construction projects.
Other Democratic candidates have widened the scope of the message, delivering a pitch that the system itself is broken.

"The problem is that the people's elected representatives don't represent the people. They represent the donors and special interests," Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., said in an April campaign video. "Corruption is why things don't work for ordinary people."
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has hammered the claim that Republicans have betrayed their vow to bring down costs.
"The wealthy and well-connected are cashing in. What are Republicans doing to lower costs for everyone else? Absolutely nothing," Jeffries wrote Friday.
Rhetoric and results
Democrats' push appears to be resonating with voters, even as large swaths remain skeptical of both parties.
Respondents to the CNBC survey gave Democrats a 4-point edge over Republicans, 35% to 31%, when asked which party would do a better job dealing with government corruption.
But that gap grew to 17 points in Democrats' favor among voters who said corruption was their most important issue.
And independents, by a 15-point margin, said Democrats would address corruption better than Republicans – though 41% of those respondents think neither party would do a good job.
The apparent rise in concern about corruption is welcome news to critics of the president who have long lamented that Americans have become numb to scandal in the Trump era.

That shift is taking place because voters are feeling the impact of inflation and connecting it to what they see in Washington, said Brian Lemek, executive of the Democrat-backing political action committee Defend the Vote, in an interview.
"It's the only thing people are talking about right now," said Lemek, whose group briefed candidates on the issue in June.
Voters are "looking at the reality that their costs are high" and "making the connection between this corrupt and broken system and their high costs," he said.

Additionally, survey respondents overwhelmingly opposed the idea of elected officials, including the president and members of Congress, personally owning or trading stocks in individual companies that have contracts with the federal government. That should not be allowed, 93% of voters said in the poll.
A similar proportion – 89% – said that companies owned, or invested in, by a sitting president's immediate family members should not be allowed to receive contracts from the federal government.
"This definitely ties back to the corruption issues that we've been talking about," said Alicia Simmons of Hart Research Associates.

nytimes.com/2026/10/24/us/politics/democ.headline: Why Democrats Could Find It Hard to Win the Senate Despite Their Strong Polls

paragraphs.text: Democrats have a hefty advantage in national polls. President Trump is playing

, campaigning through deep-red corners of the country that he won by overwhelming margins just two years ago. And assumptions that Democrats will win control of Congress have become conventional wisdom in many quarters, from longtime political observers to social media to the oddsmakers in prediction markets.
But as Democratic dreams of midterm victories grow bigger, some strategists quietly worry that expanding expectations are crowding out signs of a more challenging political reality.

Control of the Senate hinges on victories in red states that favored Mr. Trump by significant margins in 2024, including some that Democrats have not won in decades. Republicans are outspending them by eye-popping amounts in key races. And after its performance in 2024, the Democratic Party as a brand still remains unpopular among voters.
All of that has left some in both parties wondering: Could the much-discussed blue wave end up looking more like a splash?

“The election can be summed up in the following sentence: Can huge amounts of Republican money defeat huge Democratic advantages in issues, candidates and political climate,” said Senator Chuck Schumer, the minority leader from New York.

Strategists in both parties believe it is increasingly unlikely that Republicans will be able to hold on to their House majority. But among Democratic donors, activists and voters, hopes of winning control of both chambers have grown so high that some fear any other result could feel like falling short.

“I am concerned that we have an overheating of expectations,” said Molly Murphy, a pollster who worked on the 2024 campaigns of former President Joseph R. Biden Jr. and former Vice President Kamala Harris. “People often assume in a wave you win everything, and what happens in a modern wave is you win far more than normal.”
The kind of broad wins that once defined wave elections are largely a thing of the past, Ms. Murphy said, destroyed by gerrymandering that has left relatively few House seats truly competitive.

In 2018, the most recent midterm election considered a landslide election, Democrats won 41 House seats and control of the chamber. But Republicans gained two Senate seats and expanded their majority.

This year, there’s near-universal agreement among politicians, strategists and activists that Republicans face steeper political headwinds than Democrats. Mr. Trump’s approval rating hit a new low this week, views of the economy are dismal and Democrats lead by 11 points on the generic ballot — a measure often used to gage a party’s strength.

The sharp deterioration of the national political environment for Republicans has transformed the electoral map, forcing their candidates on the defensive in surprising places. This week, Senate Majority PAC, the main super PAC for Senate Democrats, began airing $1.2 million in television ads in Mississippi — a state that hasn’t elected a Democratic U.S. senator since 1982.

That’s a striking reversal of expectations from two years ago, when Democrats began plotting a midterm strategy and winning control of the Senate seemed nearly impossible. Then, Republicans — and some Democrats — scoffed when Mr. Schumer publicly discussed recruiting a Democratic candidate for Senate in Mississippi.

The question is whether the Democrats’ momentum is strong enough to lift their candidates in deep red states to victory. To win control of the Senate, Democrats must flip four Republican-held seats, and keep all of their own.

Of the 10 Senate battleground contests, four feature Republican incumbents: Senators Dan Sullivan of Alaska, Jon Husted of Ohio, Susan Collins of Maine and Roger Marshall of Kansas. And five are happening in states that Mr. Trump won by 11 points or more in 2024.
“Structurally, the Senate is built to be Republican, and the question is whether this wave can breach that levee,” said Liam Donovan, a Republican strategist. “It is incredibly hard.”
Polling, early-voting turnout and the results of recent special elections suggest that Democrats are far more enthusiastic than Republicans this election cycle.

But those measures, particularly early-vote returns, can be misleading. Turnout can flip on Election Day, particularly if Republicans successfully leverage their campaign war chest and Mr. Trump’s tour through Republican strongholds to drive their supporters to the polls.

“Trump is probably going to do some good in these red-leaning states when he comes in,” said David Kochel, a veteran Republican political strategist from Iowa, where Mr. Trump held a campaign rally on Thursday. “There’s still a lot more Republicans in Iowa and Kansas than there are Democrats.”

In Sioux City, Iowa, on Thursday night, Mr. Trump offered plenty of MAGA red meat, attacking Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, and urging Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for governor in Ohio, not to take down an ad featuring the estranged mother of his opponent that has drawn bipartisan backlash. And, Mr. Trump told the crowd, he had the “right” to run for a third term.
“I’m asking you to pretend I’m running,” he said, repeating a frequent refrain. “Pretend I’m on the ballot.”
Can the polls be trusted?

This year, as in several recent election cycles, Democrats harbor considerable anxiety about the accuracy of polling. Some strategists worry that pollsters are oversampling Democrats, particularly in red states, who may be more likely to respond to questions about the election.
A historical assessment of congressional polls conducted by The Economist this week found that the more partisan a state, the more the polls have underestimated the strength of the dominant party.
If that trend held true this year, it would temper Democratic expectations in states like Alaska, Texas, Ohio, Iowa and Kansas.
And even if the polls favoring Democrats turn out to be accurate, many individual Senate races are quite close, in some cases within the margin of error.

“There will be two explanations if the wave is just a ripple,” said Howard Wolfson, a veteran Democratic strategist. “One is there is a massive polling error. The second is that the Democrats didn’t have enough money to put enough races into play and make the races that were in play sufficiently competitive.”
G.O.P. financial advantage

Republicans currently have an advantage of about $650 million in general-election advertising, according to a review of past and future ad reservations across federal and state races by AdImpact, a media-tracking firm.

Their edge is most pronounced in the Senate: In the seven races that the Cook Political Report rated as tossups, Republicans are outspending Democrats on advertising by more than $320 million, according to a separate tally by AdImpact.

The lack of Democratic funds limits the party’s ability to mount aggressive campaigns in the kind of districts that would fuel a wave, said Mr. Wolfson, a political adviser for Michael R. Bloomberg, the former mayor of New York City, who spent about $80 million bolstering Democrats this fall.
So far, the polls haven’t shown significant shifts since more money started pumping into races.

But the spending is being felt not only in the barrage of campaign ads, said Jason Roe, a Republican strategist based in Michigan, but also in efforts to push Republican voters to the polls. Republicans have embraced a version of the strategy that helped them capture the White House in 2024, focusing on driving loyal Republican voters who typically skip midterm elections to the polls.
And just as in 2024, they have gotten plenty of outside help, including from Elon Musk, who has quietly funneled more than $276 million into building a huge turnout operation to help Republicans.
The impact of that work might not be clear until Election Day.
“I have never seen more money spent on the ground in my life — it is obscene,” Mr. Roe said. “If you are a Republican voter, you are going to get harassed to no end to turn out.”
He added: “The question is: How many of those people are so unhappy with Trump or Republicans that they don’t vote for us when they get there?”
Unpopular with voters

Some Democrats also worry that their party’s still-battered brand could hurt their support in November. Even as Democratic candidates gain support, polling shows lingering disapproval of their party overall.

Just 28 percent of voters said they are satisfied with the Democratic Party, in the recent New York Times/Siena poll, eight points lower than satisfaction with the Republican Party and the share of voters who approve of Mr. Trump’s job performance.
Republicans have tried to capitalize on that skepticism by casting Democratic candidates as far-left radicals who want to turn the country into “a socialist hellscape.”

Matt Bennett, a vice president at Third Way, a centrist think tank that presses for a more moderate Democratic approach, worries that some of the party’s more progressive candidates, including Senate nominees Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Troy Jackson in Maine, are underperforming Democrats competing in traditional red states.
Is there a scenario in which Democrats win in red states but squeak by in blue ones? Mr. Bennett doesn’t rule it out. Midterms, he said, can produce strange results.
“Every single one of the Senate races is on a knife’s edge,” Mr. Bennett said. “The results could be super weird.”

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv0ld9571511o.headline: Three released without charge after fatal Waterford arson attack
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv0ld9571511o.author: BBC News

paragraphs.text: Three people, who were arrested in connection with a suspected arson attack which killed four family members in the Republic of Ireland, have been released, gardaí (Irish police) have said.

Philip and Kim English and two of their children - nine-year-old Jayden and 12-year-old Callum - died after their home in Birch Avenue, on the outskirts of Waterford was set on fire earlier this month.
A man aged in his 20s and a woman in her 30s were previously charged in connection with the attack.
On Saturday, gardaí said three people - two women in their 30s and a man in his 50s - who were arrested on Tuesday have been released without charge.
A fourth person, a man in his 20s who was arrested on Thursday, remains in custody.

nytimes.com/2026/10/24/science/space/ste.headline: Some Buy Telescopes. These People Build Them From Scratch.

paragraphs.text: Nearly every summer for the past 100 years, stargazers have made the bumpy trek to the top of Breezy Hill, in the woods of Springfield, Vt., to honor the age-old tradition of making telescopes by hand.

The three-day gathering, hosted by the Springfield Telescope Makers club, is called Stellafane. In the century since the club’s first convention, Stellafane has fostered a community bound by a love for the stars and a deep commitment to the craft.

The event has done more than just nurture a hobby, club members say. Stellafane has imbued generations of stargazers with skills that seeded the optics industry, contributed to cosmic discovery and influenced both space exploration and national defense. It also helped spur the rise of amateur astronomy across the globe.

But the world looks different from the way it did 100 years ago. Telescopes are widely available now and often cheaper to buy commercially than to build from scratch. Handiwork is becoming a thing of the past. Widespread light pollution has led to a loss of dark skies. Stellafane’s attendance has waned, and the club’s membership is graying.
Still, club members believe their craft, as well as the convention and community built around it, is too important to lose.

Stellafane has long served as a nucleus of “innovation and invention,” according to Douglas Arion, a club member who produced a documentary about the convention that premiered in August. “We are one of the few groups still really doing this,” he said of amateur telescope making. “And if it dies, we’re pretty much killing it off.”

Stellafane’s roots stretch back to 1920, when telescopes existed mostly in the realm of the wealthy. That began to shift when Russell Porter, largely considered the founder of the amateur telescope-making movement, gathered 16 people in a Springfield basement. He instructed them through the grinding, polishing and tuning of a chunk of glass into an atomically smooth mirror — the key component of a reflecting telescope.

The Springfield Telescope Makers was established in 1923 and completed construction of a pink clubhouse atop Breezy Hill the next year. The founders named it Stellar Fane, a phrase derived from Latin meaning “shrine to the stars.” That soon contracted to Stellafane.

Interest in telescope making exploded after Scientific American published a series of instructive articles in 1925 about the club’s activities. A handful of tinkerers congregated in 1926 on Breezy Hill, where they compared designs, shared techniques and scanned the stars with homemade telescopes. Stellafane, the convention, was born.

Attendance at what became an annual event ballooned, eventually reaching into the thousands. Over the next decades, the convention and its site earned a kind of legacy status among stargazers. “A trip to Stellafane is considered a pilgrimage,” read a 1989 form to register the club grounds as a national landmark.
The event heightened interest in observing the universe, even among those with no formal training.

“From my perspective, Stellafane ‘invented’ amateur astronomy,” Ken Slater, the webmaster of the Springfield Telescope Makers, wrote in an email. Before, most amateurs were armchair astronomers, he said. They could read about the stars, “but they could not afford a telescope to explore the night sky themselves.”

Today, a worldwide network of amateur astronomers, including many Stellafaners, monitors the sky 24/7 to observe solar system collisions; uncover new stars, comets and asteroids; contribute to eclipse science and more.

Stellafane offered one of the first venues for amateurs to connect about an otherwise solitary hobby while camping together under the stars. It also gave telescope makers a watering hole from which to perfect their techniques, which to this day can produce mirrors with a surface accuracy within a few millionths of an inch, as the random motions of grinding and polishing by human hands wash out systematic errors that can happen with machines.

Over the years, Stellafane’s annual competition also inspired imaginative ways to mount those mirrors into telescopes: Some people crafted tubes from old bicycle rims and built tripods from crutches and broken hockey sticks. In 1966, one attendee arrived with a telescope inside a hollowed-out bowling ball; ads for a strikingly similar design, available to purchase commercially, appeared a decade later.
Telescope makers also developed a suite of automated software tools — to focus their scopes, process images and the like — some of which have found their way into professional astronomy endeavors.

Inspired by their craft, many young Stellafaners went on to pursue related careers. One helped develop the optical systems on a Cold War spy plane; another did the same for an Apollo lunar landing simulator. They brought their expertise to the optics on the Keck telescopes in Hawaii and to multiple NASA missions, including the Voyagers and the James Webb Space Telescope. The corrective lenses that fixed the Hubble Space Telescope in 1993 were in part crafted by an optician who passed through Stellafane.

“There’s always a time when something useful comes up and you say, ‘Oh, well, I’m familiar with that from the kind of things you learn building a telescope,’” said Mitchell Revalski, an astronomer at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, which manages operations for the Hubble and the Webb. Dr. Revalski added that attending Stellafane as a teenager helped him finish his first scope — which now lives in a corner of his office — and largely inspired his future career as an astronomer. He is now a member of Hubble’s camera team.

Despite their reach, Stellafane and the Springfield Telescope Makers largely flew under the radar for decades to those outside of the astronomy community. Members describe the club as historically introverted. Old accounts often called the makers “telescope nuts” doing who-knows-what in the woods, a portrayal they embraced.
“It was sort of like a secret society,” Mr. Slater said.
That reputation may have hurt the club in the long run. Its current demographics skew older, white and male — evidence of a history that was not the most inclusive, club members acknowledged.
“We need to fix that,” Dr. Arion said, “for the survival of the club, for the survival of the art.”

The Springfield Telescope Makers spent more than a year strategizing for their second century as they approached the 100th anniversary of Stellafane this past August. Plans are in motion to expand the membership — currently invite-only, and requiring the completion of a telescope-worthy mirror — to include a more diverse crowd.

Some have expressed the need for more local outreach. Others are pushing for an affiliate membership class, which would allow telescope-making enthusiasts beyond New England to support the club. Katie Shusdock, a club board member who planned the convention this year, thinks that modernizing Stellafane would help attract younger people.
“It’s currently quite rustic,” said Ms. Shusdock, 29, who joined the club’s mirror-making classes at age 11. “I have big, big dreams of a showerhouse.”

Stellafane has evolved since 1926. Some 800 people attended the convention in August, and many brought with them scopes not built by hand, but purchased. They set up shop in a clearing, acquired by the club in 1986 to support the event’s expansion, east of Breezy Hill. This year’s agenda included a daylong workshop with professional astronomers, treasure hunts for children and a talk on using artificial intelligence for amateur observing.

But the heart of the event remains the same. The most dedicated attendees still spend months, even years, grinding a mirror and finding clever ways to house it in a telescope. They place their handcrafted portals to the stars in front of the pink Stellafane clubhouse and share trade secrets well into the night.
Cecilia Detrich, the president of the Springfield Telescope Makers, who is Ms. Shusdock’s mother, describes it as an “almost religious” experience.

Some makers carry on the tradition to design specialty scopes that cannot yet be found commercially. Others come because they take pride in creating something with a precision surpassing that of machines.
And then there are those who embody the truest spirit of the French word “amateur” — they craft telescopes for the love of it.
Stellafane “is more than just a location, more than just a club, more than just an annual convention,” Ms. Detrich said.

“I’m hoping that in another 100 years, people will be celebrating the bicentennial right here on Breezy Hill,” she added, “continuing to share their love of space, science, telescope making and the night sky.”

nytimes.com/2026/10/24/science/dig-peaco.headline: What Amy Poehler’s New Series, ‘Dig,’ Gets Right About Archaeology

paragraphs.text: A distinctive rubber bucket used for moving excavated dirt, known as a zembeli. A mass spectrometer needed for carbon dating ancient artifacts. And a laser theodolite, which helps map the coordinates of a dig site with extreme accuracy.

Such tools are more commonly found at archaeological excavations and laboratories than they are on sitcom sets, but they all feature in “Dig,” a new comedy series starring Amy Poehler and Hugh Laurie that is scheduled to premiere on Peacock on Nov. 23.

Getting the science — not to mention the history — right was crucial to creating the sets and dialogue for the show, which follows four researchers who make a once-in-a-lifetime discovery while digging near a fictional town in Greece.

Not included among those scientists is Joseph L. Rife, an anthropologist at Vanderbilt University who specializes in the ancient Mediterranean. But Dr. Rife played a different role in the production — archaeology consultant.

The show’s plot might be fictitious, but for the titular dig to come off as believable, it was Dr. Rife’s job to make sure the site and the science around it looked real (or at least real for a television show shot on the Universal Studios backlot).
In recreating the archaeological site at the center of the plot, “the nuts and bolts had to be accurate,” Dr. Rife said.

Getting those fundamentals right meant portraying the work of classical archaeology, the study of material artifacts related to the cultures of the ancient Mediterranean through excavation. (Think ancient Greece and Rome, but also related civilizations like the Etruscans and Minoans.)

Such archaeologists work to understand the complex cultures of ancient societies, including their religious beliefs, politics and economies. But unlike researchers studying some other parts of the ancient world or periods of prehistory, classical archaeologists are aided by an abundance of complementary sources — including art, architecture and literature that have survived millenniums.
“You not only excavate the buildings where assemblies met,” Dr. Rife said, “but you can also read the speeches they gave.”

Using known pieces of art and literature, archaeologists can determine where to dig, and they can date newly uncovered artifacts to fixed timelines. (Such techniques were instrumental in uncovering some of the region’s most famous sites, including Pompeii and Troy, as well as in excavating wonders like the Colosseum and the Parthenon.)

Dating objects along an established chronology through the use of art and epigraphy (the study of ancient inscriptions etched into hard surfaces like stone) is important to the show’s not-to-be-spoiled discovery. That moment, Dr. Rife said, was intended to mimic a “realistic archaeological discovery.”

Kate Myers, the author of the novel “Excavations” on which the show is based, said getting the objects right was important for the production because an appreciation of artifacts is central to archaeology.

“So much of working in archaeology is this deep respect for the objects and for the process of uncovering,” said Ms. Myers, who studied archaeology at the University of Pennsylvania, and whose own experience working on a dig inspired the book.
Verisimilitude, however, wasn’t just a matter of getting the artifacts right. Set designers also had to build sets that duplicated dig sites and laboratories.

“We got notes about what the soil would look like and how the trenches should be laid out,” said Dan Bishop, the production designer, who built the show’s sets. “We were able to model and draw plans for burning pits, stones for floors and the way walls are put together on a dig site. We spent a lot of time studying limestone.”
Small details mattered, including zembelis, rubber buckets made from recycled tires that are “emblematic” of dig sites across the Mediterranean.

On prominent display in scenes of the lab is a spectrometer, a machine that separates atoms by mass-to-charge ratio, allowing scientists to calculate the age of a sample based on the radioactive decay rates of certain isotopes.

And in the background of several other scenes, viewers can see a laser theodolite, a surveying tool that projects a visible laser used to map excavation grids and that can track the location and depth of artifacts.

For inspiration, Dr. Rife brought the show’s producers to working excavations in Greece, including to the southern village of Kenchreai, where the archaeologist has been conducting excavations since 2002. They also visited digs in the ancient cities of Isthmia, Sicyon and Epidaurus.
Most of what is discovered at a typical dig are mundane pieces of broken pottery — shards of pots, jugs and bowls that have been untouched by human hands for thousands of years.

It is these everyday objects that allow archaeologists to piece together the lives of people who would otherwise be forgotten. A discarded pot or the remains of a meal can reveal how people ate, worked and lived — and, collectively, tell a story that a single extraordinary artifact cannot.
Treasures, like the show’s plot-turning discovery, are rare. But archaeologists like Dr. Rife prefer it that way.
“I would be much more excited to excavate a garbage pit in an impoverished house than I would a piece of gold jewelry,” he said.

fortune.com/2026/10/24/halloween-candy-s.headline: America skimps on Halloween as high fuel prices force shoppers to buy small bags of candy and abandon large sizes
fortune.com/2026/10/24/halloween-candy-s.author: Dee-Ann Durbin, The Associated Press

paragraphs.text: Halloween candy sales are off to a slow start this year as U.S. consumers grapple with high living costs and eye-popping chocolate prices.

Halloween candy sales fell 6.7% in the month ending Oct. 17 compared to the same period last year, according to NielsenIQ, a market research firm. Nielsen also noted an 11.7% decline in candy sales in mid-September, erasing the preseason gains that Halloween candy enjoyed the previous two years.

Chris Costagli, a vice president and food thought leader at NielsenIQ, said high gas prices have worsened Americans’ concerns about affordability, and that’s dampening demand for Halloween treats. As of Friday, the average price of a gallon of regular gasoline in the U.S. was $4.29, up nearly 40% from the prior year.

“I think what you’re seeing now is a consumer that’s spending so much additional money on fuel and housing and clothing and food,” Costagli said. “Some of the decisions they’re making about Halloween candy, it’s not necessarily because, ‘I notice it’s more expensive than last year,’ it’s, ‘I can’t afford it this year because I’ve paid so much more for so many other things. I just don’t have the financial means to buy it this year.’”
Small bags of candy were the only sizes seeing sales growth through mid-October, Costagli noted. Large and extra-large bags were seeing the biggest declines.

U.S. candy prices have been climbing faster than the rate of inflation for several years. As of September, candy and gum prices were up 44% over a five-year period, according to government data. Prices for all food eaten at home rose 22.5% in the same period.

This week, discount grocer Aldi was advertising a 135-piece variety pack of Mars Inc. chocolate bars – including Milky Way, Trix and Snickers – for $19.87. That’s almost the same price consumers paid for a 250-piece variety pack five years ago.

Cocoa prices are the main culprit. Global cocoa prices reached a record high of $10,710 per metric ton in January 2025 because of poor weather in West Africa – which supplies 70% of the world’s chocolate — and speculative trading in the cocoa futures market, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Cocoa prices had been falling steadily since then, and hit $3,241 per metric ton in March. But they began climbing again in the spring as the Iran war disrupted Africa’s fertilizer supplies. The El Niño weather pattern is also expected to hurt production, with hot, dry conditions expected through February.

But Costagli noted that even in cases where prices are lower than last year, consumer demand is muted. The average price of non-chocolate Halloween candies, like gummies and lollipops, was $6.08 per pound in the nine weeks ending Oct. 17, which was about 3% lower than last year, according to Nielsen data. But that didn’t lead to a bump in sales.

Sally Lyons Wyatt, a global executive vice president and food industry adviser for the market research company Circana, said one way U.S. consumers have been handling higher grocery prices is by making smaller and more frequent trips to the supermarket and buying products right before they intend to use them. That makes her wonder if shoppers are waiting until closer to Halloween to buy candy this year.

“People are very intentional and thoughtful about what they want to consume, not just for holidays, but in general,” she said. “I do believe we will still see softness overall with candy, but I don’t think Halloween is doomed.”
The National Confectioners Association, a trade group that represents candy makers like Mars, Smarties Candy Co. and Ferrara Candy Co., said it remains optimistic about Halloween sales.
“We are just now entering the peak period for Halloween and consumer enthusiasm remains incredibly strong,” the group said Friday in a statement.

aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/24/ukraine-sa.headline: Ukraine says Starlink restored as attacks continue in Russia and Ukraine
aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/24/ukraine-sa.author: AFP, AP and Reuters

paragraphs.text: Ukraine says restrictions on its military’s Starlink satellite connections have been lifted after more than a week of disruption that hampered drone operations against Russian forces.

Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said on Saturday that Starlink and Starshield connections were stable on equipment travelling above 400 kilometres per hour (250 miles per hour). He credited talks with Washington and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s diplomacy.
Recommended Stories

Ukraine relies heavily on Elon Musk’s SpaceX satellite services for communications and drone missions. However, who ordered the restrictions remains unclear, with US President Donald Trump denying responsibility while defending Elon Musk.
The disruption further strained relations between Kyiv and Washington, already under pressure over Trump’s agreement to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel and allow US imports.

Trump also called earlier this month for Ukraine to have a new president, then suggested on Monday that someone other than Zelenskyy should negotiate for Kyiv. The exchanges follow their public confrontation at the White House in February 2025.
Talks planned in Abu Dhabi

The lifting of the Starlink restrictions comes as the United States seeks to revive peace negotiations between Moscow and Kyiv. Negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the US are expected to meet in Abu Dhabi in the first half of November, more than four years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed the planned negotiations on Friday, while Zelenskyy also announced agreement on technical-level meetings.
It comes as Trump credited his wife, Melania Trump, with securing a local ceasefire in Oleshky, in southern Ukraine’s Kherson region, which Russian forces have occupied since 2022.
Subsequent Ukrainian and Russian statements putting the ceasefire’s start on October 27, with the humanitarian operation planned for October 29.
Deadly attacks continue

A Russian missile strike on Lozova, in Ukraine’s northeastern Kharkiv region, killed a man and wounded two others on Saturday, regional Governor Oleh Syniehubov said, while in northern Ukraine, a Russian attack on Chernihiv on Friday killed a man and wounded at least 25 people, local authorities said.

Shelling in Kramatorsk killed one person and wounded six, including three children, according to Donetsk officials. In nearby Sloviansk, attacks on Friday killed a 62-year-old woman and wounded four people, Mayor Vadym Lyakh said.

Ukraine reported strikes inside Russia on Friday and overnight into Saturday, including on Togliatti’s Togliattikauchuk petrochemical plant, a major synthetic rubber producer. Mayor Ilya Sukhikh confirmed industrial damage but reported no casualties.
Ukraine also said it struck Oryol’s Proton electronics plant, which it says makes missile components. Regional Governor Andrei Klychkov reported three deaths in an attack on an unidentified facility.
Authorities in Russian-occupied Crimea reported power cuts after overnight Ukrainian attacks.

Russia’s Defence Ministry said air defences intercepted a SCALP cruise missile, four Neptune missiles and 1,297 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones over 24 hours, TASS reported. The figures could not be independently verified.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/24/the-boox-palma.headline: The Boox Palma 2 Pro finally got me to stop reading on my phone
techcrunch.com/2026/10/24/the-boox-palma.author: Aisha Malik

paragraphs.text: The $400 Boox Palma 2 Pro is a smartphone-sized e-reader designed for people who want to read books, articles, and documents on a small E Ink display. However, it offers more than just a dedicated reading experience because it runs Android and supports Google Play, giving you access to third-party apps. Think of it as a cross between a Kindle and a compact Android tablet.

What drew me to reviewing the Palma 2 Pro was its size. When I’m not reading a physical book, I like to lie on my side and read at night before bed. Most e-readers are squarish and hard to hold without something like a PopSocket, and they can feel too big for reading while lying down. So even though I own a Kindle, I often ended up reading on my iPhone simply because it was more comfortable in my hand. But, reading on your phone for too long can of course cause eye strain. The Palma 2 Pro ultimately solved this problem for me during the two months I spent testing it.

The device’s front-lit screen lets you choose between cool and warm lighting. This was a big plus for me because when I’m reading in bed at night, I don’t want to disturb my sleeping husband with the light. While you can lower the brightness on a smartphone, the Palma 2 Pro can be dimmed to an exceptionally low level. Even when reading in complete darkness, I could see the screen clearly without straining my eyes or disturbing my husband.
Not only was the Boox Palma 2 Pro easier on my eyes, but it was also noticeably lighter than my iPhone, weighing just 175 grams and making it even more comfortable to hold.

And since it’s pocket-sized, I ended up carrying it everywhere, from the doctor’s office to the airport, especially since it fits in my small, everyday purse that isn’t big enough for a Kindle. So, in moments when I would normally scroll on my phone, I was getting some reading in instead.

Since it’s not a locked-down e-reader, you can download apps like Kindle, Kobo, and Libby, as well as apps for audiobooks, podcasts, read-it-later services, and email. This means that you don’t have to use the built-in reader app, and can choose to read on your preferred app.

Access to apps turns the compact E Ink device into a versatile tool for reading, research, and productivity. It’s worth noting that while scrolling through these apps, animations and some interfaces may feel sluggish because not all apps are optimized for E Ink. And while the device is capable of displaying color, images will definitely look less vibrant than they would a smartphone screen.

For me, the Palma 2 Pro became a dedicated device for reading and listening to audiobooks, which allowed me to enjoy the best of both worlds without the usual distractions that come with a smartphone.
The Boox Palma 2 Pro also features a rear camera for scanning documents, a built-in speaker for listening to audio without headphones, and a hybrid SIM slot for cellular data on the go.
The device is compatible with a stylus, so you can take notes and mark up PDFs. However, I can’t speak to that experience since I didn’t receive a stylus with my review unit.

As for battery life, the device lasted about 5–7 days, which worked for me but could be a downside for people who are used to Kindles, which can last for weeks on a single charge. Additionally, if you want to get more juice out of the device, you can just turn off Wi-Fi.

One downside I found, especially for an e-reader at this price point, is that there’s quite a bit of ghosting. Text from a previous page can linger on the screen when you turn to the next page or return to the home screen. There’s a refresh button in the navigation bar that quickly clears it, but it may get annoying for some users to repeatedly have to do that.

I think the Boox Palma 2 Pro is a great device for a very specific type of reader: someone who wants a smartphone-sized device for comfort, portability, as well as access to apps. If you’re someone who loves your Kindle, I don’t think this device is for you. But if, like me, you’re tired of reading on your phone and dealing with eye strain or headaches, the Boox Palma 2 Pro is a great option.

Of course, the price is quite steep for an e-reader, so you’ll have to decide whether the added versatility and portability are worth the extra cost. It’s worth mentioning that Boox is launching a non-Pro Palma 3 soon for $340 that features a black and white display and replaces the Palma 2.

Aisha is a consumer news reporter at TechCrunch. Prior to joining the publication in 2021, she was a telecom reporter at MobileSyrup. Aisha holds an honours bachelor’s degree from University of Toronto and a master’s degree in journalism from Western University.

cnbc.com/make-it/2026/10/24/sewing-works.headline: An ex-bookkeeper spent $375 to launch a sewing business: 'I hadn't felt so sure about something like that in a long time'
cnbc.com/make-it/2026/10/24/sewing-works.author: Jennifer Liu

paragraphs.text: Eric Lugo didn't know that when he launched his sewing workshop business, Stitch Lab ATX, as a side project in May 2025, it'd become his full-time focus within weeks.

Lugo also couldn't have predicted it'd become so successful within two years that offerings would grow fivefold, classes would regularly sell out and he'd start getting requests to host private events.

The idea came to him a few years ago: Lugo learned to sew from his grandma when he was 5 and got serious about it as a teen, eventually launching his fashion brand, Casa Amiré, and becoming his friends' go-to guy for tailoring and alterations help. Dresses needed hemming, jeans needed shortening. Lugo was happy to lend his talents, though the requests piled up.
So one day, in April 2024, he thought: What if he taught his friends how to fix their clothes themselves?

"It really made me think: Wow, this is — I think — a pretty important skill that a lot of people don't know how to do," Lugo, 29, of Austin, Texas, tells CNBC Make It. He could fill that gap. "I think I have enough knowledge after you know 14 [or] 15 years to be able to teach other people, and so I went from there."
A $375 investment

For months, while in between jobs and selling wares from his fashion brand, Lugo couldn't stop thinking about launching a sewing workshop. Around August 2024, he got a bookkeeping job for a local PR firm and shelved the idea. But by the beginning of 2025, it was back on his mind. He mapped out the classes he'd offer and how he'd get the word out.

By April, Lugo put money into it. He spent $375 to buy eight sewing machines, sourced second-hand from Facebook Marketplace, and set up shop in a friend's warehouse space that wasn't in use outside of business hours. Lugo gathered friends and family members to test-run his curriculum.

Stitch Lab ATX held its first classes in early May, Lugo says, with a few sign-ups for one-on-one private lessons and a handful of students taking his "crash course" workshop covering beginner-friendly basics, like learning how to thread a machine and sewing a straight line.
Then Lugo's circumstances changed fast: Toward the end of May, he was let go from his day job. It wasn't a question that he'd go all-in on his studio.

"Not even 10 minutes after I had just gotten laid off and gotten off of that Zoom meeting, I called my boy that has the warehouse, and I said, 'Dude, I just got laid off. Are you cool with me just going full-send with Stitch Lab?'" Lugo says. His friend was 100% in.
"I honestly hadn't felt so sure about something like that in a long time, if ever," Lugo says.
A rise in DIY hobbies
It took some time for things to get moving.

By his count, Lugo held around four to six classes in those early months. Sometimes just two or three people would show up, even though he could host up to 10. Lugo says demand picked up around September 2025 once he started partnering with local businesses to host pop-up sewing events (like a sip-and-stitch at a brewery) and spreading the word on TikTok.
Today the lab offers around two dozen classes per month and can fill up quickly when spots open up a month in advance, Lugo says.

Sessions typically cost $65 to $85 and last about two-and-a-half hours. Classes range from beginner-friendly lessons, like learning how to use a machine, to teaching intermediate skills, like hemming pants or installing a zipper. Students can sign up for special workshops to make a specific project, like a flower tote, or book open sewing time at the warehouse space. Lugo also takes requests to teach at special events, like for a bachelorette party or corporate offsite, averaging about one a month.
Lugo says he draws a salary from the business, which is his primary source of income.

Stitch Lab's success coincides with a trend of many Americans paying up to invest in their hobbies, even as the costs of goods and materials rise, leading to a trend of what Bank of America refers to as "funflation." Spending on hobbies, ranging from arts and crafts and hobby shops to retailers selling skiing, hiking, camping or scuba diving gear, grew 7.9% in August 2026 from the year prior, according to the bank's analysis of its card data.

To help some students offset these costs, Lugo in August began a monthly giveaway initiative called Sew It Forward, where entrants can comment on a Stitch Lab social media post about why they want to learn to sew, for the chance to win a free new sewing machine, supplies and a free class with the studio.
"I'm thankful for the support that I've received," Lugo says, "and so I want to put all that back into the community now that I'm in a position to do so."
A growing sewing community

Stitch Lab also stands out during a time when people, especially young adults, are craving community-oriented, offline social events. There's even a resurgence of so-called "grandma hobbies," like knitting and scrapbooking, as people seek relaxing pastimes that keep them off their phones.

In the warehouse dotted with sewing machines and early 2000s or reggaeton music streaming from the sound system, Lugo says he aims to build Stitch Lab up as a fun, creative "judgment-free zone" that can "feel like a home for people."
As an Afro-Latino founder, he says, "this is a safe space for Latinos, for people of color."

"I think community is needed, especially today with so much that's happening in the world," he adds. "No matter who you are, where you come from, you have a safe space to be around other people, learn the same thing ... and just have fun."

Stitch Lab ATX's future plans are already taking shape. Lugo says he just hired two part-time instructors to his team, which will allow them to expand to upward of 30 workshops per month. He still aims to keep classes relatively intimate to support one-on-one help and small-group socializing.
Lugo even sees his business expanding beyond Austin, with his sights set on New York City, hotspots across California and even Mexico City.
"I just want to continue to do what I'm doing all around the world," he says.
