thehill.com/opinion/judiciary/6169577-ju.headline: ‘You have this superpower’ — how the left is weaponizing jury nullification
thehill.com/opinion/judiciary/6169577-ju.author: Jonathan Turley, opinion contributor

paragraphs.text: “You have this superpower.”

That statement from Qiana Johnson is part of reported training material for residents to engage in “jury nullification,” whereby jurors ignore the law and incriminating facts in a given case to nullify any prosecution.

Notably, Johnson is the newly elected clerk of Prince George’s County Circuit Court in the Maryland suburbs of Washington. She is part of a growing left-wing movement gaining traction with voters that calls for radical changes to the U.S. legal system.

The effort is to engineer “Twelve Angry Men” scenarios on real juries — but unlike in the movie, the jurors are actually being trained to ignore evidence and deliberations in favor of political outcomes.

In her election campaign for her current job, Johnson had to overcome questions about her own criminal record. But many voters are willing to give others a second chance when they show evidence of rehabilitation and contrition. The more immediate concern might be embracing a practice that is expressly barred by courts.

Johnson is part of a new investigation by the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee into groups training citizens to engage in jury nullification — including Free DC and Harriet’s Wildest Dreams, where Johnson was reportedly a board member.
One such document allegedly declares, “You have this superpower, and that superpower is you are able to nullify that goddamn jury.”

Far-left professors have long advocated that juries use jury nullification. Georgetown Law professor and MSNBC legal analyst Paul Butler has long advocated that Black jurors engage in nullification in cases involving Black defendants. Butler wrote in the Washington Post in 2016: “Confronting the racial crisis in criminal justice, jury nullification gives jurors a special power to send the message that Black lives matter.”

The problem of biased jurors has long plagued the legal system. It can work both ways in ignoring the law to refuse or secure convictions. Past cases involving President Trump and other Republicans have raised bias concerns over the jury pool in cities such as Washington, D.C., and New York City.

But jury nullification is different; it is a direct assault on the very foundation of the American court system. The juror is the thumping heart of that system — a group of empowered citizens who swear to consider cases without prejudice or prejudgment.

It is not a crime to advocate jury nullification. Moreover, there are legitimate concerns raised by investigations into such groups. about chilling the rights of free speech and association. In my view, such advocacy is protected speech under the First Amendment.

But that is not always the case for lawyers, who can face professional consequences. Many courts bar lawyers from arguing for jury nullification. Calling for jury nullification can also present sanctionable conduct for lawyers in a given case.

Even if this is protected speech, voices in both parties need to denounce these efforts. It effectively encourages jurors to lie when they take their oath to follow the law and to shed any outside bias or prejudgment. It is an effort to enlist jurors in using cases to achieve political and social goals at the expense of the rule of law.

The professors and pundits supporting these campaigns are actively seeking a hostile takeover of the courts without explaining to these citizens the implications of such dishonesty. Indeed, Comer has detailed how groups like Freedom Trainers are allegedly seeking to enlist potential jurors while, according to the committee, instructing trainees not to “signal the agenda.”
Instead of addressing the impact of politicizing our jurors, these groups are portraying nullification as “a powerful tool for ensuring fairness and justice.”

These efforts are coming at a time of full assault on our judicial system from the left. Leading Democrats are calling for the packing of the Supreme Court, to reverse decisions with which they disagree. Every leading Democratic candidate for the 2028 presidential nomination has now thrown the court to the baying mob.
Former Democratic presidential nominee Hillary Clinton is only the most recent, declaring, “We should seriously look at expanding the court while the Democrats are in power.”

From the trial jury to the Supreme Court, many on the left now seek to take control of institutions that have long been the rock of this Republic. If successful, justice will become merely an extension of politics.

What is so disconcerting is that there is no longer any pretense of principle. Law professors are demanding that pledges to pack the Court be used as litmus tests for politicians, and senators are calling for an instant liberal majority on the Court to carry out the “will of the people.”
Liberal professors have long demanded revolutionary change to “reclaim America from constitutionalism.”

The attack on the American jury may be the most insidious of these efforts. Our legal system invests average citizens with the power to do justice. Every community plays a role in upholding the principles of blind justice. As with court-packing, jury nullification is a previously odious practice now being portrayed as a noble cause. It is part of the conditioning of voters to accept foundational changes to our constitutional system, to further a radical agenda harmful to the nation.

The juror’s role was indeed a “superpower,” but not the one these professors and pundits are pushing. It was a power against prejudice and partisanship; it was the power of doing simple justice in a nation committed to the rule of law.
Jonathan Turley is a law professor and the New York Times best-selling author of “Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution.”

engadget.com/2290733/macbook-neo-a18-pro.headline: The MacBook Neo Uses An iPhone Chip, And It's Just Good Enough
engadget.com/2290733/macbook-neo-a18-pro.author: Roger Fingas

paragraphs.text: A smartphone chip in a laptop sounds like a mess, but it results in a solid laptop for the money.

In retrospect, the MacBook Neo was Apple getting ahead of the curve. With tariffs and soaring memory prices in effect, the company must have known there was only so long it could keep the cost of its previous entry-level laptop — the MacBook Air — at a reasonable level. Sure enough, just three months later, the Air shot up by $200 to a new baseline of $1,300. Even at its current $700 price tag, the Neo is a comparative bargain.

Of course, the Neo achieves these savings by making compromises. The biggest by far is the use of a reproposed iPhone processor instead of an M-series chip like those found in other modern Macs, as well as the iPad Air and iPad Pro. Until the Neo launched, I had serious doubts about how well a phone chip could handle a desktop-level operating system.

The good news is that it handles macOS far better than you might think. There are some notable limitations, but these are mostly to be expected. The real question is whether you should wait for the anticipated refresh, which could be a big deal if it's not priced out of the budget sphere.
How an iPhone chip helps and hinders the MacBook Neo

The Neo is equipped with an A18 Pro, a processor originally designed for 2024's iPhone 16 Pro. In fact, it's scaled down slightly in this case. Whereas the 16 Pro's chip had a six-core CPU paired with a six-core GPU, the Neo drops to five GPU cores. You're getting inferior graphics performance, despite scaling up to a 13-inch display and potentially more demanding workloads.

What's strange is that for the most part, it's not a big deal. In our own testing for our MacBook Neo review, the laptop was able to juggle multiple web browsers, a TV show, photo editing in Pixelmator Pro and the game Oceanhorn 3 without much trouble. Arguably, this speaks to how overpowered iPhone chips have been for some time.

That said, the Neo can struggle with advanced tasks. While it's capable of vanilla 4K video editing, for example, its 8GB of RAM means that it can't process special visual effects without coming to a crawl. Many apps also require an M1 processor or better, including games like Assassin's Creed Shadows. Remember that minimum requirements are just that, and not a guarantee of best performance. If you want a truly smooth experience, you'll be far better served by the MacBook Air. Its latest iteration sports not just an M5 chip, but at least 16GB of RAM, which is the realistic baseline on today's best laptops.

The Neo's port technology is extremely limited, too. It's equipped with only a 10Gbps USB 3 port, a 480Mbps USB 2 port and a 3.5mm headphone jack. While you can plug in a 4K, 60Hz DisplayPort monitor via that USB 3 connection, there's no support for daisy-chaining or any kind of Thunderbolt accessory. The MacBook Air has a major win by upgrading those USB ports to 40Gbps USB 4 (with Thunderbolt 4), plus a dedicated MagSafe power connection.
Should you wait for the MacBook Neo 2?

Almost certainly. According to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, a 2027 refresh will upgrade the Neo to the A19 Pro chip used in the iPhone 17 Pro, as well as 12GB of RAM. While 12GB still isn't 16GB, an extra 4GB may be enough to smooth out some of the edge cases where the current model falters. Remember that you can't upgrade the RAM in today's MacBook post-purchase, so it's better to plan ahead now than get bottlenecked in the future.

That thinking about longevity especially applies in the current market. While the A18-based Neo might be good enough for most apps today, there's no guarantee that will be the case five years down the road. Apple is rolling ahead full-steam with AI features in macOS 27, some of which already require an M3 chip and 12GB of RAM. The second-generation Neo will still only get a slice of what Apple has planned, so it's not as if it will be a perfect fit for, say, heavy AutoCAD use. Yet you'll be in a slightly better position if you wait for the A19 hardware.

If you need a Mac immediately, the first-gen Neo will do. If an app works today, it probably isn't going to fall out of support anytime soon, since the laptop was only launched in March 2026. We suggest you go hunting for a refurbished model to save a few dollars, though.

aikido.dev/blog/python-packages-vulnerab.headline: Node2Shell evolves to HTTP2Shell. Brotli flaw (CVE-2026-111497) blast radius affects many libraries & apps using HTTPs.
aikido.dev/blog/python-packages-vulnerab.author: Dania Durnas

paragraphs.text: TL;DR
On Friday, October 23rd, it has become known that this CVE affects other major languages and service applications using HTTP, where patches are not yet fully available.

Check if you are decoding Brotli as a dependency within your libraries. Stay on guard for wider announcements and be ready to upgrade as soon as possible. If there is no patch available for a library or application that may be affected, we recommend disabling Brotli decoding until patches become available.
Update 4:12PM PT:
What is Brotli?

Brotli is a lossless compression algorithm and data format developed by Google. It’s a way to make data smaller for storage or sending over the internet. Software then unpacks it to recover the original data. It’s widely used for HTTP compression to compress web content such as HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
What is CVE-2026-111497?

CVE-2026-111497 is an out-of-bounds write in the Google Brotli decoder affecting versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms. This is the same Brotli decoder flaw behind Node2Shell announced a couple days ago. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted Brotli-compressed stream to corrupt memory, leak sensitive data, crash the process, or potentially execute arbitrary code. It carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 (Critical), and Node.js is affected through its bundled Brotli library.

A bug makes the Brotli decoder keep accepting more bytes when it should reject the data. Those bytes can overflow a small working buffer and damage the program’s memory. An attacker can use that damage to control what runs, such as their own code.

OpenAI found this in February reported it as unauthenticated remote code execution that works in both directions, so a malicious client can take over an unpatched server and a malicious server can take over an unpatched client that accepts compressed responses.

The root cause was fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn't recognized as a security issue at the time and no release shipped with the fix until now. That means every project that bundles Brotli has to ship its own update.

You’re exposed if any environment has Brotli 1.2.0 or earlier or brotlicffi 1.2.0.x installed, since HTTP clients such as requests, httpx, and aiohttp load these packages automatically when they’re present. Upgrade to Brotli 1.2.1 or brotlicffi 1.2.1.0 and rebuild any container images that bundle them. As of October 23, advisory databases don’t map the CVE to either PyPI package, so pip-audit, Dependabot, and Safety won’t flag vulnerable versions yet.
You can see what we’ve tracked here in Aikido Intel.
As for unaffected software, Apache’s standard mod_brotli does not decode Brotli
For CVE-2026-111497, update the affected runtime or Brotli library:
• Node.js: upgrade to 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1, or a newer supported release in the corresponding release line.
• Native Brotli / libbrotli: upgrade to 1.2.1 or later. For older release lines, use patched 1.0.10 or 1.1.1.
• Python packages: upgrade Brotli to 1.2.1 or later and brotlicffi to 1.2.1.0 or later, wherever installed.
• curl / libcurl: update its Brotli dependency to 1.2.1, a patched older release, or the vendor’s security-fixed package. Bundled or statically linked copies require an updated application build.
• Bun: upgrade to 1.4.4 or later. Rebuild compiled executables that bundle Bun.
• Envoy: upgrade to 1.40.0, 1.39.3, 1.38.6, or 1.37.8, or a newer release in a supported branch. 1.36.12 also includes the fix, but the 1.36 branch is unsupported.
• Istio: the fix is included in 1.29.9, 1.30.6, and 1.31.2. Use a newer supported release in the corresponding line; the 1.29 branch is end of life.
• Operating-system packages: install the vendor’s security update. Vendors may backport the fix without changing the upstream version number.

• Other HTTP servers, reverse proxies, API gateways, and HTTP clients: update the affected runtime or Brotli library they use. Where Brotli is bundled into the product, install the product vendor’s release that explicitly addresses this CVE. For managed services, confirm remediation with the provider.
Update dependency locks, rebuild affected applications and container images, redeploy, and restart services. Verify that running workloads use the patched components.
What to do if you can't upgrade yet
These workarounds reduce exposure while you prepare the upgrade:

• Python applications: where Brotli support is optional, uninstall both Brotli and brotlicffi from affected environments. Remove dependency extras such as httpx[brotli] and any other requirements that would reinstall them, then regenerate dependency locks and rebuild/restart workloads. HTTPX, Requests, and urllib3 retain gzip and deflate support without these optional packages. However, a server that sends Brotli anyway may produce an unreadable response or an application error; automatic fallback is not guaranteed. Uninstalling both Python packages and restarting workloads removes the decoding paths provided by those packages for incoming and outgoing data. It does not remove separate Brotli decoders bundled into other runtimes, libraries, or products.

• Incoming HTTP requests: reject requests whose Content-Encoding includes br at the reverse proxy, load balancer, or application middleware, before any vulnerable decoder processes the body. Match br case-insensitively, including within lists of encodings.

• Outbound HTTP requests: remove br from Accept-Encoding. Also disable Brotli response decoding or reject responses whose Content-Encoding includes br before decoding begins. Ensure this check occurs before automatic body processing; checking after the client has downloaded and decoded the response is too late.

Changing Accept-Encoding alone is insufficient: a malicious server can send a Brotli response regardless of what the client advertises, and urllib3 selects its decoder from the response’s Content-Encoding header.
Keep these controls in place until affected components are patched and verified. Review coverage as vendors confirm additional affected components or attack paths.
How Aikido helps with CVE-2026-111497

Aikido flags vulnerable versions of Brotli and brotlicffi in your repositories, container images, and dependencies, including when they arrive as transitive dependencies. Your dashboard shows which services still run a vulnerable version, so you can upgrade the ones that call outside servers or accept compressed request bodies first.
Once you've upgraded, Aikido checks if the finding is gone.
The timeline

Brotli is a widely used compression library from Google. On Wednesday, October 22nd NodeJS disclosed CVE-2026-111497, dubbed “node2shell,” wherein a Node.js process that decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data can be made to leak memory or run arbitrary code. Users were exposed if their app or a library decompresses bad Brotli data (e.g. the built-in fetch(), body-parser).

The next day, Python released a security update that patches the same flaw; Python packages were also vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497. Brotli flaw may affect even more languages and service applications, given how widely integrated the library is downstream. It turns out OpenAI had found this back in February.
Techincal details of CVE-2026-111497

The flaw sits in DecodeBlockTypeAndLength(), which handles block switches, the points where a Brotli stream changes which Huffman tree it uses. In vulnerable versions the function returns a plain boolean, and BROTLI_FALSE can mean either "this stream is malformed" or "I need more input." Callers can't tell the two apart, and on the fast path the decoder discards the return value entirely.

A crafted stream can declare a single block type and then exhaust that block's length, which forces a switch that can't succeed. The decoder then either reports that it needs more input for a stream that's complete, or keeps decoding with the block state it already had. That second path leads to the out-of-bounds write.

The upstream fix, google/brotli commit 0ed4268, makes the function return an error code and adds a new error, BROTLI_DECODER_ERROR_FORMAT_BLOCK_SWITCH (-17). Decoding now stops on a format error on both the safe and fast paths. OSM diffed the Brotli 1.2.0 and 1.2.1 source distributions and found that 1.2.1 differs only in the version bump and the decoder changes from that commit.
Brotli vulnerabilities in Python libraries (CVE-2026-111497)

The Brotli flaw behind Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497) affects Python. Two PyPI packages, Brotli and brotlicffi, compile the same vulnerable Brotli decoder that Node.js bundles. An official advisory was posted on GitHub. Brotli has 82.8 million downloads per month.

You're affected if any Python environment you run has Brotli 1.2.0 or earlier, or brotlicffi 1.2.0.x, installed. Popular HTTP clients such as requests and httpx load these packages automatically when they're present. Some packages automatically install Brotli as a dependency such as Scrapy, while others require explicit mention of it. An attacker can reach the vulnerable decoder by sending a malicious Brotli response to a request your app makes, or by sending your app a request body compressed with Brotli. That means an app can be exposed without importing Brotli anywhere in its own code. It’s a popular transitive dependency, so check your systems.
To fix it, upgrade to the patched releases:
• Brotli -> 1.2.1
• brotlicffi -> 1.2.1.0

The release notes for both fixed versions don't mention the CVE. As of October 23, advisory databases don't map it to either PyPI package yet, so pip-audit, Dependabot, and Safety won't flag these versions.
Who is affected by CVE-2026-111497 in Python?
You’re affected if any of your Python environments have one of these packages installed:
Your code doesn’t have to import either package. These HTTP clients advertise Accept-Encoding: br and decode Brotli responses automatically:
• urllib3 (and therefore requests) when Brotli or brotlicffi is installed
• httpx with the brotli extra
• aiohttp when Brotli is installed
• Scrapy, and anything built on the clients above
Attacker data can reach the decoder through two routes:
• Outbound requests. Your app fetches a Brotli response from a server an attacker controls, such as through a webhook delivery, URL preview, crawler or “fetch this URL” feature.
• Inbound requests. Your framework or middleware decodes a request body sent with Content-Encoding: br, which is the Python equivalent of the Express 5 case in Node.js.
How to fix CVE-2026-111497 in Python
The fix is a package upgrade, and it takes four steps:

• Upgrade whichever package you have installed with pip install -U "Brotli>=1.2.1" or pip install -U "brotlicffi>=1.2.1.0". If you use a lockfile with Poetry, uv, or pip-tools, update the constraint and regenerate the lockfile.
• Rebuild your container images and any wheels that bundle either package. An image built on a vulnerable version stays vulnerable until you rebuild it.
• Check every environment you run, including laptops, CI runners, servers and containers. Many projects pull in Brotli through an HTTP client extra, so look at your full resolved dependency tree.
• Rely on a manual check for now. pip-audit, Dependabot and Safety won't report this until the advisory databases map the CVE to the PyPI packages.
If your Python Brotli bindings came from a Linux distribution package instead of PyPI, the fix comes through your distribution, so check its security advisory as well.
What is the Python Brotli vulnerability (CVE-2026-111497)?

Python Brotli vulnerability refers to CVE-2026-111497, the Brotli decoder flaw known as Node2Shell, as it affects Python packages on PyPI. The CVE record pairs CWE-252 (unchecked return value) with CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write).
How serious is CVE-2026-111497 for Python, and is it being exploited?

The CVE record gives the flaw a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2, and Node.js rates it high severity. OSM built Brotli 1.2.0 and 1.2.1 with AddressSanitizer and ran a crafted stream through both. Version 1.2.0 consumed all of the roughly 23 MB stream and kept reporting that it needed more input, whether the stream arrived in one piece or in chunks as small as one byte. Version 1.2.1 rejected the stream with error -17 every time.

OSM didn't pursue memory corruption or code execution in the Python extension. The decoder code is the same code that researchers exploited against an unmodified Node.js 24.22.0 build, as Imperva and others reported. For Node.js, The Hacker News reported no exploitation in the wild as of October 22.

Treat it as urgent anyway. The bug is a memory-safety flaw in a component that handles untrusted network input, and the fix is a routine version bump. Services that call outside servers or accept compressed request bodies should go first.
How to check if your Python app is exposed
• Check installed versions with pip show Brotli brotlicffi in each environment, and with docker run --rm <image> pip show Brotli brotlicffi for each container image.
• Find what pulls the packages in. Run pipdeptree -r -p Brotli to see which dependencies require it, and search your lockfiles with grep -i brotli poetry.lock uv.lock requirements*.txt.
• List the outbound HTTP calls that go to servers you don't control, and any endpoints that decode Content-Encoding: br request bodies.
• Upgrade the services that match step 3 first, then the rest.

If you're reproducing the bug from Python, brotli.decompress() raises a generic brotli.error: decoder failed for any error, so you can't see which error code fired. A Decompressor() fed the crafted stream incrementally will never finish on 1.2.0.
FAQ
Which versions fix CVE-2026-111497 in Python?
Brotli 1.2.1 and brotlicffi 1.2.1.0, along with any newer releases.
Do I need to import Brotli in my code to be affected?
An installed package is enough. urllib3, requests, httpx and aiohttp use Brotli or brotlicffi automatically when either is present and decode Brotli responses from any server your app calls.
Will pip-audit or Dependabot flag this?

Not yet. As of October 23, the CVE record, OSV and the GitHub Advisory Database don't list either PyPI package. OSM is submitting PYSEC entries and a PyPI package mapping for the GitHub advisory so that tooling picks this up.
Is there a workaround?

Uninstalling Brotli and brotlicffi removes the vulnerable decoder, and HTTP clients fall back to gzip and deflate. Rejecting Brotli-encoded requests at the edge reduces inbound exposure, but it doesn't protect against Brotli responses your app fetches.

marketwatch.com/story/everyones-talking-.headline: Everyone's talking about Roth conversions, but here's how few people really do them - and why you shouldn't have FOMO about it

paragraphs.text: You have to do the math to figure out your best tax strategy in retirement, and converting might not be for you
Do you want to pay tax on your retirement money now or later?

There's no hotter topic in retirement than Roth conversions. But for all the ballyhoo, the number of people who actually follow through with a Roth conversion is small compared with the number who hold money in tax-deferred accounts.

The Investment Company Institute, which tracks industry data, reported that 1.6 million Roth conversions happened in 2023, based on the most recent available IRS data. The total amount converted was $36.7 billion, out of about $17 trillion held in traditional IRAs in the U.S. The average amount converted was just under $23,000.

There's nothing to suggest these numbers are changing dramatically. The number of conversions was 1.5 million in 2021 and 2022, according to ICI. Fidelity said just 2% of its 20 million or so IRA customers made a Roth conversion transaction in 2025 an that the number had not changed much so far in 2026.

"People are hungry for it, but the dollars, from what we see, are still pretty small. There's basically a lot of engagement without a lot of transactions," said Rita Assaf, Fidelity's vice president of retirement and college products.

It turns out that while the interest is genuine, there are still serious barriers for most people. Namely, there are a few criteria for the conversion to be worthwhile: You need the money on hand to pay the tax, the knowledge that you'll actually benefit from paying that tax now versus later, and the know-how to complete the complicated transaction.
Doing the math

Running the numbers to determine whether a Roth conversion will be beneficial is not an easy task. If you're on your own with the decision, you have to turn to online calculators and self-directed software programs like Boldin and MaxiFi, which are available for a fee. Online forums and advice columns can provide feedback, but that would just be based on a cursory overview of your situation. You can easily run into walls, which may explain some of the discrepancy between the number of people who have an interest in Roth conversions and the number who actually do them.

Assaf said Fidelity cannot tell from the anonymized data if those completing conversions had help from advisers but that she would presume they did. "I can say that Roth comes up as a planning topic for retirement, and clients expect that their adviser would bring it up - or the clients bring it up," Assaf said. "I have a feeling most of [the conversion activity] is coming from advisers doing planning, more so than it is self-directed, but that's just me taking a guess."

Professional financial advisers use software to run projections, but even that is not perfect. Run your scenario through three different programs, and you will get three different answers. Elizabeth Buffardi, a fee-only financial planner based in the Chicago area, developed her own spreadsheet to run analyses for clients, because none of the software appealed to her. One key aspect she found lacking in off-the-shelf solutions was that they measured for a few decades but not for an entire lifespan. She likes to stretch out her scenarios until the IRA owner in question turns 101.

When Buffardi is doing the math, she wants to see if the client will end up paying more or less in lifetime taxes as the result of a conversion. That's an equation that incorporates educated guesses, considering that future tax rates are unknown, but the best she can do is project the current system through future years.

For some clients, the resulting savings are small, a function of the size of their IRAs and the difference between their current tax rate and their future tax rate. She has seen the difference be as little as $15,000 or $25,000 in lifetime taxes.

"You don't need to pinpoint it the way I do, but I like to give people a number," Buffardi said. When the amount they are saving is low, people tend to balk at the Roth conversion. They don't see why they should shell out tax money now for a small amount of savings down the road.

More often, when considering account balances of more than $1 million, the lifetime tax savings is closer to $100,000 or $200,000. That's when clients begin to take action, especially if they are facing high required minimum distributions later in life. Required minimum distributions can add layers of complication to a retirement plan, such as triggering the Medicare surcharge known as IRMAA and higher taxation of their Social Security benefits. Buffardi has seen the lifetime savings go as high as $1 million.
Tax aversion

The first step of a Roth conversion is to take money out of a tax-deferred account and pay the tax due, and then move it to the Roth account. The best scenario is to pay that tax with cash on hand, because then the full amount of the conversion can go into the Roth account to grow tax-free.
This stops a lot of people in their tracks. Either they don't have enough money or they don't want to shell out that much to pay the tax.

Another consideration is the endgame for the money. If someone plans going to spend down whatever is in their IRA by the time they die, then there's no need to convert. If any money left in the account will be earmarked for a charity, the more tax-efficient strategy is to leave it where it is.

Roth conversions make the most sense for married couples with large IRA balances, because after one spouse dies, the other will have to pay taxes as a single person on the same amount of money. They also come into play for people who going to leave the money in those accounts to heirs. "A lot of the clients I have are very concerned about leaving good assets to kids," Buffardi said. An inherited IRA has to be emptied in 10 years, into a regular brokerage account in most cases, and this generally happens when the account owner's adult children are in their peak earning years, with their own kids in college. "They end up saying, this money would be really helpful if I weren't giving half to the government and half to college," Buffardi said.

There's a lot of hype around Roth conversions, which is why some younger people are inclined to make them, Assaf said. But there's a better avenue for those investors, she said. "Do you know you could be eligible for Roth contributions? They're looking at the back door when they could go through the front door," she said. "Do the math. Don't just believe the hype."

npr.org/2026/10/23/nx-s1-6013613/israeli.headline: Israeli PM pledges massive military operation after West Bank checkpoint attack
npr.org/2026/10/23/nx-s1-6013613/israeli.author: Ruth Sherlock

paragraphs.text: The Israeli military is demolishing homes and forcibly removing hundreds of Palestinians from a neighborhood in the city of Hebron in the occupied West Bank following an attack by Palestinian gunmen on an Israeli checkpoint that killed two soldiers and wounded three others.

In response to that attack yesterday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces a tough election on Tuesday, vowed to launch a military operation in the West Bank "on a scale not seen since the Six Day War," when Israel first occupied the West Bank almost 60 years ago.
"We will act to demolish this place, to change it completely," Netanyahu said in a televised speech from the location of the attack, close to the Palestinian city of Hebron.

He likened the plan to an Israeli military assault against two long-standing Palestinian refugee camps in the northern West Bank last year in which the Israeli army displaced tens of thousands of Palestinians. Human Rights Watch said those expulsions amounted to war crimes, a charge that Israel rejects.

On Friday afternoon, the Israeli military had already begun bulldozing homes close to the site of the shooting. The Israeli human rights group B'Tselem is calling on foreign governments to act to prevent "another wave of ethnic cleansing and war crimes."

Commenting on the attack, the Israeli military told NPR that soldiers were positioned behind concrete barriers at the checkpoint when two gunmen opened fire on them. A firefight continued for about 20 minutes before Israeli soldiers killed the attackers.

This comes amid a surge of violence and land seizures by Israeli settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. The United Nations Human Rights Office for the occupied Palestinian territory has described it as a "new level of dehumanization of Palestinians."

Israel imposed widespread closures in Hebron on Saturday, making movement difficult in and around the most populous city of the occupied West Bank. Israel regularly imposes restrictions on movement across the Palestinian occupied territory with some 925 checkpoints, roadblocks, earth mounds and other barriers.

Analysts tie the wide-scale Israeli response to Friday's attack to the Israeli national elections on October 27, claiming this is an effort by Netanyahu to appear strong to voters. According to polls, Netanyahu and his main opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, are neck and neck in the race. Neither candidate currently has enough support to form a government.

"For Netanyahu, his ticket before the election is, 'I'm Mr. Security,'" Danny Citrinowicz, a senior researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies in Tel Aviv, told NPR. "In order to show that he is the protector of Israel, he will take harsh measures in order to show the Israeli public that he supports them and he's defending them."

This is a view shared by other analysts, who see this latest military action more as an effort by Netanyahu to remain in power than a closely thought-out strategy to improve Israel's long-term security. Citrinowicz called Netanyahu's response — to evict families from their homes in the neighborhood the attackers came from, without evidence of a connection to the gunmen — "collective punishment."

"The way to prevent [more attacks by Palestinians] is not collective punishment. It's by giving hope," Citrinowicz said. "Distinguish between those who want to commit terrorist attacks and arrest them and those who just want to live peacefully and help them to live peacefully, with an economy that works, with everything they need for stability.
Additional reporting by Daniel Estrin in Tel Aviv and James Hider in Washington D.C. This story was edited by Samantha Balaban.

aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10/24/ballon-d.headline: Ballon d’Or 2026: Can Kylian Mbappe’s Real Madrid and France record win it?
aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10/24/ballon-d.author: Manasi Pathak

paragraphs.text: He may not be the bookmakers’ favourite or last season’s top goalscorer, but Kylian Mbappe has left no stone unturned in his media push to win the upcoming Ballon d’Or.
The 2025-26 season, on which the award is judged, left the Real Madrid talisman without a trophy for club or country.
Recommended Stories

On an individual note, however, the France captain set records, which he hopes will finally land him the coveted award that carries no cash prize but, alongside the accolade, increases a player’s worth and status.

“Being the all-time top scorer in World Cup history, overtaking all the great legends in the history of the sport in the most important tournament there is, is something that really stands out,” Mbappe said last month.
“Who am I voting for? Myself.”
In an award voted for entirely by journalists, Mbappe believes he is the most deserving contender in the run-up to Monday’s ceremony in London.
But how does his performance compare with other shortlisted nominees? Al Jazeera breaks it down:
World Cup exploits with France headline Mbappe’s bid

The 2026 FIFA World Cup in North America marked another spectacular individual campaign for Mbappe, who not only won the Golden Boot for the top scorer for the second successive campaign but also became the all-time top scorer in World Cup history.

His 22 World Cup goals in as many matches keep him at the top of a star-studded list that includes Argentina’s legend Lionel Messi in second place on 21 and German ex-international Miroslav Klose third on 16.
Madrid see a Real return from Mbappe

Beyond international duty, Mbappe also enjoyed an excellent individual campaign with his club, Real. His tally of 25 goals earned him the honour of La Liga’s top scorer, while he was also the Champions League’s leading marksman with 15 goals.
Those numbers have made Mbappe confident he will win the prestigious Ballon d’Or for the first time.
“I was top scorer in all the biggest competitions, and I think that this could be a good year for me, and I really feel it,” the ex-PSG star said.
No silverware weakens Mbappe’s case
Despite Mbappe’s solo brilliance, there is nothing in his trophy cabinet from last season to put forth a strong case.

Amid a turbulent campaign first under Xabi Alonso and then Alvaro Arbeloa, Real finished second in La Liga and were bundled out of the Champions League by Bayern Munich in the quarterfinals, leaving Mbappe and Los Blancos ending a second straight season without major trophies.
To make things worse, France came fourth at the World Cup after losing to Spain in the semifinals and England in the third-place playoff.

Even though Mbappe was often the lone hero in many of Real or France’s games, he failed to win a trophy, unlike his close contenders Lamine Yamal, who won the World Cup with Spain and La Liga with Barcelona, and Bayern’s Harry Kane, whose three trophies last term include a Bundesliga title.
Mbappe shrugs off trophyless season for France and Real Madrid
Those differences do not seem to bother Mbappe, though.
“They won’t announce a team in the envelope; they will announce a player,” Mbappe told RFI radio station, referring to the Ballon d’Or ceremony.
“The ability to perform individually and produce eye-catching moments – that’s what stands out to people for an award like this.”
While Mbappe’s self-promotion has been rampant in recent months, his club manager, Jose Mourinho, has also backed the 2018 World Cup winner.
“We know who has made history this summer, and he’s not from PSG or the Spanish national team,” Mourinho said.
History suggests trophies matter in Ballon d’Or triumph
Over the last decade, every Ballon d’Or winner won at least one trophy during the years they were crowned the best player.

Ousmane Dembele, the 2025 winner, enjoyed a trophy haul that included leading PSG to their first-ever Champions League title, while Spain’s midfield maestro Rodri won the Euro 2024 with Spain and the Premier League with Manchester City among his accolades when he was named the Ballon d’Or winner two years ago.
The last time a player won the Ballon d’Or without a major trophy in his cabinet was in 2013 and coincidentally featured another Real player: Cristiano Ronaldo.
At that time, Ronaldo lifted his second Ballon d’Or, also ending Messi’s four-year winning streak.

The forward earned the award purely for his individual brilliance, scoring 66 goals for club and country, in a season when Portugal failed to progress beyond the 2012 World Cup playoffs and Real were the league’s runners-up.
Ronaldo’s 2013 triumph proves that while odds are not in Mbappe’s favour, he still has a slim chance.
After nine nominations and a third-place finish in 2023, many would argue that Mbappe’s moment to kiss the coveted Ballon d’Or trophy is long overdue.

theatlantic.com/national/2026/10/what-sh.headline: What Shifting U.S. Support May Mean for Ukraine

paragraphs.text: Editor’s Note: Washington Week With The Atlantic is a partnership between NewsHour Productions, WETA, and The Atlantic airing every Friday on PBS stations nationwide. Check your local listings, watch full episodes here, or listen to the weekly podcast here.

President Trump’s dismissal of Russian aggression against Ukraine has prompted bipartisan backlash. On Washington Week With The Atlantic, panelists joined to discuss what this may mean for the Ukrainians, and more.

“We have to remember that Ukraine has seen the United States pull back its support even before this,” Nancy A. Youssef, a staff writer at The Atlantic, said last night. In the past, the U.S. has limited the number of weapons it sends to Ukraine, and “this week, we saw the United States not delivering promised interceptors,” Youssef added.

“The challenge for Ukraine is twofold: It is the inconsistency in the United States’ support and the inability for Europe to come back and provide that support,” Youssef argued. “And that Russia is as close as it’s ever been to Washington.” These two factors make “the war harder for the Ukrainians,” she noted.

Joining the editor in chief of The Atlantic, Jeffrey Goldberg, to discuss this and more: Leigh Ann Caldwell, a chief Washington correspondent at Puck; Stephen Hayes, the editor and CEO of The Dispatch; Zolan Kanno-Youngs, a White House correspondent at The New York Times; and Youssef.
Watch the full episode here.

aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10/24/aston-vi.headline: Man City beaten at Aston Villa as perfect Premier League start ends
aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10/24/aston-vi.author: AFP

paragraphs.text: Manchester City’s perfect Premier League start came to a crashing halt in a 2-1 defeat at Aston Villa as Nicolas Jackson’s double extended an upturn in form for Unai Emery’s new-look side.

Enzo Maresca had become the first manager to win his first seven Premier League games in charge of a new club, but failed to find a solution to City’s struggles at Villa Park, where they have now lost in each of the past four seasons.
Recommended Stories
After Jackson blasted home the opener after just six minutes, Villa relied on a brilliant goalkeeping display from Zion Suzuki to keep City at bay.
Erling Haaland briefly levelled early in the second half only for Villa to respond on the hour mark when Jackson drilled home Ibrahim Mbaye’s cross.

Four years on from Emery’s arrival, which has transformed the club from a sleeping giant into a Champions League club, the Spaniard is working more magic despite seeing the spine of his squad in recent seasons decimated.
Six players from the side that started Villa’s victory in last season’s Europa League left during the transfer window.
But the recruitment of the likes of Jackson, Suzuki, Mbaye and Johan Manzambi is already paying dividends after a slow start to the campaign.
Until now, City have managed to shrug off the cloud hanging over the club’s Premier League future to keep winning on the field.
The 10-time English champions are appealing a guilty verdict on over 100 charges of breaking financial rules between 2009 and 2018 that could lead to swingeing sanctions, including relegation.
There was little sign of that distraction affecting Maresca’s men, but they were made to pay for two sloppy defensive errors.
A heavy touch by Marc Guehi presented Jackson with possession for the opening goal as he cut inside Elliott Anderson and blasted high past Gianluigi Donnarumma.
City largely dominated the remainder of the first half, but could not find a way past Suzuki.
Iliman Ndiaye, Rayan Cherki and Abdukodir Khusanov were all denied before Ndiaye struck the post.
City’s pressure finally told on 52 minutes when Haaland powered in a header from Ndiaye’s cross for his 13th goal in 10 appearances this season.
Josko Gvardiol nearly completed the comeback when Suzuki turned his blistering drive onto the crossbar moments later.
Instead, it was Villa who got the decisive third goal.
Mbaye was played in behind the City defence and from his cross, Jackson’s low effort should have been saved by Donnarumma.
The visitors pressed in vain for another equaliser to allow Arsenal the chance to move level on points at the top of the table when they host Everton later on Saturday.
A sixth win in seven games in all competitions for Villa lifts them up to sixth.

marketwatch.com/story/young-americans-ar.headline: Young Americans are giving up on car ownership. It's a path to financial freedom for some.

paragraphs.text: With vehicle prices soaring and ownership increasingly out of reach, some young adults are discovering that life without a car leaves them with breathing room to spend on other things
The average car has gotten so expensive that giving one up can provide young Americans with greater control over how they spend their money.

When Nick Renteria moved from Boston to Los Angeles for school, he rented a car for about $350 a month. His parents covered the rental cost while he paid for gas, but he hated sitting in traffic, parking and feeling disconnected from the city.
When he finished his program, Renteria, 24, decided he didn't want a car at all.
He moved to West Hollywood, selecting a neighborhood where he could bike to work, use public transportation and altogether avoid the expense of owning a vehicle.

The decision has paid off over the past two years. While a roommate with a car and a similar income struggled financially, Renteria found he could afford to go out with friends and enjoy the city, even while working part-time jobs.
"L.A. is actually kind of affordable if you don't have a car," he said.

For generations of Americans, owning a car has often been a symbol of independence. But, for some younger adults today, that notion is being turned on its head. The average car has gotten so expensive that giving one up can sometimes translate into gaining something equally important: greater control of how they spend their money.
"L.A. is actually kind of affordable if you don't have a car," said Nick Renteria, who went car-free two years ago.
And there are signs that younger Americans are shifting away from car ownership as a symbol of success.

The share of households younger than 35 that owned a vehicle last year fell to 79.4% from 82.1% in 2019, according to data from the Federal Reserve. Meanwhile, over the same period, vehicle ownership among Americans 75 and older rose to 83% from 80.1%. Younger adults have replaced the oldest Americans as the demographic with the lowest vehicle-ownership rate.

Other data suggest that young people are changing how they get around. Among adults 29 and younger, 48% drove themselves in their own car at least once a month this year, down from 53% in 2023, according to YouGov surveys. Meanwhile the share who rode as passengers increased to 54% from 45%. This was the only method of transportation to become more common among Generation Z adults during this period.

Those surveys gauge transportation habits and not necessarily car ownership. But, taken together with the ownership data, they point to a shift in the relationship between young Americans and personal motor vehicles.
The high cost of car ownership
The financial case for young Americans not owning a car is becoming increasingly compelling.

As the rising cost of vehicles, maintenance, insurance and loan payments deter young Americans from buying cars, many are migrating toward ride-sharing, carpooling and car-sharing options, and using delivery services, instead - and some say they prefer those alternatives to having a car of their own.

New vehicles now sell for more than $50,000, on average, and used cars for $27,000. Meanwhile, those who finance their vehicles face average interest rates of 6.35% for new cars and 11.19% for used cars, pushing up the average monthly payment to $765 for new cars and $542 for used cars, according to Experian.

And purchasing a car is only the beginning. Maintenance and insurance costs have increased dramatically since the pandemic, while gas prices have crossed $4 a gallon, on average, this year due to the war in Iran.
The average annual cost to own and operate a new vehicle is now $12,863, according to AAA.
More on this: Cars have become unaffordable for many Americans. Here's what the numbers show.
For younger Americans navigating a difficult job market, expensive housing and student-loan debt can consume a substantial chunk of income.

In a 2025 survey, common concerns hindering Gen Zers from buying a car included not being able to afford the type of car they wanted (30%), interest rates being too high (32%) and costly maintenance (28%), data shared with MarketWatch by Enterprise Mobility show.
On top of that, remote work and online shopping trends, as well as the proliferation of new delivery services, make it easier to forgo car ownership.
Last month, about one out of five workers ages 25 to 34 worked from home at least some of the time, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Meanwhile, Gen Z adults said online shopping (54%) and working from home (48%) have reduced their need to drive over the past few years, and more than 20% cited rideshare services, according to a Mercury Insurance survey in June.

In a separate poll, 29% of Gen Z members said they have used peer-to-peer car-sharing platforms, and, among them, 43% did so at least biweekly or monthly. Convenience and cost savings were the top reasons given among all survey respondents.
To these young Americans, such options have made owning a car a luxury, not a necessity.
For Xenna Smith, 27, selling her Subaru in Raleigh, N.C., last year was partly a money decision and partly about peace of mind. "I just felt a lot of anxiety," she told MarketWatch.
In addition to safety concerns as driver, "it was just costs and costs and costs," she said.
Now, Smith bikes or rides the bus almost anywhere she needs to go, and walks to buy groceries. Her apartment, which costs $1,500 a month, has a gym, a pool and bike parking.

In a typical month, she now spends less than $40 on transportation for the occasional Lyft and bike maintenance, compared with $600 when she had a car. Through a $25 annual membership at bike advocacy group Oaks and Spokes, she gets her bus pass for free.

While renting a car, ride-hailing apps (like Uber and Lyft), and public transit all come with their own costs, average transportation spending for households with no cars are lower at every income level - including the top 20% of earners - compared with households that own or lease at least one automobile, according to the Bureau of Transportation Statistics.
'I can afford my student loans now, my rent's comfortable, and I actually am saving money for once.'Xenna Smith, Raleigh, N.C.

There are tradeoffs. Not having a car makes it harder to see people who live out of town and can require extra effort and be physically demanding, Smith said. She also said she wished drivers would "stop being so aggressive to cyclists."

On the other hand, "I can afford my student loans now, my rent's comfortable and I actually am saving money for once," she said of having gone car-free. "I'm not contributing anything bad to the environment, and I'm making myself better physically."
Smith's experience underscores an important point: Going without a car isn't necessarily about giving something up. For some, it's about deciding what they would rather be able to afford.

When Sabrina Rae Santoro, a 33-year-old entrepreneur, moved from northern Scottsdale, Ariz., to Old Town Scottsdale earlier this year, she decided to give up her Mercedes. The loan payment, insurance, gas and maintenance cost about $1,000 each month, but she was only using the car to drive 20 to 30 miles each week because she normally works from home.

"Anybody that knows me knows, like, I am a car girly," Santoro said, but "I simply ran the numbers and worked out a location where everything that I need is pretty much five to 10 minutes away walking, or a short drive," she told MarketWatch.

Now, Santoro uses the on-site gym at home, has her groceries delivered, and shops on Amazon. To get around, she uses Lyft, which runs $450 to $500 a month. Compared with when she owned her car, "I'm spending half [as much on transportation], and the funny thing is, I still go everywhere I want to go. I don't limit myself," she said. "It's actually an improvement in quality of life. I feel free."
Sabrina Rae Santoro, a 33-year-old entrepreneur, decided to give up her Mercedes and says not owning a car has improved her quality of life. "I feel free," she told MarketWatch.

Living in cities with robust public transportation can ease the transition. "It's been a huge relief" financially and mentally to go car-free and not have to worry about maintenance and repairs, said D.J. Hargrave, a 30-year-old who sold his Honda when he moved to Chicago last year.
Hargrave's car expenses ran about $1,000 per month, and, when he sold his Accord Sport back to the dealership, he had to pay about $3,000 in negative equity.
Now, Hargrave relies on Chicago's network of buses and trains with a $75 monthly pass and spends less than $200 a month on Uber rides.

"Younger generations of consumers are doing a lot of math, and they don't believe that owning things is the way to go, or that they can ever own things to the same extent older generations have, so they make different choices," Jeremy Robb, chief economist at Cox Automotive, told MarketWatch.
As young people also delay getting married and have fewer children, "there are lifestyle choices that may mean they don't need to have a car, especially on the family side," Robb added.
Related: America's renter generation is trying to build wealth by investing in stocks instead of owning a house
Car-industry response

These transportation trends are showing up especially in sales of new cars. Drivers ages 18 to 34 made up 9.7% of new vehicle registrations in August, down from 12.7% five years earlier, according to automotive-data company Mobility Global.

"Younger and less affluent buyers have largely left the new-vehicle market," Sam Fiorani, vice president of global vehicle forecasting at AutoForecast Solutions, told MarketWatch. At the moment, the U.S. car industry lacks options below $30,000. The loss of entry-level models such as the Ford Focus, Chevrolet Cruze and Nissan Versa over the past decade has "eliminated several key products that brought first-time buyers into the market," he noted.

Historically, "whenever the U.S. market moved too far upmarket, a new competitor helped rebalance prices," Fiorani said. "In the 1950s, it was Volkswagen. In the 1960s, it was Toyota, followed by Honda in the 1970s. Hyundai arrived in the 1980s, followed by Kia in the 1990s."
However, protectionist regulations and tariffs are currently preventing lower-cost cars from China from entering the U.S. market, eliminating a potential source of entry-level vehicles, he said.
From the archives (April 2026): Americans would love this $25,000 hybrid SUV - but it's not available here yet

It's hard for car companies to "make money on vehicles" that cost less than $30,000 now, Tom Libby, director of loyalty solutions and industry analysis at Mobility Global, told MarketWatch, but recent developments show there is consumer demand.
The Ford Maverick, unveiled in 2021 at $20,000, has "done very, very, very well," he said. It now costs $30,000.
Meanwhile, Slate Auto, the new electric-vehicle startup backed by Jeff Bezos, is taking preorders for trucks with roll-up windows that start at $25,000.

Even at lower prices, car makers will have to confront young consumers who are looking for alternatives to ownership. Dominic Berardi, a 21-year-old student in Orlando, Fla., has a car, but moved downtown and got a job as a server close by "because I was already planning to restructure my life around the transit that exists here, if at all possible."
For Berardi, independence no longer means having a car waiting outside. It means freedom from reliance on one.

What personal-finance issues do you want to see covered in MarketWatch? We would like to hear about your financial decisions and money-related questions. You can write to us at readerstories@marketwatch.com. A reporter may be in touch to learn more. MarketWatch will not attribute your answers to you by name without your permission.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/24/these-clever-a.headline: These clever apps show off the iPhone Duo’s potential
techcrunch.com/2026/10/24/these-clever-a.author: Sarah Perez

paragraphs.text: It’s been a long time since I’ve been genuinely excited about a new iPhone.

For years, a new iPhone meant a device that was thinner, faster, and had a camera that came with incredible upgrades. At some point (and Apple devotees can debate which year’s model this was!), a new iPhone became an incremental upgrade. Slightly better, slightly faster. Maybe there was a new button to learn, a new charging cable, or a new notch on the screen, but the iPhone itself remained the same rectangular glass and metal handheld it always was.
The iPhone Duo changes this, allowing Apple to enter the market for foldable phones with a phone that, while imperfect, is whimsical, fun, and, yes, actually exciting.

It’s hard to say when the urge to acquire the iPhone Duo first kicked in. I’ll admit that it wasn’t during the official announcement, which left me feeling puzzled about the device’s potential. Do I actually want a phone that folds, I wondered? Was propping up the phone as a little tent to watch Netflix worth all that extra money? (The Duo starts at $2,000).

As it turned out, the desire for the Duo grew on me as I saw developers embracing the new foldable design to create Duo-optimized apps. Apple’s software development community, after all, is what keeps me locked into the iPhone. Apple developers are active, creative, engaged, and still often build for iOS first – a must if you like trying things early.

Of course, the initial Duo reviews have pointed out how many mainstream iOS apps have not yet been made ready for the Duo, which is true. Many of the apps you use every day were not optimized by launch day, meaning they’re surrounded by black bars, have their controls in odd places, or have to be enlarged with a tap, similar to the early days of running iPhone apps on iPad.
But the developers who have specifically built for the Duo sparked my interest. Soon, my inbox was filled with pitches for clever apps I couldn’t yet try unless I got my hands on a Duo. Hello, FOMO.

The best of these don’t just adapt their apps to display correctly on the foldable form factor, but make use of the fact that there are different displays of different sizes – and they incorporate that into the design of the apps themselves.
Below are some of my early favorites, tested on a review unit provided by Apple.
Netflix

Let’s start with the basics. Netflix is one of Apple’s hand-picked partners for the Duo launch, and had its streaming app Duo-optimized by the time the device shipped, alongside others like the MLB app, NYT Cooking, Slack, my preferred calendar app Fantastical, and others. But Netflix is the perfect showcase for what I expect will be a regular Duo use case: watching movies and TV.

The streaming app hasn’t just been expanded to fill the screen; it takes advantage of the fact that there are two different screen sizes to build for. On the outer screen (the display you see when the device is folded), you can scroll through Netflix’s short-form, TikTok-like “Clips,” then open up the device to continue watching videos on the larger matte-screen inner display. The transition between the two experiences feels as seamless as unfolding the Duo itself, as the content automatically adapts to the new screen size.

As I personally find myself watching most TV on my phone these days, as opposed to big screen in the living room, I appreciate having the option to shift from a phone to a larger screen with one device. This is going to be one of my most-used apps, I think.
Deck-Man (Formerly Duo-Man)

Look, I called it back in September. I have to credit Deck-Man, which was previously known as Duo-Man, as being the first app that made me want to get a Duo. Designed by indie developer Vidit Bhargava at a hackathon, the music player takes clever advantage of the Duo’s two screens to imitate how Walkman cassette players used to function.

The playful app reimagines the cassette player as a digital experience with retro vibes, allowing you to browse through your favorite albums as cassettes, then load them into the player. You can then control the playback with play, pause, fast-forward, and rewind controls, as you would on a hardware device, complete with authentic-sounding clicks and cassette sounds that were recorded from a real portable cassette player.
With the Duo open, the cassette appears to play on the right side of the screen, next to album imagery on the right. When closed, Deck-Man’s interface looks like the front of a Walkman.

The app has appeal not only because it built something that could only exist on a hinged, foldable device like the Duo, but also because it taps into the growing demand for retro tech, which is partly a cultural response to the speed at which the AI industry is shipping out products. Retro tech, like dumbphones, digital cameras, vinyl, CDs, and landlines, recalls an older time when tech use was intentional, not just baked into every aspect of our lives.
Honestly, if you buy a Duo and don’t install Deck-Man, I’m convinced you just don’t know how to have fun.
TypeDraw

The TypeDraw app is designed to be a personal notebook, something that looks like a virtual Moleskine of sorts — it even has an elastic closure band. But there’s a certain charm to using this app specifically on the Duo, whose form factor makes it look a lot like a little notebook when closed.
Inside TypeDraw, you can type using a font that’s your own handwriting or pick from one of a dozen fonts designed by its creator, Phil Traut.

You can also choose which kind of paper you want to write on, like lined, grid, or dotted pages, and pick your ink color. You can also draw and sketch to create colorful images that accompany your handwritten text, which makes it feel a lot more like using a real-life notebook as your journal or diary, and not some boring to-do app.
The pages curl as you flip through them, and you can even pull on the elastic band to produce a twang animation that’s just silly and fun.
Wakeout

Wakeout, the workout app that’s a former Apple App of the Year winner, has also approached its Duo optimization thoughtfully by designing different user interfaces for each postion the phone can be in. The app, which offers a series of mini movement breaks that feel more like games than exercise, works when the Duo is closed, open, in tent mode, or sitting open like a laptop computer.

For instance, when the Duo is open like a book, the view is split across the hinge with the movement game videos on the left, but when it’s open like a laptop, the videos shift to the vertical screen. You can also put it into tent mode, which is great for watching the videos with the Duo propped up on your desk. (Most people use Wakeout at work, when they take quick stretch breaks after sitting at a desk for too long.)
If the app is running on a closed Duo, its row of navigation tabs becomes a slim side menu in the column beside the camera, allowing the phone’s small screen to use the full display.
Flighty

Already my favorite travel app, Apple Design Award-winning Flighty tells you everything you need to know about your upcoming flight, from gate updates to delays to airport conditions and even the type of aircraft you’re flying.

But on the iPhone Duo, when open, the app takes advantage of the expanded screen space to spread its map to the edges, letting you see more of your flight’s path on a globe that spins under your fingertips.

When the Duo is open, your flight details move over to the left side of the screen, but it doesn’t fill that side of the screen. Instead, most of the display is taken up by the image of the globe, allowing you room to zoom in on different flight paths more closely as you plan your travels.
The app also works in split screen, which means you can keep track of your flight while also doing something else — like watching your favorite TV show.

Plus, Flighty added a new feature called En Route Mode just for the Duo. In this mode, the Duo is folded into the tent shape and then placed on a flat surface — like your airplane’s tray table. That way you can watch your flight’s progress via Wi-Fi while you do something else, like listen to music, read a book, or watch a movie from the in-flight entertainment’s seat-back screen.
Tiny Computers

Designed specifically for the Duo (and for tech enthusiasts, who are also the Duo’s first customers), Tiny Computers is a playful way to reconnect with older technology. The app ships with 10 retro computers that you can play with, including the Macintosh, Commodore 64, IBM PC, Amiga 500, Windows 95, ThinkPad, iMac G3, iBook G3, PowerBook G4, and Windows XP.

You’re meant to set up the Duo in its open “laptop” mode to toy around with these old-fashioned devices, which feature clicking keyboards, working command lines, paint programs, floppy disks, and even some desktop games. But it’s not just an old computer exhibit – there’s a game element too, as you can look for hidden files and secret commands to earn a medal.
There are no ads, subscriptions, or in-app purchases, either – just a $3.99 one-time fee.
Sky Guide

Sky Guide is that classic stargazing app that I still open from time to time when I’m outdoors enjoying nature, wondering whether that bright light up there is a star or a planet or what the constellation right next to Orion is called.

The company is another of those that Apple gave a shoutout to in its press release about all the new Duo-optimized apps, and it’s easy to see why. It’s just so much easier to track the night sky when you have the larger display on the Duo unfolded, offering a more immersive, edge-to-edge map that moves as your position and orientation change. This one will be broken out on the next camping trip or nighttime walk, for sure.
MD Vinyl
Maybe I’m just a sucker for retro music apps, but MD Vinyl did not disappoint with its Duo-optimized music player.

This app’s widget already has a permanent place on my regular iPhone’s Home Screen purely for the aesthetics, which includes a tiny, spinning record and a display that shows you the song title and artist you’re streaming, alongside the player controls.

Now for the iPhone Duo, the virtual vinyl record gets to use more of the screen. Plus, you can even pick up the record player’s arm and place it on the spinning disk to start the music or remove it to stop it.
Pico Cam

Before the Duo, Pico Cam offered a tiny, playful camera app for taking virtual Polaroid-style pictures, which eject from the phone’s Dynamic Island (the pill-shaped cutout at the top of the screen). You can also shake the picture to get it to develop faster, then decorate with little stickers and share with friends.
Now optimized for the iPhone Duo, Pico Cam can be used when the phone is both open and closed, with the latter giving you more screen space to see your photo gallery after pictures are taken.
Honorable Mention, sorta: Toastie

Remember when the iPhone first came out, and there was that app that would make it look like you were drinking a beer when you tilted the phone to your mouth? Toastie is the iPhone Duo version of that same type of ridiculous experience.
I wouldn’t call Toastie a “killer” app, of course; it’s far too silly for that. But it’s a pretty fun toy to play with — if you ever dare to hand over this expensive device to a kid.

The app, cheekily described as the “world’s most expensive toaster” (a reference to the Duo’s exorbitant price), lets you follow a recipe to create a piece of toast with butter, cheese, or any of the other numerous toppings, then close the Duo to let the toast cook.
Open the phone too soon, and your toast will be undercooked, losing you the 5-star review you’re after.
You definitely don’t need this app, but what’s another $2.99 when you’ve already dropped a bundle on the phone itself?
We expect more interesting apps to come as developers get their hands on the iPhone Duo in the weeks ahead.

thehill.com/homenews/campaign/6170033-jo.headline: José Andrés joins fight against proposed DC foie gras ban
thehill.com/homenews/campaign/6170033-jo.author: Ford McCracken

paragraphs.text: World renowned chef José Andrés is entering the battle over Washington’s proposed ban on foie gras, a delicacy which animal rights activists have called cruel.

Andrés responded to a proponent of the ban, labeled as Initiative 86 on D.C.’s ballot, in a post to the social platform X — appearing to argue serving the French specialty made with fattened duck liver is no different ethically than making other meat-based dishes.

“Let’s ban beef and pork and chicken … and also vegetables too because is [sic] a study that says that maybe indications of suffering,” Andrés wrote. “We have children hungry in USA and the World … lets end hunger and then we talk.”

Foie gras is a delicacy made from duck liver which is enlarged via force feeding before slaughter. Washington animal rights activists are pushing for the ban over concerns about cruelty, putting them at odds with the city’s restaurant industry.

Andrés owns restaurants all over the world and has long been an advocate for addressing world hunger. He founded the World Central Kitchen, a nonprofit which aims to provide meals to those impacted by natural disasters.

But Andrés is not the only restaurant owner pledging to fight the ban. Bart Hutchins, owner of Butterworth’s in D.C., authored an op-ed in The Washington Post defending the use of foie gras and the practice by which it is made.

“Ducks are not humans,” Bart wrote. “This overfeeding is something the bird does naturally. Before their annual migration, ducks gorge — they stuff themselves with excess food … What foie gras farming does is amplify a natural biological process rather than invent a cruel one.”
Hutchins announced on X that Butterworth’s will be having a “Foie Gras at the End of the World” event with a four-course tasting menu, available every day Oct. 27 through Election Day.

The Butterworth’s owner told Axios D.C. he would continue to serve foie gras even if it is banned, and if the ballot initiative passes, he would rather move his restaurant to Virginia than stop offering the delicacy to its patrons.

cnbc.com/make-it/2026/10/24/quit-marketi.headline: I quit my marketing job to walk dogs for 4 months: It's 'one of the most valuable professional experiences I've ever had'
cnbc.com/make-it/2026/10/24/quit-marketi.author: Sally Simmons

paragraphs.text: One early morning in 2022, I found myself watching a dog walker on TikTok and thinking: I want her job.
It felt ridiculous. I was finishing up my MBA and navigating the next chapter of my career with a focus on prestige and financial success.

But soon after relocating from Kentucky to California in October 2021, I burned out. I had transitioned into a remote healthcare marketing role, living on the West Coast but still working East Coast hours and completing my second year of business school from afar. While everyone around me seemed to be heading to the beach and enjoying the sunshine, I spent my days inside, glued to a computer screen.
The dog walker I followed online seemed to have everything I was craving: fresh air, movement, flexibility and a job that didn't revolve around emails and Zoom meetings.
During a long drive, I joked with my husband, "I think I'm going to quit my job and walk dogs." The joke quickly became a plan.
My season as a professional dog walker

Within the span of just a few weeks in the spring of 2022, I quit my job, graduated from business school, traveled to Europe for an old roommate's wedding and then flew to Texas to speak at the Latino Franchise Symposium. While I was there, I created my Rover profile. I highlighted my experience volunteering at animal shelters in college, pet sitting for friends and caring for animals throughout my life.
Before I even made it back home to California, I had my first meet-and-greet scheduled with a potential client. Shortly after, I landed my first booking. I was thrilled.

At first, I intentionally priced my services below what seemed typical in my area to build reviews, charging about $15 for a drop-in visit and about $17 for a 30-minute walk. Some days I had just one client. I was able to start small because I had savings to tide me over, along with a partner whose job provided steady income and benefits.
Still, I treated it like a real business from day one. I accepted nearly every opportunity that came my way, taking dogs on midday walks, housesitting on weekends and boarding dogs in my apartment.

I sent thoughtful updates to the dog owners filled with photos, detailed notes and plenty of emojis. I shared bathroom break tallies, funny moments and anything unusual they should know. If I stayed overnight, I brought in packages, cleaned up after myself and made sure their home looked exactly as they had left it.
My goal wasn't simply to complete the booking. It was to become the person people trusted with a member of their family.

The reviews started rolling in. As my profile gained traction, I gradually increased my rates, eventually charging $23 for a drop-in visit and $84 for overnight stays. By the time I left the platform four months later, I had earned a five-star rating with 30 reviews, built a roster of recurring clients and filled my calendar.

One of my favorite memories came when a family asked me to care for their dogs during their wedding weekend. I spent two and a half days at a beautiful resort and dressed the dogs in tiny tuxedos before they walked down the aisle.

It reminded me that this work was about helping families enjoy some of the biggest moments of their lives with peace of mind. Years later, we're still friends. They now have a daughter, and my daughter and I recently attended her first birthday party.
A new definition of success

Some days I walked more than eight miles, logging over 18,000 steps as I explored neighborhoods I otherwise never would have discovered. I spent hours outside instead of sitting behind a desk. Sometimes I listened to podcasts or music. Other times, I simply enjoyed the quiet.
Those walks gave me space to think. I reflected on what success actually meant, what I wanted my career to look like and, perhaps more importantly, how I wanted my days to feel.

Before Rover, success meant getting promotions, landing bigger clients and climbing the corporate ladder. Walking dogs challenged that definition. I realized I didn't want to chase an impressive title as much as I wanted to chase a lifestyle that gave me energy.
Ironically, it was during one of those walks that I received the phone call offering me the marketing job I still have today. I paused on the sidewalk, accepted the offer and then finished the walk.

Returning to marketing wasn't a difficult decision. By then, I was pregnant with my first daughter and needed the stability, benefits and predictable income that came with a full-time role. When an excited dog chasing a squirrel pulled me to the ground early in my pregnancy, it became clear that my season as a professional dog walker was coming to an end.
Still, I think about those four months often. People sometimes assume dog walking was a gap or detour in my career. I see it as one of the most valuable professional experiences I've ever had.

It reminded me that passion is visible, no matter what kind of work you're doing. It reinforced that the skills that matter most — showing up, listening, caring deeply, building trust and making small, consistent changes — translate to every career.

And even though I'm back in marketing, my days look different than they did before my dog-walking era. These days, you'll find me logging off at 5 p.m. to go play outside with my family before dinner, walking near the ocean after a hard week, having kitchen dance parties to shake off the day, taking calls while walking my own dog or squeezing in a lunchtime workout. The fresh air and sense of presence give me the balance I craved when I was glued to screens on a schedule dictated by someone else's time zone.

Those four months taught me something my MBA never could: Success isn't just about finding a job that sounds impressive. It's about building a life you genuinely enjoy living, even if it doesn't look like the one you originally imagined.

Sally Simmons is a marketing leader and holistic health coach based in California. After years building strategies for global brands, she found unexpected lessons about business, connection and success during a four-month chapter as a professional dog walker. Today, she brings those lessons into her work helping people create healthier, more balanced lives.
